Saudi Arabia wants into the F-35 club. What will membership cost?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:52:18 UTC
02:52:18 KST

Saudi Arabia wants into the F-35 club. What will membership cost?
The Trump administration has approved a potential sale of F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia as part of a $24.3 billion package that also includes engines, equipment, and spare parts. For Riyadh, the decision opens the prospect of a substantial improvement in its air capabilities, while allowing Washington to demonstrate its willingness to deepen relations with one of its most important Middle Eastern partners. Yet political disagreements and negotiations over the terms still stand between State Department approval and the arrival of the aircraft at Saudi air bases.
The significance of the decision extends well beyond an arms contract, as Saudi Arabia increasingly seeks to broaden its relationships with competing centers of power. Viewed in this context, Trump’s initiative can be understood as an attempt to preserve America’s position as the kingdom’s principal strategic partner and prevent further drift away from Washington. The challenge, however, is that commercial interests, the protection of sensitive technology, and commitments to Israel do not always point towards the same policy.
How Washington hopes to keep Riyadh close
Saudi Arabia values its partnership with the United States, but wants to determine for itself how far that partnership should shape its wider policies. Relations with China, cooperation with Russia, and the development of regional ties allow the kingdom to reduce its dependence on any single external partner. This does not mean Riyadh is ready to abandon US-led security arrangements, but it does make Saudi leaders less receptive to demands that Washington might once have regarded as a natural part of an alliance.
For the United States, the risk lies in the gradual erosion of its privileged position. Even if the kingdom continues to purchase American weapons, it may increasingly turn elsewhere for political support and economic opportunities. As those relationships deepen, Riyadh gets more options, while Washington has fewer opportunities to secure concessions by threatening to restrict cooperation.
An offer of F-35s could make the American partnership more attractive at a time when its advantages can no longer be taken for granted. By opening access to an aircraft Saudi leaders have long sought, Trump is signaling a willingness to accommodate the kingdom’s ambitions. For Riyadh, the symbolic importance is considerable, since acquiring such aircraft would affirm its standing among America’s security partners.
Washington’s practical gains, however, would come from the longevity of the relationship. Advanced combat aircraft require continuing support contracts, keeping the Riyadh connected throughout their service life. Once Saudi Arabia has invested heavily in the aircraft, infrastructure, and personnel, moving away from that system becomes more difficult and expensive. A defense contract can therefore reinforce ties that outlast changes of administration and individual diplomatic disputes.
Dependence on aircraft support does not, however, automatically translate into a willingness to coordinate oil policy or relations with third countries. Riyadh may see no contradiction in working with Moscow on energy and expanding economic ties with Beijing. This creates a potential mismatch of expectations, as Washington may view the sale as a means of securing closer strategic alignment, while Saudi Arabia sees an opportunity to simply strengthen its defense.
Washington’s willingness to proceed could convince Saudi leaders that their existing approach is working. If closer relations with America’s competitors are followed by more attractive American offers, Riyadh has an incentive to continue pursuing them. Trump must then decide how much independence he is willing to accept from a partner in order to retain influence over it, and at what point accommodation becomes more than his administration is prepared to concede.
Why Trump’s approval does not settle the debate in Congress
Trump’s first term demonstrated that arms sales to Saudi Arabia can become the subject of serious domestic political confrontation. In 2019, Congress passed resolutions opposing several arms transfers to the kingdom and the United Arab Emirates, but the president vetoed them and the Senate failed to override him. That episode does not establish that lawmakers will stop the present sale, but neither does it justify assuming that the president’s decision will be implemented without resistance.
The process does not require an affirmative vote of approval from Congress, as the administration can proceed after the statutory review period unless a legislative prohibition takes effect. Opponents need to turn political objections into enforceable restrictions and, if the president exercises his veto, assemble enough support to overcome it. A demanding threshold, if the White House retains the backing of most Republicans.
With the F-35, the central objection concerns the protection of sensitive American technology. Saudi Arabia’s relations with China raise questions about how reliably third parties can be denied access to the aircraft, associated equipment, and information. Such concerns could resonate with lawmakers who broadly support Trump but place the preservation of America’s technological advantage above the benefits of a particular contract.
Critics in Washington may also invoke Riyadh’s cooperation with Russia through OPEC+ and its refusal to join sanctions against Moscow as evidence of the kingdom’s limited willingness to support American foreign policy. Yet political grievances should be distinguished from risks to a specific weapons program, since an independent oil policy is not in itself a threat to military technology. These issues may become intertwined in public debate, even though a serious assessment of the sale requires different answers to each.
Supporters can argue that refusing the sale would only strengthen Saudi Arabia’s determination to cultivate alternative partners. The same ties with Moscow and Beijing can thus support opposing conclusions. Some will see them as grounds for withholding access to advanced weapons, while others will see a reason to offer Riyadh closer cooperation while American influence remains substantial.
The congressional debate is therefore likely to concern both whether the sale should proceed and what commitments Saudi Arabia should undertake. The administration will have to explain which restrictions would genuinely protect the technology and how compliance could be verified. More credible safeguards would make it harder for opponents to build a broad coalition, but excessively stringent demands could provoke resistance from the buyer.
Where Israel draws the line
For Israel, the central question is how a stronger Saudi Arabia would affect its own security. Washington seeks to improve the defense capabilities of its Arab partners while preserving Israel’s qualitative military edge, and the F-35 makes reconciling those objectives particularly difficult. The arrival of such aircraft in the hands of another regional power would matter even if their configuration differed from Israel’s.
Riyadh is unlikely to receive F-35s with the full range of capabilities available in the Israeli variant, but differences in equipment and weapons would not eliminate every concern. Saudi air power would gain new capabilities, and the implications for Israel’s regional advantage would depend partly on how quickly the kingdom could master the aircraft and integrate them into its armed forces.
A stronger Saudi air force would not directly diminish Israel’s own combat capabilities, but could alter the relative balance and constrain Israel’s freedom of action. This is the context in which concerns about air superiority should be understood. Israeli military planning must account for both present relations with neighboring states and the changes that could occur long-term while the aircraft are in service.
Israeli officials have used similar arguments when opposing a possible F-35 sale to Türkiye, warning that it could disrupt the regional balance of power. That example illustrates Israel’s sensitivity to the wider availability of such capabilities, although it does not make the Turkish and Saudi cases identical. The identity of the buyer, the nature of bilateral relations, and the proposed terms of delivery will all affect the intensity of Israeli opposition.
Israeli leaders can be expected to use diplomatic pressure and support from allies in Congress to either to stop the sale or secure restrictions. Negotiations could cover the weapons available to Saudi aircraft, particular technological capabilities, and additional measures to strengthen Israel’s own defenses. None of these arrangements should be treated as settled, however, since the eventual compromise will depend on every party’s willingness to accept its political costs.
For Trump, this creates an uncomfortable dilemma. The more substantial the offer to Riyadh, the stronger Israeli objections may become, while every additional restriction introduced to reassure Israel could make the package less attractive to Saudi Arabia. If Saudi leaders interpret the terms as confirmation that their country will always occupy a subordinate position, the deal could undermine the very confidence in the partnership that Washington hopes to build.
What a compromise might look like and what happens if it fails
The most plausible next phase is a prolonged negotiation in which a high-profile political announcement is translated into concrete obligations. Washington will seek to protect sensitive technology and provide assurances acceptable to Israel, while Riyadh will press for a purchase with meaningful military value that preserves its political independence.
A compromise appears more attainable if restrictions focus on the security of the program itself, including access to equipment, the handling of data, and engagement with third parties. If Washington tries to make the sale conditional on a broader revision of Saudi relations with China and Russia, resistance from Riyadh is likely to intensify. Saudi leaders need to be able to justify the agreement in terms of their own national interests while retaining the right to make decisions that do not always satisfy the United States.
The kingdom will also have to weigh the value of the capabilities it would acquire against the restrictions attached to them. Overly demanding terms could reduce the deal’s appeal, but walking away would carry costs of its own, requiring alternative approaches to modernization and an assessment of how long those alternatives would take. Serious dissatisfaction with particular conditions might therefore become part of the bargaining process without necessarily bringing negotiations to an end.
Another possibility is that political approval remains in place while implementation is delayed for an extended period. The administration could continue to describe the deal as evidence of a stronger partnership, while Riyadh waits for clarity on configuration, personnel training, and delivery schedules. Yet a promise gradually loses its power to sustain a partner’s interest, particularly if every delay appears to bring another set of political conditions.
The outright collapse of the sale would not mean an immediate rupture in Saudi-American relations, which encompass far more than a single weapons program. It could nevertheless reinforce the view in Riyadh that even an understanding with the US president does not guarantee a predictable outcome. The Saudis would then have further reason to broaden its pool of suppliers and reduce its exposure to decisions taken in Washington.
Successful delivery, however, would not guarantee that Saudi Arabia abandons its effort to balance relationships among competing powers. It could deepen military cooperation with the United States while maintaining economic ties with China and energy coordination with Russia. Washington would be able to claim that it had retained a vital partner, while Riyadh could argue that an independent foreign policy had secured new concessions.
The practical signs of progress will be agreed terms, committed financing, infrastructure preparations, and a credible delivery schedule. The deeper strategic outcome will emerge later, when American and Saudi interests diverge again over an important issue. Only then will it become clear whether the F-35 has helped forge a closer political alliance or strengthened military cooperation between two states that continue to pursue calculations of their own.

The Guardian view on the Lib Dems: Ed Davey wants Tory voters without losing the left | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:51:32 UTC
02:51:32 KST

Sir Ed Davey’s speech at the Liberal Democrat party conference was a calculated appeal to voters who recoil from a rightwing bloc associated with Brexit, nationalism and reactionary politics. That’s not a bad place to start. But he wants this message not to be lost in the headlines about his party’s £17bn tax giveaway aimed at disillusioned Conservative voters. To walk that line, his address sought to present Reform UK’s politics as an existential threat to Britain, appealing directly to left-leaning tactical voters. At the same time, he told moderate Tories that only a vote for the Lib Dems can reliably block both Reform and a Conservative-supported Nigel Farage premiership.
It’s a clever strategy. Too clever, think some in his party, who yearn for clearer dividing lines. Yet the Lib Dem leader is nothing if not ambitious. He claims that his party could have more MPs than the Conservatives after the next election. In 2024, the Lib Dems won 60 of their 72 seats from the Tories; they were also second in a score of Conservative-held seats. That electoral geography pushes the Lib Dems as replacing the Conservatives as the respectable, pro-market opposition, while Reform occupies the space of the nationalist right. The logic is that in a multiparty system under first past the post, it may no longer be necessary to be a national party. Sir Ed might become kingmaker as the parliamentary expression of a liberal southern tendency.
Rejoining the single market would be in Britain’s interests. But presenting the move as a frictionless growth policy obscures the major change involved in accepting common rules and institutions. Sir Ed’s tax cuts may be smart politics, parking Lib Dem tanks on Tory territory. But they are a world away from his 2024 election image as the champion of carer’s allowance, NHS funding and local sewage protests. That leftwing stance importantly allowed him then to tap into tactical anti-Conservative voting.
Raising the personal allowance to £15,000 allows Sir Ed to speak to almost every taxpayer in a cost of living crisis, while increasing the higher-rate threshold to £56,000 targets professionals in the south on whom his electoral strategy depends. The trouble is that the tax cuts are a promise, but the growth – from closer ties to Europe – that “pays” for them is a forecast. Choosing tax cuts over public investment leaves the Lib Dems exposed to competition from the left, from Labour and the Greens.
Sir Ed is trying to detach economic liberalism from the socially conservative nationalists and link it to a pro-European and socially liberal party. He’s right to say that “people feel powerless”, but the examples that Sir Ed uses to demonstrate their lack of agency – unsafe maternity care, inadequate disability provision and polluted rivers – largely arise from failures of collective provision or state regulation. Their solutions require capable public institutions and more resources.
The political scientist Paula Surridge wrote that continued Lib Dem success depends on them being seen as a safe alternative for liberal-left voters. The cultural and social liberalism he sells would reassure this group. But tax cuts might disquiet them. Sir Ed is betting that these tactical voters care more about defeating the nationalist right than the Lib Dems’ economic programme. That was the case in 2024. After years of the public dealing with high prices, it may be harder to land that message next time.

Trump is expected to press Zelensky to accept a Russia-Ukraine energy truce at their NYC meeting
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will meet with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on the evening of September 22. According to The Guardian, Trump is expected to press Zelensky at the meeting to agree to an energy ceasefire with Russia.
The Ukrainian and U.S. leaders spoke by phone on Sunday, September 20. Sources told the Financial Times that their conversation was about “diesel, diesel, diesel.” The next day, Trump discussed the idea of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine with French President Emmanuel Macron. Macron called the conversation “very constructive” and promised to raise the issue at his meeting with Zelensky as well.
Trump is unhappy with Ukrainian strikes targeting Russia’s diesel production and has already asked Zelensky to halt the attacks. On September 13, he explicitly blamed Kyiv for rising fuel prices, emphasizing that the war between Russia and Ukraine — not the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran — was responsible.
As early as September 14, Trump said Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. Sources told the Financial Times that the announcement was premature. People familiar with the Kremlin’s position told the newspaper that Putin would not agree to such a deal because attacks on energy facilities during the winter could give him additional leverage over Kyiv.
Since then, Russia has struck energy infrastructure in Kyiv, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, and the Sumy and Odesa regions. An employee of Zaporizhzhiaoblenergo was killed in one of the strikes. After Russia’s overnight attack on September 22, residents of seven Ukrainian regions were left without electricity.
Ukraine, in turn, has attacked the Syzran, Yaroslavl, Moscow, and Kuybyshev oil refineries. Trump said the repeated attacks had caused Russia to lose control of its diesel industry — and that “The whole World suffers” as a result.
The Kremlin called an energy ceasefire “a good idea” but said keeping refineries operating safely and increasing production of petroleum products would not solve “global problems” — lifting sanctions on shipments and ensuring the safety of tankers were far more important.
Zelensky said Russia and Ukraine see the problem completely differently: Moscow is thinking about the oil and gas trade, while Kyiv is thinking about electricity in people’s homes. He proposed that Russia “put on the table” a list of facilities to be covered by the ceasefire. On Monday, Zelensky listed the targets Russia must stop striking:
Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible.
Zelensky and Trump are scheduled to meet at 8:15 p.m. Moscow time. According to Reuters, the outcome of the talks is difficult to predict. The news agency pointed to the two leaders’ public meeting in Washington in February 2025, which ended in a heated exchange broadcast live.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
Russia attacked Kramatorsk on Monday, September 21. Donetsk regional police said Russian forces struck the city with KAB-250 aerial bombs, Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, and drones. One person was killed, and seven others were injured, including two children. Eight apartment buildings and 17 private homes were damaged. The photographs show the aftermath of the strikes.

“Brazilian democracy belongs to Brazilians,” Lula said towards the end of his speech. “Brazil will remain a sovereign country.”

The comments came as Trump was expected to use his own UN address on Tuesday to assert US power in the region. Israel just pardoned a soldier who executed a wounded Palestinian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:50:51 UTC
02:50:51 KST

On March 24, 2016, two Palestinian suspects stabbed an Israeli soldier in the occupied Palestinian city of Hebron, moderately injuring him in the shoulder and hand. One suspect, Ramzi al-Qasrawi, was immediately killed by Israeli gunfire, while the other, Abdel Fattah al-Sharif, was shot several times and lay incapacitated on the pavement.
Eleven minutes later, Elor Azaria, an Israeli soldier and medic, arrived on the scene. He walked over to al-Sharif, who still lay unconscious, pointed his gun at him, and shot him in the head from point-blank range.
The entire incident was caught on film by B’Tselem volunteer Imad Abu Shamsiyeh, who had a perfect view from his apartment across the street.
Elor Azaria was pardoned for his murder of al-Sharif yesterday on Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement. He wasn’t, however, pardoned by God, but by Israeli President Isaac Herzog.
Herzog issued a statement accepting Azaria’s request to “erase the remaining criminal record” of the former soldier so that he could “continue on with his life.” The President stated that “the passage of time” and the “sorrow” Azaria had supposedly expressed were penance enough.
But what “sorrow” was this? Although Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz was the one pushing for the pardon as of last July, the military itself advised against it. The opposition to the move from the military Chief of Staff, Eyal Zamir, specifically pointed out that Azaria had “refrained from expressing remorse and taking responsibility for his actions, even a decade after his conviction.”
This was apparent from the first moment Azaria finished his prison sentence (which was reduced from Murder to Manslaughter and from 18 months to 9). He returned to a hero’s welcome and bragged that he would “do it again”:
“I’m completely at peace with myself. I did the right thing, I followed my truth, and there was no need for any of what happened,” Azaria told Israel Hayom. “I have no regrets. There’s no doubt in my mind. Take me back to those seconds in the incident in Hebron — I’d be doing exactly the same thing. Because that was the proper way to act.”
Azaria had thought this one out, and executing an incapacitated Palestinian was fully consistent with his ideology.
The judge in his case opined that he was just a “normal person” whose life was interrupted by “his current complication.”
By “normal,” the judge doubtless meant that Azaria was no different from the rest of Israeli society. Both Azaria and several members of his family had made genocidal statements online going back to 2014. Not much has changed since, with four out of five Jewish Israelis supporting the starvation of children in Gaza. These days, such views remain the norm in Israel.
An army of executioners
The erasure of Azaria’s criminal record goes beyond symbolic gestures. Criminal records in Israel prevent Israelis from working in specific fields and sectors, especially anything that is related to security or the military. But with his record now expunged, Azaria is suddenly eligible to return to the army.
This wasn’t lost on Israel’s hardline National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who expressed his elation at Azaria’s pardon, which he found “very moving and gratifying,” and called on the Israeli army’s Chief of Staff to allow Azaria to “return to the military if he wishes.”
A very similar thing happened months ago when the soldiers responsible for gang-raping Palestinian prisoners in the Sde Teiman torture camp were cleared of all charges by the Military Advocate General, with Defense Minister Katz calling for them to immediately return to military service.
Ben-Gvir also added that Azaria would never have been given a criminal record for his actions “had the rules of engagement been different.” Here, he is referring to the onerous rules that don’t give automatic permission for soldiers to execute Palestinians as they lie unconscious in the street.
Herzog the genocidaire
Of course, Herzog himself is an inciter of genocide. In October 2023, he infamously said that there were “no uninvolved” civilians in Gaza, stating that there was “an entire society out there” that was responsible for the October 7 attacks. He has continuously tried to gaslight those who pointed out that such statements were incitement to genocide, claiming that they were taken “out of context.”
But make no mistake, Herzog’s views are far from outliers. At least three out of every four Jewish Israelis share the perception that there are “no innocents in Gaza.” This view is highest among right-wingers, but even among self-identified Israeli “leftists,” about 30% shared this view.
It’s important for Herzog to be seen as popular among a broad cross-section of the Israeli public, as the President’s post is meant to be a ceremonial role that unites the nation. In this, the President has succeeded, because at least everyone can agree on genocide.
At the time of the Elor Azaria case, a substantial political drama ensued, with many calling for Azaria’s immediate and total pardon — including the left-wing Labor leader, Shelly Yachimovich — meaning that pardoning Azaria is far from a right-wing niche idea.
Who knows, with Azaria’s growing popularity, and his criminal record totally expunged, he might return to the military to murder more Palestinians before becoming Prime Minister. Maybe even President.

The Guardian view on Keynes in the West End: James Graham’s latest play captures the zeitgeist | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:50:31 UTC
02:50:31 KST

Still only 44, James Graham has become a formidable chronicler of our national story. On themes such as the rise of Rupert Murdoch, social upheaval in post-industrial Britain and the neuroses of the England men’s football team, the playwright and screenwriter has made it his vocation to read the signs of our times and write them up for the stage.
Graham’s new play goes a bit further back in history, but its subject matter is characteristically of the moment. Opening this week in the West End, The Standard of Living offers a portrait of the sentimental and intellectual passions of John Maynard Keynes (played by Rory Kinnear), as the great economist makes his name between the first and second world wars. As Keynes rails against the laissez-faire ethos of the age, he seeks to devise a theory of growth that justifies state intervention on people’s behalf in the wake of the Great Depression.
A month out from the first budget to be delivered by Andy Burnham’s government, the contemporary relevance is not hard to spot. Ever since the prime minister pledged to bring an “end to 40 years of neoliberalism” and launch a new era of public investment to bring about growth, his opponents have sought to characterise that project as a reckless Labour version of Trussism. Discussion of the nation’s political direction has been reduced to a numbers game relentlessly focused on bond yields, debt levels and what markets will or will not countenance.
John Healey may or may not take a seat in the stalls during the play’s scheduled run. But just as Graham’s Labour of Love presciently addressed the Labour party’s problems in its red wall heartlands, and Dear England explored a nation’s insecurities through sporting anxiety, his latest offering captures the zeitgeist in a way that goes beyond the contents of the chancellor’s budget briefcase.
The economic historian Robert Skidelsky, who died this year, observed that “our age has eerily come to rhyme with Keynes’s”. In the aftermath of the 2008 crash, nationalist threats to the global order have multiplied and the far right has been able to mobilise popular discontent at declining living standards. Whether progressive governments can negotiate the fiscal room for manoeuvre to allow them to respond effectively is a key issue of our time. Meanwhile, the existential threat posed by unregulated artificial intelligence has taken the laissez-faire debate on to new and alarming territory.
Graham and Nicholas Hytner, the director of The Standard of Living, are too skilled to allow such echoes to add up to a sombre night out. Keynes’s marriage to the Russian ballerina Lydia Lopukhova, for example, is deftly exploited to make dance a metaphor for what a graceful balance of economic forces might look like. Perhaps the highlight of the evening thus becomes a vigorous pas de deux across the stage involving Keynes and his free-marketeering rival, Friedrich Hayek, choreographed to the rhythm of an argument about interest rates.
Ideas, art, love affairs and the bohemian excesses of the Bloomsbury set all compete for audience attention. At a time when the common good risks being undermined by market imperatives, algorithmic abstractions and rogue AI agents, Graham has once again produced a play that poses the right question at the right time: how can humans take back control?

Police believe they have foiled ‘imminent’ attack on Manchester’s Jewish community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:50:25 UTC
02:50:25 KST

Police believe they have stopped an imminent plot to attack Jewish communities in the Manchester area.
The announcement on Tuesday follows the arrest of two men on Sunday at 2.45pm in Manchester and comes during the Jewish holy month.
Counter-terrorism investigators were unusually explicit about the alleged attack plot, which was halted after an operation lasting several months. Police believe they have detained the main suspects and any materials they may have been planning to use.
Deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said: “This has been a long-running proactive investigation which has led to the disruption of what we believe to be a plot to target the Jewish community in the Manchester area.”
  The arrests and official confirmation of a suspected attack plot comes almost a year after an Islamist-incited attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur left two people dead, with the attacker shot dead by police.
Arrests were made hours before this year’s Yom Kippur started, with police fearing any plot might be “imminent”. The Jewish festival of Sukkot falls on Friday, with other holy days to follow.
Evans added: “We are acutely aware this news will cause further concern to the Jewish community, as well as the wider public, especially given the significant High Holy Day period.
“I want to reassure them we are working incredibly closely with colleagues in Greater Manchester police and partners to ensure we’re doing everything we can to keep them and the wider public safe.”
The two men in their 30s were arrested under section 41 of the Terrorism Act, meaning police suspected they were terrorists. Police will not officially say what the motive was, nor the nationality or ethnicity of those detained.
The Guardian understands that a far-right motive is thought to be unlikely. Sources stress the investigation is at an early stage. Islamist extremism is among possible motives under consideration, and given a spate of recent attacks against Jewish targets, investigators are searching for any sign of a state link. Investigators are increasingly finding it difficult to determine motive until much later in an investigation, if at all.
The UK’s terrorism threat level is now at its second highest level of severe.
The investigation was led by CTP in London and the two men arrested have been taken to a police station in the capital for questioning.
Warrants for their further detention have been granted, meaning they can be held until Sunday.
The arrests led to searches in Epworth Street, Liverpool, and Lancaster Road, Salford, which police say have now been completed. Examination of electronic devices such as mobile phones is under way.
Evans added: “Counter Terrorism Policing continue to focus our efforts on identifying and disrupting those who wish to cause harm in our communities.
“As we have shown with these arrests, where we suspect there could be a threat to the public, then we will not hesitate to investigate and take action.
“We are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry and we anticipate these will continue over the coming days as this investigation continues.
“Importantly, we do not believe there to be any ongoing threat to the public in relation to this matter, but as ever, we would ask that people remain vigilant and contact police with any concerns.”
The Community Security Trust (CST), which works to keep Jewish communities in the UK safe from attack, said: “This is utterly chilling, coming so close to the anniversary of the terrorist attack at Heaton Park Synagogue last year, and is another reminder of the serious terrorist threat facing Jewish communities in this current time.
“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and alert, and to report any suspicious activity to police on 999 and then to CST.”

Explainer-US expands its prosecution of 2021 assassination of Haiti's president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

Explainer-US expands its prosecution of 2021 assassination of Haiti's president
Sept 22 - The United States over the weekend dramatically expanded its prosecution of the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moise, indicting 30 people allegedly involved in the plot and flying 18 suspects out of Haiti and to the US.
The indicted include an alleged mastermind of the plot, 17 former Colombian soldiers, and a notorious gang leader linked to the abduction of 1 Canadian and 16 US missionaries just months after Moise's assassination.
WHAT CHANGED THIS WEEKEND?
While US prosecutors secured the indictment in August, they did not unseal it until the weekend.
Announcing what he called "the next major phase" of the case, US attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason A. Reding Quinones said on Saturday that prosecutors were expanding their prosecution of people tied to Moise's murder.
Prosecutors allege the conspirators, operating in Haiti and Florida, hired Colombian mercenaries impersonating Drug Enforcement Administration agents to kidnap and ultimately kill Moise, and then install a US-Haitian doctor as his replacement.
According to the latest indictment, the plotters used a web of companies and pandemic-era loans to fund the plot, shipping body armor and other items to Haiti under fraudulent labels such as "medical x-ray vests."
A dozen people have previously pleaded guilty or were convicted in US court proceedings related to the assassination. Five received life sentences.
WHO WAS INDICTED?
Joseph Felix Badio, a former Haitian government official who worked in an anti-corruption unit, is the highest-profile defendant in the new US court case. Accused of masterminding the plot against Moise, Badio was rolled into a Miami court in a wheelchair on Monday.
Badio has said he is innocent and being made into a scapegoat. Gang leader Vitel'homme Innocent, who remains at large in Haiti, was also named. Innocent rose to international attention when the US alleged that he helped another gang carry out the 2021 kidnapping of 17 US and Canadian missionaries. Washington later offered a $2 million reward for information leading to his arrest.
In a rare interview with CNN two years ago, Innocent did not deny his followers have kidnapped people, but blamed this on a state of corruption, and said he hoped to defend himself from these allegations in court.
The latest indictment centers on Innocent's alleged efforts to help a Colombian mercenary and Haitian senator, both now serving life sentences after pleading guilty, evade capture after Moise's murder.
Prosecutors also charged five others accused of helping channel pandemic-era loans into funding the plot.
WILL THIS MAKE A DIFFERENCE?
Haitian political analysts said the latest indictments are another sign of a broken judicial system in Haiti, where five years of investigation into Moise's murder have failed to yield a single trial.
Others, however, hoped the US case could deliver long-awaited accountability.
"It's often a domino effect," said political analyst Chantal Elie on X. "One person speaks, another is arrested, a new name appears. Those we thought untouchable could in fact, not be so."
But Wolf Pamphile, who heads the Washington-based Haiti Policy Institute, said the indictment would not necessarily increase US pressure against gang leaders like Innocent in Haiti, where he faces serious charges.
"They know where he lives, they just can't get to him," he said. REUTERS

An Israeli couple in their 30s say they were subjected to unusually invasive security searches while crossing into Egypt’s Sinai Peninsula through the Taba border crossing on Saturday, including alleged intimate touching and a full strip search.
The woman, identified only as S., told ynet that an Egyptian female security officer touched her groin, buttocks and chest shortly after she passed through a metal detector, before officers had even finished examining the couple’s luggage.
Her partner, identified as O., was later taken behind a curtain for a separate search, where the couple says a male security officer touched his groin over his clothing. S. said she was then taken behind the same type of curtain and ordered to remove all of her clothes.
“It was a very traumatic experience,” she said.
According to S., the couple entered the crossing late Saturday night, when the terminal was nearly empty.
“We were the only ones going through security,” she said. “We put our bags through the scanner, and before they even came out, my partner went through the metal detector. I went through after him, and immediately afterward the woman working security started patting me down, before they had even seen what was in the bag or had any suspicion about anything.”
“She ran her hand over my groin, my buttocks and my chest,” S. said. “Those were mainly the places she touched, rather than other parts of my body.”
After officers discovered rolling papers in her partner’s luggage, she said, the inspection intensified.
“They started turning everything upside down. They smelled everything, checked everything. They completely emptied our bags.”
S. said her partner was then taken behind a curtain by a male security officer.
“He touched him in the groin over his clothes,” she said.
When O. emerged, S. said the female officer took her behind a curtain as well.
“It wasn’t a room, just a curtain,” she said. “She told me to take off my shirt. I wasn’t wearing a bra. Then she told me to take off my skirt. I was left in my underwear, and then she asked me to take that off too.”
S. said the officer did not speak English and communicated largely through gestures.
“I said, ‘What?’ and she said, ‘Yes, yes, take it off.’”
According to S., the officer then instructed her to spread her legs and conducted a visual inspection.
“She asked me to spread my legs and looked at me down there in a very invasive and disturbing way,” she said. “It felt like harassment, like she was enjoying it and smirking at me. It was very extreme. It was a very unpleasant experience. Mostly, I was just shocked.”
S. said she did not fully process what had happened until after the couple left the crossing.
“It was a very destabilizing experience,” she said. “Only when we got out of there did I understand that something wasn’t right. I felt terrible that I hadn’t said anything while it was happening.”
“I felt that what was happening wasn’t right and wasn’t legal. It didn’t make sense to me that this was happening, but I didn’t say anything at the time and didn’t ask questions. It happened very quickly, and I just wanted it to end so I could get out of there.”
She said the experience left her confused and shaken even after the couple continued their journey.
“We stopped at a gas station and bought a few things, and I paid much more than usual without even asking how much it cost,” she said.
The couple have traveled to Sinai before, S. said, but had never experienced anything similar at the crossing.
“We’ve been to Sinai before and never experienced this, not even anything close,” she said. “It won’t stop us from going back to Sinai, but I hope that by then I’ll understand whether this is legal and know how to respond if it happens again.”

NATO's top generals gathered in Copenhagen, and Ukraine was at the center of the table. The Alliance's Military Committee, its 32 chiefs of defense and two strategic commanders, met to reaffirm support for Ukraine, accelerate its readiness, and appoint a new chairman, Ukraine's General Staff said.

Ukraine anchors the agenda
The annual conference, held in Copenhagen and chaired by Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone alongside the Alliance's two strategic commanders, followed up on decisions from the recent NATO summit in Ankara and centered on deterrence, defense, and new technology, with Ukraine running through it all, according to the NATO Representation in Ukraine.

The chair calls out Russia
Cavo Dragone framed the moment bluntly. The Alliance had again seen "the reckless behavior of Russia, including airspace violations, drone incidents, hybrid activities," he said at a joint press conference. He credited allied forces for their swift responses to those incidents and vowed the Alliance would defend every inch of its territory.
Germany's Breuer takes the helm
The chiefs have also elected General Carsten Breuer, Germany's chief of defense, as the next chair of the Military Committee, NATO's highest military body. He will take over in the summer of 2027 for a three-year term, succeeding Cavo Dragone.
Breuer, Germany's chief of defense since 2023, was the front-runner, and his selection, backed by Washington, hands the role to Europe's largest military spender and signals Germany's growing weight in the Alliance's command.

Sudan’s historical famine echoes through latest hunger crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:45:55 UTC
02:45:55 KST

Sudan’s historical famine echoes through latest hunger crisis
Sudan’s war-driven famine revives memories of past famines as war drives displacement and food shortages.
Sudan’s collective memory has long carried stories of famine-induced tragedies. Now, as war pushes the country deeper into a catastrophic food crisis, historians and humanitarian activists fear that some of those horrors are being repeated.
The ongoing war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which erupted in April 2023, has plunged the country into one of its worst modern food crises, with conditions deteriorating sharply since 2024.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Erdogan slams Israel’s ‘genocidal mindset’ in blistering UN address
- list 2 of 3‘Deadly hazards’: Behind Sudan gold mine collapse, a wartime desperation
- list 3 of 3Undeterred by fines, Al-Shaair pays tribute to Palestinian girl Wafaa Akila
Sudan has endured severe famines before, often triggered or made worse by drought and other environmental shocks. However, the current hunger crisis, which has triggered famines in Sudan in 2024 and 2025, has been brought on by a man-made factor: war.
Past starvation
One of the earliest recorded major food crises in what is now Sudan occurred in 1684, during the Funj Sultanate. The crisis, which lasted several years, brought severe grain shortages across central Sudan. Historical accounts describe people driven to desperation, and in some cases forced to eat dog meat. The hunger triggered mass displacement, as well as a deadly smallpox outbreak.
Similar climate-driven crises were recorded in 1750 and again between 1835 and 1838 during a period of Ottoman-Egyptian rule, exacerbated by severe drought and low water levels in the River Nile.
The famine most deeply embedded in Sudanese popular memory occurred between 1888 and 1889, during the rule of Khalifa Abdullahi al-Taashi.
Drought, locust infestations and conflict combined to cause widespread hunger and death. Some historical estimates put the death toll at more than one million people, although precise figures from the period are difficult to establish. The crisis was reported to have been so severe that some families shut themselves inside their homes to die rather than going out to beg for food.
Sudan experienced more periods of food shortages during the 20th century. Droughts and poor harvests during the colonial period of the first half of the century forced the authorities at times to import grain from abroad.
Then, in 1984, during the rule of President Jaafar Nimeiri, a devastating drought hit western Sudan, including Darfur and Kordofan, where there were widespread crop and livestock losses, displacing hundreds of thousands of people from rural areas to the capital, Khartoum.
Man-made catastrophe
Unlike many of those historical crises, the current famine is distinctly man-made.
War has disrupted agricultural production and trade, forced farmers to leave their land, and made it difficult to move food and humanitarian aid across the country.
Abdullah al-Tijani, a social historian and humanitarian activist, noted the unprecedented scale of the current disaster.
“Most previous famines were often confined to specific regions, as happened in 1984, or areas in southern Sudan before its secession in [2011], while the capital and major cities continued to have the necessities of life and services,” al-Tijani told Al Jazeera.
This time, he said, hunger and the collapse of basic services have spread across the entire country.
“A comprehensive food crisis has struck the heart of major urban and agricultural centres in the states of Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar, Darfur, and Kordofan, causing millions of citizens to be displaced inside and outside the country,” al-Tijani added.
He pointed to what he described as the “systematic destruction of infrastructure, disruption of large agricultural projects, and targeting of markets, bakeries, and crops, along with disrupting the banking system and communication networks, which isolated entire regions”.
Al-Tijani also cited the “restrictions on humanitarian access and delays in granting transit permits for relief workers”. He accused the warring parties of using control over food supplies as a tool of war, while warning that international funding has fallen short of the size of the crisis.
Lost agricultural potential
The scale of the crisis is stark because of Sudan’s agricultural potential. The country has immense resources, including roughly 200 million acres (81 million hectares) of arable land, abundant water from the Nile, and extensive livestock resources, but Sudan’s potential as a global breadbasket remains unfulfilled.
Mohammed Abdul Rahman, an economic researcher, explained that the current food security crisis reflects a clear development gap, and a longstanding weakness in Sudan’s agricultural sector compounded by war.
“Wars and armed conflicts are among the most influential factors on food production,” Abdul Rahman said, “along with the displacement of farmers from their lands, the absence of political stability and agricultural policies, weak funding and government guarantees, and reliance on traditional farming methods.”

Hours after again threatening to destroy Iran’s regime, US President Donald Trump struck a markedly more optimistic tone Tuesday, saying Tehran wants to negotiate and that relations between the two countries are “developing” as he prepared to meet Arab leaders on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Trump told world leaders earlier Tuesday that he faced what he called a major decision between reaching an agreement with Iran and taking far more destructive military action against the Islamic Republic. At the same time, he predicted that a deal would eventually be reached after the US midterm elections in November. Iran has also signaled a willingness to revive negotiations, while Arab governments have been working to arrange high-level US-Iran contacts in New York.
Later, during a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Trump again expressed confidence that Washington and Tehran could eventually reach an agreement.
“They want to talk to us. They’re talking to us. Even today they’re talking to us. The relationship is developing,” Trump said. “But we cannot allow them, and they understand, we cannot allow them to have a nuclear weapon.”
Burnham’s first in-person meeting with Trump was expected to focus heavily on the Middle East, including the Iran war and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Britain has also agreed to provide limited defensive aerial refueling support to Saudi Arabia as Riyadh confronts renewed Houthi attacks from Yemen.
Trump is also due to meet Gulf leaders and senior officials in New York for talks expected to focus on the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict and what comes next. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman were invited to participate, with Iraq and Jordan also joining the discussions.
Several of the same Gulf governments pressed Trump in August to hold off on a major new strike against Iran, believing an agreement with Tehran could still be within reach. A month later, no such agreement has been concluded.
The Gulf states arrive at the talks increasingly concerned about their own vulnerability. Iranian missile and drone attacks during the war have exposed limits in the security protection offered by the large US military presence in the region, prompting governments to explore both stronger defense arrangements and direct diplomacy with Tehran.
The New York talks are therefore expected to go beyond the question of whether Washington and Tehran can reopen negotiations. Regional governments are also seeking greater clarity over the security guarantees the United States is prepared to provide as they confront the fallout from the Iran war.
The Houthi threat is also expected to feature prominently. The Iran-backed group has expanded its territorial control in Yemen around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia, creating another security challenge for Gulf governments already contending with Iran and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has repeatedly sought greater US military assistance against the Houthis, but Trump has so far stopped short of joining Riyadh’s campaign directly. That hesitation has fueled questions in the kingdom over the extent of Washington’s commitment to its defense, even as the broader US-Saudi military relationship remains extensive.
For now, Trump is publicly leaving both options open on Iran: renewed diplomacy and the threat of further military force. His remarks Tuesday suggested that, despite the warnings delivered from the UN podium only hours earlier, contacts with Tehran have not stopped.
“The relationship is developing,” he said.

Lithuania Moves to Scrap Ban on Weapons of Mass Destruction and Military Bases

Lithuania Moves to Scrap Ban on Weapons of Mass Destruction and Military Bases
Lithuania's Seimas has backed removing a constitutional clause that bars both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from the country's territory.
This was reported by Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT on September 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The measure passed only the consideration stage, and two further votes on adoption remain before the amendment can take effect. According to LRT, 99 lawmakers supported the change, 13 opposed it, and five abstained.
LRT noted that most of the opposition came from the Nemunas Dawn faction, with nine of its members voting against it and four abstaining. Agrarian lawmaker Valius Ąžuolas and three members of the Mixed Group also withheld support.
Article 137 currently states that neither weapons of mass destruction nor foreign military bases of other states may be stationed on Lithuanian territory. The proposed amendment would delete that provision outright.
Seimas Speaker Juozas Olekas indicated that the first adoption vote is scheduled for October 6 and the final vote for January 12 next year. LRT added that lawmakers must vote twice more, with a three-month interval between the ballots. At least 94 of the 141 members must back the amendment for it to pass.
Debate on the floor exposed sharp divisions over deterrence. Laurynas Kasčiūnas, an elder of the opposition Homeland Union—Lithuanian Christian Democrats faction, described nuclear weapons as one of the most effective deterrents.
He credited them with “keeping the Cold War from turning hot.”
He argued that Lithuania was the only country in the region still bound by such a restriction, pointing to Latvia, Estonia, Poland, and Finland as states without such a limit.
"Russians do not attack the strong," Kasčiūnas told the chamber, per LRT.
Remigijus Motuzas, the social-democrat chair of the Seimas Committee on Foreign Affairs, emphasized that Lithuania should not obstruct NATO's nuclear deterrence or become the alliance's weak link. He warned that the country could not afford to be less protected than other NATO members.
Opponents pushed back. Nemunas Dawn leader Remigijus Žemaitaitis claimed the amendment was unnecessary and maintained that only a referendum could change the article.
Ignas Vėgėlė of the Mixed Group cautioned that the deleted text also lifts the ban on foreign military bases, asking whether Lithuania might cede land it would neither control nor manage.
Liberal leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen framed the vote as a way to ensure Lithuania would not appear weaker than its allies.
The vote comes amid a wider European debate over nuclear deterrence.
The Financial Times separately reported in early June that the US was weighing the deployment of nuclear weapons in several additional NATO countries in Europe.
The vote followed a rapid sequence of steps toward the same goal.
On September 9, the Seimas Committee on Legal Affairs voted 7-2 to strike the constitutional provision on nuclear weapons.
Moscow reacted within days: on September 11, Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev warned that Lithuania would be wiped from the map if a confrontation over nuclear deployment ever erupted, claiming NATO allies would not come to its defense.

Global Oil Prices Drop as Saudi Arabia Restarts East-West Pipeline After Drone Attack
Saudi Arabia has officially restarted operations on its East-West Pipeline and is preparing to resume crude exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu on September 22, Reuters reported, citing industry sources.
The critical pipeline was shut down on September 13 following targeted drone attacks, which completely halted crude loadings at the Yanbu port.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Drone strikes on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline were launched from Iraq’s Maysan province, leading Baghdad to fire local security commanders, according to the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD).
The FDD said the attack was executed by a splinter network of Iran-backed militias operating outside established command structures.
Following the disruption of maritime oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, Saudi Arabia—OPEC’s leading exporter—has relied heavily on the East-West Pipeline to safely reroute approximately 4 million barrels per day (bpd) to the Red Sea coast.
This bypassed volume accounts for nearly 4% of total global supply, Reuters wrote.
Sources briefed on the matter indicated that while the pipeline is active, it is currently pumping at a reduced rate. State energy firm Saudi Aramco is working to restore the full 4 million bpd capacity, though a security source cautioned Reuters that achieving full resumption could take several weeks.
Saudi Aramco has not yet publicly commented on the operational timeline.
The news of restoring supply channels immediately eased global oil markets. Traders reacted to the pipeline’s restart with a sell-off, driving Brent crude futures down by more than $2 a barrel to their lowest price point since September 8, Reuters reported.
In the immediate term, the active pipeline will resume supplying Aramco’s Red Sea coastal refineries. According to Reuters, at least one cargo was scheduled to load at Yanbu on September 22, bound for China.
Meanwhile, trading sources confirmed that oil markets are preparing for renewed Saudi maritime loadings, with tankers already being repositioned to Egypt’s Mediterranean Port Said and Sidi Kerir terminals for ship-to-ship transfers.

Ukraine and Syria Sign Deal on Demining and Drone-Based Mine Detection
Ukraine and Syria have signed an intergovernmental agreement aimed at strengthening cooperation in humanitarian mine action, including land clearance, specialist training, and the use of Ukrainian technologies for detecting explosive hazards, Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy and Environment reported.
The agreement was signed in Damascus by Ukraine’s Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment Ihor Bezkaravainyi, who is visiting Syria, and Syria’s Deputy Minister for Emergency Situations and Disaster Management Mustafa Munir.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under the agreement, the two countries will cooperate on clearing land affected by hostilities to enable its return to productive use. Ukraine will also provide training for Syrian specialists in humanitarian demining and non-technical survey.
Bezkaravainyi said Ukraine’s experience and technologies could support Syria’s mine action efforts, particularly the use of drones for remote mine detection and mapping contaminated areas.
“For Ukraine, it is very important to share our experience in mine action with countries that, like us, have suffered contamination from explosive remnants of war. I am convinced that close cooperation in humanitarian demining is the beginning of broader cooperation between Ukraine and Syria that will not be limited to the mine action sector,” Bezkaravainyi said.
Munir, in turn, highlighted Ukraine’s progress in detecting and neutralizing explosive hazards, noting the direct impact of demining efforts on agriculture and global food security.
Ukraine has accumulated significant practical experience in clearing territory contaminated by mines and unexploded ordnance. In the first six months of 2026 alone, Ukrainian Defense Ministry demining teams inspected and cleared 4,715 hectares of liberated territory.
The Main Directorate of Mine Action, Civil Protection and Environmental Safety reported in July that the work covered 831.85 hectares of agricultural land, 186.33 kilometers of railway tracks, 16.14 kilometers of roads, and 6.72 kilometers of power lines.
During the same period, specialists detected and destroyed 1,914 explosive devices, helping restore access to farmland and critical infrastructure. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, a total of 482,330 explosive items have been removed, according to the directorate.
Alongside conventional demining operations, Ukraine has increasingly incorporated domestically developed robotic systems into missions in hazardous battlefield environments. In June, the Defense Ministry announced the addition of the Vepr unmanned ground vehicle to Ukraine’s battlefield evacuation fleet.
The Vepr robotic ground complex, which can be used for logistics, casualty evacuation, and combat support, has been deployed on the frontline since 2024. Its developers have since upgraded the platform based on combat experience and feedback from Ukrainian troops, adapting it to evolving battlefield conditions.

Shock therapy threatens post-Assad peace in Syria: analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
17:42:34 UTC
02:42:34 KST

Shock therapy threatens post-Assad peace in Syria: analysis
President Shara relies on Hayat Tahrir al-Sham veterans as key advisers and policymakers
TEHRAN – A number of economic policies adopted by new Syrian leader Ahmed al-Shara has made the people’s lives “even harder,” says a senior nonresident fellow at the Center for International Policy.
“As the country has proceeded in its political transition under President Ahmed al-Shara… living conditions for most Syrians have only become worse,” Sam Heller wrote in Foreign Affairs published on September 22.
“Costs have soared, and a promised post-Assad economic boom has not materialized,” he noted.
Heller highlights inexpert decisions by the government, saying, “The president relies on a handful of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham veterans as key advisers and policymakers.”
Heller also says the government “has in large part reined in revenge attacks and sectarian killings, although pro-government partisans perpetrated two massacres of minority Alawites and Druze last year.”
The text of the article titled “Syria’s imperiled transition” reads as follows:
In Syria today, nearly everyone seems to be struggling. People of all classes and backgrounds can barely afford food, rent, utilities—the basics of a dignified life. The country is attempting to leave behind half a century of tyranny and 14 years of civil war for a new and freer political order. It is also recovering from an economic collapse so precipitous that it ultimately helped topple the dictator Bashar al-Assad in 2024. As the country has proceeded in its political transition under President Ahmed al-Shara, however, living conditions for most Syrians have only become worse. Costs have soared, and a promised post-Assad economic boom has not materialized. Syria’s new government has offered citizens some symbolic victories, including an end to international isolation, but, for most people, it has not delivered materially. In fact, a number of its policy choices have made their lives even harder.
Of all the problems Syria now faces, including intercommunal violence and the possible fragmentation of the country, the economy is the biggest one. Yet the country’s new leadership has insisted on austerity measures that have made the cost of living even more unbearable for the average Syrian.
Syria is by no means the only country experiencing an affordability crisis. But it is one of the world’s most politically fragile states. If the new government cannot provide for ordinary Syrians, it risks unrest that could derail the country’s post-Assad transition.
Syrian rebels led by the Islamist faction Hayat Tahrir al-Sham ousted the Assad government in December 2024. Shara, the group’s leader, eventually assumed the presidency and has since overseen the consolidation of the country’s new institutions and its postwar recovery.
His administration has scored some real wins. After decades of political isolation, Syria has gained the support of regional and global powers, including the United States, and secured the removal of most international economic sanctions. Shara’s government has for the time being kept the country from breaking apart; after defeating Kurdish-led forces in Syria’s northeast earlier this year, it is now working to reintegrate the formerly semiautonomous region. It has in large part reined in revenge attacks and sectarian killings, although pro-government partisans perpetrated two massacres of minority Alawites and Druze last year. And Shara has mostly shielded Syria from the effects of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, even as it has spread elsewhere through the region.
Where the new Syrian government has fallen short is in its management of the economy. Of course, reviving commerce and industry was going to be a formidable challenge for any post-Assad government. Fourteen years of civil war displaced more than half the country’s population and caused the economy to contract by more than 50 percent. The World Bank has estimated that the war caused more than $108 billion in physical damage, largely in and around three economically vital cities, Aleppo, Damascus, and Homs. The World Bank reckons that two-thirds of Syrians now live in poverty, with an income below $3.65 per person per day. According to the UN Development Program, 90 percent of Syrians are living in poverty, and 66 percent in extreme poverty.
By the last several years of Assad’s rule, conditions had grown miserable. In fact, economic collapse contributed to the regime’s implosion in December 2024, as half-starved Syrian soldiers abandoned the front lines in the face of a rebel advance. In these circumstances, even an amply resourced, expert-led government would now struggle to restart the economy. The Shara government is neither of those things.
Of all the problems Syria now faces, the economy is the biggest one.
Syrians, impoverished by economic mismanagement and war, cannot afford even the bare necessities. The cost of living far exceeds the average citizen’s income. Based on the current unofficial exchange rate, World Food Program estimates that monthly needs for a Syrian household of five, including food and utilities, cost about $197. The Syrian Center for Policy Research, a Damascus-based think tank, puts the monthly abject poverty line at roughly $255. Yet the official monthly minimum wage is equivalent to only $95. Many Syrians depend on remittances from relatives abroad to get by.
To make matters worse, the cost of living in Syria has been rising steadily. The World Food Program calculates that the cost of essentials increased by 34 percent between July 2025 and 2026. Syrians’ purchasing power has been further diminished by a weakened currency, which initially strengthened after December 2024 but has since approached Assad-era lows.
More than 80 percent of Syrians lack reliable access to sufficient food. A joint assessment by the government and World Food Program found some improvement on this front from 2024 to 2025, but only insofar as the proportion of food-secure Syrians increased from 11.1 to 18.4 percent. After a severe drought that limited agricultural production in 2025, ample rainfall this year should improve the availability of domestically grown food. But it is unclear whether Syrians can actually afford to buy from local markets.
Housing costs have also skyrocketed. According to the Syrian Center for Policy Research, rents increased almost 66 percent between May 2025 and May 2026. After trying to live elsewhere, many people have returned to homes and neighborhoods shattered by the war after they found themselves unable to afford the rents in less damaged areas. Costs are biting even for middle-class and upper-middle-class Syrians, who need to contend with rents that have doubled or tripled, as well as rising school tuitions.
Although much of Syria’s hardship can be chalked up to the devastation of war and decades of Assad-era mismanagement, some of the country’s problems are the product of the Shara government’s policies. The country’s new leaders have undertaken a shock therapy program of economic liberalization without, it seems, fully accounting for the acute vulnerability and poverty of most Syrians.
The Shara government increased price of subsidized bread by 1,400 percent
In the Assad government’s final, most threadbare years, it slashed subsidies that it could no longer afford. The Shara government has gone even further. Months after taking power, it increased the price of state-subsidized bread—the staple of the Syrian diet—by nearly 1,400 percent. Although the state has since held the price of a standard bread bundle steady, it has repeatedly shrunk the amount of bread per bundle. Early this year, the government massively increased electricity tariffs, in some cases by as much as 800 percent. This new pricing effectively shifted the cost of restoring the country’s power infrastructure to consumers and businesses; many people have simply stopped paying impossibly high bills.
Syria’s new authorities brought fuel prices in line with global averages early on, sharply increasing costs for farming, transportation, and other sectors. On September 13, the government raised fuel prices again—40 percent in the case of diesel—while citing global energy markets and ongoing repairs to a key Syrian refinery. Protests erupted across the country in response to the price hike. They are the largest demonstrations since Assad’s ouster.
The Shara government has tried to compensate for inflation by increasing public-sector salaries: in March alone, it approved a 50 percent raise. The benefit of these higher wages is diminished by continuing inflation, however, and it has not been distributed equally. The government laid off hundreds of thousands of Assad-era employees last year, even as it hired many of its own loyalists, including for the newly reconstituted military and security services.
The Shara government has additionally opened the country to most imports, dismantling strict controls that conserved foreign currency reserves and protected local manufacturers. Syrian producers already working in adverse conditions now struggle to compete with cheap imported goods.
The economic challenges facing the Shara government are daunting. It inherited a state that was effectively bankrupt. The government has projected some revenue from customs duties and consumption-related fees and taxes, and it is working to position Syria as a regional trade hub by developing road and rail links and embarking on new pipeline projects. It has retaken control of the country’s northeast, which is comparatively rich in natural resources and farmland. Yet restoring oil and gas production in the northeast will require substantial investment, and increasing wheat production might be a net drain on government coffers.
Foreign governments have not supported Syria to the extent Damascus may have expected. The United States has helped reconnect Syria to international financial networks and encouraged investment in the country, but it has not made large commitments to its recovery or convened a “friends of Syria” conference to mobilize donors—as it did for Iraq, for example, in 2016. Persian Gulf Arab states such as Saudi Arabia and Qatar have sent some assistance, including support for public-sector salaries, but they have not agreed to keep Syria afloat financially. Their ability to further support Syria is also in question as these powers deal with the effects of the Iran war.
The World Bank has provided grants, but the Shara government’s decision to eschew international loans has likely cut off Syria from additional liquidity in the near term. The government has not spelled out why it rejects international borrowing, although Shara has said he doesn’t want Syria “to live on assistance, or on politicized loans.” Humanitarian aid has in any case fallen away; earlier this year, cuts to donor funding, especially from the United States, forced the World Food Program to end its subsidized bread program and halve general food assistance.
More than 80 percent of Syrians lack reliable access to sufficient food.
Shara has envisioned a recovery powered by private investment, not aid. Yet he seems to have believed that investment would be more forthcoming. Many of the memorandums of understanding that his government initially announced with would-be investors have not translated to real commitments. Significant obstacles to foreign investment persist: the security situation is still unsettled, and Syria lacks legal and regulatory frameworks and a fully functional financial system. Investments that have been announced skew toward real estate megaprojects that seem disconnected from the country’s development needs.
The Shara government is short on economic expertise. The president relies on a handful of Hayat Tahrir al-Sham veterans as key advisers and policymakers. Their experience in governing is limited to running a small rebel-held enclave in northwestern Syria between 2017 and 2024. Shara has stripped power from legacy state institutions such as the ministries of economy and transportation and concentrated it in a handful of newly created, opaque entities linked to the presidency, including a so-called sovereign fund meant to manage a vast portfolio of state-owned assets and property appropriated from business figures linked to Assad.
The lack of know-how shows. Major policy announcements, such as this month’s fuel price increase, are abrupt and seemingly made without real study or outside consultation. And although reliable economic data has long been hard to come by in Syria, the Shara government has sometimes presented dubious figures. In March, Shara himself announced that the Syrian economy had grown between 30 and 35 percent the previous year. The Syrian Center for Policy Studies estimated that the real growth rate in 2025 was only 0.3 percent.
Patience running thin
Although the policies of the Shara government have not foreclosed an eventual recovery, they have likely delayed it and made life harder for ordinary Syrians. If basic needs are not met soon, people could lose faith in the country’s post-Assad political order.
According to polling by the magazine Syria in Transition, 52 percent of Syrians disapproved of their government’s performance in June—up from 44 percent in April. A majority of respondents in both April and June said they struggled to cover their living expenses at least once a month, and in April (the latest month with available data), 66 percent said the government was not doing enough to curb high prices. Between April and June, the number of respondents pessimistic about the country’s trajectory jumped from 30 to 46 percent.
Immediately after Assad’s fall, Syrians were willing to excuse their new government’s shortcomings. Nearly two years later, they seem more ready to express frustration. That discontent probably won’t take the form of armed struggle because Syrians are, on the whole, tired of war. But they are increasingly mounting smaller-scale protests and strikes to demand economic relief and improved public services.
Syrians don’t have endless reserves of patience for Shara’s government.
Economic hardship also adds to Syria’s general combustibility, making other political and sectarian issues potentially more explosive. The Shara government is now trying to reintegrate the Kurdish northeast, including by folding Kurdish militias into the national military. At the same time, though, it is removing subsidies in the formerly semi-autonomous region—which had its own economic regime for years—hugely increasing the cost of fuel and other essentials for people living there. On the Mediterranean coast, meanwhile, authorities are trying to establish a functional relationship with the Alawite community at a time of acute economic stress. Alawites not only face the same cost-of-living pressures as their fellow Syrians but also have suffered disproportionately from public-sector layoffs and the dissolution of the Assad’s military and security services. Many are afraid to leave their villages because of safety concerns. On the coast and elsewhere, rising prices and mass unemployment are a recipe for social instability.
A Syria that is poor and violent is in no one’s interest. After years of misery and bloodshed, the country needs a chance, finally, to recover. Now, as the Shara government tries to revitalize the economy, it needs to do so with social stability in mind. The authorities must prioritize affordability so that the country’s most vulnerable are not casualties of liberalizing reforms. The government should develop new subsidies for bread, electricity, transport, farming, and industrial production while the country is emerging from economic collapse. Its international partners, meanwhile, need to provide Damascus with the resources to deliver meaningfully for ordinary citizens, and to provide a social safety net as it pursues structural reforms. Investing in energy and real estate won’t be enough to revive Syria.
The government also needs to open more channels of communication with the public to build confidence and manage discontent as Syrians endure what was always going to be a difficult transitional period. That means communicating frankly and transparently about the rationale for its economic decision-making, consulting with Syrian businesses, and empowering the newly formed parliament to play a meaningful oversight role.
Syrians were relieved to see Assad finally go, but they don’t have endless reserves of patience for Shara’s government. The country’s new leaders need to improve material conditions for ordinary Syrians immediately, or risk losing the people’s trust.
