Can AI reason without words? A small model puts the idea to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Can AI reason without words? A small model puts the idea to the test
Skipping the words could make some AI reasoning more efficient
AI may be able to reason without putting every step into words.
Many of today’s AI systems tackle difficult problems by generating intermediate steps in lengthy, chains of words before arriving at an answer— a technique often called chain-of-thought reasoning. That approach can improve performance on some tasks, but it also means an AI model may generate many words, or tokens, on the way to a relatively short answer. Each token takes computing power to produce, so longer reasoning can make answers slower and more expensive to generate.
A small, experimental AI system called BDH-CQ takes a different approach. It can solve some reasoning puzzles without spelling out its intermediate thinking, researchers report in a paper submitted August 10 to arXiv.org. The work asks whether AI needs language at every step of reasoning, and whether doing more internally could make some reasoning cheaper.
In training, AI models are often shown a few examples before they try a new problem. Many keep those examples in front of them as they work. But on reasoning tests, BDH-CQ (DH is short for Dragon Hatchling) instead uses each example to update a fixed-size memory, which stays the same size as it takes in more examples, so it does not have to keep going back through everything it has already seen.
“Once the query arrives, the model doesn’t write out its thinking in words at all,” says complexity scientist Zuzanna Stamirowska, CEO of AI company Pathway. Stamirowska says the model works through a problem internally without turning each step into words. “Nothing in between ever converts into language,” she says.
Stamirowska and colleagues said the model solved nearly three in 10 puzzles on the public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation set when given two attempts. The result showed that a small model could solve some new reasoning problems without spelling out its intermediate steps. The benchmark tests ask AI systems to infer visual rules from a few examples and apply them to new puzzles. The tests are like human student exams.
The model did better on some puzzles than others. For example, it handled some tasks involving turning or moving shapes but struggled more with color changes and some combinations of rules. On harder ordering and nesting puzzles, the model did better after seeing an example of similar difficulty.
The process with fewer words may help keep computing costs down, Stamirowska and colleagues say. They estimate that each puzzle query costs about $0.00070 to run, about one-eleventh as much as GPT-5.6 Luna on the same benchmark test, though the two costs were calculated differently. The study has not been peer-reviewed.
The finding is “an interesting efficiency result,” says computer scientist Yuntian Deng of the University of Waterloo in Canada. But he says it does not show that BDH-CQ’s underlying architecture is better than other approaches.
“Specialized small models [like BDH-CQ] are a promising route to efficient reasoning,” Deng says. But more testing is needed to separate the effects of the model’s design from how it was trained, he says. Without written-out reasoning, the model is harder to inspect, Deng says. But even a written chain of thought may not faithfully show how the model reached its answer.
The BDH-CQ model was built specifically for ARC-style problems, which makes it hard to compare directly with general-purpose AI systems, says machine learning researcher Jonas Geiping of the ELLIS Institute Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems in Germany. But he called the approach “neat” and noted that it can tackle test problems without retraining.
For Deng, the study raises a broader question: Does AI need to put all of its reasoning into words?. “Human language is useful for communicating reasoning, but it need not be the most efficient representation for every intermediate computation,” Deng says.

Trump spoke early on the first day, following Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in keeping with the tradition under which Brazil opens the debate and the US – being the host country – speaks next.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham were among the other leaders scheduled to address the assembly during its opening day
Commander Warns Russian Groups Could Reach Zaporizhzhia
During his UN address, Trump expressed confidence that Washington could help broker an end to the war, although he did not announce a ceasefire or any negotiating framework between Kyiv and Moscow.
“We’re working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done,” Trump said, according to Clash Reports.
“It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand. They’ve had it,” he continued.
The president presented his approach as one of direct intervention rather than prolonged diplomacy. “I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day. I do not believe in letting problems fester. They only become harder to solve,” Trump said.
However, no further details about Washington’s resolution to bridge the fundamental differences between Kyiv and Moscow had been offered.
On Monday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that there had been no progress in negotiations, although Moscow hoped trilateral talks would eventually resume.
In July, Bloomberg reported that the Kremlin no longer planned to return any occupied Ukrainian territory as part of a future peace deal. Instead, Putin reportedly intended to keep occupied areas of the Sumy and Kharkiv regions as permanent buffer zones, while continuing his push to seize all of the Donetsk region.
Kyiv categorically rejects any settlement requiring it to surrender territory and maintains that a peace agreement must respect Ukraine’s internationally recognized borders and sovereignty.
Renewed US mediation earlier in September
Trump’s most recent speech follows a renewed US mediation earlier in September.
Special US envoys Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5 during talks lasting more than three hours, then traveled to Kyiv on Sept. 6 for their first visit to the Ukrainian capital as Washington’s intermediaries.
Prospects for a direct Trump-Zelensky meeting in New York initially appeared uncertain.
As of Sept. 19, Zelensky was absent from the list of bilateral meetings publicly outlined by US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz, while two senior Ukrainian officials told Suspilne that no meeting had been finalized.
The situation changed following a Sunday, Sept. 20 telephone discussion between the two leaders, who agreed to meet with “ideas for de-escalation steps.” By Tuesday, the bilateral talks had been added to Trump’s schedule, with Reuters reporting that Zelensky was among at least 11 leaders the US president planned to meet during UNGA.
The discussions are expected to center on air defense – particularly US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapons Ukraine relies on to successfully deter Russian ballistic missiles – as well as energy and security.
Kyiv is urgently seeking additional protection ahead of its fifth winter of war, as the country prepares for intensified Russian attacks against critical infrastructure, such as heating, power and water supplies.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Polezhayev had signed a contract with the Russian Defense Ministry shortly before sentencing. In October 2024, an appeals court suspended proceedings in his criminal case after receiving a request from the commander of his military unit confirming that he was serving under contract.

Ukraine Downs 350,000 Russian Drones Since Start of Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:56:00 UTC
00:56:00 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Downs 350,000 Russian Drones Since Start of Year
Ukrainian defense forces have neutralized more than 350,000 Russian drones since the start of the year, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Defense.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Every confirmed strike was recorded on video in the DELTA combat system and verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster, the ministry reported.
It described DELTA as the “digital core” of modern battlefield management, saying the platform allows forces to analyze each recorded shootdown and more quickly scale effective countermeasures.
The ministry provided a breakdown of the total tally:
- around 220,000 fixed-wing drones destroyed by unmanned systems units of the Defense Forces;
- roughly 100,000 copter-type drones downed by those same units;
- 31,000 Shahed-type drones were brought down by unmanned systems units, mobile fire groups, and army aviation.
Destroying fixed-wing drones denies Russia the ability to conduct reconnaissance in Ukraine's rear, strike targets, or adjust long-range fire against civilian sites and critical infrastructure, the ministry noted.
Downing copter-type drones, it added, prevent Russian forces from locating and hitting Ukrainian positions and equipment along the front.
Each destroyed drone represents potentially saved lives for Ukrainian troops and civilians, the ministry noted.
The tally reflects an intensifying campaign by Ukraine's drone forces against Russian aerial and ground targets.
In a single 24-hour period in early September, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces struck or destroyed 2,379 Russian targets, including 379 drones across copter, fixed-wing, Shahed, and Gerbera types.
Between September 1 and 9, those units reported hitting 18,580 targets, including 3,726 Russian personnel.

Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:55:57 UTC
00:55:57 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Is Dropping More Glide Bombs on Ukraine Per Day Than US Did During Iran Air Campaign
Russian forces dropped 8,766 guided aerial bombs on Ukraine in August 2026, bringing the daily rate of their use above that recorded for guided bomb strikes during the recent US air campaign against Iran.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on September 22, Russia used an average of 283 aerial bombs equipped with Universal Gliding and Correction Modules, known as UMPK, per day during August. The outlet based its comparison with US operations on Pentagon data and research by the Royal United Services Institute.
During the US-led Operation Epic Fury against Iran, American aircraft employed an estimated 211 to 237 guided aerial bombs per day, according to Militarnyi’s calculations.
The comparison concerns the rate at which guided aerial munitions were released rather than the overall scale, capabilities, targets, or operational conditions of the respective air campaigns.
Russia’s current rate remains below that recorded during the main phase of the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003. Militarnyi estimated that US and coalition aircraft used roughly 509 precision-guided munitions per day during that period.
The 2003 Iraq campaign involved extensive use of precision-guided weapons. US Air Force data shows that 19,948 of the 29,199 munitions employed during the initial campaign were guided weapons.
Russia’s UMPK kits and the US-developed Joint Direct Attack Munition, or JDAM, are based on a broadly similar approach: adding guidance and control systems to existing stocks of conventional free-fall bombs rather than producing an entirely new weapon.
The US Air Force describes JDAM as a guidance kit that converts conventional unguided bombs into precision weapons using inertial navigation and GPS guidance.
Russia has pursued the same general concept with UMPK-equipped bombs, allowing aircraft to release modified conventional bombs from greater distances. RUSI reported in February 2025 that Russia had ordered more than 70,000 UMPK glide-bomb kits for that year alone as production expanded during the full-scale war.
The August figure illustrates the continuing expansion of Russia’s use of glide bombs against Ukraine. During the final ten days of July, Russian forces also struck Pavlohrad, around 75 kilometers from the front line, three times with guided aerial bombs, according to Militarnyi.
The outlet said the attacks could indicate renewed use of the jet-powered UMPB-5R extended-range bomb.
Russia has also expanded production of other relatively low-cost precision weapons. In September, The Wall Street Journal reported that Russia was rapidly moving new jet-powered systems, including the Geran-5 drone and Banderol cruise missile, from battlefield testing into serial production, with both weapons estimated to cost around $100,000 each.

The target, who currently leads an all-Ukrainian non-governmental organization and works as a kickboxing coach in the capital.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to SBU investigators, the operative—an unemployed resident of the temporarily occupied eastern Ukrainian city of Melitopol—was recruited by the FSB after Russian intelligence offered to drop a criminal case against her involving illegal drug possession.
She subsequently completed a training course at an FSB-run facility in Melitopol, receiving instruction in operational security, land navigation, and marksmanship.
Following her training, the operative was routed through Belarus into Zhytomyr before arriving in Kyiv. While in the capital, she frequently changed hotel accommodations and deployed counter-surveillance measures to detect potential monitoring. Under directions from her FSB handler, she retrieved a pistol and ammunition from a concealed cache in a Kyiv forest park zone.
In this way, Russia hoped to kill a Russian opposition figure who had been fighting for Ukraine since 2022—first in the Kyiv region and then on the Eastern Front.
SBU counterintelligence officers intervened before the attack could take place, detaining the suspect near the victim’s workplace as she reconnoitered the area to set up a firing position.
A search of her hotel room yielded the firearm, ammunition, and a smartphone containing direct communications with her Russian handler, whom the SBU has formally identified.
The suspect has been served a notice of suspicion under Part 2, Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law). She remains held in custody without bail and faces up to life imprisonment with confiscation of property if convicted.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:53:40 UTC
00:53:40 KST

A Ukrainian fund is investing in a Danish defense startup, a reversal for a country far better known for taking in foreign capital than for sending it abroad. Resist.UA is backing BlueShadow, a maritime security firm run by a former US Navy submarine commander but largely engineered in Ukraine, to build defenses for coasts and undersea cables against drones and hybrid attacks.
BlueShadow is registered in Denmark, but almost its entire engineering team works in Ukraine, and it folds gear from more than 15 Ukrainian suppliers of drones, sensors, and communications into a single system.
Resist.UA, which signed a letter of intent to join the company's €2 million pre-seed round, runs a new €50 million fund, Resist 2.0, designed to bring Ukraine's battlefield-proven technology to global markets.
Ukraine engineers the Danish startup
The company was founded in 2025 and is led by Charles Maher, a former commander of a US Navy nuclear submarine, according to Defender Media.
This summer, it registered as a Ukrainian legal entity and builds on Ukrainian components, planning to fit its maritime platforms with M-Fly's RB-220 gimbal, a day-and-night targeting sensor used until now only on flying drones.
The two sides first met in January 2026 and formalized the partnership as BlueShadow raised its round and Resist.UA launched its second fund.
The systems guard the sea
BlueShadow is building two of them. BlueDragon, still in development, is designed to shield Ukraine's coastal cities, ports, and shipping lanes from drone strikes. BlueSentry, which the company plans to launch in October, is aimed at protecting ports, offshore wind farms, undersea cables, and maritime borders from hybrid attack, the kind of sabotage that has repeatedly damaged Baltic Sea infrastructure.
"This partnership will fuel the next phase of our mission to protect people, infrastructure, commerce, and natural resources at sea," the company said.
Ukraine's defense tech turns outward
Ukrainian defense technology, tested in real combat, has drawn growing investor interest, and Ukrainian figures are now building funds to channel it: the former Defense Minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, is raising what he calls the country's largest defense-tech venture fund.

Commander Warns Russian Groups Could Reach Zaporizhzhia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:53:00 UTC
00:53:00 KST

Small Russian infantry groups could reach Zaporizhzhia this winter, the commander of Ukraine’s 1st Separate Assault Regiment, Dmytro Filatov, said in an interview with the Real Front YouTube channel.
Filatov, known by his call sign “Perun,” said Russia could intensify offensive operations during the winter and search for weak points in Ukrainian defenses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I think that this winter we will record the approach and entry into Zaporizhzhia – not of troops, but of individual groups,” Filatov said.
He identified the Stepnohirske area and the Dnipro River’s southern bank as possible directions for such attempts. According to the commander, dense development along the river could help Russian troops infiltrate toward the city.
Filatov said Russian forces had come close to Zaporizhzhia last year. He warned that even the appearance of isolated groups near the city could have a major psychological effect on Ukraine’s partners and encourage the Russian military and President Vladimir Putin.
Filatov warns of wider Russian pressure
Filatov said worsening weather could allow Russian forces to increase pressure across the entire front line.
He said some Russian units had already been transferred to the Dobropillia direction, where they are attempting to advance toward Kramatorsk. According to Filatov, Russia is also trying to shift Ukraine’s attention toward Donbas and force Kyiv to redeploy troops from other sectors.
Russian Ex-Mayor Who Left Prison for Ukraine War Dies From Combat Wounds
“On the Zaporizhzhia front, the number of strikes and sorties has decreased – the intensity has fallen. Yes, we are operating less on this sector. I think the enemy’s redeployment to other directions is part of its strategy in response to our actions here,” Filatov said.
He argued that Ukraine must strengthen its defenses in Donbas while preserving the initiative and continuing to pressure Russian weak points.
Filatov said Russia’s initial objective in the Zaporizhzhia region was to encircle and capture Orikhiv, before advancing toward Zaporizhzhia. Capturing the city would allow Russia to block one of Ukraine’s major industrial centers, which has a degree of energy autonomy because of its hydroelectric power plant. Ukrainian forces, however, managed to stop the Russian advance.
Southern Grouping rejects imminent-entry claims
The Southern Grouping of Ukrainian forces rejected reports that Russian troops are likely to directly enter Zaporizhzhia this winter.
“There are currently no grounds to speak of a high probability of such a development,” Anastasiia Shevchenko, a spokesperson for the Southern Grouping, told Ukrinform.
Shevchenko said the front line is about 30 kilometers (19 miles) from Zaporizhzhia, making a covert advance over that distance highly unlikely. Ukrainian drone systems monitor Russian personnel and direct fire toward detected groups.
She also said there have been no changes in Russian military activity indicating preparations for a direct entry into the city. Russia has not abandoned its goal of capturing Zaporizhzhia, she said, but currently lacks sufficient forces and equipment to advance directly toward it.
Ukrainian forces have recorded attempts by small Russian infantry groups to infiltrate near Mali Shcherbaky, Stepove, and Shcherbaky in the Orikhiv direction. Shevchenko said those attempts had not succeeded.
Similar warnings were made last year
The latest warning echoes reports and forecasts made during Russia’s advances in the southern Zaporizhzhia region last year.
Russia had concentrated assault formations near Orikhiv after advancing through the Hulyaipole area. Russian forces captured Hulyaipole in early 2026 and then pushed toward Orikhiv, increasing pressure on the route to Zaporizhzhia.
Late last year, Russian forces also had intensified attacks around Hulyaipole, including attempts to break through and advance deeper into the region.
A recent Kyiv Post opinion analysis described Russian pressure on Orikhiv from several directions and attempts to use forward positions to threaten Ukrainian supply routes.
However, those warnings did not mean that Russia was certain to capture Zaporizhzhia, rather described a possible military route and potential risks. The same applies to Filatov’s current prediction: individual Russian groups could attempt to approach the city, but there is no confirmation that Russia is preparing or capable of capturing Zaporizhzhia.
For now, the Southern Grouping says the threat is being monitored, while Ukrainian forces continue to block Russian infiltration attempts along the Orikhiv and Stepnohirske sectors.

Unknown

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sept. 22 he would use tariff authorities granted to him by the new Russia sanctions bill if necessary to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
The legislation, spearheaded by the late Senator Lindsey Graham and signed by Trump last week, authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian oil and gas, among other measures.
"Last week, in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham, I signed a powerful new law passed by Congress, providing me with enormous new tariff authorities," Trump said in his address at the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
"And, if necessary, I will have to use them. It's time to stop the killing," he told the audience that included Russian and Ukrainian officials, including President Volodymyr Zelensky.
While Trump's U.N. address covered a broad range of topics, from Gaza and the war in Iran to artificial intelligence, he briefly touched on peace efforts in Ukraine.
"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," the U.S. president said, suggesting that a deal will come "more quickly than people understand."
The comments come hours before Trump's expected meeting with Zelensky, where the two leaders are set to discuss the possibility of a Russia-Ukraine pause in strikes against energy facilities and targets on the Black Sea.
Recent weeks saw Washington start a fresh push to broker an end to the war, an effort that hit a deadlock earlier this year amid Moscow's territorial demands and the U.S.-Iran war.

Iran expands rail routes to China, targets higher-value exports: TPO

Iran expands rail routes to China, targets higher-value exports: TPO
TEHRAN- At a press conference, Amir Roshanbakhsh Ghanbari, deputy for international business development at Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), said Iran is negotiating with China to develop rail routes for goods transit, with part of Iranian cargo already moving to China via Yazd Dry Port. He said transport is a fundamental trade issue and current conditions impose restrictions.
Last year, Iran exported about 155 million tons and imported about 42 million tons, much of it by sea. With trade routes limited, TPO has divided responses into short-, medium- and long-term measures. Short-term steps include increasing capacity of executive agencies, managing borders, and using border provinces. At Bazargan, he said, higher traffic and truck queues partly stem from limited acceptance capacity on the other side, so not all problems can be managed domestically.
Rail capacity is limited: each train has about 55 wagons and carries about 1,500 tons, compared with about 100,000 tons for a ship. Moving the same amount by truck would require about 3,000 trucks. Therefore, rail and land capacity must be used alongside sea routes. Alternative routes require cooperation with neighbors and trade partners, with infrastructure on both sides.
Ghanbari said recent conditions showed the need to reform trade governance and transport infrastructure after the current period. Otherwise similar import-export problems could recur. Trade finds its way, but when main arteries are blocked, alternatives must exist.
The 30th National Export Day will focus on trade infrastructure and sustainable routes, starting Monday, 20 Mehr. A joint event with the Ministry of Roads and Urban Development will examine transport and sustainable export routes. The second day will address higher export value and services.
For National Exemplary Exporters, 367 applicants entered evaluation; 277 completed files reached final assessment: 235 in goods, 26 in knowledge-based goods, and 16 in services. There are 42 commodity groups and seven service groups.
The average value of Iran’s exported goods is about $300–350 per ton, while some knowledge-based and high-tech products can reach $1,500–2,500 per ton. Services exports reached about $3 billion in 1404, including $1.8 billion in technical and engineering services, up from $790 million in 1403.
TPO also launched an Export Atlas, providing commodity-and-country trade data, competitors, intermediaries, monthly growth charts, and provincial production and export shares. Other planned meetings will cover financing, export management companies, standards, trade laws, diplomacy, and exporters’ demands, including direct importer-exporter transactions.

cast aluminum turns heart forms into sculptural furniture in LOVE collection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:45:32 UTC
00:45:32 KST

LOVE collection translates the heart into sculptural objects
Istanbul-based designer Sami Savatli introduces LOVE, a two-piece collectible design collection comprising the LOVE Chair and LOVE Side Table. Conceived at the intersection of design and sculpture, the collection explores how structure, material, and gesture can transform familiar forms into objects with an independent spatial presence.
The LOVE Chair takes the familiar outline of the heart as its point of departure, but removes it from conventional symmetry and symbolism. Rather than appearing as an applied motif, the form emerges directly from the structure of the chair. Lines extend, divide and reconnect, moving between silhouette and support, while shifts in volume allow the object to read differently from each viewpoint. The LOVE Side Table develops the same language without repeating the heart literally. Its branching structure carries the movement of the chair into a more compact form, connecting the two pieces through proportion, rhythm and construction rather than visual repetition.
Hand-finished cast aluminum shapes LOVE Chair and LOVE Table
Both pieces are produced by designer Sami Savatli in Istanbul in cast aluminum and individually finished by hand. Subtle irregularities in surface, texture and reflection are retained as part of the making process, giving each object its own material character. As light moves across the aluminum, the collection shifts between solidity and visual lightness, reinforcing its sculptural presence. Positioned between collectible design and sculpture, LOVE retains the function of furniture while establishing an autonomous presence within space.

Iran offers to reopen Strait of Hormuz – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:45:26 UTC
00:45:26 KST

Iran offers to reopen Strait of Hormuz – media
The Strait of Hormuz could reopen within seven days if the US eases military pressure and lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, according to media reports citing a senior Iranian official.
The strait is one of the world’s most important energy routes, normally carrying around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Shipping has largely stopped since the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, disrupting supplies and driving energy prices higher.
Tehran has proposed that Washington declare its readiness to resolve the conflict through diplomacy and agree on a timeline for further steps, the official told Reuters on Tuesday. The proposal was conveyed to the US through mediators last week as world leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly.
The event is a “golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy,” the official said, adding that the Iranian delegation had full authority to revive negotiations. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC that the administration was prepared to speak with Tehran if negotiations had the prospect of producing a positive outcome.
The official noted that there were no plans for Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and US President Donald Trump to meet directly at the General Assembly, although Trump signaled on Sunday that he would be open to such a meeting.
Iran has set broader conditions for ending the conflict. Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday that Tehran had conveyed seven demands to Washington through mediators, including an end to hostilities, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and the lifting of the naval blockade.
Previous attempts to halt the fighting have been fruitless. A memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June was followed by renewed hostilities, while no face-to-face talks are known to have taken place since July.
US government data show that oil flows through Hormuz fell from 21.6 million barrels per day in the final quarter of 2025 to 4.9 million in the second quarter of this year.
Tensions rose again this week after Trump said he was in “deciding mode” over Iran and weighing further military action, economic pressure, or a deal. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by warning that another US attack would prompt Tehran to expand the scope of the conflict and use different weapons.
Washington has also threatened further economic pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that companies providing Iranian airlines with fuel, airport services, or ticketing could be denied access to the US dollar system.

Austrian ex-billionaire Benko found guilty of insolvency fraud at retrial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:45:04 UTC
00:45:04 KST

Ex-billionaire Benko convicted at Austrian retrial, sentence increased
VIENNA, Sept 22 - An Austrian court found former property tycoon Rene Benko guilty on an additional insolvency fraud charge at a retrial on Tuesday, increasing his prison sentence to 30 months from the original two years.
The case was the first to emerge from a wider criminal investigation into the collapse of the property group Benko founded. Signa's failure in 2023 became Austria's biggest post-war bankruptcy and left investors across Europe nursing losses.
A court in Innsbruck, Benko's home city, convicted him in October on one count of insolvency fraud over a €300,000 ($344,000) transfer to his mother in late 2023, when Signa was already in financial difficulty. The court found the transfer was intended to put the money beyond creditors' reach.
It acquitted him on a second count relating to an advance rent payment of about €360,000 for a house in Innsbruck that prosecutors said made no economic sense. After appeals from both sides, Austria's Supreme Court upheld the conviction and ordered a retrial on the second count.
Benko pleaded not guilty, arguing that he thought his company could avoid bankruptcy when the payments were made.
"Regarding this part of the case that had to be retried, a panel comprising magistrates and a judge at the Innsbruck State Court found the defendant guilty and sentenced him to 30 months in prison," the court said in a statement, adding that the maximum possible sentence was 10 years.
Benko was convicted over the rent payment but acquitted over additional operating expenses for the house that had also been paid in advance, the court said.
His time in custody since his arrest on January 23 of last year would count towards his sentence and he remains in custody in Innsbruck, it added.
Benko was convicted of insolvency fraud in a separate case in December and handed a 15-month suspended prison sentence. REUTERS

Banned White House outlets cover Trump at UN as court hearing looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:44:34 UTC
00:44:34 KST

Banned White House outlets cover Trump at UN as court hearing looms
- President Trump banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from White House grounds, accusing them of reporting "FICTION and LIES," prompting a lawsuit alleging First Amendment violations.
- The banned outlets covered Trump's UN visit using UN-issued media passes, while other networks suspended White House pool coverage, leading to the launch of a "Trump TV" government stream.
- The court hearing is set for Sept 23, with administration officials denying the outlets are banned, claiming only restricted workspace access at the White House.
AI generated
NEW YORK - As CNN, MS NOW and Politico await a court hearing on Sept 23 over President Donald Trump’s decision to ban them from the White House grounds, reporters from the news outlets covered his visit to the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 22 using media passes issued by the UN.
“I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me, you shouldn’t be here,” Trump said on Sept 22 as he entered the United Nations building and addressed a group of reporters. “You said you weren’t going to cover me.”
CNN has not said it would stop covering Trump.
Trump announced the ban on Sept 18 on social media, saying the three news outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States,” and defended it in another post on Sept 21.
The news outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration on Sept 21, saying the action violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.
They are seeking a temporary restraining order to block Trump’s action in federal court in Washington, DC, with a hearing scheduled for Sept 23 before US District Judge Timothy Kelly.
Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He also has filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets.
CNN is one of the five news organisations – along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC – that make up the primary White House television pool. They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.
CNN had been scheduled to cover Trump’s trip to New York for the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 21, but was not able to provide a pool feed.
In response, the other major TV networks suspended presidential pool coverage.
In an effort to fill that void, the White House launched a “Trump TV” stream on Sept 21. The White House said the stream will run videos and highlights of what it calls the Trump administration’s achievements. A press freedom advocate said it amounted to “a steady diet of government propaganda.”
During an interview on NBC’s Today show on Sept 22, Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not answer a question about whether he will be making changes to his travelling press pool.
When asked whether media outlets should be banned because the president does not like their coverage, Rubio repeated a sentiment expressed by Vice-President J.D. Vance a day earlier, falsely stating that the outlets were not banned, when they have in fact lost access to the White House grounds.
“They’re not banned... We’re not closing CNN... They’re just not allowed to work from the workspace at the White House,” Rubio said. REUTERS

How Russians again disappointed the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:44:31 UTC
00:44:31 KST

How Russians again disappointed the West
The legislative elections in Russia have become a major topic in global media. The Times even published an editorial with the impressive headline ‘Potemkin election’.
Apparently, the author is unaware of the fact that his apparent witticism is out of place. He must also be ignorant of the origins of the term ‘Potemkin village’. Had he done some research, he would have known that Field Marshal Potemkin did not show Catherine the Great and many foreign ‘observers’ (as the people who accompanied her would be called today) fake villages. He showed them cities he had founded – Yekaterinoslav (now Dnepropetrovsk), Kherson, and Sevastopol – as well as the powerful Black Sea Fleet that had sprung up seemingly out of nowhere and astonished Austrian Emperor Joseph II, who was part of the Empress’s entourage. If the authors of The Times believe these ‘Potemkin villages’ never existed, they should have a look at the modern map of Novorossiya and Crimea.
In terms of significance, the current State Duma elections may be compared to Catherine the Great’s journey to southern Russia. That trip demonstrated to the entire world that the map of Europe had fundamentally changed and that the once-wild steppes had become an integral part of the Russian Empire. It was precisely for this reason that back then, the purveyors of fake news rushed to concoct tales about ‘Potemkin villages’ – just as today, they try to slander the elections held in Russia’s historic territories, in the very cities founded by Potemkin nearly 250 years ago.
I’d like to note how dramatically the perception of the elections has shifted in Western media over a short period of time. Just a week and a half ago, The Sunday Times published an extensive ‘analytical’ piece on why the elections were important. The author expressed hope that they would reveal “discontent” with the government and suggested that the results would demonstrate that “Russians’ patience is wearing thin” and that, in frontline regions, “the Kremlin will … begin to lose the provinces.” There was no shortage of such articles leading up to the vote.
However, yesterday, in the wake of the elections, The Spectator published a frustrated piece arguing why the results of these “rigged” elections should be ignored. The author is clearly disappointed with voter turnout and the results in those so-called “Potemkin villages” – specifically the regions of Crimea, Donbass, and Novorossiya, which have again become part of Russia. “Most Russians want the war over, but they seem to be blaming the new inconveniences – from internet blockages to lines for gas – on Kiev, not the Kremlin,” the article states.
Some might say, ‘So what if two different authors have two different opinions? That only demonstrates the pluralism of the free European press.’ But here’s the catch: both articles were written by the same person – Mark Galeotti, Britain’s top ‘expert on Russia.’ This stark contrast in the evaluation of the same event stems from the genuine disappointment among Western elites who have again misjudged the outcome of Russia’s elections.
They failed to understand Russians 250 years ago and fail to understand them today. They genuinely believed that Zelensky’s “influence operations,” strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and warehouses, and the killing of civilians would sow unrest – if not across Russia as a whole, then at least in the territories most affected by Ukrainian air raids. They failed to grasp that this would actually cause the opposite reaction. The elections demonstrated that the residents of these territories do not see themselves as separate from the rest of the country.
This is why European politicians are gritting their teeth; it’s why Kaja Kallas issued a notice before the voting, declaring that elections in “occupied” territories would not be recognized; and it’s also why they resurrected the tale of ‘Potemkin villages’, knowing as little about Russians today as they did hundreds of years ago.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

Russia quietly modernises bomb shelters in Moscow and St Petersburg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:43:51 UTC
00:43:51 KST

Tens of millions of roubles have been allocated for repairs to shelters across Moscow districts and St Petersburg metro stations as Ukrainian drones struck another Russian refinery on Sunday, as the Kremlin's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.
Russia is quietly modernising bomb shelters in Moscow and St Petersburg, with procurement data showing tens of millions of roubles being allocated for repairs that have not been publicly announced, as Ukrainian drones intensify strikes on Russian territory.
State procurement records, reported by Russian independent media, show 39 million roubles (€400,000) allocated in early September to restore nine facilities in three districts of Moscow's South-West administrative region, an area home to dozens of research institutes and defence contractors.
Work is due to be completed by 30 November and covers entrances, internal partitions, doors and utility systems including water, electricity, sewage, ventilation and communications.
Further funds have been earmarked for shelters in Moscow's eastern Novogireyevo district, and a major overhaul is planned in New Moscow for a shelter built in 1971 that includes its own diesel power station.
Tenders worth 200 million roubles (€2 million) were published at the start of summer for repairs to shelters in 17 districts, mainly in Moscow's eastern region.
In St Petersburg, the metro operator published a contractor search in early September to build bomb shelters at nine stations, four compartments and 35 kilometres of track.
The project involves large-scale adaptation of both operating and unfinished stations to civil defence requirements, including air filtration and pressurised air supply systems.
'End war, choose peace'
The Kremlin has increasingly felt the heat of Ukraine's strikes on its energy and business sectors, in Kyiv's ongoing bid to strip Russia's war machine of as much funding as possible.
On Sunday night, Ukrainian drones struck the Moscow refinery in Kapotnya, halting operations due to fires at primary oil processing units, according to reports.
In August, Ukrainian rocket developer FirePoint and former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov said the Ukrainian armed forces could begin striking Moscow with new ballistic missiles by the end of the year.
"Moscow should not be building layered rings of air defence at the expense of other regions, but ending its brutal war and choosing peace," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"There are steps for de-escalation on the table: in energy, in food security. What is needed is political will."
Moscow and St Petersburg's civil defence infrastructure largely dates to the 20th century and consists of command bunkers for government and military communications, and mass shelters for civilians, including the metro.
Recent inventories in St Petersburg found many shelters in need of repair, and a significant portion of basement space in residential buildings has passed into private hands.
Ukraine's metro systems — particularly in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro — have functioned as round-the-clock bomb shelters since Russia's full-scale invasion began in early 2022, with tens of thousands of people at a time sheltering in them during Moscow's daily air raids.
In frontline regions without a metro, purpose-built underground schools have been constructed so children can attend classes. Ukraine's public education system has also shifted to remote formats because of the persistent threat of Russian air strikes.

Ukraine to be enabler of EU’s future security architecture – MEP
Member of the European Parliament Rasa Jukneviciene, a member of the security and defense committee, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“We need Great Britain on board. We need Norway on board, and especially we need to integrate Ukraine into our security architecture. Current alliances like NATO and EU are not able to accept Ukraine as soon as possible, so when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen mentioned in her state of the union address last week the European Security Council, in my understanding, and I know that it is also the same understanding that she has, and Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, that this is the idea of how to integrate Ukraine deeper into the whole security architecture,” Jukneviciene said.
She is convinced that for many in Brussels, Ukraine “is now no less important for our European security as the United States.”
“Both are equally critical, although in different ways. The US is important through their enablers, including space intelligence and all those capabilities we don't have yet and will not have in the nearest future. And Ukraine is important with their defense experience and what they are doing now. They stopped Russia on their borders, and we, of course, are thankful very much,” the MEP said, adding that Ukraine will become an enable of Europe’s future security architecture.
She added that another important participant in the process is Canada, which is already carrying out a mission under NATO’s enhanced forward presence project in the Baltic states, serving as the “framework nation” for the project in Latvia.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 16, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that the EU needs its own version of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty for urgent consultations in the event of a security threat to an EU member state, as well as a new body – a European Security Council that would also include Ukraine.

EU may extend Russia sanctions until 2029 without Russian oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman, with vote still to come
The Committee of Permanent Representatives of the EU (Coreper) reached a preliminary agreement on 22 September to extend sanctions against Russia for 36 months while removing Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.
Source: a European Pravda correspondent citing two European diplomats speaking on condition of anonymity
Details: Diplomats in Brussels again reached a preliminary agreement on 22 September to extend sanctions against Russia over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity while removing two Russian billionaires from the list.
"Coreper again discussed the extension of sanctions, and there is hope that agreement can be reached on the Irish presidency's compromise proposal," one source said.
The diplomat added that the sanctions are expected to be extended for 36 months, i.e. until 22 September 2029.
The two Russian oligarchs will be removed from the sanctions list, and the decision will be adopted through a written procedure due to begin shortly.
Another diplomat confirmed to European Pravda that EU ambassadors have apparently agreed to remove Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.
Background:
- An attempt to adopt a compromise decision via written procedure was launched on the evening of 21 September.
- However, during the written voting procedure Latvia initially objected in private and then publicly opposed the compromise. Any decision requires unanimous approval.
- Currently, personal sanctions against Putin, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, former Ukrainian MP Viktor Medvedchuk, former Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych and roughly 3,000 other individuals and legal entities responsible for the war against Ukraine remain in force until midnight on 22 September.
- The current sanctions regime, the list for which the EU began compiling back in 2014, covers individuals and legal entities responsible for actions that undermine or threaten the territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence of Ukraine.
- Since 2022, it has included Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, Russia's ruling elite and leading oligarchs, as well as former Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych.
- As reported by European Pravda, on 14 September, Coreper extended the sanctions regime for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty for seven days as Slovakia and France continued to insist that the two Russian oligarchs be removed from the list.
- European Pravda sources in French diplomatic circles explained why Paris wants to lift sanctions on Usmanov. It later emerged that France plans to "exchange" Usmanov's delisting for the release of several French citizens who are currently in prison in Azerbaijan.
- The last extension of personal sanctions took place on 14 March. On that occasion, too, Slovakia pushed until the last minute for Fridman and Usmanov to be removed from the list.

EU ambassadors extend sanctions over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity for 3 years instead of 6 months, remove 'certain individuals' from list
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:39:58 EEST
00:39:58 KST

Ambassadors – the permanent representatives of European Union member states – after a lengthy discussion, finally decided to extend sanctions for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity by three years, rather than six months as had been the case previously; "certain individuals" were excluded.
A spokesperson for Ireland, which currently holds the EU Council presidency, announced this to reporters on Tuesday in Brussels following the conclusion of a meeting of the Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper).
The spokesperson said that, following completion of the written procedure, the Council was expected to approve the extension of the sanctions regime related to Ukraine's territorial integrity. He said the continuation of the regime had resulted from a complex compromise providing for its extension for 36 months, until September 22, 2029.
The spokesperson stressed that, as a result, restrictive measures under the regime concerning Ukraine's territorial integrity would continue to apply to nearly 3,000 individuals and legal entities, while the possible addition of many others to the sanctions lists was also under consideration. He explained to journalists that the lists had previously been reviewed and assessed every six months and that the decision to extend the regime for 36 months would increase the stability and predictability of the EU sanctions system.
At the same time, a decision was made to remove certain individuals from the sanctions lists under the regime. The spokesperson added that maintaining the regime had been one of the key priorities of the Irish presidency, without specifying either the number or the names of those removed.
Sanctions over violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity, first imposed on March 17, 2014, have traditionally been extended every six months. The most recent decision to extend the sanctions was made on April 23 of this year.
As is well known, sanctions for violations of Ukraine's territorial integrity – which were first imposed on March 17, 2014 – are extended every six months. The most recent decision to extend the sanctions was made on April 23 of this year.
A point of contention arose over Slovakia's demand to remove Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions lists. Most countries opposed this, while simultaneously proposing to extend the duration of the sanctions from six months to three years. Amid reports that decisions regarding both the Russian individuals subject to sanctions and the duration of the sanctions would be adopted, Latvia issued a categorical objection, echoing Ukraine's position that any easing of the sanctions is unacceptable.
The list includes more than 3,000 individuals and legal entities. Among them are Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, and others.

17-year-old detained in Poland over alleged plans for terrorist attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:35:27 UTC
00:35:27 KST

Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said the teenager had planned "a mass terrorist attack," including on a school and a mosque.
Authorities in Poland have detained a 17-year-old accused of preparing an attack on a school and a mosque.
A court has ordered that the teenager, named as Paweł G, be held in pre-trial detention for three months.
The case is part of an ongoing investigation by Poland's Internal Security Agency (ABW) looking into individuals active in online neo-Nazi and extremist circles.
On 18 September, ABW reported the detention of two minors who were active in groups bringing together people linked to such ideologies.
At the time, officials stressed that the investigation was ongoing, with officers analysing the detainees' contacts and checking whether other individuals may have been involved.
This led investigators to Paweł G.
Officers from ABW in Katowice then detained him and searched his home, securing electronic devices and data carriers that were then subjected to detailed analysis.
According to ABW's findings, Paweł G., like the minors detained earlier, was active on the Telegram and Discord platforms, where groups linked to neo-Nazi and extremist communities operated.
He took part in discussions about previous terrorist attacks and their perpetrators. In some exchanges, participants also raised the possibility of carrying out further attacks.
Members of these groups examined, among other things, the methods used by those responsible for earlier attacks and treated them as a potential source of inspiration.
ABW further established that Paweł G. is believed to have belonged to the Atomwaffen Polska group and to have co-created the Bierut Soldier ZNB group. Both contained content and symbols referring to neo-Nazism, along with discussions of violence and terrorist activity.
Alleged attack plans
The most serious of the charges brought against Paweł G. concerns the preparation of a terrorist attack.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said Paweł G. had planned "a mass terrorist attack," including on a school and a mosque.
"There is no and will be no leniency for fascism, hatred and the planning of bloody attacks in Poland," the minister wrote on X.
"Anyone who raises a hand against the security of Poles will face the full severity of the law. Security is not an area for compromise. It is the foundation of our community," Żurek added.
Prosecutors are also examining information about planned purchases of weapons and military equipment, as well as the collection of materials linked to the activities of terrorist organisations.
The two remaining charges relate to participation in an organised criminal group. According to investigators, the group was involved in activities including preparing offences of a terrorist nature, promoting Nazism and fascism, and inciting hatred.
The likelihood that the suspect committed the offences with which he is charged is said to be supported by the evidence gathered during the investigation.
Particular weight is attached to the results of the search of his home and the analysis of his phones and other seized data carriers.
During the search, officers reportedly found, among other items, knives, a bayonet for an AKM-type rifle, as well as books, patches and other materials bearing fascist and Nazi symbols.
Analysis of the data stored on the seized devices is also said to have revealed correspondence about the planning of mass attacks, including a potential attack on a school and a mosque.
The conversations reportedly covered the surveillance of potential targets, methods of carrying out attacks and issues related to obtaining weapons, ammunition and military equipment. Messages were also said to contain information on the use of grenades and Molotov cocktails.
Paweł G was questioned as a suspect. He refused to make a statement.

Last September, Poland downed four of 19 Russian drones. This September, drone reached NATO’s missile shield in Redzikowo, and troops guarding it called 112
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:33:33 UTC
00:33:33 KST

An unknown drone has flown right up to the US missile-defense base in northern Poland, and how the military responded has raised questions about how well the site is protected from the air. Rather than shoot the drone down near Redzikowo, a cornerstone of NATO's missile shield, the unit followed a set of procedures that included a call to 112, Poland's civilian emergency line, Onet reported.
Meanwhile, European intelligence officials are considering the possibility that Russia could test NATO’s resolve in the near future. According to one official, a potential attack could occur “within months, not years," The Guardian reports. 
Surveillance systems detected the drone about half a kilometer from the base on 15 September, where it operated for roughly five minutes.
This incident is linked to a similar one in 2025. Almost a year ago, also in September, around 19 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace. Poland shot down only four Russian drones with modern Polish F-16s and Dutch F-35s. Meanwhile, Ukraine downs 87.4% of Russian long-range drones. Poland only shot down 17-21% of the drones that entered its airspace.
The base sits at the heart of NATO's shield
Redzikowo hosts the US Navy's Aegis Ashore installation, an American component of NATO's missile-defense system and one of the most sensitive military sites in Poland. It matters strategically to Poland, NATO, and the US. While American personnel guard it, Poland has taken primary responsibility for its security and assigned a dedicated unit.
Even before the base opened, there were efforts to secure anti-drone systems for it, on the logic that a site best protected from the ground can stay exposed from the air.
The ministry keeps its methods quiet
The Polish Defense Ministry says it established where the operator was flying from, notified the relevant services, including the police, and treats every case of unauthorized drone activity near a guarded site seriously. What it will not say is whether it tried to neutralize the drone, or whether the anti-drone and electronic-warfare systems at Redzikowo were used at all, citing security.
Warnings pile up across the flank
The stakes are rising along NATO's eastern edge. Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament on 17 September that, by the assessment of NATO, Ukrainian, and US intelligence, Russia's plans include drone and missile strikes on countries backing Ukraine, Poland among them, possibly staged to look "accidental" and test whether Article 5 means anything. Warsaw insists it is ready and will hit back at any attack. The Redzikowo drone, and the four-of-nineteen record behind it, are why that confidence keeps drawing questions.

Trump TV: Can the US president bypass mainstream media?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:33:22 UTC
00:33:22 KST

Trump follows in Hugo Chavez’s footsteps to launch his own TV channel
Trump has launched his own channel amid an ongoing rift with the White House press pool.
United States President Donald Trump launched a round-the-clock YouTube channel run by the White House on Monday.
The move follows his banning of CNN, MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), and Politico from reporting from the White House on Friday, prompting five major television networks to suspend coverage on Monday morning in protest.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US proposes AI safety notification mechanism in talks with China
- list 2 of 4Iran’s military says US preparing to resume strikes
- list 3 of 4CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
- list 4 of 4Trump-GCC Summit in New York: What does each side want?
The spat has triggered a wave of lawsuits from broadcasters, with the president warning on Saturday that he might ban other outlets for broadcasting what he claims is “fake news”.
Alongside his own social media platform, Truth Social, Trump appears to be trying to bypass mainstream media. But is this possible, and has anyone tried it before?
What is Trump TV?
‘Trump TV: The Essentials Station’ is not a conventional television network but a 24-hour online video stream.
There are no anchors, no reporters and no original journalism. Instead, it broadcasts speeches, administration announcements, ceremonial events and selected highlights from Trump’s presidency.
How did Trump’s latest feud with mainstream media begin?
On Friday, Trump said he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, prompting a flurry of condemnation from several major media outlets and media rights watchdogs.
On Truth Social, he accused the outlets of propagating “fake news”. He added that the outlets “constantly write or report fiction or lies” about the Trump administration, but did not give any examples.
On Monday, the banned outlets sued the Trump administration for denying them their First Amendment rights.
Trump responded to the suit in a statement posted on Truth Social, lashing out at what he called the “fake news people”, and saying that “the Oval Office … should be treated with Decorum, Respect, and Dignity, not defiled by Third Rate Clowns”.
“No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialise and demean,” the president added.
The television news pool then announced it was suspending its coverage of the president’s events.
The White House broadcasting pool is made up of five networks – ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC. They take turns filming the president, providing live feeds that are picked up by the networks and outlets around the world.
When the White House blocked CNN from the rotation on Monday, the other four refused to replace the network.
The result was an awkward broadcast in which a White House ribbon-cutting ceremony attended by Trump, surrounded by workers in hard hats and safety vests, was broadcast by US news outlet Newsmax with only live visuals and no audio because no television press pool was present.
Other news outlets also showed solidarity with the press pool. The Associated Press (AP) joined several news organisations, including The Washington Post and The New York Times, in deciding not to publish photographs taken by the White House photography pool of presidential events on Monday.
The same day, Trump launched his own channel.
How has Trump tried to bypass mainstream media in the past?
Trump has long tried to bypass mainstream media by communicating directly, often in capital letters alongside AI-generated depictions of himself, on his own social media platform, Truth Social.
Last year, he also sought to bar AP reporters from the White House Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico – which lies partially in Mexican and other waters – to the Gulf of America. AP has taken legal action against this.
Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has pursued other legal actions against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.
His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation with ABC over renewal of its broadcast licences.
Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media.
Some outlets that he favours, such as Fox News and Newsmax, often carry his events in full, while podcasters and online streamers considered friendly to him often give him long, unedited interviews.
Have other leaders launched their own media channels?
Yes. One of the best-known examples is Venezuela’s former president Hugo Chavez.
From 1999 to 2012, he hosted Hello, President, a Sunday television and radio show that often ran for several hours per episode.
Chavez sang, took calls from viewers, attacked his opponents and sometimes announced major policy live on air.
He also made heavy use of cadenas, or broadcasts that all Venezuelan channels were legally required to carry at the same time.
Chavez’s successor, Nicolas Maduro, who US forces abducted and imprisoned on guns-and-drugs charges in January during a Trump-authorised lightning military raid on Caracas, kept the same model during his presidency.
He hosted his own weekly programme on state television, most recently called Con Maduro+, continued using cadenas, and became an active user of TikTok and other social media.
India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also followed a similar strategy.
Since 2014, he has hosted Words from the Heart, a monthly radio address via state broadcaster All India Radio, in which he talks directly to citizens without interviewers or questions.
He also has his own official NaMo app, through which he sends messages direct to the general public, rarely accepting questions directly from the press.
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro used Facebook Live during his 2019 to 2023 presidency, holding live weekly broadcasts, usually on Thursday evenings and often filmed in a casual setting at his official residence.
He used the broadcasts to make announcements, attack journalists and criticise Globo, Brazil’s largest media group.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele often announces major decisions on X rather than through press conferences.
In 2020, amid a dispute with independent outlets, he launched a government news programme on the state channel Canal 10 which broadcasts three times a day. His government also runs a daily newspaper dedicated to official messaging.

Trump threatens Iran with ‘hell’ at UN, predicts deal after US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:32:10 UTC
00:32:10 KST

President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend an increasingly interventionist foreign policy, casting himself as a leader willing to use American military, diplomatic and economic power while declaring that the United States would continue to put its own interests first.
“While others have talked, I have acted,” Trump said. “While others have spoken of peace, I have made peace. While others have ignored threats, I have confronted them.”
Much of the speech focused on Iran and the nearly seven-month war that has reshaped the Middle East and disrupted global energy markets. Trump defended his decision to go to war alongside Israel earlier this year and said Tehran had rejected previous efforts to reach an agreement that would prevent it from obtaining nuclear weapons.
Trump said he now faced what he called a “big decision” over whether to reach a deal that would allow Iran to recover or move toward far more destructive military action.
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he asked, before saying he nevertheless expected an agreement after the November midterm elections.
Trump said Iranian leaders were waiting to see how Republicans performed in the midterms, though he stressed that he himself was not on the ballot.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’m going to help them,” he said, adding that his principal concern remained ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.
He also rejected reports that concerns over depleted US ammunition and interceptor stocks were constraining his military options, saying the United States possessed large quantities of weapons and was replenishing them rapidly.
Trump called on other countries to join Washington in economically isolating Iran until it ends attacks on commercial shipping, abandons its nuclear ambitions and stops supporting terrorism.
The war with Iran has complicated Trump’s effort to portray his foreign policy as a series of successful peace interventions. The Wall Street Journal reported that the White House is seeking to present his international record as a collection of tangible wins for Americans ahead of the midterms, even as the wars involving Iran and Ukraine continue to weigh on energy prices and global trade.
Trump invokes Oct. 7 and Gaza deal
Trump also invoked Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, accusing Iran of supporting the terrorists responsible and arguing that Tehran could never be permitted to operate under the protection of a nuclear arsenal.
He said Iran’s supreme leader had celebrated the massacre and described the threat posed by a nuclear-armed Islamic Republic as one the United States could not ignore.
Trump then pointed to Gaza as evidence of what he described as his ability to turn conflict into negotiated outcomes.
He recalled that when he addressed the General Assembly a year earlier, the Gaza war was still underway and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. His administration’s 20-point plan was later endorsed by the UN Security Council, and the Board of Peace was established to oversee the postwar framework. The board says the ceasefire brought the return of all hostages and is now focused on demilitarization, Palestinian civilian administration, reconstruction and humanitarian assistance.
Trump thanked Qatar, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and other countries contributing to Gaza, saying their money was reaching areas where humanitarian needs remain acute.
He also praised countries that have committed personnel, police or training to Gaza stabilization efforts, including Indonesia, Morocco, Albania, Kosovo, Kazakhstan, Egypt and Jordan.
The Board of Peace is scheduled to meet on the sidelines of the General Assembly to review implementation of the Gaza framework and discuss its next priorities.
Ukraine, Greenland and Venezuela next
Trump devoted less time to Russia’s war against Ukraine, saying his administration was continuing efforts to bring the conflict to an end.
His diplomatic agenda after the speech underscored how much unfinished business remains.
He was scheduled to meet separately with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Gulf leaders, with the Iran war expected to feature prominently in the regional discussions. The continuing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine have both contributed to pressure on global energy markets.
Trump was also expected to sign an agreement expanding the US military and commercial presence in Greenland after nearly two years of pressure on Denmark, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Another meeting was set with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, whose government has entered into an arrangement giving the Pentagon a stake in the country’s oil sector. Trump has argued that closer US involvement in Venezuelan energy production will help lower fuel prices at home.
The meeting is politically sensitive because Rodríguez was a senior figure in the government of Nicolás Maduro, who was removed in a US military operation earlier this year. Trump has emphasized cooperation with Rodríguez while moving more slowly on a transition to democratic government, according to the Journal.
Xi summit looms
Trump’s UN appearance also comes on the eve of a three-day state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The two leaders are expected to discuss artificial intelligence, rare earth minerals and Taiwan, among other issues. The Journal reported that Trump, who previously took a more confrontational approach toward Beijing, is now seeking a less adversarial relationship and wants to avoid a deepening economic and military confrontation.
The summit is expected to focus heavily on optics and the broader relationship rather than major new agreements.
Trump’s packed schedule reflects the contrast at the heart of his UN message: he presented himself as a president who has already delivered peace through decisive action, even as some of the largest crises he has confronted remain unresolved.
His Iran policy captures that tension most clearly. Trump threatened Tehran with potentially devastating consequences while simultaneously predicting that diplomacy would ultimately prevail.
“The president is open to a meeting with him or anybody,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian ahead of the speech, while cautioning that Iran’s supreme leader remains the country’s ultimate decision-maker.
For Trump, the message to the General Assembly was that willingness to negotiate and willingness to use force are not contradictory elements of his foreign policy.
“While others have spoken of peace,” he told world leaders, “I have made peace.”

Trump threatens to send Iran 'into hell' if war carries on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

Trump threatens to send Iran ‘into hell’ if war carries on
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon generated applause throughout the chamber.
- The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
NEW YORK — President Trump threatened to escalate the war with Iran by “annihilating” the Islamic Republic if it fails to negotiate a deal over its nuclear program, delivering a defensive speech justifying the mission at the United Nations on Tuesday.
His remarks come more than six months into a war that has grown increasingly unpopular at home, with fewer than a third of Americans approving of the president’s handling of the conflict, according to recent polls.
“I have a big decision to make,” he told world leaders gathered at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, with Iranian diplomats in attendance.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again?
“Do I drive them into hell,” he continued, “with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, increasing inflation and energy prices due to disruptions in commercial shipping traffic through key waterways in the Middle East.
Defense officials say the conflict has also placed a huge burden on U.S. munitions stockpiles, as Iran continues firing ballistic missiles and drones at American assets and bases throughout the region.
But Trump denied that the war has depleted U.S. stocks. “That’s not true,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “We must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
The rise in global gas prices has sparked protests around the world. But Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon — an issue that for decades united the international community — generated applause throughout the chamber.
The president’s actions stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the U.N. and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Launching Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump projected the campaign would last roughly six weeks, with the stated objective of disabling Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear infrastructure. He also vowed a day would soon come when the Iranian people could rise up against their government and reclaim their country.
More than six months later, the Islamic Republic stands. Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to test U.S. air defenses across the Middle East, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains depressed, and talks over the future of Iran’s nuclear program have collapsed.
Explaining his decision to start the war, Trump said that he decided not to let the problem of Iran’s nuclear work “fester,” and warned that its ballistic missile program was being designed as a shield to protect its nuclear program from foreign attack.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional nuclear shield,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully no more.”
The United States has repeatedly offered a deal with Iran that would open up economic cooperation between the two nations in exchange for an end to their nuclear work, he said.
“They absolutely refused,” he added. “That was a big mistake.”

This year’s El Niño just broke another sobering record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:30:29 UTC
00:30:29 KST

Sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean have broken a new record, climate scientists say. This is yet another signal that this year will see an exceptionally strong El Niño.
El Niño is a cyclic climate pattern that influences weather around the globe. It typically brings heavy rains to the southern U.S., for instance, and dry conditions to other parts of the country, such as in the Pacific Northwest.
Researchers determine an El Niño year by analyzing ocean temperatures in a specific part of the equatorial Pacific that serves as a bellwether for extreme weather conditions to come. And now, climate scientists say, this region is incredibly, unusually warm—much more so than it’s ever been since we started keeping track more than a century ago.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Sea surface temperatures in this region are 3.05 degrees Celsius (5.49 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than usual, the highest anomaly seen since 2015, in which such temperatures were 3.02 degrees C (5.44 degrees F) above normal, noted climate specialist Jeff Berardelli in a social media post.
Kim Wood, an associate professor of hydrology and atmospheric sciences at the University of Arizona, said in a social media post that the region’s sea surface temperatures have been “unparalleled” for this time of year “for a while.” Based on a measurement that accounts for background warming of ocean temperatures as a result of climate change, this year's El Niño hasn’t yet hit an all-time high, but it is hotter than it’s ever been for late September.
No matter how you slice it, the new record is a sign of what experts say will be a brutal El Niño. “This is probably going to be the superlative El Niño event of our lives so far,” says Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources (UCANR).
That’s bad news for an already warming planet. As Scientific American previously reported, El Niño events typically raise global temperatures, which puts this year, as well as 2027, at risk of being among the hottest years ever recorded.
Additional reporting by Andrea Thompson.
