Russian forces take multi-level approach to striking targets in Ukraine — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:09:19 UTC
00:09:19 KST

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The Russian military is taking a systematic, strategic, and multi-level approach to striking targets in Ukraine aimed at eliminating the military-industrial potential of the Kiev regime as a whole, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the Institute of Law and National Security at the Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (RANEPA), told TASS.
He noted that a key aspect of the Russian strikes against Ukraine’s industrial sector is the systematic nature of the elimination of the Kiev regime’s military-industrial potential, in which not only production sites are destroyed, but also the entire industrial base that supports them, including the chemical, metallurgical, and energy sectors, which ensure the continuity of the industrial cycle.
"We can conclude that our Defense Ministry is employing a systematic, strategic, and multi-level approach to target selection, one that is based on very thorough intelligence and information preparation," the expert said.
He also noted the increased effectiveness of strikes by the Russian Armed Forces due to the expansion of their arsenal of precision weapons. "These strikes, sometimes carried out in a redundant manner, serve two purposes: first, to overcome the remnants of the enemy’s air defense system, and second, to ensure the destruction of key and critically important military-industrial facilities," Stepanov noted.
The expert added that all of this is complemented by the simultaneous destruction of logistical routes, primarily naval military-technical traffic organized by NATO countries to supply components and raw materials to the Ukrainian armed forces, as well as checkpoints to cut off land communications. "Taken together, the elimination of industry, energy, and logistics will guarantee that the Kiev regime is deprived of the capability to launch strikes against our territory," he concluded.

Standoff with Trump administration sidelines UN refugee agency deputy, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:09:17 UTC
00:09:17 KST

Standoff with Trump administration sidelines UN refugee agency deputy, sources say
GENEVA, Sept 22 - The Trump administration is refusing to work with the newly appointed deputy head of the United Nations refugee agency, exposing tensions between the agency and one of its top donors at a time of acute funding pressures, diplomats said.
Tressa Rae Finerty, an American who took up the role of Deputy High Commissioner at UNHCR earlier this month, has taken leave as she seeks a waiver from the US government that would allow her to carry out aspects of her duties, according to seven diplomatic sources.
Her treatment by Washington, which previously considered cutting ties with the agency, is seen by several of the diplomats as a retaliatory response after UNHCR opted against Washington's preferred candidate, Simon Hankinson.
A State Department spokesperson said it could not comment on pending legal issues. "...We work with and through UNHCR when doing so advances US foreign policy interests," the spokesperson said.
Finerty did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The standoff comes as UNHCR grapples with one of its worst ever funding crises following aid cuts by the Trump administration and others, at a time of record global displacement.
Finerty, a career US diplomat who previously served as charge d'affaires at the US Mission to the UN in Geneva, is currently unable to interact directly with US officials because of post-employment restrictions that apply to former US government personnel, the sources said.
Violations of the restrictions, designed to prevent conflicts of interest, could in theory result in a prison sentence.
UNHCR told Reuters that Finerty requested a partial waiver from the US government late last month.
"This relates, in particular, to her participation in multilateral meetings that US Department of State officials attend," UNHCR said in a statement.
"We are hoping for a speedy and favourable resolution to this matter," it said, adding that the agency's operations and reform agenda continued "at full pace".
KEY ROLE FOR DONORS
The failure to obtain a waiver is seen as highly unusual because they are granted routinely for other former US staff entering the global body, diplomats and UN staff said.
The deputy high commissioner is traditionally one of the agency's most important interlocutors with major donors, including the US, diplomats and former officials said, adding Finerty’s situation may make it challenging for UNHCR to fundraise with the US.
The US, which has withdrawn from dozens of other UN entities under President Donald Trump, had long been the agency's largest donor.
According to UNHCR data, Washington contributed more than $800 million in 2025, accounting for nearly a quarter of the agency's $3.6 billion in contributions. That dropped to around $110 million this year. REUTERS

ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger disclosed the figures in comments to Russian newspaper Vedomosti published Tuesday.

The organization does not provide a breakdown of how many missing people are Ukrainian or Russian because information collected during its tracing operations is confidential.
“Over the past four years, we have made significant progress on humanitarian issues,” Spoljaric Egger said, adding that more families had received information about the fate of missing relatives.
The total does not represent only confirmed battlefield disappearances. It includes people reported missing in connection with the international armed conflict, including military personnel, prisoners of war, and civilians whose relatives have lost contact with them.
The sharp rise in the recorded number is also partly linked to a change in the ICRC’s methodology.
Since 2025, the organization has counted both formalized tracing cases and preliminary requests that have not yet completed the documentation process. The change increased the overall number of cases in its system and means the latest figure cannot be directly compared with earlier totals.
The ICRC receives information about prisoners of war through official lists exchanged by Russia and Ukraine. Its representatives may also visit detention facilities and collect oral or written messages for prisoners’ relatives.
Russian Ex-Mayor Who Left Prison for Ukraine War Dies From Combat Wounds
Such visits can allow the organization to confirm that a person previously listed as missing is alive, although the ICRC has repeatedly faced criticism in Ukraine over limited access to Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
Separate Ukrainian data indicates that Russian families are searching for large numbers of soldiers who disappeared during Moscow’s invasion.
Ukraine’s “I Want to Find” project said in August that it had received 210,766 requests concerning missing Russian military personnel since its launch in January 2024.
The largest number of requests that included a location was connected to the Pokrovsk district of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, where relatives sought information about approximately 29,000 Russian troops, primarily reported missing during 2024 and 2025.
More than 12,000 requests were linked to the Bakhmut district, while over 8,000 concerned Russian personnel reported missing in Russia’s Kursk region. Ukrainian forces controlled part of that region from August 2024 until April 2025.
Russian internet users searched the phrase “missing in the special military operation” on Yandex almost 120,000 times in July 2026, according to search data cited by the Belarusian outlet Vot Tak.
The ICRC has warned that determining the fate of people missing during armed conflicts can take decades, even after the fighting ends. The Geneva Conventions require warring parties to record information about detainees and cooperate in efforts to locate missing people.

HAIKOU /China/, September 22. /TASS/. China’s southern Hainan Province plans to use more low carbon technologies based on the experience of the zero carbon demonstration zone of the Boao Forum for Asia (BFA), China News Service (CNS) reported.
According to the news portal, as part of China’s 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), the Hainan Free Trade Port will actively introduce green technologies and efficient waste recycling methods under a government plan aimed at comprehensive optimization of the current urban and rural development model. Sun Shuhua, chief engineer of Hainan’s housing department, said earlier that the province’s authorities added these tasks to the list of priority areas for high-quality growth.
The news portal noted that, under the goals set, Hainan will not only summarize the experience of the zero carbon demonstration zone in the settlement of Boao located on the eastern coast of Hainan Island, but will also find ways to introduce more green technologies used there. The authorities are preparing different scenarios for their application in residential areas and parks, while qualified specialists are studying the related market mechanisms to take the project to the national and even international level.
Hainan plans to improve green building standards for structures that will be primarily characterized by extremely low energy consumption. Such buildings should account for 40% of the total civil construction area in the near future.
According to Sun Shuhua, over the next five years, companies operating in the province or promoting cooperation with it will also improve supply chains for materials and components needed to build high-quality green houses with smart technologies.
Under the 15th Five-Year Plan, Hainan has already launched a pilot project dubbed "Cool City" for Haikou, the province’s administrative center, and Sanya, a leading resort city on the island’s southern coast. One of the main goals is to make life more comfortable in the tropical climate. Urban greening will play a key role in this program that will also cover older neighborhoods. Hainan is expected to see more cozy alleys, parks and shady boulevards.
Boao Forum for Asia’s environmental project
China’s central authorities and Hainan administration have been developing the zero carbon demonstration zone in Boao since 2022. A high-tech system on Dongyu Island at the mouth of the Wanquan River, where the BFA complex is located, provides efficient air circulation and cooling in buildings and uses solar energy to illuminate the surrounding area.
The Boao Forum for Asia was founded in February 2001 and has been held on the eastern coast of Hainan Island since 2002. As many as 29 Asian countries are its participants. This platform for developing multilateral cooperation is often referred to as the "Eastern Davos." The Chinese government is focused on the forum’s development, considering it a tool of soft diplomacy. In 2026, around 2,000 people from 60 countries and regions attended the conference. The next forum will take place from March 24 to 27, 2027.

Metal detectorist finds record-breaking trove of ancient Roman coins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:39 UTC
00:04:39 KST

Man's metal detector wouldn't stop beeping, leading to record-breaking trove of ancient Roman coins
An amateur archaeologist who discovered several Roman silver coins in a field in western Germany realized he had stumbled upon something bigger when his metal detector kept beeping.
Oliver Riedl called the authorities for help, and a group of experts who began digging immediately discovered a total of 934 Roman silver denarii. It is the biggest coin treasure ever found in Germany from the time of Roman Emperor Hadrian, the local office in charge of archaeological monuments said Tuesday.
"It was clear to me that there was something bigger buried here," Riedl said, describing how his metal detector continued signaling even after he had found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne a year ago.
The hoard of coins, which weighs 3.1 kilograms (6.8 pounds), went on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn on Tuesday.
The majority of the coins date from the time of the Flavian emperors (A.D. 69–96), and the oldest one was minted in 148 B.C., the museum said in a news release.
The collection of coins was probably buried deliberately in the second quarter of the second century A.D., according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland.
"Of course, we can only speculate about the motives, but it's very likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks didn't exist back then," Erich Classen, state archaeologist and the director of the office, said in a statement.
Classen said it wasn't clear why the treasure was never recovered before, adding that "perhaps the owner died before that could happen, without being able to pass on the knowledge about the coins."
Treasure troves from ancient Roman times or other distant eras are not uncommon. However, few from the second century are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling, the archaeological office said, adding that it was difficult to estimate the coins' value at the time.
However, the pay of Roman legionaries, which is well documented in written sources, provides a point of reference.
"At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year. However, about half of that was withheld for food and equipment," said Rahel Otte, a research associate at the archaeological office.
"A legionary would therefore have had to save all of his disposable income for about six years to amass the Wesseling hoard," Otte said. She added that it remains unclear exactly who ultimately amassed this considerable fortune.
 The Cologne area was under Roman control roughly from 39 B.C. to A.D. 459. The Romans established a presence in the region under General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure their empire's border along the Rhine River, setting up a military outpost which later became Colonia Agrippina - today's Cologne.
 
Treasures from the Roman era have been found across Europe in recent years.
In February, metal detectorists in Wales found two lead ingots that date back to the Roman era, the first of their kind to be found in the region.
In 2024, a hoard of Roman coins worth over $125,000 was found during a construction project in central England. That same year, metal detectorists in Poland helped discover a large cache of ancient Roman coins.
Also in 2024, a collection of ancient silver Roman coins was unearthed on a small island in the Mediterranean Sea, officials said this week.

Trump announced a “massive” potash deal with Belarus—Lukashenka said the same day there is no spare potash to sell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

US President Donald Trump announced a "massive deal" to buy Belarusian potash at prices far below what the US pays Canada, but Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka publicly contradicted him the same day, saying Belarus has no spare volumes to sell.
Washington has spent a year courting Lukashenka with sanctions relief and envoy visits in pursuit of both prisoner releases and trade openings—but the potash episode shows the limits of that courtship when the dictator's own supply chain cannot deliver what the US President has already promised his voters.
Trump promised cheaper potash for American farmers
Trump wrote on Truth Social on 21 September:
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer. Canada is the world's largest supplier—the US takes 53% of Canadian potash exports, and 80% of the potash American farms use comes from Canada. Canadian potash remains exempt from US tariffs despite the ongoing trade war between the two countries.
The announcement came as Trump's trade dispute with Ottawa deepened—he recently called Canada a "terrible trade partner," and on 16 September European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership, which Trump said could be a "hostile act."
Lukashenka said all output is contracted
The same day, Lukashenka told officials Belarus cannot deliver. "Even if we wanted to supply potash to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes—everything is contracted," he said during a meeting with the head of Belarus's State Customs Committee, Uladzimir Arlouski.
Arlouski reported that 85% of all Belarusian exports and imports now move eastward—primarily to China, other Asian countries, and Russia. Budget revenues grew almost 3.5% over eight months, and 5.2% so far this month.
A deal built on sanctions relief and prisoner swaps
The potash announcement followed a year-long US effort to engage Lukashenka. Washington lifted sanctions on Belarus's potash industry in exchange for the release of hundreds of political prisoners. US special envoy John Cole has played the central role, meeting Lukashenka last week and securing the release of 25 prisoners—far fewer than the 200 he had previously promised.
Over the course of Cole's effort, at least several hundred people have been freed, among them Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski and Siarhei Tsikhanouski, husband of the internationally recognized winner of Belarus's 2020 presidential election. But human rights groups and freed prisoners say Lukashenka runs a "carousel"—arresting new political opponents to replace the ones he releases. Lukashenka denied this. "There are no political prisoners in Belarus," he claimed during last week's meeting with Cole.
With US midterms six weeks away on 3 November and the Republican Party struggling in the polls, Trump has been scrambling for wins on fuel and food prices. The same week, he urged Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian refineries, blaming Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran for record US diesel prices—a move a senior European official told Politico was a search for "scapegoats."

European drugmakers say they are ‘losing ground’ to US and Chinese rivals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:10 UTC
00:04:10 KST

Some of Europe’s biggest pharmaceutical companies have said the continent is “losing ground” to rivals including the US and China in developing new drugs and attracting investment.
The chairs of nine companies, including Britain’s AstraZeneca, GSK and Denmark’s Novo Nordisk, wrote to Andy Burnham and the national leaders of other European countries on Tuesday to call for action to “safeguard our companies’ future”.
The letter, entitled Europe is Losing the Pharma Investment Race – But the Comeback is Within Reach, called on governments to treat medicines as strategic infrastructure, secure health sovereignty and act now to restore Europe’s competitiveness.
It argued that the pharmaceutical sector is one of Europe’s great postwar achievements that is supporting millions of highly skilled jobs and generating an EU trade surplus of more than €220bn (£188bn). “But this hard-won inheritance is at risk,” the letter said.
“In our boardrooms, we see Europe losing ground to global competition. Over $600bn in pharmaceutical investment has been announced in the US and China in the last two years alone.
“European governments must create conditions that attract investment in next-generation medicines before it’s too late,” said the letter, which was also signed by the chairs of Germany’s Boehringer Ingelheim, Italy’s Chiesi group, France’s Sanofi and Ipsen, and Novartis and Roche of Switzerland.
Europe’s share of global pharmaceutical research and development has fallen from 43% in 1990 to 31%, according to the European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA).
The continent’s share of commercial clinical trials – where new medicines are tested for safety and efficacy before they are submitted for regulatory approval – has halved to 9% from 18% a decade ago. Only 4% of clinical trials are focused on cell and gene therapies.
China has overtaken Europe in clinical trials, pharmaceutical patents, and the development of new medicines. The country’s share of global clinical trials rose from less than 10% to almost 30% over the same period.
Almost half (49%) of newly approved therapies did not reach European patients last year, up from 46% in 2019; those drugs that do take nearly 600 days on average. This varies hugely from country to country: from a median 56 days in Germany to 1,201 days in Romania, according to data from the EFPIA.
The industry body has said the root causes of unavailability and delay to accessing new medicines range from the speed of regulatory processes to insufficient budgets in some European countries.
Closing the clinical trials gap alone could generate €53bn and create 82,000 jobs in Europe, the nine pharma companies argued in the letter.
“We ask national leaders to work with us to reverse Europe’s declining competitiveness, unleash a new era of medical discovery, and secure health sovereignty. We recognise the fiscal pressures many face. But just like defence or energy, modern medicines should be treated as vital infrastructure and not be left to others to provide,” the letter said.
It was signed by industry leaders including Michel Demaré, the chair of Britain’s biggest pharmaceutical company, AstraZeneca; Jonathan Symonds, his counterpart at GSK, the country’s second-biggest drugmaker; Lars Rebien Sørensen, the chair of the Wegovy and Ozempic maker, Novo Nordisk; Severin Schwan at the Swiss company Roche; Giovanni Caforio at fellow Swiss firm Novartis, and Frédéric Oudéa at France’s Sanofi.
It comes after a public row last year between the industry and the UK government over drug pricing and availability of new treatments to patients. Ministers agreed in December to spend billions of pounds a year extra on medicines supplied to the NHS after pressure from Donald Trump, who argued that high drug prices in the US were subsidising lower prices elsewhere.

Ukraine Has Pushed Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Into a Repair Trap
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:02:06 UTC
00:02:06 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Has Pushed Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Into a Repair Trap
Ukraine’s repeated strikes on Russia’s Black Sea Fleet have created a growing maintenance problem for Moscow, leaving damaged warships with few safe places where they can undergo lengthy repairs without becoming stationary targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk on September 22, Russia is struggling to conduct full-scale maintenance at its Novorossiysk base, while its primary repair infrastructure in temporarily occupied Crimea has become increasingly difficult to use because of Ukrainian strikes.
For major repairs, Russian vessels need to enter dry dock and remain immobilized for extended periods—making them considerably more vulnerable to Ukrainian attacks.
“Therefore, there can currently be no talk of any prolonged repairs or maintenance,” Pletenchuk said.
The pressure comes as Russia’s naval missile capability in the Black Sea has also narrowed. Pletenchuk said Moscow currently retains two surface ships capable of carrying cruise missiles, as well as two submarines that have recently seen little operational use.
Russian surface vessels have also continued to suffer damage. Pletenchuk named the Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov frigates, as well as a Buyan-M-class small missile ship, among vessels that have been struck.
Novorossiysk has become the main refuge for much of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian attacks made operations from temporarily occupied Crimea increasingly dangerous.
However, concentrating ships there has created another vulnerability: vessels requiring serious maintenance must remain in predictable locations long enough to undergo repairs, potentially exposing them to further strikes.
Russia’s main Black Sea Fleet repair facilities remain in temporarily occupied Crimea, but Ukrainian operations against military infrastructure on the peninsula have significantly complicated Moscow’s ability to rely on those bases.
Despite the reduced activity of Russian warships, the threat from the Black Sea region remains. Pletenchuk said Russia continues to rely primarily on missiles, drones, and aircraft for attacks against Ukraine.
He added that Russian aviation remains active in the operational area, while Ukrainian strikes against military targets in temporarily occupied Crimea are aimed at further reducing Russia’s ability to launch attacks from the peninsula.
Earlier, on September 9, Ukraine struck Russia’s naval hub in Novorossiysk with missiles and drones, hitting at least three Black Sea Fleet vessels, including the Kalibr-capable frigate Admiral Essen. Separate imagery also indicated possible damage to the Admiral Makarov frigate and a Buyan-M-class missile ship.

For the amendment to take permanent effect, parliament must approve it in two more votes held three months apart: the first on October 9, the second on January 12. At least 94 of the 141 lawmakers must support it for the amendment to pass.
In early June, the Financial Times reported that the United States was negotiating the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland and the Baltic states, citing sources who said the talks involve American bombers capable of carrying nuclear weapons. Lithuanian authorities confirmed that they are holding these talks and are considering corresponding amendments to the Constitution.
In September, the Kremlin said that Lithuania would be “in the crosshairs” of Russian nuclear weapons if it stationed a nuclear arsenal on its territory.
American dual-capable aircraft able to carry nuclear weapons are currently stationed in six NATO countries: Belgium, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Turkey.
Russia stationed its nuclear weapons in Belarus after the start of the full-scale war with Ukraine.

Reform UK turns to YouTube to sidestep UK broadcast rules, reach voters

Reform representatives and candidates have faced a series of allegations over racist, antisemitic and anti-Muslim remarks, while some party figures have also faced scrutiny over links to far-right activists.
Earlier this month, Reform home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf was accused of "straightforward racism" by a government minister after questioning whether a Somali-born British politician who came to the UK as a child was "British".
Several Reform councillors have also been identified as members of a Facebook group linked to the far-right Patriot Platform, although some have denied links to the organisation or distanced themselves from it.
Farage himself has faced renewed scrutiny over his past rhetoric and associations, including allegations about racist and antisemitic comments dating back to his school years, which he has denied.
Online content accessible in Britain remains subject to legislation including the Online Safety Act, which Capon said "could help [curb the channel's use of discriminatory language] to an extent", but warned that "it won't deal with everything".
The venture would therefore give Reform a powerful platform from which to communicate directly with supporters while avoiding some of the regulatory requirements that apply to conventional television broadcasters.
Reform's links to GB News
Reform UK is already closely linked to GB News, where Farage currently hosts a prime-time programme three nights a week.
GB News presenter Matt Goodwin also unsuccessfully stood as a Reform candidate in February's Gorton and Denton parliamentary by-election.
The launch of Reform's own channel, however, could put the party in direct competition with a broadcaster that has provided considerable airtime to Farage and other figures associated with Reform.
GB News has recorded a higher average television audience than both Sky News and BBC News, but the prospect of Reform building its own digital platform appears to have prompted concern about whether some viewers could be drawn away.
On Friday night, GB News presenter and former Conservative MP Jacob Rees-Mogg made a direct appeal to his audience.
"I know you are wonderful, clever people and will remain loyal to GB News," he said.
The BBC has also repeatedly found itself in Farage's sights.
The Reform leader has said he would strip the broadcaster of the licence fee, one of its principal sources of funding.
He also accused the BBC of "double standards" after the corporation's Today programme questioned him over allegations that he made racist and antisemitic remarks while at school.
The emergence of a Reform-controlled channel would allow Farage and other party figures to reach viewers without relying on interviews or appearances on traditional broadcasters, where politicians can face independent questioning and editorial scrutiny.
£72 million funding boost
Reform's push into digital broadcasting comes shortly after the party received two donations totalling £72 million from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
The enormous injection of cash gives Reform considerable resources to professionalise and expand its political and communications operations, including its push into digital media.
Capon said the money would make it considerably easier for the party to establish its own broadcasting operation.
"I think that that piggy bank that's been thrown at Mr Farage and Mr Tice, that's definitely going to help with this," he told The New Arab.
The unprecedented donations have also intensified scrutiny of the influence extremely wealthy individuals can exercise over British politics and the country's political finance rules.
The planned channel could allow Reform to pour some of its new resources into producing and distributing its own political programming directly to voters, bypassing the editorial scrutiny that comes with appearing on independent broadcasters.
It would also give the party much greater control over how Farage and other Reform figures are presented, what issues they focus on and which voices are given a platform.
That prospect is particularly significant as political parties increasingly use social media and online video to circumvent traditional media organisations and communicate directly with voters.
For Reform, its own channel could become a permanent platform for its political messaging at a time when the party has acquired unprecedented financial resources and continues to face scrutiny over the rhetoric and conduct of some of its representatives.
Reform UK did not respond to The New Arab's request for comment.

What’s behind French protests against a new police bill?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:01:19 UTC
00:01:19 KST

What’s behind French protests against a new police bill?
Critics say controversial law will give police officers a ‘licence to kill’.
France was rocked by protests on Sunday against proposed legislation that would grant additional protections to law enforcement officials using firearms in the line of duty.
The new law, which critics say will grant police officers a “licence to kill”, comes amid mounting allegations of police brutality in recent years, particularly against immigrant communities in the banlieues – outlying suburbs – of Paris and other major cities.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Russia seizes assets of French firms, summons UK envoy over Ukraine support
- list 2 of 3Lebanon security talks in Paris to focus on post-UNIFIL alternatives
- list 3 of 3Macron and Aoun discuss efforts to back Lebanon’s army, end Israeli attacks
So what is the new law, why is it controversial and where have protests taken place?
Where are protests taking place and what are they about?
Thousands of people marched in France over the weekend against the proposed law which would grant armed police and gendarmes the presumption of self-defence if they use their weapons while carrying out their duties.
This means that complainants against police brutality would have to prove that a police officer was not acting in self-defence.
A petition against the bill lodged by Issam El Khalfaoui, whose son was shot dead by a police officer in 2021, on the website of the National Assembly, gathered 730,000 signatures earlier in the year, but a parliamentary law committee dismissed it in July.
Thousands of people marched in the French capital Paris over the weekend while many other protests were organised in cities across France. Police said about 8,200 people demonstrated in the southern French cities of Lyon and Toulouse alone.
Protests were also held in Marseille, southern France, and Rennes, in the country’s northwest, where officials said eight people were arrested and three police officers were injured when projectiles were thrown at them.
Left-wing politicians, rights groups including Amnesty International, France’s magistrates’ union and the country’s League of Human Rights also participated in the protests.
What is the new police law coming in?
Draft bill 691 aims to establish a presumption of legitimate self-defence or of legality for law enforcement officials when they use their firearms in the line of duty.
In other words, the proposition would mean that officers who killed someone in a shooting incident would be presumed to have acted within the limits of the law, unless there was proof to the contrary.
The text says the presumption of self-defence “may be rebutted if the judicial investigation demonstrates that the use of weapons was manifestly disproportionate or contrary to the principle of absolute necessity established by law”.
Deputies in the National Assembly approved the bill in July. A vote on the proposed legislation will now take place in the Senate, the upper house of the French parliament.
Why is this new law being brought in?
A longstanding demand of France’s far-right National Rally party, the legislation was proposed by Member of Parliament Eric Pauget, from France’s right-wing Les Republicains (LR) party.
Proponents of the law, including French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, say it is an important legal measure, required to protect police officers working in dangerous conditions, particularly when tackling organised crime.
What have the responses to the proposed law been?
Nunez told the French parliament in July that “it does not lead to penal irresponsibility – at any moment, if the circumstances are reunited, any prosecutor can reverse this presumption”.
But critics say the measure amounts to a “licence to kill”.
Mathilde Panot, president of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, condemned the bill, saying “the police kill already”.
Addressing crowds in Paris during Sunday’s protest, she said, “In the Republic there can be no organised police impunity. In the Republic, there cannot be a category of citizens who have the right of life or death over other citizens.”
Pouria Amirshahi, a left-wing lawmaker representing French residents overseas, also condemned the bill.
“There will be more deaths – if you authorise someone to use their firearm with the idea that they won’t be accountable, then they will just shoot,” said Amirshahi. “This law grants police impunity.”
Amnesty International’s Cedric Picard, who took part in the Marseille protest, said, “We are afraid police violence would only grow with this law.”
Why is this new law controversial?
The United Nations has condemned the proposed law, saying it could “legitimise and normalise” violence against civilians.
“The duty to investigate every potentially unlawful killing rests with the State,” said Morris Tidball-Binz, United Nations special rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions.
“It cannot be displaced, in law or in practice, by requiring victims or their families to rebut a legal presumption that the use of potentially lethal force was lawful before the facts have been independently established.”
Tidball-Binz said that if the proposed legislation is adopted, it would violate Principle 9 of the UN Basic Principles on the Use of Force and Firearms by Law Enforcement Officials, which mandates strict limits on the use of lethal force.
Marie-Laure Geoffray, also of Amnesty International, echoed Tidball-Binz’s statement in July, saying that the law would slow down investigations into police violence, as the burden of proof would fall on the victims or their families rather than on the police.
Critics have warned the new law could trigger a rise in fatal shootings and a sharp decline in public trust in the police.
Do other countries have this law?
Pauget, the MP who put the bill forward, said Italy’s anti-protest law is similar in nature.
Proposed by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right wing government and adopted in June 2025, the law introduced harsher penalties for protest-related offences, including property damage and sit-ins deemed disruptive, and granted broader powers to law enforcement officers.
It also allowed intelligence agents to commit certain “crimes” for national security purposes without facing prosecution.
That law similarly prompted widespread demonstrations across Italy, with human rights organisations accusing the government of criminalising dissent, limiting civil liberties and restricting the right to protest.
When has the French police been accused of brutality?
The French government has come under pressure from activists and the public over repeated allegations of police violence and harassment, largely against Black and Arab men and boys in the suburbs (banlieues) of Paris and other major cities in France in recent years.
Furthermore, the number of fatal shootings by police in France is among the highest in Europe and continues to rise.
The agencies that carry out investigations of police in France – the IGPN and IGGN – recorded 69 people killed by police or gendarmerie officers in 2024, compared with 49 in 2023 and 50 in 2022.
Below are some of the most high-profile incidents across the country over the past decade:
- In June 2023, Nahel Merzouk, a 17-year-old boy of Moroccan and Algerian descent, was shot dead by police in Nanterre, west of Paris, while in the driving seat of a rental car. The incident prompted nationwide protests against police violence. The police initially maintained that Nahel had driven his car at the officer. But this was contradicted by mobile phone footage, which showed two officers standing by a stationary car, with one pointing a weapon at its driver. In March, a French appeals court ruled that Florian M, the policeman who shot and killed the teenager, should stand trial for violence that led to the death.
- In August 2021, Souheil El Khalfaoui, a 19-year-old man of North African descent, was shot and killed by a trainee police officer during a traffic stop in Marseille’s Belle de Mai neighbourhood. Authorities initially ruled the shooting a matter of “absolute necessity” after Souheil allegedly reversed his car towards police, but the case was reopened following family appeals regarding withheld CCTV evidence. The incident set off protests, which intensified after Romain Devassine, the officer involved in the shooting, performed as a BMX rider in the Paris Olympics opening ceremony. The investigation into El Khalfaoui’s death remains ongoing. Devassine has not been formally indicted, placed under arrest or suspended from duty.
- In July 2016, Adama Traore, a 24-year-old man of Malian descent, died in custody after being restrained and apprehended by police following a dispute over an identity check. His death triggered nationwide protests over police brutality. There was another resurgence in demonstrations in 2020 despite COVID-related restrictions, with protesters drawing parallels with the circumstances of the murder of George Floyd in the United States. In 2020, French medical experts exonerated the three police officers involved in the incident, dismissing a medical report commissioned by the young man’s family that said he had died of asphyxiation. Earlier this year, France’s top court ruled against reopening an investigation into Traore’s death, confirming a previous decision to dismiss the case against the arresting officers.

Parsons researchers warn of plastic toxicity in American manufactured homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:00:43 UTC
00:00:43 KST

Parsons researchers warn of plastic toxicity in American manufactured homes
Researchers at Parsons School of Design's Healthy Material Lab have released a study that raises concerns about the "many substances harmful to human health" in a typical prefabricated American home.
Called Manufactured Homes: An Analysis of Health and Environmental Impacts of Common Building Materials, the study highlighted potential negative health effects associated with manufactured homes.
Manufactured homes have been popular among Americans for the last century and peaked in the 1970s, with as many as 500,000 delivered per month. That number is now closer to 100,000 per month, according to data from the US Census Bureau.
"Significant health and environmental risks"
"The extensive use of petrochemical-based materials in contemporary manufactured housing poses significant health and environmental risks," said the Healthy Material Lab Study.
"Plastics and their associated toxic additives are found in nearly every major surface within a manufactured home, including flooring, paint, cabinetry and insulation."
The fossil-fuel plastics mentioned in the research include polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride and polypropylene, with the majority found in kitchens and bathrooms.
Healthy Material Labs executive design director Jonsara Ruth told Dezeen that the presence of potentially toxic plastic material in homes is a problem across the building industry. However, manufactured homes may pose a greater risk due to the drive for affordability.
"It's true, petroleum-based plastic materials are now widespread in new American homes, not just manufactured ones," said Ruth.
"But manufactured housing offers a unique lens: it's where affordability and conventional construction intersect most starkly, often resulting in material choices that externalize health and environmental costs."
Ruth cited the research of Dr Shanna Swan, who has shown the relationship between plastic exposure and the Green Science Policy Institutes Six Classes framework, which outlines harmful chemicals.
"Longstanding reports, dating back to the 1990s, discuss the increased use of petrochemical-based materials in housing and associated health concerns," said Ruth.
"Famously, the FEMA trailer crisis after Hurricane Katrina highlighted the dangers of high formaldehyde exposure in temporary homes."
The move to healthy affordable homes
The study's results are based on information on materials taken from a single home sold by Northstar Systembuilt in Minnesota, as its sample.
Researchers at Healthy Material Lab called the company, posing as buyers to ask questions about the materials.
"We selected one of the most affordable models from one of the largest manufactured home manufacturers in the US," said Ruth.
"While this isn't a statistically representative sample, it's a typical example of conventional, low-cost manufactured homes."
Ruth said she was confident that the material findings were "consistent with what is often found in affordable, conventional residential construction in the US".
Northstar Systembuilt did not respond to Dezeen's request for comment.
According to Healthy Material Lab, the research's goal was to demonstrate that healthier materials could be used in the construction of these homes. Linoleum flooring could replace vinyl, for example, or wood finishes could be chosen instead of plastic ones.
"We're not arguing against manufactured homes," said Ruth, who added there were some examples of manufacturers trying to improve materials, such as a 2000 collaboration between Enterprise Community Partners and Clayton Homes.
"In fact, we're arguing for healthier, low-carbon prefabricated housing at an affordable price point."
The negative effects of plastic on the body have been examined at length in recent years, especially the ubiquity of microplastics. The National Institute for Health showed the potential for microplastics exposure in the indoor environment, though it did not go so far to claim negative health effects from the exposure.
In 2021, Dezeen took a look at the variety of plastics used in the architecture and design industries.
In 2024, Denmark's Natural Material Studio created a home interior completely free of fossil-fuel-derived products.

Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.
I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window. With her liver failing, her skin was a ghostly apricot. June – I called her Nan – had been stalked by the king of terrors, the emperor of all maladies: cancer. That son of a bitch.
The cancer was in her pancreas. Odds of survival? “Not good” – putting it lightly. The maths, putting it darkly: it’s the 12th most common cancer worldwide, the sixth most common cause of cancer death. The World Health Organization says it is “one of the cancer types with the least favourable prognosis”. It was not favourable for my grandmother.
June died nine years ago. Lately I’ve been thinking about alternate futures – the ones in which my grandmother, and the many millions diagnosed with cancer each year, are still here. The thoughts creep in as we are bombarded by artificial intelligence chief executives making bold proclamations such as “AI will cure cancer in five to 10 years” or “AI will cure cancer in our lifetimes”. Those claims stand in contrast to apocalyptic scenarios, including AI being responsible for human extinction before 2030. AI, we hear, is both saviour and annihilator.
Park the world-ending scenarios and you’ll find there has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer. If there is a future where a supposed AI apocalypse is averted, then it may be one in which cancer therapy has been completely redefined. But just how far can AI take us towards a cure?
Today AI is being turned toward drug development, treatment plans and, in some places, it’s being used clinically, studying imagery of lungs for early signs of malignancy and helping to remove brain tumours. Words like “efficiency” and “personalised care” are everywhere; the notion AI can free up time for doctors and medical professionals to get away from the busywork abound.
Cancer is not a single disease
Even with such positive advances, speak to clinicians, oncologists and researchers working at the coalface and you quickly find there is tension between the more grandiose claims of big tech and its race to “solve” disease, and the deliberate, considered progress of science.
“Until AI can actually think and do experiments itself at scale, I’m not sure that we’re going to find a cure for all cancer or medical illness in the next 10 years,” says Sherene Loi, a medical oncologist who specialises in breast cancer treatment at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne.
But Loi and other cancer experts the Guardian has spoken to believe there will be efficiencies for treatment, diagnostics and pathology services that will bear fruit, heralding more personalised and more equitable cancer care.
Cancer is not a single disease. It’s a catch-all term that describes the uncontrollable growth of abnormal cells. Typically, we describe cancers based on the location within the body that they are found: breast, prostate, lung, brain, blood, pancreas. These are complex, highly variable diseases, affecting a variety of different cells and underpinned by a host of genetic changes. In addition, cancer outcomes depend on many factors, including the biology of the disease and the treatments available. A single cure for cancer is not only unlikely but nigh on impossible.
Just take the brain. Though not all are cancerous, “there are more than 100 types of tumours in the brain, much more than in any other single organ”, says Felix Sahm, a neuropathologist at the University Hospital Heidelberg. “There are so many unresolved questions in brain tumour research and brain tumour care.”
We’ve made great leaps in cancer survival rates over the past century; chemotherapy and radiation have enabled solid tumours to be cured, monoclonal antibodies ushered in more direct targeting of abnormal cells, and emerging treatments are rewriting how we combat the disease. But, as Loi notes, “Human disease is very complex.” So where does AI fit in?
A shadow on a scan
“AI can improve several parts of that process by helping us identify risk, detect disease, characterise tumours, select treatments and monitor,” says Ajit Goenka, a radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.
Medical imaging, in particular, stands to benefit from advances in AI and machine-learning models. Training models on huge amounts of patient data, such as CT scans, X-rays or tissue samples, enables those models to detect changes or patterns that may be imperceptible to the human eye.
Goenka has been exploring the early detection of pancreatic cancer with machine-learning tools since 2021, before the release of ChatGPT fully turned the public’s head toward generative AI. Since then, OpenAI and its rival Anthropic have pushed into new realms beyond chatbots: partnering with companies to accelerate access to treatment; striking deals with research centres; and working with pharmaceutical companies to incorporate large language models and AI into drug discovery.
Goenka noticed that some patients who developed pancreatic cancer had undergone CT scans months or years before diagnosis. Those scans were interpreted as normal but Goenka reasoned there could be microscopic, measurable changes invisible to a radiologist. “We began studying whether quantitative imaging and machine-learning methods could detect that signal,” he says.
In a proof-of-concept paper published in 2022, he confirmed that hunch. Machine-learning tools can detect pancreatic tumours, including in pancreases that appeared normal, before clinical diagnosis. Further studies by Goenka’s group have explored how robust and reproducible the method is and whether it is useful across institutions. The opportunity, he says, is to identify evidence of cancer earlier. My grandmother’s pancreatic cancer appeared as if out of nowhere, a shadow on a scan. Goenka’s models may have been able to see it sooner, which could have improved her outcome.
Reducing the duration of uncertainty
Sahm leads a European multi-disciplinary collaboration called EUcanAI, which is using agentic AI to improve the way brain tumours and central nervous system cancers are treated. The idea is that “every single chunk of this journey gets informed by the previous one and informs the next one in the sequence, so that it gets more efficient, quicker and less cumbersome for a patient”, he says.
He provides one example of a teenager who presented with a tumour in his brain stem. The expectation was that it was fatal, based on imaging and the patient’s age. The patient went in for surgery, his tumour was biopsied and rapidly sequenced to determine the mutations driving his disease.
Traditionally, these results go to a board of specialists to discuss the next steps in surgery and treatment. But today, these results can be delivered during a surgery, saving patients time and money. Sahm imagines a world where agentic AI accelerates this process even further – a surgeon could biopsy and image a tumour, then have an AI provide answers about the kind of mutation and potential drugs that may treat it. Sahm says this work is already happening in trials but stresses it is not yet routine.
The key for Sahm is a more tailored journey for each patient that “reduces the duration of uncertainty”. It’s about providing a wholly optimised approach to managing a patient’s cancer journey. He also notes it could provide more patients with better care.
This was a common thread in discussing AI tools for cancer diagnostics. “I think it will help with regards to equity of care, and access to care,” Loi says.
For instance, she says, in rural communities or locations that do not have cancer facilities or access to specialists or specialist diagnostic tools, access to machine-learning models could help medical professionals provide faster, more complete answers.
Can AI ‘solve’ disease?
The dream of curing cancer is one that big AI firms constantly seed. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, has suggested that within a decade, cancer – and many other diseases – could be cured. The Google DeepMind spin-off, IsoLabs, has a bold mission statement to “solve” all disease.
Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, has similar lofty goals, suggesting the ability to solve disease might just be a problem of how much computing power backs our AI systems. “Maybe with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer,” he wrote. As AI firms experience growing backlash to the environmental cost of datacentres, the argument that just a little more compute could offer life-saving opportunities could be hard to sell.
But Emilia Javorsky, a physician and scientist at the Future of Life Institute, argues the opposite: “We cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure it.”
In her March essay on AI and cancer, she outlines the complicated process of developing and testing any new medication. “Thirteen years into the AI drug discovery movement, we still lack a single [Federal Drug Authority]-approved drug that cleared the full bar of regulatory approval, reimbursement, and clinical adoption,” she says.
Javorsky argues that curing cancer is a noble goal but the research community must be smart about where investment goes. It’s not intelligence that limits progress but the data, regulation and incentives that surround cancer research.
Even if all the data from research across the world was placed into these models, would that be enough to solve these diseases today? What about in five or 10 years? For Sahm, there are biological truths we are yet to uncover. In his work, he still encounters rare, unknown pathology that doesn’t “fit into a box”. While AI may be able to devise technology or tools to understand rare subtypes, it’s only as good as its training data.
The complexity of human physiology and biological processes comes up a lot in discussions with those working in cancer. Although AI may speed up the process of, for instance, hypothesising and creating new drugs that can treat specific forms of cancer, it is fundamentally limited in applying those learnings to the real world. “Someone actually has to go back and do the experiment, right?” Loi says.
An article published in The Australian newspaper in March revealed that a Sydney data scientist had been able to synthesise a bespoke cancer vaccine for his dog, Rosie, by uploading her genetic information to ChatGPT. And while some were astounded by the development, others noted that the hard work had still been done by humans in a lab.
Even if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape. Sahm notes that the majority of AI-assisted or AI-led research being performed is experimental and remains in clinical trials. Even if AI tools were deemed safe for test patients, he says, the EU lacks a clear regulatory path to allow them to reach the market. “That ends up in a lot of AI research going on, a lot of surprising and promising things happening … but also surprisingly few of those really being applied,” he says.
The most vocal proponents of AI – those building the models – may make grand claims about cures but on the ground the reality is different. There’s a lack of understanding of cancer complexity, many researchers working in the space argue.
But it’s clear that AI does provide a sense of hope for clinicians and researchers. Alone it cannot dethrone the king of terrors; it cannot bring down the emperor of all maladies. Curing cancer will require more than extra-efficient computation.
“AI can come up with a million hypotheses,” Loi says – but we will still need humans to help understand which of them are true.
“Technology,” says Goenka, “is only one part of the answer.”

Meet the ‘fire amoeba,’ a record-breaking survivor of extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A single-celled blob living in a California hot spring has smashed a heat tolerance record for an entire domain of life.
The newly described “fire amoeba” can grow at 63° Celsius (145° Fahrenheit), a temperature that’s fatal to all other known eukaryotes, researchers report September 22 in Cell. Eukaryotes include all life-forms with nuclei and organelles, such as plants, fungi and animals.
Little was known about the genetic adaptations of microbial eukaryotes that live in extreme environments. From 2023 to 2025, microbiologist Beryl Rappaport and her colleagues brought water samples from geothermal hot springs in California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park into the lab. There, the team tried to grow any amoebas they found and study their DNA.
“We set up cultures at a few temperatures, with the hottest being 57° C because that is the highest temperature previously described for an amoeba,” says Rappaport, a member of microbial ecologist Angela Oliverio’s lab at Syracuse University in New York.
After seeing an amoeba growing at 57° C that looked different from the previous amoeba record holder Echinamoeba thermarum, the team cranked up the temperature. The mystery microbe continued to replicate and thrive at a blistering 63° C, above the eukaryote record of 60° C held by some algae and fungi. This resilient amoeba could even survive up to 70° C by entering a dormant state.
The researchers named the amoeba Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which means “fire amoeba from the Cascades,” after the volcanic mountains where it was discovered.
Some other, simpler microbes like bacteria and archaea can tolerate much higher temperatures. For instance, archaeon Methanopyrus kandleri holds the heat record for all life and can grow at 122° C.
The fire amoeba appears to share some adaptations with these kinds of organisms, like chemical features on the surface of its proteins that discourage the harmful clumping that happens at high temperatures.
The amoeba can also pivot between two body shapes, which might help it deal with rapidly fluctuating temperatures in its hot spring environment. “One slower [form] seems suited to foraging and one faster [one] seems useful for escaping if temperatures become suboptimal,” Rappaport says.
Even more heat-tolerant eukaryotes may yet to be discovered. “As far as we know, there is no reason why 63° is the hard limit,” Oliverio says. “We don’t really know what the upper temperature limits are.”

"The very nature of the KLA – criminal at its core – still awaits a proper legal assessment," Zakharova concluded.

EU removes two Russian billionaires from sanctions list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:58:32 UTC
23:58:32 KST

BRUSSELS — Two of Russia’s wealthiest men could soon be free to operate inside the EU after the bloc moved to lift restrictions on them and their empires as part of a high-stakes diplomatic play.
Capitals struck a deal on Tuesday to cut Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, five diplomats told POLITICO, granted anonymity to speak frankly.
For more than a week, France had been holding up the EU’s entire framework of individual sanctions in an unexpected standoff, risking the expiry of the 3,000-odd listings if they weren’t renewed. Earlier talks ended without a deal Monday night after Baltic nations initially refused to sign off.
Advertisement
Paris launched a surprise campaign earlier this month calling for sanctions to be dropped on mining and telecoms billionaire Usmanov and citing a “national security” issue at play. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had long been asking for the delisting of banking magnate Fridman, who is suing the country for access to assets frozen by the Grand Duchy.
A number of countries — including Nordic and Baltic nations — had warned the move could jeopardize the entire sanctions list, leading others to lobby for their own narrow interests. The breakthrough came after Latvia, which had been the most vocal opponent, agreed to abstain on the plan.
As part of the deal, the current selection of names will be frozen for three years, effectively sidelining further debate until 2029. The agreement was due to take effect if capitals submitted their written consent by 6 p.m. on Tuesday.
“It is done,” said one of the diplomats. “The question is what Baltic countries got in return.”
Latvia defends deal
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs defended Riga’s climb-down, saying Latvia would “continue to advocate for the imposition of additional EU sanctions on Russia.” In a statement on the Latvian government website, the PM also noted that his had been “the only EU member state” to oppose the removal of “politically motivated individuals” from the individual sanctions list “until the very end.”
At the same time, he revealed, French President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks with Latvia on its accession to France’s nuclear deterrence initiative, and “also expressed his commitment to strengthening France’s military presence in Latvia, especially in the field of air defense.”
“Such a commitment will strengthen not only the security of Latvia but also of the entire NATO eastern flank,” he added.
Advertisement
EU capitals have struck a deal to remove Russia’s Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list.@benjaminhaddad called the outcome a win for European solidarity.
France had riled other EU members by announcing its support for Usmanov at short notice, saying only that it was related to “a specific national security issue” and that Paris “wishes to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.”
Still, its European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad called Tuesday’s outcome a win for European solidarity.
“We keep a very strong united front on the sanctions on Russia,” Haddad told POLITICO. “We have these discussions. You have consideration of national security and others among member states. But the most important is that we’ve shown once again our unity and our resolve to put economic pressure on Russia for its war of aggression.”
Ukraine slams 'shameful' arrangement
Kyiv led criticism of the sanctions list maneuver, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha describing the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman as “shameful and unjustifiable.”
“Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” he wrote on X.
The Financial Times reported that the delisting was part of a deal that could see French nationals released from detention in Azerbaijan. Paris has significantly stepped up its role in the South Caucasus in support of Armenia, a pro-EU democracy that has spent decades locked in conflict with Azerbaijan.
Advertisement
But some were concerned about the precedent that could set. “If the reports are confirmed, Europe must not turn sanctions into a bargaining chip,” said Latvian MEP Rihards Kols, a member of the Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee. “France has every right and duty to seek the release of its citizens. But the price cannot be relief for a Russian oligarch sanctioned for his links to the Putin regime.”
Ukraine’s Sybiha noted that member countries could still individually push back against the transaction. “There is still a way to spoil the celebrations in Moscow, he wrote. “I urge all EU member states to announce now that they will impose their own national sanctions on these two individuals [Usmanov and Fridman].”
The Latvian PM promised Latvia would do just that, and would “continue to use all legal instruments at its disposal to prevent the release of these persons’ funds and economic resources in Latvia.”
Info impasse
A handful of countries privately expressed frustration that further information had not been provided at Coreper, the meeting of ambassadors where sanctions rollover decisions are taken.
“Ambassadors were told that there are national security reasons. Coreper is not the right place to discuss those in detail,” said a senior French diplomat who was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the sensitive discussions last week. “Member states were told a week ago that if they needed more precision, they could get it through the appropriate channels.”
Usmanov has consistently denied supporting Russia’s war effort, rejected the idea he is an oligarch, and campaigned for his removal from the sanctions list. Fridman has likewise argued the seizure of his assets is unlawful.

Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:58:30 UTC
23:58:30 KST

Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.
The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.
The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.
The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.
France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.
The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.
Goals downgraded
The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.
Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.
But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”
Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.
“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.
A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
- Published
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.
France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.
Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.
Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.
Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.
The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".
It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.
Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.
His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.
This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.
However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

Latvia gives in to France's demands to lift EU sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, diplomats say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:58:15 UTC
23:58:15 KST

EU officially extends sanctions against Russia — at cost of delisting 2 oligarchs in Putin's inner circle
Key developments:
- The European Union agreed to extend 3,000 sanctions against Russian individuals and entities for another 36 months after reaching a deal on Sept. 22.
- The agreement calls to lift sanctions against two Russian oligarchs with Kremlin ties: Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov.
- The deal came after Latvia agreed to allow the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman in order to prevent the sanctions regime from lapsing altogther.
- The push to delist Usmanov and Fridman was driven by France and Slovakia, with France's motive reportedly connected to a prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.
- Latvia will pursue its own national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman, while Ukraine has called on other EU states to follow suit.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Union on Sept. 22 finalized a deal to extend its package of sanctions against Russia for another 36 months.
In exchange for extending the 3,000 sanctions, two Russian oligarchs closely associated with Russian President Vladimir Putin have been removed from the list.
The news comes just hours after three diplomats told the Kyiv Independent that Latvia had agreed to stop opposing a plan by Slovakia and France to remove Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the EU sanctions.
"The Council decided today to prolong the restrictive measures targeting those responsible for undermining or threatening the territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence of Ukraine for another 36 months, until 22 September 2029," the Council of the European Union said in a press release announcing the agreement.
The sanctions regime includes travel restrictions, asset freezes, and economic limitations against 3,000 individuals and entities, most of them Russian.
"In the context of the sanctions' review, the Council also decided not to renew the listings of three individuals and one entity, as well as to remove three deceased persons from the list."
While the statement did not disclose the identities of the delisted persons, two of them are oligarchs Fridman and Usmanov. The identity of the third individual and the delisted entity have not been revealed.
Latvia holds out as long as it can
The Franco-Slovak push to delist Usmanov and Fridman led to a weeks-long delay in renewing the European bloc's 3,000 sanctions on Russia.
"In maintaining the (sanctions) regime we have reached a difficult compromise," said a spokesperson for the European Council Presidency.
In exchange for the delisting, EU ambassadors agreed to extend the sanctions for three years rather than the originally planned 12 months, the compromise that appeared to have been reached the previous day.
"What signal does this send? Frankly, astonishing and embarrassing," said Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk on social media.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in response to the compromise.
Sybiha called on individual EU member states to impose their own national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman in the wake of the extension deal.
All EU votes on sanctions policy require unanimity, which gave France and Slovakia leverage in securing the deal.
Initially, Latvia went public on the night of Sept. 21 to oppose the Franco-Slovak plan, with the country's Foreign Minister Baiba Braze writing on social media: "The Latvian government's stance has been unwavering. EU sanctions against Russia must be strengthened, not weakened."
That strong stance garnered the support of President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised Latvia just two hours before Riga backed down.
Now, instead of voting against the compromise, Riga will abstain, which allows the measure to go ahead but without Latvia's blessing.
"This was not a choice between a good and a bad solution, but between a bad and a much worse one," said Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs.
Three national diplomats said that they understand Belgium and Lithuania have also committed to abstaining because they do not support the move, but equally cannot allow 3,000 listings to evaporate.
Riga will also impose national sanctions against Usmanov and Fridman, according to a Latvian government press release; something which Sybiha called on other EU countries to do.
A press statement from the Estonian government confirmed that Tallinn also abstained on the vote, and that it would likewise re-sanction the two men nationally.
"Estonia did not support lifting sanctions on these two prominent Russian businessmen, as they continue to support the aggressor and contribute to its aggression," said Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna.
Earlier on Sept. 22, Latvia had demanded to postpone the decision for two weeks, so that the vote would be taken after an upcoming parliamentary election in the country, where delisting the two men would be a politically toxic move.
"Choosing to stand up for further sanctioning of these persons, we achieved a result that is more beneficial for Latvia, Ukraine and Europe in the long term," Kulbergs said.
The Latvian government press release goes on to mention a series of new commitments from France to Latvia, including the start of negotiations to join France's nuclear deterrence initiative, and to bolster France's military presence in the country, "especially in the field of air defense."
read also
The oligarchs France advocated for
The two sanctioned individuals, Fridman and Usmanov, are both considered members of Russian leader Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group, whose subsidiary provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine, and reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
The Ukrainian-born tycoon was also the owner of Sense Bank — formerly known as Alfa-Bank, one of Ukraine's largest banks — before its nationalization in 2023.
Usmanov made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Both men have repeatedly disputed the claim that they have close ties to the Kremlin.
Slovakia, has repeatedly requested the delisting of Fridman and Usmanov, but had always been unsuccessful, until France joined the push to delist Usmanov.
The Financial Times first reported that Paris wanted to delist Usmanov because Azerbaijan made it a condition for releasing two prisoners with French nationality.
Reuters reported that an Azeri diplomat confirmed they want Usmanov to be delisted, but denied trying to influence decision-making.
And national diplomats from six different countries confirmed the FT's claim to the Kyiv Independent.
Why Azerbaijan is trying to negotiate a prisoner swap with France to delist an Uzbek-Russian oligarch over any of its own sanctioned citizens or companies has not been publicly explained.
Reuters reported only that its Azeri diplomatic contact described Usmanov as a "renowned philanthropist and public figure."
With the agreement to rollover the other sanctions complete, they are expected to remain in force until at least Sept. 22, 2029.

Rasa Juknevičienė, a Member of the European Parliament and a member of the Committee on Security and Defense, spoke about this in an interview with Ukrinform.

“It's easy to promise things to people. But we should be explaining people that our future will not be the same as now, we will have no such welfare if we are small, fragmented, and weak, if Russia is next to our borders and does the same as they are doing in Ukraine . It’s important to remind this already today. I don't know if everyone can accept it because it's really difficult for many people to understand that truth,” the MEP concluded.

Amnesty urges UEFA to suspend Israel, calls Nations League participation ‘unconscionable’
