Seyma Erkul Dayanc
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
Human rights organization Amnesty International on Tuesday called on UEFA and FIFA to suspend Israel’s football association, saying its Nations League participation is “unconscionable” because of the association’s support for settlement-based clubs.
“It’s unconscionable that the Israel men’s football team will participate in the UEFA Nations League this autumn despite clear evidence that Israel’s football association continues to support illegal settlements,” Steve Cockburn, Amnesty International’s regional director for Europe, said in a statement.
“UEFA and FIFA should have suspended the Israel Football Association (IFA) over its refusal to exclude clubs based in illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories,” Cockburn said.
He said the continued participation of settlement-based clubs in Israeli leagues “violates FIFA statutes and international law.”
He added that UEFA and FIFA funding to the IFA “risks contributing to the sustainability of Israel’s illegal occupation, settlements and violations of international law.”
Israel is set to play in League B's, Group B3 alongside Austria, the Republic of Ireland and Kosovo.
The league phase begins Thursday, with Austria hosting Israel, according to UEFA.
Israel will also play the Republic of Ireland on Sept. 27 and Oct. 4, and Kosovo on Oct. 1 and Nov. 14, before hosting Austria on Nov. 17.
Amnesty said opposition to Israel’s participation has grown in Ireland, where football associations, players, activists, trade unions and politicians have called for sanctions, a boycott or suspension.
The Football Association of Ireland has also asked UEFA to consider suspending Israel, according to the rights group.
“Sport should never be used as a public relations spectacle for states committing atrocities,” Cockburn said.
“As the Israel team travels to Europe, Palestinian families are being displaced and dispossessed, their land stolen, their olive trees uprooted and their histories erased by settlers with the support of the Israeli military,” he said.
“The beautiful game should bring people together, not rubber-stamp apartheid,” Cockburn added.
Amnesty said it wrote to FIFA and UEFA in October 2025 to call for the IFA to be suspended unless clubs based in Israeli settlements were excluded from Israeli competitions.
FIFA announced in March 2026 that it would take no action against the IFA over the participation of settlement-based clubs, according to Amnesty.
The Palestinian Football Association subsequently appealed the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Russia’s Yak-130M combat trainer effectively hunts low-speed targets, such as enemy strike UAVs, thanks to the aircraft’s maneuverability at various speeds, the state corporation Rostec reported.
"Because the aircraft itself is highly maneuverable and responsive at a wide range of speeds, we have enabled it to effectively engage low-speed targets, such as enemy combat UAVs," Rostec noted.

The "heart" of the Yak-130M is the AI-222-25 turbofan engine manufactured by the United Engine Corporation (UEC). This nonafterburning turbofan produces a maximum thrust of 2.5 tons. And for flight safety, the engine’s operation is monitored by an automated control system that guarantees high reliability, Rostec stated.

Oliver Riedl called the authorities for help and a group of experts who began digging immediately discovered a total of 934 Roman silver denarii. It is the biggest coin treasure ever found in Germany from the time of the Roman emperor Hadrian, the local office in charge of archaeological monuments said on Tuesday.
“It was clear to me that there was something bigger buried here,” Riedl said, describing how his metal detector continued signalling even after he had found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne, a year ago.
The hoard of coins, which weighs 3.1kg (6.8lb), went on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn on Tuesday.
The collection was probably buried deliberately in the second quarter of the second century AD, according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland.
“Of course, we can only speculate about the motives, but it’s very likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks didn’t exist back then,” said Erich Classen, a state archaeologist and the director of the office.
Classen said it was not clear why the treasure had not been recovered, adding that “perhaps the owner died before that could happen, without being able to pass on the knowledge about the coins”.
Treasure troves from ancient Roman times or other distant eras are not uncommon. However, few from the second century are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling, the archaeological office said.
It said it was difficult to estimate the coins’ value at the time of their burial, but the pay of Roman legionaries, which is well documented in written sources, provides a point of reference.
“At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year,” said Rahel Otte, a research associate at the archaeological office. “However, about half of that was withheld for food and equipment.
“A legionary would therefore have had to save all of his disposable income for about six years to amass the Wesseling hoard,” Otte said. She added that it remained unclear exactly who ultimately amassed this considerable fortune.
The Cologne area was under Roman control roughly from 39BC to AD459. The Romans established a presence in the region under General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure their empire’s border along the Rhine River, setting up a military outpost which later became Colonia Agrippina – today’s Cologne.

Fertilizers: End the free pass for the merchants of death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:53:49 UTC
23:53:49 KST

Fertilizers: End the free pass for the merchants of death
A worker operates a crane to lift sacks of Apaviva NPK(S) phosphate fertilizer at the PhosAgro-Cherepovets fertilizer plant, operated by PhosAgro PJSC, in Cherepovets, Russia, on Dec. 2, 2021. (Andrey Rudakov / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Alan Riley
Visiting Professor at the College of Europe
Ever since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Russian fertilizer industry has had a sanctions-free pass.
One can see why such a free pass was granted. When it came to Russian fertilizer exports, both the U.S. and the EU prioritized food security. They did not want to increase food prices and reduce food security by banning Russian fertilizer.
While that was an understandable reaction, it overlooked the role that fertilizer plays in munitions production.
Fertilizer production is inherently dual-use, and in wartime it is critical. As a result, that food security free pass has enabled and enriched the Russian fertilizer industry and Russia's financial capacity to wage war.
In addition, it has provided the Russian military with the explosives it needs to continue its attacks against Ukraine. The only truly significant sanctions that have fallen on the Russian fertilizer industry are those that fall from the sky in the shape of Ukrainian drones.
The EU has only belatedly begun to limit Russian fertilizer imports, and the U.S. has no tariff or sanction regime at all on the sector.
The most significant part of the fertilizer industry, and that which makes up approximately 75% of globally traded fertilizers, is a nitrogen-based one. The ultimate source of nitrogen fertilizer is a fossil fuel, usually natural gas, which is used to produce ammonia, the base product for all nitrogen fertilizers.
However, in addition to producing fertilizers to assist food production, the ammonia-based product can be used to produce downstream chemical precursor products vital for explosives, such as nitric acid and ammonium nitrate.
During the war, these downstream products vital for explosives production have been produced in large quantities by the Russian fertilizer industry.
The two principal producers are Eurochem and Uralchecm. We know, for instance, from Reuters and Bloomberg reports that Eurochem shipped 5000 tonnes of nitric acid from its Nevinnomyssk Azot plant to the Russian munitions industry between 2022 and 2024.
To give some sense of the impact of 5000 tonnes of nitric acid, it can provide the key explosive filling ingredient for 500,000 large caliber shells.
Uralchem provided 27,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate and 6000 tonnes of nitric acid from its Bereznki plant in the same 2022-2024 period.
Toaz, which is also controlled by Uralchem, is one of the world's largest producers of ammonia, the base chemical for most explosives, and therefore, from the point of view of the Russian state, is a critical chokepoint in its explosives production supply chain.
The food security focus of European and U.S. policymakers has, until recently, led them to wholly ignore the security threat posed by the Russian fertilizer sector.
Even now, the EU has only imposed limited progressive tariffs on Russian fertilizers, which began to be imposed in mid-2025.
The U.S. situation is worse. There are still no tariffs or sanctions whatsoever on Russian fertilizers entering the U.S. While Brussels and Washington have taken a long time to recognize the security threat posed by the Russian fertilizer industry, this is not the case in Kyiv. Ukrainian drones have hit the Nevinnomyssk plant at least seven times, and the main Togliattiazot ammonia production facility controlled by Mazepin at least three times.
The sanctions regime on both Russian fertilizer executives and their companies remains fragmented to non-existent to being shot through with loopholes.
There are no corporate sanctions on the Russian fertilizer sector, and only a limited tariff regime for fertilizers entering the EU; personal sanctions remain fragmented.
It is true that various Russian actors sought to avoid sanctions. If we take the two principal owners of Eurochem and Uralchem at the onset of the war, like other owners in the sector, they had tried to reduce their nominal control of their companies to avoid sanctions.
Andrey Melnichenko at Eurochem handed his wife control of his companies via a trust, and Dmitry Mazepin at Uralchem nominally reduced his shareholding of Uralchem to 48% from 100%.
Western courts, however, have not been convinced by such mechanisms. For example, in North-West 2 v. Societe Generale, the English High Court was not particularly impressed by this "trust maneuver" and held that Melnichenko still owned and controlled Eurochem.
Still, their corporate entities have not been subject to sanctions.
It is true that both Mazepin and Melnichenko have been subject to personal sanctions. Nevertheless, those sanctions have been fragmented. So while Melnichenko is subject to U.S. and EU sanctions from a number of third states, Mazepin has been sanctioned by the EU, not the U.S.
Given their role and that of their companies in underpinning the Russian war effort, there is a compelling justification for comprehensive Western sanctions both on the individuals who ultimately control and run these companies and the companies themselves.
This argument is reinforced by their proximity to the Russian leadership. The de facto owners of Eurochem and Uralchem were at the meeting of business leaders at the Kremlin on the first day of the war, and have both been condemned by the EU courts as close to the Russian leadership.
That proximity in respect of Melnichenko is underlined by his recent article in the Economist, in which he pleaded for the West to understand Russia's legitimate concerns. An article that could not have been written and published without the highest level of clearance from within the Kremlin.
Equally, Mazepin, in his long-running ‘corporate raid’ to control and then sustain his control over the ammonia firm Togliattiazot, was only possible due to his proximity to power, which gave Mazepin his capacity to deploy state resources to carry out and sustain that raid.
It should be possible for the Western allies to ensure that comprehensive personal sanctions are imposed on the de facto owners, shareholders, board members, and managers of the Russian fertilizer sector. After all, they are collectively benefiting from the death and suffering being inflicted on Ukrainian civilians in this war.
It is admittedly more difficult to just cut off Russian fertilizer flows. However, it is possible for the West to develop alternatives both for itself and the wider world.
Critically, the key source feedstock, natural gas, exists in enormous quantities in the United States. Yet the U.S. remains a significant importer of fertilizer. The U.S. could transform fertilizer production rather like the way it went from being a net importer of liquid natural gas (LNG) to being the world's largest exporter of LNG; it has the resource base to become the world's largest fertilizer exporter.
In so doing, it would secure food supplies and push the merchants of death in the Russian fertilizer industry out of global markets.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the targeted restrictions last week against foreign nationals whom Washington says are responsible for, or complicit in, policies involving uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination and the incitement of violence against minority groups in South Africa. No individuals were named when the policy was announced.
Ramaphosa was speaking to journalists on the sidelines of the ANC Veterans League fundraising golf day at the Johannesburg Country Club in Woodmead on Monday. He said the government had taken note of the restrictions but remained prepared to engage with Washington. ”We are quite willing and prepared to continue engaging with the United States as we engage with all other countries in the world,” the president noted.
”Where there are challenges, we will go in with our dignity, with our sovereignty to engage with those countries without bowing our heads and treating those nations respectfully and expecting them to treat us also respectfully,” Ramaphosa added.
The president said the US remained an important market for South Africa and that both countries had products they needed from each other. He also said discussions between South Africa and the US had been under way for some time, including on trade and tariff issues. The US had also raised ”the so-called five issues”, and South Africa had responded to a number of them, he stressed.
Asked what had happened to the discussions, given the latest announcement, Ramaphosa answered he could not explain what had prompted the move. ”So I just don’t know what happened. Only they can answer and say what exactly happened,” he said.
Ramaphosa noted South Africa remained willing to negotiate with the US to resolve the challenges in the relationship. ”We also trade with them and there are certain things or products that they need from us that we also need from them,” he said. ”So that in itself should bring about the state of equilibrium. So as we deal with each other, as states that respect each other, we will find solutions.”

Navigating the Regulatory Framework for Anti-Wrinkle Injection Clinics Across the European Union  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:51:13 UTC
23:51:13 KST

The aesthetic medicine industry has experienced remarkable growth throughout the European Union over the past decade, with anti-wrinkle injections becoming one of the most sought-after non-surgical cosmetic procedures. As millions of Europeans seek to maintain a youthful appearance through treatments such as botulinum toxin injections and dermal fillers, the regulatory landscape governing these procedures has evolved significantly. Understanding the complex framework of rules, standards, and guidelines that govern anti-wrinkle injection clinics across the EU is essential for both practitioners and patients seeking safe, effective treatments.
1. The EU Medical Device Regulation Framework
At the heart of anti-wrinkle injection regulation in the European Union lies the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) 2017/745, which came into full application in May 2021. This comprehensive regulatory framework classifies most injectable products used in aesthetic medicine, including dermal fillers, as medical devices. The regulation establishes stringent requirements for the safety, performance, and quality of these products before they can be marketed within the EU.
Under the MDR, manufacturers must demonstrate that their products meet essential safety and performance requirements through rigorous clinical evaluation and conformity assessment procedures. Products must bear the CE marking, indicating compliance with EU legislation, before they can be legally placed on the market. This harmonised approach across member states aims to ensure a consistently high level of patient safety whilst facilitating the free movement of medical devices throughout the single market.
Botulinum toxin products, however, fall under a different regulatory category. These are classified as prescription-only medicines and are governed by pharmaceutical legislation, including the centralised authorisation procedure overseen by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). This distinction is crucial, as it subjects these products to even more stringent pre-market approval processes, including extensive clinical trials and ongoing pharmacovigilance requirements.
2. Professional Qualifications and Training Standards
Whilst the EU has harmonised product regulations, the requirements for practitioners administering anti-wrinkle injections vary considerably across member states. Each country retains the authority to determine which healthcare professionals may perform these procedures and what level of training they must possess.
In most EU countries, medical doctors are permitted to administer anti-wrinkle injections, though some nations extend this privilege to dentists, nurses, and other healthcare professionals under specific conditions. The United Kingdom, before Brexit, required practitioners to be registered healthcare professionals, and many EU countries have adopted similar frameworks. Countries such as France and Germany maintain particularly strict requirements, generally limiting these procedures to qualified medical practitioners or those working under direct medical supervision.
The European Committee for Medical Laser Applications (ECMLA) and other professional bodies have advocated for standardised training programmes across the EU, recognising that the quality and safety of aesthetic procedures depend heavily on the skill and knowledge of practitioners. Many member states now require practitioners to complete specialised training in aesthetic medicine, covering topics such as facial anatomy, injection techniques, complication management, and patient assessment.
3. Clinic Licensing and Operational Standards
The establishment and operation of anti-wrinkle injection clinics within the EU are subject to national healthcare regulations, which can vary significantly between member states. Most countries require clinics offering injectable aesthetic treatments to register with relevant health authorities and comply with specific operational standards.
These standards typically encompass requirements for clinical premises, hygiene protocols, equipment standards, patient record-keeping, and emergency preparedness. Many jurisdictions mandate that clinics maintain appropriate resuscitation equipment and that staff receive training in managing potential complications such as allergic reactions or vascular occlusion.
In Ireland, for instance, clinics such as Facial Rejuve in Dublin must adhere to strict healthcare standards whilst operating within a regulatory environment that is continuously evolving to address the growth in aesthetic medicine. Several EU countries have implemented inspection regimes to ensure ongoing compliance with established standards, recognising that regular oversight is essential to maintaining patient safety.
4. Advertising and Marketing Regulations
The promotion of aesthetic medicine services is subject to stringent regulation across the European Union, with member states imposing various restrictions on how clinics may advertise anti-wrinkle injection treatments. These regulations aim to protect consumers from misleading claims and ensure that marketing communications are responsible and accurate.
The EU's Unfair Commercial Practices Directive provides a baseline framework prohibiting misleading and aggressive commercial practices, which applies to the advertising of aesthetic treatments. Additionally, many countries have specific rules governing healthcare advertising, often requiring that promotional materials be factual, balanced, and not exploit patients' anxieties about their appearance.
Several member states restrict the use of before-and-after photographs in advertising, recognising the potential for such images to create unrealistic expectations or fail to represent typical results. Others require that any marketing claims about treatment efficacy be substantiated by appropriate clinical evidence. Practitioners and clinics found to breach advertising regulations may face sanctions ranging from warnings to fines or restrictions on their ability to practise.
5. Patient Consent and Information Requirements
Informed consent has become a cornerstone of aesthetic medicine regulation throughout the EU, with increasing emphasis placed on ensuring patients understand the nature, risks, and limitations of anti-wrinkle injection treatments before proceeding. This aligns with broader principles of medical ethics and patients' rights enshrined in EU law.
Most member states require practitioners to provide patients with comprehensive written information about proposed treatments, including details of the products to be used, potential side effects, alternative options, and realistic expectations regarding outcomes. Patients must typically be given adequate time to consider this information before treatment, and their consent must be documented.
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) also significantly impacts how clinics handle patient information, requiring robust data protection measures and clear policies regarding the collection, storage, and use of personal health data. Clinics must ensure that patient records are maintained securely and that data processing complies with GDPR principles.
6. Emerging Regulatory Trends and Future Developments
The regulatory landscape for anti-wrinkle injection clinics in the EU continues to evolve in response to the sector's growth and emerging safety concerns. Several member states have recently strengthened their regulatory frameworks, introducing more rigorous requirements for practitioners, clinics, and product manufacturers.
There is growing momentum towards greater harmonisation of standards across the EU, particularly regarding practitioner qualifications and training requirements. Professional organisations and regulatory bodies increasingly recognise that the current patchwork of national regulations can create inconsistencies in patient safety standards and complicate cross-border practice.
The European Commission has signalled its commitment to enhancing consumer protection in aesthetic medicine, with discussions ongoing about potential EU-level initiatives to establish minimum standards for non-surgical cosmetic procedures. These developments may include requirements for practitioner registration, standardised training curricula, and enhanced reporting systems for adverse events.
Additionally, increased scrutiny of social media marketing and the influence of non-medical aesthetics providers has prompted calls for stronger enforcement of existing regulations and the development of new rules addressing the unique challenges posed by digital platforms and mobile treatment providers.
7. Conclusion
The regulatory framework governing anti-wrinkle injection clinics across the European Union represents a complex interplay of harmonised product regulations and diverse national requirements for practice standards, professional qualifications, and clinic operations. Whilst the EU's Medical Device Regulation provides a consistent foundation for product safety, significant variation persists in how member states regulate practitioners and clinics offering these increasingly popular treatments.
For patients, understanding this regulatory landscape is crucial to making informed decisions about where and from whom to seek treatment. Reputable clinics operating within robust regulatory frameworks offer the greatest assurance of safety and quality. As the aesthetic medicine sector continues to grow, ongoing regulatory development and enhanced enforcement will be essential to protecting patient welfare whilst supporting the legitimate practice of aesthetic medicine throughout the European Union.

Old-age retirement at 67 years, six months in 2029 - State General Accounting Office
Italy

16:50:43 CEST
23:50:43 KST

Mandatory old-age retirement in Italy
will rise to 67 years and six months in 2029, the State General
Accounting Office (RGS) said Tuesday.
                                    
                                       
				In 2029, the age for old-age retirement will be 67 and a half,
while in 2031, it will rise to 67 years and 8 months, according
to estimates by RGS regarding "Medium- to long-term trends in
the pension and health/social care systems." To qualify for
early retirement—regardless of age—individuals will need 43
years and four months of pension contributions in 2029, and 43
years and six months in 2031 (one year less for women).
                                    
                                       
				In 2027, the old-age retirement age will be 67 years and one
month, rising to 67 years and three months in 2028. For early
retirement, 42 years and 11 months of contributions will be
required in 2027, and 43 years and one month in 2028.

EU agrees to lift sanctions on Russian oligarchs in ‘shameful’ compromise deal

- Ukraine condemned the decision as "shameful and unjustifiable," urging EU members to impose national sanctions on the two oligarchs.
- The deal avoids sanctions lapsing, includes over 3,000 individuals like Putin, and was influenced by political pressures and potential prisoner release negotiations.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - EU countries on Sept 22 agreed a compromise deal to prolong sanctions on Russia that will see oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov removed from the blacklist, diplomats said.
As time ticked down to a deadline, diplomats said that Latvia agreed to drop its veto after days of bitter opposition to efforts to secure the exemptions led by France.
Ukraine has lashed out against the push to remove the asset freezes and visa bans on the two billionaires, arguing the European Union should instead be ratcheting up pressure on Moscow.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha afterwards called the EU’s move “shameful and unjustifiable” and called on EU countries to impose “national” sanctions on Usmanov and Fridman.
“Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans,” Sybiha said on social media. “But there is still a way to spoil the celebrations in Moscow. I urge all EU member states to announce now that they will impose their own national sanctions on these two individuals.”
The agreement sees the EU’s sanctions on some 3,000 other individuals and entities over the war in Ukraine extended for three years.
The list includes Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The compromise will involve an extension of the regime for 36 months, until Sept 22, 2029,” a spokesman for Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, said.
“The decision was also taken to delist certain individuals under the regime.”
EU countries had been wrangling furiously after France joined Slovakia in demanding Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov be removed from the blacklist.
Luxembourg then seized upon the demand by Paris to insist that if sanctions were lifted on Usmanov, then they should be lifted for Fridman as well.
Officials in Paris have cited “national security” concerns for their request on Usmanov, but refused publicly to give details.
A senior diplomat in Brussels told AFP that Paris explained the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg has pushed for Fridman to be removed. Diplomats said the move comes as he is suing the country for €15 billion (S$21 billion) for freezing his assets under EU sanctions.
The demand from France in particular riled other EU member states who argue that removing people for political reasons sets a dangerous precedent.
“It really sends the signal that you can blackmail your way to delisting,” said one EU diplomat talking on condition of anonymity. “It’s shocking that France is the one blocking it all.”
The Kremlin seized on the EU standoff to say it backed taking Usmanov and Fridman off the blacklist, and that the bloc should lift sanctions on “all Russian businessmen”.
‘Need stability’
Without the agreement, the EU risked seeing the sanctions lapse.
Now the agreement to prolong the sanctions for 36 months - up from the previous six-month extensions - means the EU should skip this particular headache for the forseeable future.
EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas insisted that the bloc needed “stability” by settling the future of its sanctions.
Metals tycoon Usmanov and banking magnate Fridman are among dozens of Russian businessmen suing the EU over the sanctions.
Both were added to the sanctions list after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 over allegations that their businesses provided significant revenues to the Kremlin. AFP

Russia is holding Ukraine’s south with convicts: 69 percent have records. And they’re fighting where civilians live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:49:20 UTC
23:49:20 KST

More than two-thirds of the Russian soldiers holding the Zaporizhzhia front carry criminal records. Ukraine's "South" grouping says a third of them enlisted to escape prosecution, most are over 30, and no fresh reinforcements are arriving, spokesperson Anastasia Shevchenko told Ukrinform.
The reasons they signed up track with that: 31 percent enlisted to dodge criminal liability, 24 percent for money, 26 percent on ordinary contracts, and 13 percent through mobilization. It is Russia's prison pipeline in a single snapshot, a model that has pulled well over 100,000 inmates into the war with pardons and suspended sentences and thrown many of them at Ukrainian lines in disposable assault waves.
"It is worth noting that 69 percent of the Russian personnel have a criminal record," Shevchenko said.
The model dates to Wagner's prison recruiting in 2022 and has run under the Defense Ministry since.
A middle-aged force holds the line
The men are not young. More than a third, 36 percent, are between 31 and 40; another 24 percent are 41 to 50; 31 percent are 21 to 30; and just 9 percent are 20 or under.
This is a force of grown men with records, not fresh conscripts, and it points to who Russia can still find willing to fight in the south: people with little to lose and a sentence to escape among Ukrainian civilians, women and children.
The prison pipeline runs dry
What Shevchenko did not report is any sign of that force being rebuilt. Russia has enough men and equipment to keep fighting on the Zaporizhzhia front, she says, but no substantial replenishment is coming.
That fits a wider problem for Russia: its supply of convict recruits is thinning as word of the front's lethality spreads through the prisons, with some inmates now signing military contracts only to bolt on the way to the front, in one case killing their escort to get away.
Russia's practice of replenishing its ranks from prisons is breaking down, and officials are resorting to ever more coercive measures to keep the flow going.

Irish athletes sign open letter urging national soccer team to boycott Israel matches

Both games are being played without fans in neutral countries after protests by both players and supporters in Ireland against the civilian death toll of Palestinians in Gaza.
The activist group Irish Sport for Palestine said Monday in a social media post that more than 160 Irish sportspeople had signed a letter to the Irish senior men's soccer team "urging them to act collectively with conscience & refuse to participate in their upcoming games against Israel."
This comes after the Israeli Football Association slammed Irish head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson for comments he made at a press conference last week.
Hallgrímsson was asked by reporters whether it would be difficult to keep his players focused on football during the upcoming games against Israel given the public outcry in Ireland.
"We are not playing with genocide, we are playing against genocide," he said. "We are playing against Israel; we are not playing with Israel."
Those remarks drew a strong rebuke by the Israeli football association in a social media post on Monday.
"We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way. Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach," the post read. "We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, We're playing against the coach who embodies them."
The Irish government has been one of the most vocal critics of the Israeli government in recent years over its military action in Gaza and diplomatic tensions between the two countries have reached a boiling point over the past two years.
Israel shut down its embassy in Dublin in December 2024 over what Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said was the country's "extreme anti-Israel policies."
"The actions and antisemitic rhetoric used by Ireland against Israel are rooted in the de-legitimisation and demonisation of the Jewish state, along with double standards," Saar said in a statement at the time.
The announcement had followed Ireland's announcement of its support for South Africa's legal action against Israel in the International Court of Justice, which accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The Irish government would later formally join South Africa's legal case against Israel at the ICJ.
Members of the Irish football association also passed a vote last year requesting UEFA, European soccer's governing body, suspend Israel from its competitions.
But in a statement earlier this summer, members of the Football Association Ireland reiterated the Irish men's soccer team would fulfil its obligations to play Israel in UEFA qualifying games.
"While acknowledging the strength of feeling regarding support for Palestine and the upcoming UEFA Men's Nations League fixtures … the members recognise the profound impact that any non-fulfilment of UEFA fixtures would have on Irish football as a whole and on its future development, and accordingly endorses the Association fulfilling its obligations in respect of those fixtures," the statement said.

The food was barely edible, there was mould on the detention walls, and medical care was non-existent, he said.
The Winnipeg-born Canadian was actually forced to endure the conditions twice. ICE agents took him into custody in October 2025. Herman entered the US legally 20 years ago but overstayed his visa and was forced to report to ICE at regular intervals since 2022. Then he was put in the detention center in October 2025.
Herman, who has not been convicted of any criminal offense, was ordered released by the judge in June, he was taken into ICE custody again five weeks later. The second arrest occurred when a document appealing his deportation was delayed in the mail, he said.
His troubles are not over.
Herman said he has no job and no identification, and was forced to hand over his Global Affairs Canada emergency travel document upon arrival at the Vancouver airport Aug. 26.
Even so, he is relieved that his now free and back in Canada.
“It's better than being in that inhumane conditions of that filthy, concrete, razor-wired blockhouse down south.”

Why are the Houthis fighting for Yemen’s Kahboub Mountains?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:47:25 UTC
23:47:25 KST

Why are the Houthis fighting for Yemen’s Kahboub Mountains?
Kahboub could help the Houthis consolidate control near one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
The Houthis are attempting to push into the Kahboub Mountains after seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive this month – an advance that experts say could dramatically shift the balance of power in the country’s war if successful.
The renewed fighting in recent months with forces aligned with Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government has brought an end to the relative calm that had largely held since 2022. In recent days, the conflict has moved into the rugged highlands overlooking the approaches to Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump-GCC Summit in New York: What does each side want?
- list 2 of 3Who actually has power at the United Nations?
- list 3 of 3La Liga President Tebas slams Real Madrid refereeing ‘conspiracy’ claims
The strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, and its importance is only growing as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted by the Houthis’ main ally: Iran.
Experts said taking the high ground would help the Houthis defend the newly captured coastline and make it far harder for government forces to push them back. While the mountains may not necessarily be used as a launchpad for attacks on ships, controlling them would provide defensive depth and cover for Houthi positions closer to the coast, making missile and drone operations in the Red Sea easier to sustain and harder to disrupt.
The Houthis have said they do not intend to target United States shipping and attacks would be limited to vessels linked to Saudi Arabia. But the group has repeatedly attacked ships in the Red Sea in previous years, including vessels with no clear connection to its stated targets.
The Houthi advance has taken on added urgency after The New York Times reported that US President Donald Trump came close to ordering air attacks against the Houthis on Sunday, only to call them off at the last minute. Britain, meanwhile, said it will support Saudi Arabia with defensive refuelling.
Why is Kahboub strategically important?
Kahboub, a mountainous region spanning parts of the Lahj and Taiz governorates in southern Yemen, derives much of its strategic importance from its proximity to Bab al-Mandeb. Some of its heights lie about 40km (25 miles) from the waterway, providing commanding views across a stretch of the Red Sea, through which a significant share of global maritime trade and millions of barrels of oil pass each day.
While that vantage point has considerable military value, experts said the mountains are unlikely to serve directly as a launchpad for attacks in the Red Sea. Their more immediate importance for the Houthis lies in securing the territory the group has already captured.
“The mountains are the natural wall that protects the Houthis’ rear on the coast. Controlling them would cut the coast off from the government-held south and place direct pressure on Lahj and, in the longer term, Aden,” Faozi Al-Goidi, a visiting fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera.
Securing their rear would help the Houthis prevent government forces from attacking their coastal positions from behind or severing the routes connecting their newly captured territory. Until the high ground is secured, Houthi forces stationed along the Red Sea remain vulnerable to attacks from government-held areas to the south and east.
Capturing the elevated positions, therefore, would make Kahboub less important as a potential launchpad for maritime attacks than as a defensive shield for the Houthis’ military gains along the coast.
Ewa K Strzelecka, a visiting senior fellow at the London School of Economics, told Al Jazeera that controlling the coastline, Mayyun Island and the neighbouring highlands would give the Houthis “strategic resilience”.
“Holding the coastline, Mayyun and the adjacent highlands together would give the Houthis a much deeper and more defensible position around one of the world’s principal maritime chokepoints,” she said.
Those positions would allow the Houthis to move fighters, weapons and supplies along the coast with less risk of their routes being severed from behind.
“From the high ground, the Houthis could monitor movements along the coast, around Mayyun Island and towards the chokepoint while protecting missile, drone and potentially unmanned-boat infrastructure positioned farther inland,” Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.
The battle is already proving slower than the Houthis’ rapid advance across the coastal plains. Footage circulated on X by the Taiz Military Axis Command’s media centre appears to show intense fighting between forces aligned with the Yemeni government, local fighters and the Houthis on mountain fronts. The footage could not be independently verified by Al Jazeera.
“This is not an easy battle,” said Mohammed al-Basha, an analyst and a former spokesperson for Yemen’s embassy in Washington. “The fighting is taking place across some of Yemen’s most unforgiving terrain where control of a single hilltop or mountain peak can come at a heavy cost.”
Could the Houthis isolate Taiz by controlling Kahboub?
Control of Kahboub could also place greater pressure on Taiz, a symbolically and strategically important city, as the Taiz governorate forms a bridge between the Houthi-held north and the government-held south and the Red Sea coast. Whoever controls it gains the upper hand in the movement of weapons and supplies between the interior and the southern port city of Aden. Losing it, therefore, could deal a serious blow to the government.
Murad Al-Arefi, an editor at the Sana’a Center, told Al Jazeera that taking Kahboub would “increase pressure on the southern and western approaches to Taiz” although he cautioned that it should not yet be seen as evidence of a broader attempt to encircle the city.
The immediate threat to the Taiz-Aden connection is less direct because Kahboub does not itself sit across the route. “What matters is whether the Houthis can subsequently push farther east through Al-Wazi’iyah and towards the Al-Turbah-Lahj axis, which would place much greater pressure on the southern approaches to Taiz and potentially weaken its connection with Aden,” Strzelecka said.
A further advance, therefore, could leave government forces defending several mountain fronts simultaneously while relying on fewer secure routes to move troops, weapons and supplies, leaving Taiz increasingly exposed. One of Yemen’s largest population centres, Taiz became an important centre of resistance to the Houthis after they seized Sanaa in 2014, and was besieged by the rebel group for years. A major Houthi breakthrough there, therefore, would carry symbolic significance far beyond the territory captured.
What could it mean for Red Sea shipping?
Officially, the Houthis have said their current restrictions in Bab al-Mandeb would apply only to Saudi-linked shipping.
But during its previous Red Sea campaign, the group struck or endangered ships with no clear connection to Israel – their purported target during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – raising questions about how narrowly any new restrictions would be applied. Seizing the Kahboub Mountains would further strengthen the Houthis’ position by helping them secure the coastline overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and making it harder for their opponents to push them back.
Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that the offensive showed the Houthis using their momentum to capture more territory, weaken their opponents and “dominate Yemen further”.
“This is the Houthis trying to seize more ground and diminish the capacity of their enemies while increasing their strategic ability to close Bab al-Mandeb,” Mabon said.

EU renews Russia sanctions but removes Usmanov at France's request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:47:22 UTC
23:47:22 KST

France succeeded in its push to remove Alisher Usmanov from the EU sanctions list as part of a prisoner release with Azerbaijan. A second high-profile businessman, Mikhail Fridman, was also removed.
The European Union has agreed to remove Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list after fraught negotiations that saw France link his delisting to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan, unsettling Brussels.
A second Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, was also removed after Slovakia vetoed his continued listing, several diplomats told Euronews.
Luxembourg had argued that if Usmanov was removed, Fridman should be too. Fridman has filed a $16 billion claim against Luxembourg over his frozen assets.
As a result of the changes, the asset freeze and the travel ban will be lifted.
Ambassadors sealed the compromise on Tuesday after two weeks of drawn-out talks that brought the bloc's sanctions regime to the brink of collapse.
Latvia held up the processon Monday, warning it was not the right time to ease pressure on Moscow. The Baltic country relented on Tuesday afternoon and opted for a constructive abstention, enabling the necessary unanimity.
As a way to offset the pain of delisting the two high-profile businessmen, the EU has extended its individual sanctions on Russia for an unprecedented 36 months.
Previously, the measures were renewed every six months, giving member states regular opportunities to seek concessions.
The sanctions list currently includes more than 2,600 people, organisations and entities accused of supporting Russia's war in Ukraine, including President Vladimir Putin.
"Today's decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework," said a spokesperson for the Irish presidency of the EU Council, which chaired the talks.
The spokesperson admitted the resolution was "difficult".
While the compromise keeps sanctions in place for much longer and shields them from unexpected vetoes in the future, the removal of two prominent Russian figures has enraged Kyiv, which vocally opposed the move.
As negotiations neared the final stage, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly called on the bloc to keep Usmanov and Fridman on the blacklist.
His message thanked Latvia for its opposition.
"The world needs not a political delisting, but timely and unconditional rollover of individual sanctions, until Moscow engages in serious peace negotiations and takes concrete steps to end its war against Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.
"This is the shortest path to peace we all are striving for. Every Ukrainian family is counting on EU unity and solidarity."
The appeals, though, failed to swing the balance in the room. Member states quickly realised that France had invested too much political capital and would refuse to give up its demand on Usmanov, regardless of the controversy.
"No one is happy about this," a diplomat said. "But the consensus in the room was that it's better to maintain the rest of the listings under the regime and make sure we don't have to do this circus again any time soon."
Uzbek-French deal
The EU sanctioned Usmanov in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, citing his "close ties" to Russian President Vladimir Putin and interests in "key sectors" of the Russian economy that provide "substantial" revenue to the state.
The 73-year-old businessman, whose fortune is estimated at $16.6 billion, has denied the allegations and challenged the sanctions.
Uzbekistan, alongside other Turkic states, has lobbied the EU institutions and several member states for two years to have Usmanov removed from the blacklist.
Euronews understands that Uzbek and French authorities reached a behind-the-scenes agreement under which Azerbaijan would release two French nationals from prison in return for Usmanov's delisting.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev would issue a pardon as part of the deal.
France has not confirmed the arrangement. French officials have only cited a "national security" issue and declined to provide further details, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the negotiations.
Since September 2024, Paris has warned against travel to Azerbaijan over the "risk of arrest, arbitrary detention and unfair trial".
"In the event of arrest or detention, respect for fundamental rights is not guaranteed," the French foreign ministry says in a travel notice that remains in force.
Last year, an Azerbaijani court sentenced French water-management executive Anass Derraz to 12 years in prison for accepting a bribe in 2018 from an Azerbaijani-Russian businessman in connection with efforts to free an impounded yacht.
Earlier this year, French national Martin Ryan was sentenced to 10 years in prison in Azerbaijan for spying on the military and collecting secret information for the French government. Ryan and Paris strongly contested the charges.
France updated its travel advisory in April following Ryan's sentence.

Fake passport images claim Zelenskyy and family chose Israel as homeland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:47:10 UTC
23:47:10 KST

A photo amassing thousands of views on social media allegedly shows a scan of Zelenskyy's passport, with Israel as his homeland. Not only are the allegations false, but they've been doing the rounds since 2023.
A fake photo circulating online of two alleged Israeli passports belonging to Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, allegedly shows that the Ukrainian president and his family have chosen Israel as their homeland instead of Ukraine.
The Facebook post was published at the beginning of September alongside the caption: "You can twist it any way you like, but we always come back to the same point: Zelenskyy and his family have a homeland of choice that inspires, protects and supports him in everything he does, and that homeland is certainly not Ukraine. This is common knowledge, just as it is common knowledge who his backers are at the top of the Ukrainian establishment, but people prefer to turn a blind eye so as not to disturb those pulling the strings. Shalom."
There is no truth behind these claims. The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, contacted Ukrainian official sources who denied them.
Furthermore, Ukrainian public officials are not permitted to hold multiple citizenships, unlike members of the general public, under a recent law which officially came into effect in January of this year.
Additionally, the false passport belonging to Zelenska lists the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic as her place of birth. This is inaccurate, as official identity documents issued for individuals born in Ukraine before independence routinely list Ukraine rather than the defunct Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, which was one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union from 1922 until 1991.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, also ran it through the image detector Hive Moderation, which revealed it to be AI-generated.
The fake passport appears to have been created based on a sample template published on the Council of Europe website.
Fake Zelenskyy passports resurfaced
It's not the first time false passports attributed to Zelenskyy and Zelenska have circulated online.
In April 2026, an image of an alleged Israeli passport of Zelenskyy was shared on Instagram, X and Facebook, gathering thousands of views, likes and reshares.
These posts claimed that the Ukrainian president was an agent for Israel's intelligence agency, whose main mission was "to Ukrainianise Europe and lead it to its own self-destruction".
In addition to a significant portion of the passport being cropped in the image, there is a spelling error in Zelenskyy's name.
According to the president's official website, his last name is stylised as "Zelenskyy" in English, not "Zelensky", as the alleged passport shows.
In fact, stories about Zelenskyy and Zelenska's alleged passport have been doing the rounds since at least 2023.
For instance, a photo of the first lady was shared on pro-Russian channels and in several Facebook posts.
In one of these posts, the caption can read: "While Ukrainian President Zelensky travels the world begging for money and weapons for his war, his wife spent a lovely vacation in Israel and even obtained an Israeli passport. Interestingly, is Mrs Zelensky preparing for a possible escape from Ukraine?"
All of these posts follow the same playbook: use an AI-generated passport to invent a scandal with some real elements to target Ukraine and undermine support from its allies, as Russia's war against the country continues.
These techniques are common tactics used among pro-Russian networks in their disinformation campaigns.
The posts about the alleged Israeli passports stand at odds with one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's supposed justifications for his full-scale invasion: when it began in February 2022, Putin pledged to oversee the "demilitarisation and de-Nazification" of Ukraine.
However, as the grandson of a Holocaust survivor, Zelenskyy has Jewish origins and has previously addressed the series of attacks on his religious background by the Kremlin.
"How can I be a Nazi?" Zelenskyy said in 2022, just before the full-scale invasion, in a video address directed at the Russian people in the Russian language. "Explain it to my grandfather, who went through the entire war in the infantry of the Soviet army, and died a colonel in an independent Ukraine."

Swiss passport does not guarantee visa-free entry everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:45:00 UTC
23:45:00 KST

Swiss passport does not guarantee visa-free entry everywhere
The Swiss passport takes 9th place in a global ranking, with 119 visa-free destinations and 54 countries requiring a visa on arrival or other entry formalities for Swiss citizens. A standard visa is required for 25 destinations.
There are no downsides for European destinations, according to the Passport Reports ranking published on Tuesday. As such, Swiss nationals can visit 44 European destinations without a visa. For Russia, a visa on arrival is required, and for the United Kingdom, an electronic travel authorisation is required.
The situation is also favourable for travel to North and South America, the Gulf states and the Caribbean. These destinations are all accessible either visa-free, with a visa on arrival or with an electronic travel authorisation.
In Oceania, the Swiss passport offers an overall access rate of nearly 93%, including visas on arrival and electronic travel authorisations. In Asia, this rate stands at 82%; in the Middle East, 82.4%; in Central Asia, 80%; and in Africa, 72.2%.
More
Born abroad? How to keep your Swiss citizenship
At European level, however, the Swiss passport ranks only 13th out of 47. Ahead of Switzerland are European Union countries such as Spain, Luxembourg, Belgium, France, Italy, Germany and Greece, as well as countries in Northern Europe. The differences in terms of the number of visa-free destinations and visa requirements are, however, minimal.
Singapore tops the list
Globally, according to the passport rankings, Singapore tops the list with 129 visa-free destinations, followed by the United Arab Emirates with 128. Afghanistan occupies the bottom place in the ranking, behind Syria and other countries in the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia. From Afghanistan, only three countries are accessible without a visa.
Conversely, Switzerland applies stricter entry requirements than it faces itself. In the hospitality ranking, Switzerland is in 92nd place out of the 199 countries surveyed. This means that nationals of many countries, where Swiss nationals are welcomed without difficulty, require a visa to enter Switzerland.

Passport Reports presents itself as an independent platform, with no links to any government or official body. Its aim is to present complex data on entry requirements for countries in the form of a clear and practical reference guide.

Egypt is increasing wheat purchases from France as it diversifies away from Russia and Ukraine, Reuters reported on 20 September, citing remarks made that Sunday by the country's Supply Minister Sherif Farouk, as quoted by television host Ahmed Moussa and confirmed afterwards by a ministry spokesperson.
Russian and Ukrainian strikes on each other's shipping are disrupting Black Sea trade routes used by both major wheat exporters, pushing up shipping costs and forcing grain buyers to navigate longer and more expensive alternatives. For Ukraine, a disrupted sea route means fewer or more expensive grain exports, putting pressure on farmers' incomes and the country's export earnings.
Egypt is one of the world's biggest wheat importers, and the grain feeds a subsidized bread program that tens of millions of Egyptians rely on. The supply minister also said Cairo had a 50,000-metric-ton wheat shipment en route from France, with further shipments from the country continuing, and that Egypt has stepped up its engagement with Bulgaria and Romania. Its wheat reserves cover more than six months of strategic consumption, he said.
War-risk costs climb as the high-risk zone widens
Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other's commercial shipping, and London's marine insurers widened the area they treat as high risk to the whole Black Sea. The Joint War Committee, which sets that listing for the Lloyd's market, extended its reporting requirements to the entire sea, and its guidance shapes what underwriters charge. War-risk premiums have surged as dozens of ships have been attacked in the Black Sea, and are adding hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost of every seven-day voyage.
Russia was continuing attempts to destroy Ukraine's transport infrastructure and block its exports through the Black Sea, Ukrzaliznytsia said on 30 July. More than 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports were shipped from ports in Odesa Oblast through a maritime corridor.
Ukraine's export capacity falls after July strikes
Following Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports on 10–12 July, the deepwater terminals' monthly handling capacity fell by about 2.5 million tons, from up to seven million to four or five, Barva Invest's Bohdan Kostetskyi said at the time. Industry sources told Reuters that four of 13 major terminals had stopped buying grain.
By mid-August, Ukrainian attacks and the suspension of navigation in the Sea of Azov since July had taken more than 90% of Russia's grain export capacity in the Azov–Black Sea basin offline, agricultural consultancy SovEcon said. Three Novorossiysk terminals were suspended, while the Taman terminal had halted operations in late July.
The Danube detour takes longer and costs more
Two vessels sailing from Izmail to Egypt took 26 days and an estimated 32 to 33 days, and a third bound for Izmir 28 to 29 days, against about 12 days for the Egypt run before the delays, Avalon Shipping operations manager Kateryna Kononenko told Ukrainian Shipping Magazine.

Pakistan must take credible action on crossborder terror before world believes it: MEA

India slams Pakistan over Permanent Court of Arbitration ruling
NEW DELHI: Pakistan needs to take credible action against cross-border terrorism before the world can believe what it says, the ministry of external affairs said on Tuesday, while hitting out at Islamabad over its claims regarding a recent decision by the Permanent Court of Arbitration.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal accused Pakistan of “misrepresenting facts” and spreading “falsehoods” as part of its propaganda.“Pakistan has a habit of misrepresenting facts and propagating falsehoods to serve its malicious propaganda,” Jaiswal said.“For starters, the so-called ruling is not a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration, as sought to be projected by the Pakistan minister. It is a ruling by an illegally constituted court. We see this as just one more attempt by Pakistan at distorting the reality,” he added.Jaiswal was responding to a question about Pakistan circulating a letter to the president of the UN Security Council regarding recent rulings related to the Permanent Court of Arbitration.His comments also came days after Pakistan increased the reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) chief Masood Azhar.
India had last week described Pakistan's PKR 70 lakh reward for information on Azhar as a “phoney” move and asked Islamabad to take concrete action against the JeM chief.The Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed has been linked to several major terror attacks in India, including the 2001 Parliament attack and the attacks in Pathankot and Pulwama.The group was founded by most-wanted terrorist Masood Azhar.New Delhi has repeatedly called on Pakistan to take credible action against crossborder terrorism, saying Islamabad's actions would be a key test of the credibility of its claims.
India seeks constructive ties with Bangladesh
On India-Bangladesh relations, Jaiswal said New Delhi wants positive and constructive ties with Dhaka.“India seeks positive, constructive and forward-looking ties with Bangladesh,” he said.
275 Indians missing in Nepal
On Indians missing in Nepal floods, Jaiswal said an Indian forensic team was working with Nepalese authorities to identify those still unaccounted for.“As I told you last time, we had given you a figure of 275 Indian nationals who were missing. Over and above that, several other people from the Indian diaspora and persons of Indian origin are also missing,” he said.“We have a forensic team in Nepal that is working in Kathmandu in several laboratories along with their Nepali colleagues,” Jaiswal said.He said the Indian team was working on 3,000 samples and had so far arrived at more than 1,200 DNA profiles.“The work is going on, and regarding the missing Indian nationals and missing persons, we await to hear from the Nepali authorities,” he said.
India reiterates dialogue, diplomacy on Ukraine
On the Ukraine conflict, Jaiswal said external affairs minister S Jaishankar met Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Monday and discussed recent developments.“Yes, the external affairs minister met with the Ukrainian foreign minister yesterday. During the meeting, he discussed the recent developments in the conflict,” Jaiswal said.
Jaishankar reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution.“The external affairs minister once again put forth India's point that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution,” Jaiswal said.“India, as you know, is in touch with both sides, Ukraine and Russia, and we have told them that if there is any way that India can contribute, India is ready to do so,” he added.

Trump addresses UN General Assembly amid Iran war and tensions with allies – live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:39:27 UTC
23:39:27 KST

Trump defends actions in Iran and Venezuela in UN General Assembly address amid rising tensions with allies – live
Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran and ‘drive them into Hell’ if there isn’t a deal, while also underscoring US policy on Cuba, Mexico, Greenland and AI
Trump opened his speech to the UN by commemorating the nation’s 250th anniversary and focusing not on international issues, but touting his domestic record. Tax cuts, stock market highs, crime rates, and immigration enforcement, to name a few.
He once againframed the war he launched on Iran earlier this year with Israel the same way he has to his domestic audience — as a necessary conflict to addressing a long-ignored threat. The United States, Trump said, had acted to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, while other countries ignored the issue.
Trump then re-issued his threat to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into Hell” if the regime didn’t capitulate and make a deal.” He touted his version of the war: one in which the US had defanged Iran militarily and driven the country to the brink of economic collapse. And hedged by saying he was confident Iran would make a deal after the US midterm elections – an argument he’s made to US voters.
Trump said he was “working closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine” to end the disastrous war. “It’s going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand,” he said. The US president said he had signed into law “a powerful new law” on sanctions, and “if necessary, I will have to use them.” He added: “It’s time to stop the killing.”
Trump defended his administration’s actions in Latin America – including the midnight raid to arrest former Venezuelan president Nicólas Maduro, and the oil deal he struck with his more US-friendly successor, Delcy Rodriguez. “To the victor belong the spoils,” Trump declared, justifying the deal that will funnel a share of the nation’s immense oil wealth into the US treasury.
Defending his drone strikes on boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, Trump equated the cartels he claims to be fighting with Islamist terrorist organizations. “The cartels are the ISIS of the western Hemisphere – not good people,” he said. “Like ISIS, they should be killed, exiled or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release, which is what we’re doing.”
He accused Mexico of being effectively controlled by the cartels, and said it was “unacceptable” for the US to share a border with a nation under such conditions. “So Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” Trump said.
Trump also pointed to regime change in Cuba. “My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba, where the communist regime is under great pressure, the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under,” he said. “It’s an absolutely failed state. It’s failing.”
Trump said the US has reached “an unprecedented agreement” on Greenland, with the Kingdom of Denmark. He said the deal – to be formally signed shortly after his speech – “gives the US permanent control over security and all of the needs on that territory” and that the US will build two “very major” military bases in Greenland.
Trump said he would reject any calls for a “globalist scheme” to control artificial intelligence, and made an impromptu pitch to world leaders to call the technology “super intelligence” or “SI”. Amid mounting fears over the dangers of AI as some, including leaders in the industry, call for international regulation on the technology, Trump said he would not hinder its growth. He said he believes will be “bigger than the industrial revolution,” and vowed the US would lead on AI. “We’re only going to encourage superintelligence.”
Trump strikes warm tone in meeting with UK prime minister
Andrew Sparrow
Trump also met earlier this afternoon with the the United Kingdom’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, with whom he appeared to enjoy a solid rapport – a divergence from his at-times testy relationship with Burnham’s predecessor in the role, Keir Starmer.
“I think he’s going to be a great prime minister,” Trump said of Burnham. “I think he’s got a lot of assets on his side.”
Trump added: “We talked about everything from Rolls-Royce to energy, immigration. We covered a lot.”
One point of tension in an otherwise cordial exchange: the Chagos Islands deal, a proposal by Keir Starmer’s goverment to give Mauritius sovereignty over the Chagos Islands, on condition that the US and the UK can continue to operate the Diego Garcia military base there for at least another 99 years.
“I don’t support it,” Trump said. “I think it’s a terrible deal.”
At one point the relationship between Trump and Starmer was good. But it worsened as Starmer started to criticize Trump publicly on issues like his proposal to annex Greenland, and his claim British troops avoided frontline action in Afghanistan. And the full rupture came when Keir Starmer refused to allow the US to use British airbases for attacks against Iran at the start of the war.
Members of US delegation met Iranian leadership at UN, Trump says
During a press conference alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump said some members of his team met today with the Iranian delegation, a meeting that he said lasted three hours and “went very well.”
Trump left the exact nature of the exchange – what was discussed, and what progress, if any, was made toward a deal – unclear, but said it was a “a very good meeting.” He then repeated his threat delivered to the assembled world leaders in an address earlier that morning that Iran had to choose between “potential greatness or obliteration.”
“They had a very good meeting, and they have another one scheduled in the near future,” Trump said, teasing future conversations with Iran.
Steve Witkoff, Trump’s special envoy to the Middle East, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law-turned-Middle East diplomat, sat alongside the president. Both declined to share specifics of the meeting.
“I feel very good right now,” Witkoff said when asked how he felt after the initial meeting.
“How will you feel tomorrow?” a reporter pressed him.
Trump endorses a US embargo on diesel exports in conversation with Zelenskyy
President Trump appeared to support the increasingly loud calls from some members of his party to halt the export of US diesel fuel, whose skyrocketing price has begun to ripple out through the American economy and stung Republicans ahead of the upcoming midterm elections.
“I’ve called for that too, I’ve said, ‘let’s not send out the diesel’,” Trump said, when asked about the outcry from his fellow Republicans.
He then turned to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, sitting at his side, who said the Trump administration is evaluating the feasibility of a full or partial plan. Trump declined to share a timeline for when such a ban could come down.
The subject was raised after a reporter mentioned Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, which Trump was quick to point out had damaged global diesel supplies. (The conflict between the US and Iran, which Trump launched in February alongside Israel, has also strangled global energy markets.)
“It is a serious hit on the Russians,” Trump said. “It’s also a very serious hit on the price of diesel.”
Trump, Zelenskyy speak to reporters at the United Nations
Trump is now fielding questions from reporters alongside Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the president of Ukraine.
“I think they’re going to make a deal,” Trump said, when asked what, if anything, Ukraine would have to give up to end the war. “I think’s somethings’ going to happen.”
The Ukrainians, Trump said, were “very capable people” with – and a nod here to the man sitting beside him – “very capable leadership.”
Vance, Oz announced removal of 760,000 Obamacare enrollees, alleging fraud
At a joint press conference on Tuesday, Vice President JD Vance and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, announced that the federal government was removing 760,000 enrollees from Affordable Care Act insurance marketplaces.
Those 760,000 marketplace enrollees – representing 4 percent of all Americans who obtain coverage there – were allegedly receiving benefits they weren’t qualified to get, or were not real people at all, per Vance. The vice president said the action will save $2.2 billion “for the essential services for which is meant to go.”
The removals, first reported by the Wall Street Journal, were carried out by Vance’s White House task force aimed at eliminating fraud. Critics have accused that group of primarily targeting blue states.
“This is what the fraud task force is all about,” he said.
Vance said that an additional 419,000 enrollees suspected of similar violations were undergoing further review. He accused the previous Biden administration of incentivizing healthcare brokers to enroll more people in the program while inadequately vetting for fraud.
Donald Trump to CNN at UN general assembly: 'You shouldn't be here'
Donald Trump told a CNN reporter at the UN general assembly on Tuesday that he was “surprised” the outlet was covering him, saying it ‘shouldn’t be here’ after he banned the network alongside Politico and MS Now from the White House on Friday.
“The United Nations allowed us in, sir,” a CNN reporter replied, when Trump began to protest the outlet’s presence.
“You should not be here covering me,” Trump shot back. “You said you weren’t gonna cover me, you shouldn’t be covering me.”
CNN, alongside MS Now and Politico, have sued the Trump administration for the White House ban, and other outlets in the president’s standard TV pool have paused their duties in solidarity.
Trump praises Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela's interim president, before their planned meeting
Tom Phillips
In his remarks to the UN earlier, Donald Trump hailed his new relationship with Nicolás Maduro’s successors in Venezuela, after the capture of the South American dictator during the US raid on 3 January.
“In January, at my direction, the United States military conducted a massive military operation penetrating deep into the Venezuelan capital, Caracas .... and arrested the outlaw dictator - a real criminal, Nicolás Maduro,” Trump said, as Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, sat listening in the audience.
Rodríguez, formerly Maduro’s vice president, has been a more pliant partner to the US in Venezuela, helping broker a lucrative deal granting the Trump administration access to the country’s immense oil wealth.
“We’re working closely with the leaders of Venezuela to forge a much better future for the Venezuelan people. Last month we signed the largest oil deal in history - covering 65 billion barrels of oil which will benefit both Venezuela and the United States enormously,” Trump added.
Trump is slated to meet personally with Rodríguez later today.
Trump hails 'tremendous' relationship with Denmark, Greenland as he signs Greenland deal
Jakub Krupa
At the Greenland deal signing ceremony, Trump said it “has been an amazing journey with tremendous people” with Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s PM Jens-Frederick Nielsen.
“We’re going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship,” he said.
He thanked them for the deal, and says they will be working “very hard” on its implementation.
He said the deal has been “long in the making” – “many decades, probably centuries” – and it will be “tremendous for Europe and for the US and for everybody.”
Speaking next, Denmark’s Frederiksen said “This deal is good for the United States. It’s good for Greenland, for Denmark, for the Nato alliance, and therefore also good for Europe.”
Frederiksen said any adversaries “will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland,” adding that the agreement “underlines the importance of the Nato alliance.”
In tricky, carefully worded paragraphs, she said the agreement “recognises the US defining historical and ongoing contributions to the security and defence of Greenland,” but it also “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
“I think everybody knows that we live in difficult times where we have to show our strength. If we let ourselves be divided as allies, then we do our votes a favour. We will do everything we can to prevent that from happening.”
Then, Greenland’s Nielsen said it is “a very important day for our security” that “builds on 85 years of security cooperation” since the second world war.
He stressed that “this is not only an agreement about us, but an agreement with us” and called it “a win-win”.
“It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country. This has been a key priority for us throughout this process,” he said, saying this is why Greenland “insisted on engaging in a constructive dialogue.”
“Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security. And this agreement reflects that we understand our responsibility and act accordingly,” he said.
He continued:
“Nato matters. We believe that it is vital to keep Nato strong, also in the Arctic, where the alliance has a key role to play.
This agreement should put to rest any doubt today and in the future about where Greenland’s loyalty lies.
Our commitment to this alliance and to the security we build together is not in question. We are, have been, and will remain a steadfast friend of the United States and a part of the western alliance. Your security is our security, and our security is your security.”

Jakub Krupa
