Cases of forced deployment to the front are multiplying.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:38:51 UTC
23:38:51 KST

Moscow region military contract service recruitment centre. Photo: Sergei Karpukhin / TASS
Last week, we learned that St. Petersburg resident Vitaly Smidovich had died in Ukraine. The man, who suffered from epileptic seizures, was lured with an offer to repair houses damaged by drones, recruited, and sent to the front.
Cases where people have been deceived or threatened into signing a contract with the Ministry of Defence, followed by deployment to the war, are becoming increasingly common: the number of people willing to join the Russian army is falling, while the needs of the front are only growing.
Mediazona has compiled known cases of Russian men being snatched off the streets one by one.
Kirov, May 15
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. Under the pretext of a fine for drinking beer on the street, 49-year-old Sergei Skryabin was taken from his home to a police station, and then to an assembly point.
According to his wife, “they made a passport for him in 15 minutes on a weekend,” and then, “threatening violence”, forced him to sign a contract with the Ministry of Defence, despite his diagnosed epilepsy. The medical fitness board was conducted as a mere formality in Lyangasovo village—and Skryabin was found fit for service.
From the military enlistment office, he was sent to the self-proclaimed DPR and assigned to military unit 41698, where the 5th Separate Guards Motorised Rifle Brigade is deployed.
The last time Skryabin called his wife was on July 23, 2026. Four days later, a political officer called her and said that her husband was already listed as missing in action—although, according to her information, this status was officially registered only in August.
She appealed to the prosecutor’s office, but they replied that Skryabin had signed the contract voluntarily.
“There’s also deception regarding the payments. My husband has been at war for almost half a year, but I haven’t received anything. I don’t need blood money. I want my husband returned home safe and sound,” the woman said in a conversation with Mediazona.
Penza, August 19, 2026
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. 33-year-old Alexander Stepanov was abducted by unknown individuals when he was leaving a shop in the evening, wearing shorts, a t-shirt, and flip-flops.
“Strangers put handcuffs on him and bundled him into a car. My son said they brought him to what seemed like a military enlistment office, beat him, and tore his t-shirt. Until he signed the contract,” recounted his mother, Tamara Stepanova.
At the enlistment office, according to his mother, “they made new documents for him in 20 minutes”. Similar cases have been mentioned not only in Penza but in other cities.
On August 23, Stepanov reported that he was in Donetsk. His mother sent appeals to the military prosecutor’s office, the human rights commissioner, the Ministry of Defence website, and the reception of the head of the Investigative Committee, Alexander Bastrykin. She has not yet received any replies.
Penza, July 9
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. 48-year-old Andrey Lazarov from Penza disappeared after he left his home without his phone and told his elderly mother that he would be back soon.
The next day, an unfamiliar woman called the 72-year-old pensioner. According to her, her husband and Andrey Lazarov had been detained by the police the day before, after which they were taken to an assembly point, and then “given a change of clothes and taken away” to the Rostov region.
“One guy is walking all by himself, they drive up and grab him”, she said, adding that her husband was snatched on his way to work.
Lazarov did not have a permanent job and often went on drinking binges—he had developed epilepsy against the backdrop of alcoholism. Over the following days, his relatives tried unsuccessfully to bring the man back home.
“At the enlistment office, they told me: ‘Well, he’s a drunkard anyway, so at least there’s some use for him, he’ll earn good money,’ ” recounts Lazarov’s niece. “My uncle was supposedly detained drunk and taken to the station, where he was offered an administrative offence or [an army] contract, and he chose the contract himself. I say: ‘You don’t know who you’re talking about, this person would never in his life choose war over an administrative offence!’ I understand how it sounds, but my uncle drank and didn’t bother anyone, he was just quiet and harmless. He chose this way of destroying his own life, but he didn’t harm anyone with it except himself.”
Andrey got in touch only once from someone else’s phone: he dictated his unit number, No. 90600, and told his family that he was forced to sign the contract. Since then, there has been no news of him. His family only knows that he was supposed to be sent to the Donetsk region.
Petrozavodsk, July 27–29
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. 26-year-old Petrozavodsk resident Nikita Konzhezerov was detained drunk on the street and taken to a sobering-up station at a drug treatment clinic. According to his friends, this happened at the end of July. The Barents Observer publication, citing a source close to Konzhezerov’s family, reported that “they slipped him a contract, he doesn’t even remember how it happened.”
“He didn't plan or want this at all, he’s not a military man, he doesn’t know how to fight,” the publication’s source said.
Early in the morning of July 29, Konzhezerov was put on a train and sent to an assembly point in the Leningrad region.
Shortly before this, Konzhezerov had a son, and both of his parents have disabilities. “He is the sole breadwinner in the family, and now his sudden dispatch to the service puts his family in a very difficult position,” reads a post sharing Konzhezerov’s story.
This is not the first such case in the region. The same Barents Observer reported how recruiters get people drunk and then slip them a Ministry of Defence contract.
Luga, Leningrad region; first mobilisation — September 2022, second deployment — March 2026
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. 48-year-old Roman Alfutin was mobilised in September 2022 and taken to Valuyki, a town in Belgorod region near the border with Ukraine—although, according to his sister, he did not fit the age criteria for conscripting non-commissioned officers:
“My brother was a sergeant major. He received this rank back at training camps in 2006. Well, he didn’t fit the age bracket at that time,” Alfutin’s sister told Ostorozhno Novosti. Roman also had no combat experience—he served as a staff driver.
Following the family’s appeals to the governor of the Leningrad region, the military prosecutor’s office, and the enlistment office, the decision to mobilise Alfutin was overturned; he was placed on the military register as a civilian, and he lived in Luga for almost four years.
In March 2026, several people broke into his apartment, took his documents and phone, and took him away to a unit. A few days later, he was sent in handcuffs to the “special military operation”—to the village of Markivka in Luhansk region of Ukraine. He was told that he was listed as absent without leave and had been placed on a wanted list.
The family provided his discharge documents and medical records regarding spinal problems requiring treatment, but the unit claimed that the discharge documents had been lost.
“They said that Roman is now officially listed in a completely different unit. He was mobilised into military unit 29760, but somehow he ended up in military unit 29298. At the same time, there is no discharge order for him anywhere,” Ostorozhno Novosti quotes Roman’s sister.
A court adopted a preliminary protection measure, forbidding Alfutin’s deployment to the war, but simultaneously confirmed that formally he remains a serviceman. Lawyer Maxim Grebenyuk called this a dangerous precedent: “If a serviceman was mobilised and sent to a unit, even if he was mobilised illegally... you can’t unring a bell: he is already a serviceman regardless, now try getting discharged however you can. And in practice, this is very difficult, almost impossible.”
Penza, allegedly September 26
Circumstances of detention and contract signing. 63-year-old Alexander Glebov drove his car to go for a walk along the embankment in Penza, where unknown men approached him and demanded his documents.
“They started asking why he was alone, what if he’s a drug addict, what if he’s planting dead drops,” his niece Yulia recounted on Threads and Instagram.
Mediazona tried to find out the details of her uncle’s detention, but she did not reply to our messages.
Glebov did not have his passport on him; he showed his driving licence, which was confiscated. They also took his mobile phone and drove him away somewhere. According to Yulia, her uncle was “beaten, pressured so he would sign a contract.”
She claims that Glebov is unfit for military service due to his health: he has hypertension (“he was taken away by an ambulance more than once with a blood pressure of 200”) and kidney and liver diseases.
Later, the same people brought him home—to pick up his passport and military ID. “Of course, at 63, at that moment he was very frightened, and under such pressure, he signed it. He didn’t have the strength to resist,” his niece writes.
His phone was only returned to him towards the morning—that was when Glebov called his brother and said he was being taken through Voronezh to Rostov. Later, he ended up in Millerovo, Rostov region, from where he was supposed to be sent to military unit 90600 in the Samara region.
All his life, Glebov worked as a chef and pastry cook. “What kind of rifleman or stormtrooper is he at his freaking age?” Yulia wonders.

Researchers help nursing homes use AI in dementia care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:36:53 UTC
23:36:53 KST

Researchers in Ghent are supporting residential care homes to make better use of AI in caring for people with dementia. While there are many AI applications available, they are not yet widely used in practice.
“The question for residential care homes is how they can effectively utilise AI applications in care and alleviate the workload on staff,” says researcher Ruben Vanbosseghem of Artevelde University College. The research team is looking at AI applications that can reduce administrative work, so carers have more time for the care itself.
One example is voice-activated reporting. “This can reduce the burden of record-keeping and thus free up more time for carers to provide care,” says Vanbosseghem. They are also investigating applications that can monitor residents’ surroundings, enabling more targeted care to be provided.
The researchers see benefits in AI applications for both staff and residents, such as smart incontinence products and sensors in their environment. “This means care workers do not always have to disturb residents’ sleep or rest to carry out checks, as monitoring can be done remotely,” he says. “Residents can live more independently and are disturbed less often unnecessarily during rest or sleep periods.”
Several residential care homes in West Flanders, East Flanders and Flemish Brabant are already working with the research team. The researchers are connecting residential care homes with companies offering AI applications, after which testing can take place during a pilot phase.
The Alzheimer’s Research Foundation which is funding the project. The team will work with care organisations in the coming months to test the technology in their own settings and develop a corresponding care model. By the end of the project, homes should have a clear overview of the existing technology and how they can implement it.

Nigeria performs first remote robotic surgery (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:36:21 UTC
23:36:21 KST

Nigeria performs first remote robotic surgery (VIDEO)
A Nigerian medical team has performed West Africa’s first tele-robotic surgery, remotely operating on a cancer patient from around 500 kilometers away, the hospital’s press service said on Sunday.
The procedure, a right radical nephrectomy, involved removing a kidney affected by a cancerous tumor from a patient at Nisa Premier Hospital in Abuja. Surgeons at Redeemer’s Health Village (RHV) in Mowe, Ogun State, controlled the robotic system remotely via an internet connection, Punch reported on Monday. The operation was carried out in collaboration with RoboMed Global.
“We were able to operate on a patient in Abuja, 500 kilometers away. We were able to operate on a patient with a kidney tumor, a cancerous tumor. And so that was successful,” Prof. Obi Davies-Ekwenna, the robotic surgeon who led the procedure, said. The technology allows specialists to control surgical equipment from another location, potentially giving patients access to surgeons elsewhere in Nigeria or abroad.
“It’s a huge breakthrough, and then of course, it is the first time telesurgery has been done in West Africa,” RHV CEO Adedamola Dada said, as quoted by Punch. He identified a shortage of trained personnel as a key obstacle to the wider use of robotic surgery in Nigeria and urged the government to support training for surgeons, nurses and biomedical engineers.
Several days earlier, RHV announced that it had completed its first robotic surgery, a robot-assisted radical prostatectomy, a procedure to remove the prostate gland. The hospital said the operation was part of efforts to expand access to advanced surgical care in Nigeria.
Other West African countries have also recently reported complex surgical procedures. Earlier this month, a team of Malian doctors successfully separated conjoined twin girls in an operation that lasted several hours in Bamako.
Senegal, meanwhile, has begun locally producing DREPAF, a generic version of hydroxyurea used to treat sickle cell disease. Manufactured by Teranga Pharma, it has been described as the first generic hydroxyurea treatment produced in Africa, reducing reliance on more expensive imported drugs.

Negev teen charged over 45 TikTok reposts praising Hamas, October 7 massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:36:00 UTC
23:36:00 KST

Southern District prosecutors charged a 19-year-old Segev Shalom resident on Tuesday with dozens of terrorism-related speech offenses over 45 TikTok reposts that allegedly praised Hamas, glorified attackers and included one direct call to commit a terrorist act.
The prosecution has asked the Beersheba Magistrate’s Court to keep Deif Allah Abu Rjeila in custody until the end of his trial, arguing that the number and content of the posts show that his release would endanger the public.
The case concerns material Abu Rjeila allegedly shared online. The indictment charges him with 40 counts of incitement to terrorism, 23 counts of publicly identifying with a terrorist organization and one count of directly calling for a terrorist act. The counts overlap across the 45 posts, with some reposts forming the basis for more than one alleged offense.
According to the indictment, Abu Rjeila controlled a public TikTok account under the name “deef2lla,” which had 877 followers and 5,449 likes. Prosecutors allege that he reposted material from April 24 until his arrest on August 13, becoming particularly active on an almost daily basis during August.
Abu Rjeila reposted material pertaining to Sinwar, Haniyeh and Yassin
Much of the material was originally published by accounts identified with Hamas or dedicated to commemorating terrorist operatives, the indictment alleges. The reposts included footage from the October 7 massacre and material praising Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Ismail Haniyeh and Ahmed Yassin, as well as members of other Palestinian armed groups.
One June 8 repost allegedly praised Hamas Nukhba terrorist Mu’in Muammar for killing 20 Israelis in 10 minutes on October 7. The video described the victims as “heads” and was accompanied by religious music and hashtags referring to October 7 and martyrdom, according to the indictment.
The direct-call charge concerns a separate video reposted on June 3. Prosecutors said it contained a sermon describing jihad and fighting as religious obligations and presenting them as the only means of “purifying” al-Aqsa Mosque.
Under the Terrorism Law provisions cited in the indictment, the prosecution must prove more than that the posts were offensive or supportive of violence. For the 40 incitement counts, it alleges that the content and circumstances created a real possibility that the publications would lead to terrorist acts.
Prosecutors discover detainee was inspired by October 7 massacre events
The detention request says the evidence includes records of the TikTok posts and material extracted from Abu Rjeila’s phone, including WhatsApp correspondence, gallery images and the accounts he followed. Prosecutors said he acknowledged during questioning that the phone and TikTok account were his and connected himself directly to some of the reposts.
The request also quotes him as allegedly telling investigators that he had not previously liked Hamas, but began to do so after watching videos posted following October 7. That statement appears in the prosecution’s detention application and has not been independently confirmed or tested in court.
Prosecutors argued that the volume of the material, the single alleged direct call for an attack and what they described as his intensive engagement with terrorist content establish a danger that cannot be addressed outside custody. They also argued that the continuing security situation increases the potential danger posed by alleged incitement.
Abu Rjeila was arrested on August 13 in a joint operation by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police and Border Police counterterrorism officers.

Russia spreads AI fakes claiming Jews are being paid to settle in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:35:47 UTC
23:35:47 KST

Russia carried out a large-scale disinformation campaign surrounding the Jewish pilgrimage to Uman, Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation has claimed.
CCD is a Ukrainian government body that monitors and responds to disinformation and propaganda operations directed at Ukraine. It is part of Ukraine’s National Security and Defense Council (NSDC).
A record number of Jewish pilgrims traveled to the Ukrainian city of Uman for Rosh Hashanah this year, according to local statistics. The local Cherkasy Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention reported that over 49,000 pilgrims had arrived in the city by the morning of September 11, while Israeli figures place it higher, at 52,000.
Regardless, the number surpassed even pre-war years, which typically saw between 30,000 and 35,000 pilgrims. There was also a significantly increased proportion of non-Ashkenazi Jews – Sephardim and Mizrahim – which Ukrainian Jewish media said accounted for up to half of all visitors.
Numbers aside, the pilgrimage has been the subject of media attention for another reason: Russian fake news.
Russian-controlled TikTok accounts circulated AI videos with fake pilgrims
CCD reported that during and after Rosh Hashanah, Russia-controlled TikTok account networks circulated a series of AI-generated videos in an interview format.
In the videos, fake pilgrims claim that they are supposedly moving to Ukraine permanently.
The videos also contain fabricated claims about “payments from the Ukrainian government of 200,000 hryvnias,” “special benefits,” and even alleged plans to “make Uman an independent entity.”
CCD said the campaign is “entirely disinformation.”
It said there is no “mass resettlement” of foreigners and this is an annual temporary religious pilgrimage, after which hassidic pilgrims return to their home countries.
It also stressed that Ukraine has no government programs or financial payments designed to encourage foreign citizens to relocate to the country.
“The enemy’s main goal is to exploit the heightened attention surrounding the event in order to destabilize Ukrainian society from within and artificially provoke antisemitic sentiments,” it said.
Tracing the campaign
The Israel-based, Ukrainian-founded media site Nikk traced the disinformation campaign back further, to May 2019, when then-adviser to the Russian president Sergey Glazyev published a text suggesting the possibility of mass resettlement in southeastern Ukraine of residents of Israel and other Middle Eastern countries.
At the time, Israel’s Foreign Ministry described Glazyev’s comments as conspiratorial and antisemitic.
Fast-forward seven years, an adviser is no longer needed to spread it: “All you need is AI and TikTok,” Nikk said.
Six months ago, in April 2026, researchers documented new activity by the Russia-linked Matryoshka network in the form of fake videos circulating claims that Ukraine was planning to ban Israelis from making their annual pilgrimage to Uman.
Alongside this appeared a fictional “Orthodox rabbi” who supposedly cursed Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky over the Ukraine-Israel dispute concerning Ukrainian grain taken by Russia. This same network then replaced the narrative with September’s report that Ukraine gives Jews special treatment and state money and is preparing to settle them there permanently.
Additionally, on August 17, the Russian-language Telegram channel Fikrat Shabanov published a long article describing the expected arrival of approximately 30,000 hassidim as a “rehearsal” for the future mass resettlement of Jews in Ukraine. While there is no evidence that this Telegram channel is operated by the Russian state, the content is relevant.
The Telegram article said coordination between police and border guards was described as training for the “absorption of millions of new Israelis,” while the 2026 pilgrimage was called the “last major rehearsal” before the year 5788, which begins in October 2027.
It also said that while Ukraine closed borders to some other people, Jews were allowed to arrive in the tens of thousands.
None of this is based on fact, and there is no Israeli government decision or Ukrainian government document agreeing to the transfer of territory or a program for resettling millions of people.
Nikk, however, spoke of how facts on the ground could be slightly altered to fit the “resettlement narrative.”
For example, on September 5, Ukraine’s National Police announced the arrival of Israeli police officers in Uman. The Israeli officers patrolled the areas where hassidic pilgrims were staying and visiting, together with Ukrainian police, emergency services, and the National Guard of Ukraine.
Nikk noted that, within the disinformation environment, open coordination between two law-enforcement systems “becomes evidence of preparations for mass resettlement.”
“Ukraine and Israel coordinating security for tens of thousands of Israelis – true. Does that mean they are training to resettle “millions of new Israelis” there? No.”
Another fact is partially true: There is a Ukrainian state program involving a payment of exactly 200,000 hryvnias, but it has nothing to do with hassidim, Israelis, or foreigners wishing to settle in Uman.
Essentially, the trajectory looked like this: April 2026, circulation of fake reports that Ukraine supposedly planned to prevent Israelis from entering Uman; May 2026, promotion by Russian AI networks of “population replacement” and antisemitic narratives; August 2026, references to a “Heavenly Jerusalem” in Ukraine and a supposed “rehearsal” for the resettlement of millions; September 11, references to “privileged hassidim” and a Russian state media report about the “takeover” of Uman; and September 14, an AI-generated pilgrim supposedly “confessing” to receiving money and planning to remain in Ukraine.
“There is no need even to invent one enormous fake story; it would quickly collapse,” Nikk said. “It is much more effective to take real Uman, real pilgrims, real police officers, a real Ukrainian payment of 200,000 hryvnias, and real everyday tensions surrounding Rosh Hashanah, and then slightly alter the relationships between them.
“The result is a story that never happened,” Nikk concluded.

Lithuanian parliament removes ban on deployment of nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:35:32 UTC
23:35:32 KST

VILNIUS, September 22. /TASS/. Lithuania’s Seimas (parliament) has voted to lift a ban on the deployment of nuclear weapons on the country’s territory.
After debating this issue, it referred the amendment to the constitution to a committee for consideration.
The lifting was approved with 99 votes for, five abstentions and 13 votes against.
"Nuclear weapons are the foundation of deterrence. If you refuse this, you are refusing full-fledged deterrence in your security strategy," Laurynas Kasciunas, head of the faction of the opposition party Homeland Union - Christian Democrats of Lithuania, said at the podium of the Seimas.
The Seimas resolution says that Article 137, which prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, on Lithuanian territory, will be removed from the constitution.
The Seimas will have to vote on amending the constitution twice with a three-month interval between votes. The innovation must be supported by a qualified majority - 94 out of 141. The first vote is scheduled for October 6, and the repeat vote - for January 12.

Westwood began his career on pirate radio in London before joining Capital Radio. A judge at Moscow’s Tverskoy District Court sentenced a Czech man to 13 days in jail on Tuesday for staging a protest on Red Square.
Identified as Michal Plamenek, the man was arrested for holding up a sign in English next to Lenin’s Mausoleum on Sunday afternoon, the court’s press service said in a statement.
No details were provided as to what was written on Plamenek’s sign, but the court press service said a judge ruled that the inscription was “aimed at discrediting the Russian Armed Forces.”
Police officers arrested Plamenek because Red Square directly adjoins the Kremlin, where protests are banned. He allegedly refused to listen to a request by officers to accompany them to a police station and resisted arrest.
A judge found Plamenek guilty on three separate administrative counts of discrediting the Russian military, violating protest rules and disobeying a police officer.
The judge fined Plamenek 40,000 rubles ($470) for the first violation, 20,000 rubles ($237) for the second and handed him a sentence of 13 days in jail for the third.

How Arab-Israeli air defense coordination is developing into a regional security shield - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:35:21 UTC
23:35:21 KST

Operation Epic Fury helped increase coordination between US partners and allies in the region in terms of air defenses and other types of security coordination. A recent report by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) to the United States Congress, which covered aspects of Operation Epic Fury from April to June, provided new details on the types of cooperation. Although the report was general, it shed light on an important trend in the Middle East.
The report referred to “US forces embedded in partner air operations centers across the region, which supported coordination, deconfliction, and synchronization of air defense efforts.”
It also discussed a Middle East Defense network, “an integrated missile defense architecture in the region intercepted more than 6,000 OWUAS [one-way unmanned aerial systems] and more than 1,500 ballistic missiles that targeted US and partner forces.”
In addition, the report discussed how the US partnered with Israel.
“Coordinated air and missile defense with Israel was also substantial, with US Patriot and THAAD [Terminal High Altitude Area Defense] systems operating alongside Israeli Arrow, David’s Sling, and Iron Dome systems. The United States and Israel maintained shared awareness and recurring reporting on readiness and intercept activity via embedded liaison officers in the Israeli military headquarters in Tel Aviv.”
This unprecedented cooperation is built upon foundations laid over the past few years. These include US Central Command coordinating with its Gulf partners and with Israel.
Increasing cooperation throughout the Middle East
Over the last decade, Israel and CENTCOM have increasingly cooperated. This has resulted in Israel moving from being under US European Command to being in CENTCOM’s area of operations.
The Abraham Accords paved the way for this move because it meant that Israel was able to work more openly with Gulf partners. In the past, Arab countries had generally refrained from joint exercises with Israel. This made coordination difficult, even if it occurred quietly, in other ways.
Many things have changed in the Middle East over the last decade. In the wake of the 2015 US-Iran deal, Tehran increased its role in Yemen, Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon.
At the same time, countries in the region had to deal with ISIS threats that only began to decline after 2017.
Turkey’s hostile attitude to Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates shifted considerably after 2019. Other trends began to change as well. Israel, Greece, and Cyprus became closer partners. While the COVID pandemic led to a reduction in joint exercises, there were still many opportunities for Israel, the US, and other countries to train together using advanced major platforms such as the F-35 supersonic stealth fighter aircraft.
After the Abraham Accords, there was increasing discussion about how Israel might integrate with the Gulf countries to coordinate defenses. Some saw a potential Middle Eastern defense pact, or a kind of regional NATO-style alliance. Such an alliance would require Saudi Arabia to normalize ties with Israel. Normalization did not happen.
Nevertheless, in January 2022, the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) published a report titled “A Stronger and Wider Peace: A US Strategy for Advancing the Abraham Accords.”
This report “heralded the accords as an historic breakthrough and urged the US government to seize the opportunity to start building a new Middle East defense architecture premised on bringing America’s regional partners together in common cause to counter the growing menace from Iran.”
The goal was also for Congress to help support this cooperation, as well as a “region-wide air defense network to help deter and defeat the escalating missile and drone threat posed by Iran and its terrorist proxies.” The result was the Deterring Enemy Forces and Enabling National Defenses Act (DEFEND Act) of 2022.
JINSA noted in a May 2023 report called “Build it, and they will come: A US strategy for integrating Middle East air and missile defenses,” that there were opportunities to move toward a “region-wide integrated air and missile defense.” JINSA stated that “animosities among US partners have historically acted as a severe constraint on their willingness to engage in the levels of intelligence sharing and cooperation that meaningful air defense integration would require.”
The opportunities in 2023 were clear. Israel could work with the United States and Gulf partners.
Hamas, Iran, Houthi attacks shifting sands of Middle Eastern relations
The October 7, 2023, Hamas attack was a setback to this regional integration process. Iran intended it to be a setback, and Tehran initially got its wish. Israel was forced to wage a grueling war in Gaza, and then a separate campaign in Lebanon. The Houthis attacked Israel. Iran also carried out large direct attacks using hundreds of ballistic missiles.
The Iranian attacks and the Houthi attacks led to close cooperation between the US, Israel, and regional partners against the ballistic missile and drone threat. This laid the foundations for what came next in 2025 and 2026.
The full extent of the cooperation during Operation Epic Fury is yet to be revealed. Nevertheless, the fact that air defense systems, such as THAAD, Patriots, and Israel’s David’s Sling, Arrow, and Iron Dome, were able to work together is significant.
The US is also selling more defense systems to the Gulf. As the Gulf countries modernize their systems, more opportunities for joint cooperation will occur. In the future, there will be more chances for joint exercises and drills. The tempo of war since 2023 has largely pushed off some of these drills. It remains to be seen whether Saudi Arabia will acquire the F-35. If it does, it would join Israel and CENTCOM as an operator of the fifth-generation warplane over the next decade.
The recent OIG report shed light on how Iran targets countries in the region. It also showed how the US had “been helping grow the sovereign military defense of Gulf partners for decades to counter Iranian attacks and safeguard regional stability. This has included the provision of military sales, training, and information-sharing to Gulf partners.”
This is all good news. The fact that such a large number of 6,000 drone attacks and 1,500 ballistic missile attacks were intercepted further illustrates the success.
Iran has hinted that it is developing new threats. The learning curve has already shown that Israel and other countries in the region are prepared for many of these threats. Nevertheless, the war will result in some changes. There is talk of the US shifting away from some bases in the Gulf. This could mean more deployment in Jordan or in Israel. CENTCOM will be learning many lessons alongside Israel regarding what comes next.

America’s AI Safety Dilemma and at the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:35:00 UTC
23:35:00 KST

On September 12, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing that the leading labs should deliberately slow how fast their models gain new capabilities. Within hours, his chief rivals lined up behind him: Sam Altman said OpenAI would match Anthropic’s commitment to host independent evaluators, and Elon Musk replied, “Dario is right.”
Two days later, U.S. President Donald Trump called fears of an AI catastrophe a hoax and claimed that amid the backlash against AI and data centers, “the only one that is happy about it is China.”
That exchange hangs over Xi Jinping’s arrival in Washington this week, the first state visit by a Chinese leader in more than a decade.
The AI pacing debate is a dilemma the Trump administration cannot resolve at home. There is rising pressure from the public to slow down, but the government is convinced that slowing down means losing to China. The easiest way out runs through Beijing. If Washington will not slow American AI, it can try to slow Chinese AI instead, through tighter controls on chips, compute, and access to American models. That option is tempting precisely because it is an area where the safety-minded and the competition-focused, the labs and the White House, already agree.
But Trump should know that choosing this path would also undercut the most promising AI outcome on the summit table.
Public calls to slow the pace of AI development are growing in urgency. In a new Politico poll, 63 percent of respondents saw a real chance that AI could wipe out humanity, and a CBS News/YouGov survey found that most Americans want AI development slowed, though not stopped. With the midterms weeks away, AI risk is becoming an electoral issue, and the labs’ own warnings have lent that anxiety new credibility.
The Trump administration has treated the debate as a threat to American primacy. Trump said he wants to stay ahead of China because “whoever wins AI wins.” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that there is “no day after tomorrow if China wins” on AI – “nothing [else] would matter.”
Politico’s polling showed that Americans are split, 43 percent to 37 percent, on whether falling behind other countries is acceptable in exchange for safer AI. However, Trump’s supporters have a clear opinion: people who voted for him in 2024 preferred staying in the AI race (50 percent) to prioritizing safety issues (38 percent).
Since Trump is unwilling to slow down AI development and risk falling behind, that leaves the administration searching for a way to look serious about AI risk without constraining American labs. Amodei had a suggestion. The Anthropic CEO’s plan recommended an “attempt to coordinate with authoritarian governments, to the extent this is possible, while taking seriously the challenges of verifying compliance.” Beijing is at the top of the list of authoritarian governments to talk with.
Even while calling for coordination, however, Amodei urged the Trump administration to keep “powerful AI chips or semiconductor manufacturing equipment” out of Chinese hands, close “chip smuggling operations” and remote access to data centers, “crack down on unauthorized distillation,” and harden labs against theft of model weights. Amodei explicitly agreed with Bessent that “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world.” In his framework, safety at home depends on a durable lead abroad.
That points to a clear area of overlap: the White House can embrace the “slow China” half of the AI industry’s agenda while rejecting the “slow ourselves” half. This is already playing out.
Earlier this month, the NSA, FBI, and CISA jointly accused six Chinese developers, including DeepSeek and Alibaba, of industrial-scale distillation of American frontier models. In July Bessent said Washington could sanction firms found stealing from American models. Trump and Xi are also expected to discuss whether Chinese firms can keep renting top Nvidia compute through Southeast Asian data centers, while the suspension of the Affiliates Rule, which extends export blacklists to affiliates of listed firms, expires with the Busan truce in November.
On semiconductors, restricting Chinese access would be a bigger shift. The Trump administration has cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies to buy Nvidia’s H200 chips, though Chinese customs has kept nearly all the chips out. But a restriction package lets the White House tell anxious voters it is acting on AI risk while asking nothing of American companies. The louder the domestic debate grows, the better that trade looks.
Beijing has already read the room and decided this is the most likely outcome of the United States’ AI pacing debate. China’s Foreign Ministry answered Amodei’s essay by warning that “fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition” would disrupt global AI governance. The state-run Global Times called the slowdown push a “Cold War playbook” for the sector. China’s Commerce Ministry threatened “resolute countermeasures” if Washington uses the distillation accusations to suppress Chinese firms. Among other options, China could resurrect the rare earth exports controls that were suspended under the Busan truce.
Beijing’s official line is not the whole Chinese conversation, though. This spring, two of China’s most senior AI governance figures – Xue Lan, who chairs China’s national expert committee on AI governance, and Zeng Yi, dean of the Beijing Institute of AI Safety and Governance – joined a Capitol Hill discussion convened by Senator Bernie Sanders. Xue acknowledged the geopolitical rivalry but called for “safe zones” where American and Chinese scientists can build safety standards and protocols together. Zeng, whose institute has catalogued 94 classes of AI safety threats, warned last week that AI’s catastrophic risks, including “the hidden danger of human extinction,” are mounting daily. Both Xue and Zeng helped draft China’s national AI governance principles.
The Trump administration now has a real AI safety deliverable within reach. In New York on September 20, Bessent proposed a standing China-U.S. AI dialogue with a way for each side to flag AI incidents serious enough to threaten national security. A standing channel would be a first for Trump’s second term: the AI consultations he and Xi discussed in Beijing in May were never formalized. Beijing’s response, however, was unclear.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said chip export controls were not part of the AI safety mechanism discussions. That separation is the right instinct, but Beijing is likely to see the two issues as inextricably linked. If China sees “AI safety” as a synonym for containment, voices like Xue’s and Zeng’s lose ground at home. Beijing will worry that every notification through the new channel creates a pretext for new restrictions on Chinese companies.
China-U.S. crisis management mechanisms already have a poor record. After the United States shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon that had traversed the U.S. mainland in February 2023, Beijing declined a call from the U.S. defense secretary, later explaining that Washington had not created “the proper atmosphere” for dialogue. An AI incident channel that China sees as an extension of the technology war will go quiet exactly when it is needed.
Amodei anticipated this objection and rejected it, arguing that restrictions “increase the leverage held by democracies and make an agreement more likely in the future.” That may hold for a treaty negotiated from a position of strength years from now, but not for an incident channel that runs on day-to-day trust. Amodei himself wrote that sharing information about misaligned models can have value even without formal agreements. That is exactly what a notification channel would do.
Washington can manage this dilemma without breaking the Trump-Xi summit. If the Trump-Xi summit needs a first substantive commitment, Amodei’s essay suggested a modest one: an agreement that neither side will use AI to produce biological weapons.
Beyond that, the leaders should establish the notification mechanism as a standalone safety channel, insulated from trade and technology-control disputes, and pair it with a technical track that brings government evaluators at the Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation together with experts like Xue and Zeng. That track could define what counts as a reportable incident and build shared tests for biological and cyber risks without touching the chips, compute, and model weights where the race is actually run. It would also serve U.S. primacy: if Bessent is right that the real threat to AI safety is “letting any nation other than the United States set the global standard,” Washington should want to be in the room when Chinese experts help write one.
To make cooperation on AI risk more feasible, the United States should call its restrictions what they are. Enforcement against model distillation or chip smuggling may be justified on intellectual property or security grounds, but selling it as the answer to AI risk lets the White House dodge the domestic aspect of AI safety while poisoning the bilateral effort.
The domestic question needs a domestic answer. Bessent has shown an openness to safety concerns. Testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on September 15, he rejected the liability exemption the labs are seeking, arguing that safety is best guaranteed when developers are “liable for what they build and generate.” The independent evaluators that Anthropic and OpenAI have agreed to host do not require the United States to fall behind anyone.
The pacing debate asked Washington to voluntarily slow down AI development. The administration’s answer is that China should be forced to slow down instead. That may play well at home, but it will not make American AI any safer, and it risks scuttling a China-U.S. channel on AI risk before it even begins.
Trump insists the AI race is winner-take-all. This week he can show that staying ahead of China and talking to it about shared risks are not mutually exclusive.

Lithuania’s Seimas backs move to remove constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:33:00 UTC
23:33:00 KST

Lithuania’s parliament on Tuesday backed a proposal to remove from the constitution a ban on stationing weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on the country’s territory, opening the way for a potential future deployment of NATO nuclear weapons.
The proposal received 99 votes in favour, 13 against and five abstentions during its consideration in the Seimas. The vote advances the constitutional amendment but does not itself authorise the deployment of nuclear weapons in Lithuania.
The Constitution’s Article 137 currently states that weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases may not be stationed on Lithuanian territory.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said the first vote on adopting the constitutional amendment is scheduled for October 6, with the final vote planned for January 12, 2027.
Constitutional amendments require two votes separated by at least three months, with at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers required to approve the measure at each final stage.
Remigijus Žemaitaitis, leader of the Nemunas Dawn party, opposed the proposal, arguing that Russia and Belarus could use it for propaganda purposes. He also said nuclear-armed states would be able to use nuclear weapons to defend Lithuania if necessary without removing the constitutional provision.
He argued that the relevant constitutional article should only be changed through a referendum.
Ignas Vėgėlė, a member of the parliament’s mixed group, questioned why the proposal would remove the entire provision rather than only the restriction on weapons of mass destruction. The article also prohibits foreign military bases.
“Why are we deleting this part of the sentence as well? Are we planning to hand over Lithuanian territory to military bases that we will not control or manage?” Vėgėlė asked.
He noted that Lithuania’s Constitutional Court has ruled that allied foreign military bases can operate in Lithuania if they are established by allies and remain under Lithuanian control. He argued that a similar principle should apply to weapons of mass destruction.
Laurynas Kasčiūnas, parliamentary leader of the opposition Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats, said nuclear weapons are a key component of deterrence.
He said nuclear deterrence helped prevent the Cold War from becoming a direct military conflict and argued that Lithuania should not maintain restrictions that do not apply to some of its NATO allies.
“We are the only country in the region that has this restriction. Latvia does not have it, Estonia does not have it, Poland does not have it, Finland has just removed it,” Kasčiūnas said.
He cited a hypothetical scenario in which a US allied ship carrying nuclear weapons or a nuclear-capable aircraft might need to pass through Lithuanian territory for deterrence purposes.
Kasčiūnas stressed that removing the ban would not mean Lithuania had decided to station nuclear weapons there, but said eliminating the constitutional restriction would give the country more options as part of NATO’s deterrence arrangements.
Remigijus Motuzas, chairman of the Seimas Foreign Affairs Committee and a Social Democrat, also said Lithuania should not create obstacles to NATO’s nuclear deterrence or become the weaker link in the alliance’s regional security posture.
“Lithuania must clearly show our allies and adversaries that we will defend our independence by all means,” Motuzas said. “We cannot be less protected than other NATO countries.”
He said changing the constitution would send a strong signal intended to reduce the risk of military aggression.
Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said deterrence should not be viewed as an escalation of war.
“Today’s vote is about ensuring that we are not weaker,” she said.
The proposal comes amid broader discussions in Europe about nuclear deterrence. French President Emmanuel Macron has promoted the idea of developing a European nuclear deterrence framework under which partner countries could potentially host French strategic aircraft equipped with nuclear weapons.
The Financial Times reported in June that the United States was considering deploying nuclear weapons in additional NATO countries in Europe, although no such deployment in Lithuania has been announced.

United offered flight attendants extra pay to pick up Newark trips and ease delays.

Where is the US opening new military bases in Greenland?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:31:50 UTC
23:31:50 KST

Where is the US opening new military bases in Greenland?
At least two new US bases will be established as part of a deal with Denmark and Greenland.
The US will open two military bases in Greenland as part of a deal with Denmark and Greenland, Reuters has reported.
The agreement is expected to be signed on Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. However, its text has not yet been officially publicised.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump ‘settled for less’ with new US-Denmark Greenland security deal
- list 2 of 4Trump says US has ‘permanent control’ of Greenland security: Does it?
- list 3 of 4Denmark says ‘binding’ US deal on Greenland won’t compromise sovereignty
- list 4 of 4Trump’s Greenland deal: A triumph of optics?
The move follows a tense, months-long standoff with Denmark and Greenland following US President Donald Trump’s repeated comments that Washington intended to annex the autonomous Danish territory, which is strategic for its location in the Arctic and its significant mineral resources, including rare-earth metals.
As a diplomatic row brewed last year, Trump refused to rule out a military invasion, causing fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom reject US control according to polls.
Tensions peaked in January this year when European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) alliance began deploying more troops to the island to demonstrate military readiness and to deter Washington.
Following talks with NATO chief Mark Rutte, Trump backed down, saying he would not invade the island but would, instead, work towards a deal. He also withdrew his threat to impose 10 percent trade tariffs on eight European nations objecting to the US’s attempts to acquire Greenland.
Greenland and Denmark then began negotiations with the US to de-escalate the crisis. Here’s what we know:
What’s the US-Greenland deal about?
On Friday, US President Donald Trump claimed the US had reached a deal with Denmark granting it “permanent control” over Greenland’s security “and all other needs”.
The deal allows the US a veto to prevent “adversaries” from establishing a military presence or making “sensitive investments” in Greenland without its approval, Trump said.
A US Department of State official cited by the BBC clarified that will mean non-NATO states will not be able to set up bases in Greenland and will be barred from “making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States”.
Then, on Monday, news of the two new US bases emerged.
Over the weekend, Denmark and Greenland confirmed they had reached an agreement with the US that would be announced this week, but insisted that it would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty.
In a post on Facebook, Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said, “The agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”
On Monday, in advance of the deal’s signing, Nielsen added that it would be a “significant moment following a difficult period … I look forward to signing the agreement and taking the next step with our interests, our security, and respect for our country as the clear starting point.”
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen also sounded an optimistic note in a weekend statement.
“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said.
Where will the two new bases be?
The US will re-establish one Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland, and set up another on the east coast under the coming deal, it has been reported.
The first base will be in Narsarsuaq, a settlement in southern Greenland whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base – also known as Narsarsuaq Air Base and Narsarsuaq Airport – in 1958.
The second base will be located in Mestersvig, a military outpost in the northeast of the territory that is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit.
The US maintained a heavy military presence on the island during the Cold War when American nuclear bombers and nuclear early warning systems were based there. Some 150 troops remain permanently at the northern Pituffik Space Base monitoring for missiles.
What have the reactions been to the US deal?
Trump has argued that taking control of the island, which is on the most direct route between North America and Europe, is necessary to prevent Russia and China from ramping up their own presence in the Arctic, near the US’s northern border.
Analysts say that neither country has significant influence in the region. Nevertheless, the proposed deal stipulated that the US’s adversaries cannot similarly have any Greenland bases.
Russia, responding to the agreement, has said that it was not involved in discussions.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday that “at present, the issue of cooperation in the Arctic is not on the agenda. The Americans and other Arctic states are refusing to cooperate with Russia.”
China, meanwhile, has not commented.
Earlier, over the weekend, a NATO spokesperson told reporters that the alliance was on board with the deal and said it would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”.

Hong Kong workforce to shrink by 20,000 yearly as key sectors face shortages
Predicted 2028 shortfall will narrow to 130,000, but key sectors such as aviation, tech, healthcare and construction still face crunch
Hong Kong’s workforce is forecast to shrink by around 20,000 a year until 2028 despite measures to import labour and talent, with shortages remaining most acute among skilled technical workers.
A government report on manpower projections on Tuesday found that although the labour shortfall would narrow to 130,000 by 2028, down by nearly a third from the original estimate of 180,000, the city would continue to face critical manpower challenges across key sectors.
“Due to economic transformation, the adoption of AI [artificial intelligence] and various talent and labour importation measures, the predicted manpower shortfall in 2028 will narrow to 130,000, but most critical industries, especially innovation, aviation, construction, city operations and healthcare, still face a manpower crunch,” said Ho Kai-ming, the acting secretary for labour and welfare.
“The adoption of AI is expected to accelerate and companies are likely to take a more cautious approach when hiring for entry-level positions. We believe demand for these roles will ease and some clerical jobs will undergo restructuring. Overall, fresh graduates and middle-aged clerical staff are expected to be most impacted.”

China’s Hygon moves beyond data centres with embedded processors for robotics, edge AI
Shanghai-listed firm says new chips will help bring AI from cloud servers to factory floors and industrial machines

Iris Dengin Shenzhen
Chinese chipmaker Hygon Information Technology on Tuesday launched a suite of central processing units (CPUs) for robotics and industrial edge devices, expanding beyond cloud computing and into the fast-growing market for physical artificial intelligence.
The firm unveiled its Hygon 1000 series processors, designed to be embedded into physical devices in industrial automation systems such as robotics and factory controllers, enabling computing and graphics processing to be handled locally.
Built on Hygon’s x86-compatible C86 architecture, the four-core, eight-thread CPU supports both DDR4 and DDR5 memory.

Never mind Trump – if Europe wants to save Nato, it must win over the American people | Leslie Vinjamuri
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:30:02 UTC
23:30:02 KST

At a moment when Europe is focused on persuading Donald Trump to remain committed to Nato, it needs to convince Americans, too. So the presence this evening of the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, in front of a public audience in Des Moines, Iowa, is significant. This is the home town of Trump’s ambassador to Nato, Matthew Whitaker, and the visit brings the debate over Nato’s future directly to a midwestern audience in a red state that operates far from elite foreign-policy circles in Washington. Rutte’s appearance is long overdue.
Russia’s war in Ukraine and uncertainty over the US commitment to European security have forced European leaders to confront their dependence on Washington. While some are pressing for building European capabilities as a means to separate from the US, others see greater European defence spending as essential to keeping the US engaged. Either way, European governments can’t rely solely on meetings with Trump to secure the alliance’s future.
Instead, Europe’s leaders need to look beyond Washington and take a tip from Rutte. Making the public case for Nato, the transatlantic partnership, and shared security across the middle of the country, is essential, not optional. This case should begin with the American people.
For decades, Americans have supported the transatlantic relationship because they understood that Europe’s security is closely connected to their own. Nato and the transatlantic partnership were part of a wider ambition, designed to make the world safe for democracy, not least for the growth and prosperity this created. Public support has been essential to this undertaking.
For many Americans, democracy is now failing to deliver on the promise of prosperity, and in some key areas the contrast with Europe is stark. In the Commonwealth Fund’s 2023 survey, 46% of US adults with lower or average incomes reported skipping or delaying needed healthcare because of cost, compared with 16% in each of the UK, France, Germany and the Netherlands. Populists have been quick to highlight the shortcomings of America’s democracy, and this message has resonated across swaths of the population, particularly rural voters and Americans without a university degree – both central to Trump’s electoral coalition.
When it comes to the American public, there is plenty of room for optimism, but in a political context that is ripe for populists to cultivate antagonism toward spending on foreign causes, there is little room for complacency. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ polling consistently shows that Americans support Nato and the transatlantic partnership. Its recent survey with Ipsos found that 68% of Americans supported maintaining or increasing the US commitment to Nato. Yet only 47% were confident that European allies would come to America’s defence if it were attacked, down from 62% in 2025. Public support for Ukraine has also remained substantial, even as Americans debate the scale and duration of US assistance; a 2024 survey found that 58% supported sending additional arms and military supplies to Ukraine, and the same number supported economic assistance.
European leaders would be wise to invest in a public diplomacy strategy in order to cultivate understanding among Americans outside Washington’s foreign-policy establishment. The secretary general’s decision to travel to Iowa should be seen as a crucial part of Europe’s midwest strategy. Other leading foreign policy organisations have sought to do the same. Over the summer, the Ditchley Foundation used the occasion of America’s 250th to deepen its partnerships across the US, convening roundtables in South Carolina and Illinois.
This outreach is essential to counter the persistent myth that Europeans are free-riding on America’s coattails. Europe’s renewed commitment to defence is significant, with a 20% increase in 2025 compared with 2024 among the EU’s 27 member states. This remains poorly understood in the US. Nato’s Annual 2025 report notes that all of Nato’s 32 members met or exceeded the 2% of GDP expenditure target for that year. Allies have committed to investing 5% of GDP annually by 2035 in defence and related security. The precise figures matter, but so does the broader message: that Europe is investing in the capacity to defend itself and contribute to shared security.
It would also be smart to highlight the opportunities created by this investment for American companies. Defence cooperation supports jobs and growth opportunities. It also boosts transatlantic supply chains and research partnerships. But the ties that bind Europe and America reach deeper than military procurement. The case for the alliance should ultimately be made in terms that people recognise in their own lives: the security of their jobs, the price and availability of energy, the resilience of the technology they rely on and, above all, the prospect of their families living without the threat of a wider war.
The transatlantic partnership cannot be secured through presidential diplomacy alone. European leaders should continue engaging the White House, but they must also make their case to the American public. The long-term future of Nato will depend not only on what presidents decide, but on whether citizens on both sides of the Atlantic continue to see the alliance as essential to their security, democracy and prosperity.

Albania court suspends spy chief, orders house arrest in graft probe
TIRANA, Sept 22 - An Albanian court has suspended the country's spy chief and has ordered her placed under house arrest on suspicion of disclosing classified information, as part of a wider corruption investigation, a special prosecution office said on Tuesday.
Vlora Hyseni, who is originally from Kosovo, has served as head of the Sherbimi Informativ i Shtetit (SHISH) intelligence service since 2023. Previously, she served as deputy intelligence chief in Kosovo.
Prosecutors said Hyseni was suspected of disclosing classified information to unauthorised persons in connection with a corruption case at the National Agency for Information Society (AKSHI), which manages Albania's digital public services and IT infrastructure. The special prosecution office, known as SPAK, has long been pursuing the case.
Hyseni could not be reached for comment.
Many state officials and business people have been arrested or are being investigated for misusing public money at AKSHI.
SPAK, which targets corruption and organized crime, said the measures against Hyseni were approved by an anti-corruption court to allow further investigation.
Prime Minister Edi Rama, who is in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, said he had already relieved Hyseni of her duties and, in consultation with the president, would appoint a new head of the intelligence agency.
“Everyone is innocent until a final court ruling is issued, but no one is above the law,” Rama wrote on X.
The move is another setback for Rama's government. In February, Rama dismissed his Deputy Prime Minister Belinda Balluku after corruption charges were brought against her. Parliament later declined to lift her immunity to allow her arrest. Balluku denied the allegations.
European Union officials have told Reuters they are looking closely at Rama's handling of corruption cases and that Albania's fight against crime and corruption was critical to the Balkan country's bid to join the bloc by 2030. REUTERS

Ex-Rwandan official appears at UK trial over 1994 genocide
Unknown

Ex-Rwandan official appears at UK trial over 1994 genocide
Prosecutors allege Vincent Brown incited and directed acts of violence during the early days of the Rwandan genocide.
A former Rwandan official has appeared in a court in the United Kingdom after being charged with ordering six killings during the first week of the Rwandan genocide in 1994.
Vincent Brown, a 65-year-old doctor formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is the first person to be charged in Britain over the genocide, in which more than 800,000 people, most from the Tutsi ethnic minority, were killed in over 100 days of nationwide massacres. He denied any wrongdoing.

list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Hutu and Tutsi: The history behind the divide
- list 3 of 3UK prosecutors charge first person for Rwanda genocide
On Tuesday, Brown spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and address. He did not enter a plea.
Brown faces one charge of conduct ancillary to genocide in Rwanda’s capital, Kigali, in April 1994 during the first week of the genocide. The doctor is accused of ordering six killings in four days, including of a young mother and her baby son.
Prosecutor Jane Stansfield said Brown was head of the Department of Family Health within Rwanda’s National Office of Population when the genocide began.
Originally from Kigali, Brown is believed to have entered the UK as an asylum seeker in 1998 and lived in London, where he once worked for a charity assisting refugee nurses and midwives seeking work in Britain.
Brown officially changed his last name from Bajinya when granted UK citizenship in 2004 and was first arrested in 2006. His extradition to Rwanda along with four other men was finally refused by a British court in 2017.
The Rwandan government had asked the Metropolitan Police to investigate the men for involvement in killings in the Rugenge district of Kigali that are the focus of Brown’s current trial.
Seven-year inquiry
The charges arose after a complex seven-year UK investigation that began in September 2019.
Brown’s lawyer Sam Blom-Cooper said his client welcomed an opportunity to clear his name. “These are appalling crimes, terrible murders that were committed back in 1994,” he said. “But this, finally, does represent the beginning of the end for Dr Brown.”
Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring granted Brown bail on condition that his family pay 25,000 pounds ($33,000) security. Due to the seriousness of the allegations, he transferred the case to the Central Criminal Court, also known as the Old Bailey, where Brown is due to appear on October 9.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said the trial will set an important precedent against impunity even for decades-old allegations.
“This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” she said.

Climate change has created a meta-crisis in food security, energy and the economy, says Greek expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:28:36 UTC
23:28:36 KST

Emmanuella Doussis is the UNESCO Chair on Climate Diplomacy and Professor of International Institutions at the University of Athens.
Climate change is no longer purely an environmental issue. It affects the economy, society, energy and international security, while creating new geopolitical balances and competition over critical resources, like water.
"Climate change is an economic problem, because it directly concerns states' national economies. It is a social problem, because it affects societies. It is a political problem and it is also a geopolitical problem," Professor of International Institutions and holder of the UNESCO Chair on Climate Diplomacy, Emmanuella Doussis, tells Euronews.
The climate crisis is reshaping geopolitical balances
Extreme heat and climate change are now directly linked to international competition for resources and strategic regions, Doussis explains.
The melting of Arctic ice, for example, is opening up new possibilities for trade routes, while at the same time competition is intensifying for raw materials that are vital for new technologies, such as lithium, cobalt and rare earths.
Water, and access to it, are acquiring ever-greater geopolitical significance, while climate change is also linked to food security and population movements.
"At this point we are seeing heightened competition in the search for new resources," she explains, referring among other things to the Arctic, tensions over water and rivers, as well as population movements.
Moving away from fossil fuels is creating new dependencies
A central issue in tackling the climate crisis remains the gradual move away from fossil fuels. It is, however, a process with significant economic and geopolitical repercussions.
As Doussis explains, a genuine transition to clean forms of energy will not affect all states in the same way.
"The move away from fossil fuels will weaken certain states," she says, explaining that countries which produce and export fossil fuels will have to restructure their economies and seek new sources of growth.
At the same time, she believes that states with substantial potential in renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind and geothermal, will gain ground, as will countries that possess raw materials essential for new technologies.
"Consequently, new dependencies and power relations will emerge," she notes.
The role of international diplomacy
Addressing climate change depends to a large extent on international cooperation, which has been institutionalised through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and was strengthened by the Paris Agreement in 2015.
Nonetheless, Doussis points out the limitations of the current system. States submit national plans for reducing emissions and adapting to climate change, which are revised every five years, yet there are no substantial sanctions in cases of non-implementation.
In a particularly challenging geopolitical environment, she believes that diplomacy could focus more on concrete actions and less on the constant setting of new targets.
In this context, she highlights the need for cooperation in specific fields, such as research and technology, as well as electricity interconnections, which can facilitate the faster roll-out of renewable energy sources.
Major emitters and different speeds
The role of the largest emitters is particularly important. China, the United States, India and the European Union are at the centre of international efforts, but with differing priorities and policies.
Doussis makes special reference to the United States where, as she notes, scepticism towards climate policy has grown and greater emphasis has been placed on fossil fuels.
At the same time, she notes that China has invested heavily in clean technologies, treating the green industry as one of the key sectors of the 21st century. However, it continues to invest in fossil fuels as well, which, she says, creates a complex picture of its role in the global energy transition.
Greece in a particularly vulnerable region
For Greece, the climate crisis takes on particular importance because of the country's geographical position. The Mediterranean is regarded by the scientific community as a region particularly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.
Dousi notes that the country had made significant progress with the decision to phase out lignite and the just transition plans, but she believes that in recent years there has been greater emphasis on fossil fuels.
In her view, climate policy should not be treated as a set of isolated "green" measures, but as a broader political choice that affects the economy, energy and the entirety of public policies.
"Climate change is not always to blame"
According to Doussis, dealing with the consequences of the climate crisis is just as important as reducing emissions.
Recalling the major natural disasters of recent years in Greece, she stresses that climate change cannot be used as an alibi for long-standing weaknesses in planning and infrastructure.
"Climate change is not always to blame," she notes, referring to chronic shortcomings, overly complex legislation and inadequate protection of vulnerable areas.
Water, food and population movements
The most worrying aspect of the climate crisis, according to Doussis, concerns its impact on access to basic goods.
"We will face a very large, serious problem with food security. We will face problems with water," she stresses.
Pressure on water resources may lead to new tensions between states, particularly in regions where rivers and river basins cross borders. As a characteristic example she cites the Nile and the tensions between Egypt and Ethiopia.
At the same time, climate change is expected to intensify population movements, creating yet another major challenge for international security and the management of migration flows.
The climate crisis is therefore evolving into a complex issue that goes beyond the boundaries of environmental policy. Energy, water, food security, raw materials and population movements are now all interconnected, making climate diplomacy an increasingly important field within international relations.

BiH to cut, suspend customs duties to support domestic economy

SARAJEVO, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The Council of Ministers of Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) on Tuesday adopted a decision to temporarily suspend or reduce customs duties on imports of certain goods until Dec. 31, 2027, to support domestic economy.
Under the Law on Customs Tariffs, the decision covers materials and raw materials used by BiH producers to manufacture finished products for export or to replace imported products, which cannot be procured domestically in the quality and quantities required for production.
The decision covers a range of sectors, including textiles and footwear, chemicals, metals, electrical equipment, food and automobile industries.
Since the Law on Customs Tariffs entered into force, the Council of Ministers has adopted 14 decisions on the temporary suspension or reduction of customs duties on imports of certain goods, which have previously been applied on an annual basis.
Tuesday's decision takes effect upon its adoption and will be published in the Official Gazette of BiH. It will apply from Jan. 1, 2027. ■

President Donald Trump on Tuesday focused on a wide range of threats the U.S. faces from abroad during a frequently boastful address to the United Nations General Assembly in Manhattan.
Trump, in a roughly 37-minute speech, also directly criticized the U.N. itself, and reaffirmed his view that the U.S. artificial intelligence industry should continue its rapid growth with few restraints or guardrails.
Trump defended his decision to launch a war against Iran, accusing the Islamic Republic of seeking to erect a defensive missile arsenal before making a "mad dash to a nuclear bomb."
As the war approaches its eighth month with no clear end in sight, Trump said he is poised to make a "big decision" on whether to make a deal or quickly "annihilate" the country.
He then predicted once again that a deal will be made "right after" the Nov. 3 midterm elections, claiming "it doesn't make sense for them not to."
"They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," he said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running."
"I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
At a bilateral meeting with United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham after the speech, Trump added that he believes global energy prices, which have shot up due to the war and created upward inflation pressure, will retreat right after the conflict ends.
"I think as soon as the war's over, the numbers are going to come way down," Trump said, adding, "pricing generally, because oil is the big thing."
In his address, Trump also touted a military deal with Greenland and Denmark, saying it gives the U.S. "the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places." That agreement was signed at a trilateral meeting later Tuesday morning.
Trump called Cuba an "absolutely failed state" and accused it of "coordinating with left-wing radicals and Communist networks" in the U.S.
"Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba," Trump told the assembled leaders. He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in negotiations with the island nation.
As he spoke, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the hall. The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
"The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," Trump said, pointing to his administration's intervention in Venezuela this year as proof.
"And if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.
Toward the end of the speech, Trump turned to AI — first by debuting his attempt to rebrand it "super intelligence" and also whipsawing on the U.S. government's role in putting guardrails on the technology.
The president then compared those raising concerns about AI — a group that includes some tech leaders — with those warning about climate change, which Trump also denies is a problem.
"These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster," Trump said.
He reiterated his view that winning the race for AI superiority is the key to U.S. global dominance.
"That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," he said. "We're going to keep it very, very straight and very strong. I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution."
The government will "rein things in" if needed and will lead the sector "safely and responsibly," Trump said.
But he also said, "We will only encourage superintelligence. We're going to encourage it, not rein it in."
