Iran delegation to present narrative of resilience, diplomacy at UNGA
Iranians are divided on whether the UNGA will help end the war with the US.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his team are heading to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where they are expected to express grievances about the United States’ war on Iran, but also look at ways of resolving it.
Pezeshkian, who departed Tehran on Tuesday morning local time, is joined by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other officials, and is scheduled to address the 193-member assembly on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy arrives for UN summit
- list 2 of 4Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
- list 3 of 4Can the US ban Iranian airlines worldwide – and what would it mean?
- list 4 of 4Trump-GCC Summit in New York: What does each side want?
“The issues we will raise at the UN concern expressing the plight of the Iranian nation, the crimes that have been committed against it, and the distrust that has been created,” Pezeshkian told reporters before boarding a flight out of Tehran.
He also warned that the renewed use of force by Iran’s foes would be counterproductive.
“We will make the enemies disappointed,” he said.
Araghchi, who had arrived in New York earlier, said his main goals during meetings on the sidelines will be to “defend the rights and interest of the Iranian people”.
The war started by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28 continues, with disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz that have affected global energy prices.
In the backdrop, Araghchi slammed the UN’s lacklustre performance in establishing peace and security.
“Trust in this organisation has been lost, and this is unfortunately because of its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security,” he said.
He said the Minab school bombing by the US and the assassination of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the opening day of the war would be among the issues Iran will raise at the UN.
Sina Toosi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that he believes the Iranian delegation will aim to send a message that it is “open to diplomacy”, but not willing to “de-escalate unilaterally”, as Tehran believes it did in June after the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the US.
“I expect Pezeshkian to present Iran’s current pressure campaign not as an alternative to diplomacy, but as leverage for achieving a more durable agreement,” Toosi said. “The immediate Iranian demands are … an end to the naval blockade, and respect for the Iran-Oman agreement governing transit through Hormuz. In many respects, this amounts to returning to the June understanding and actually implementing it.”
The Iranian delegation will be in New York for five days and is scheduled to return to Tehran on Saturday.
The US has denied visas to Pezeshkian’s accompanying media team and imposed tight restrictions on their movement in the country, according to the president’s office. Iranian delegates will also be barred from buying luxury goods during their stay.
Still, Pezeshkian plans to hold discussions with Iranian expatriates, intellectuals, think tanks and media in the coming days.
Regional tensions
The UNGA brings together representatives of nearly 130 countries at the body’s headquarters in New York.
This year’s assembly, which begins on Tuesday, comes as the US tightens economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump said earlier this week that he was considering a new major military assault on Iran, but wanted to hear from the Arab leaders of the region first. He is set to meet with representatives from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain in the coming days to discuss the war on Iran.
This and a military escalation in Yemen, where Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting the Iran-aligned Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, are other concerns for the assembly.
The Houthis have expanded control over the strait of Bab al-Mandeb in recent weeks after making rapid military advances in western Yemen and the Red Sea coast.
Mediation
Regional mediators – including Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye – have pushed for a diplomatic end to the crisis amid prospects of escalated conflict.
As Iran demands a return to the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, its diplomats are expected to sit down with mediators in New York as well.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera earlier this week that Tehran has communicated seven conditions to the US to reopen the strategic waterway.
These included an end to war on all fronts, the release of Iran’s frozen assets, the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports, an end to military attacks on Iranian territory, and noninterference in the country’s internal affairs. But he also said Iran remains prepared for escalated fighting, and could potentially abandon the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) depending on future US actions.
Toosi told Al Jazeera that there was a “real opening” for diplomacy, but “no guarantee of a breakthrough”.
“The fundamental obstacle is credibility,” Toosi said. “Tehran’s conclusion from the June MoU was that de-escalating first left it dependent on US commitments that Washington could reverse or simply fail to implement. That helps explain why Iran is now trying to negotiate while maintaining coercive leverage, particularly over Hormuz.”
“The UN therefore presents a potentially important opportunity because both sides have reasons to explore an off-ramp,” Toosi added. The question is whether Trump is prepared to negotiate a genuinely reciprocal agreement, rather than treating diplomacy as a mechanism for Iran to surrender its leverage first.”
Meanwhile, in Iran, there are conflicting views about how to end the war with the US, with some parties open to a peaceful resolution and more hardline factions seeking to continue or intensify the war until all Tehran’s demands are met.
Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told local media on Tuesday that Iran was prepared to use new weapons systems against the US if necessary, and pointed to its recent attacks on US warships.
But he added that the country was open to peace. “If our national interests call for it to conduct some negotiations alongside war, we must negotiate,” he said.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, had already said both options remain on the table, but said hardline factions have no end date for the war of attrition. Other factions underestimate Iran’s capabilities and believe it must surrender, he said.
“The first keeps the country in a state of perpetual crisis and the other offers national resources and dignity to the enemy on a platter,” Ghalibaf said. “Both approaches realise the enemy’s wish for disturbing the country’s cohesion and unity.”
Trump said on Sunday he would “probably be open” to meeting Pezeshkian in New York, although the Iranian government’s IRNA news service dismissed this as a “new propaganda game”.
The government’s daily Iran newspaper said New York could offer a “platform for the Iranian narrative”. The hardline Kayhan newspaper wanted Pezeshkian to turn the UN into “a courtroom for American crimes”.
Public expectations in Iran are sceptical that the UN meetings will produce any political breakthrough to end the war, which has deepened the average Iranian citizen’s economic woes.
“I think Pezeshkian going [to New York] is better than him not going, but there is no hope that anything comes of it,” one Iranian told Al Jazeera in western Tehran, on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
Another resident of the capital also said she harboured no hopes of a diplomatic resolution.
“I think if [the politicians] want to, then yes, there can be an opening, but they don’t want to,” she said.

Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:28:49 UTC
22:28:49 KST

The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review into the treatment of figures within their ranks who hold religious views, weeks after the Guardian revealed a religious discrimination claim against the party by the former candidate David Campanale.
Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam but was removed in August 2023. He has argued in a civil case against the party that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career.
Richard Newby, the former Lib Dem leader in the House of Lords, has been appointed to chair the party’s inclusion and faith review, which will examine how the party treats candidates and members of different faith and those without.
The inquiry, which has not been publicly announced, was set up in direct response to Campanale’s case, the Guardian understands, with figures at the top of the party understood to be keen to show they take the issue seriously.
The Guardian revealed last month that Campanale was seeking almost £790,000 in damages after the party admitted direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, and failures in dealing with complaints about his treatment.
The case prompted the former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes to call for an independent inquiry into Campanale’s treatment by the party, as well as an apology.
The party cannot comment on court proceedings and will instead use Lord Newby’s review to seek to answer the general question of whether people of faith are being discriminated against, and to what extent any evidence shows this.
Hughes told the Guardian he would pursue a separate investigation once Campanale’s case was resolved.
“The Newby review is explicitly not about any past or present legal case and cannot be about David’s case, which is still before the courts and with one remaining possible internal party appeal,” he said. “The review however is greatly to be welcomed and I believe it will allow the party to meet one of the two big objectives which David, [the] Lib Dem Christian Forum, I and others were seeking.”
The Newby review was announced last week to party members via an email from the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, and president, Josh Babarinde, days before the start of the party’s conference in Brighton.
It will examine whether candidate approval, selection and deselection processes are inclusive of different faiths, whether candidates receive adequate support, the operation of complaints and disciplinary processes, and training for local party officers.
A Lib Dem source said: “This review offers no remorse, no apologies to members misled so badly nor contrition towards the victims of breaches including Campanale and other Christians who once formed a bedrock of activists among our party’s nonconformist tradition. All should have had an apology by now.
“As it stands, the review looks like a ploy to impress a court judge as the review of Campanale’s case is meant to be published right before damages are considered.”
Another source said: “The review doesn’t recognise the pain [Campanale’s case] brought on members, and it has to be asked why key individuals refused to act when they received complaints or requests to investigate complaints around Campanale’s deselection.”
Campanale submitted a schedule of loss that puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance” or “loss of political capital”.
In his claim, Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022 he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”.
Questions have emerged within the party about the remit of the review. A number of Lib Dem figures and activists have also privately criticised its lack of formal announcement. One figure questioned whether Newby would have access to complaints and candidate selection material, and whether the review would extend beyond religious faith to other protected beliefs.
There is a particular concern among some members about whether the review will examine the party’s treatment of people with gender-critical beliefs. In a motion passed at party conference on Monday, members rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”.
The party’s conference fringe programme over the weekend included discussions about Christian nationalism and political use of religion.
The Lib Dems previously said the party was “home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians”, but have declined to comment.

Häkkänen faces no-confidence move over Israel visit
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:28:30 EEST
22:28:30 KST

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen faces a no-confidence move in parliament after his visit to Israel and meeting with Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz prompted criticism from opposition parties. The Greens have questioned who approved the meeting and whether it reflected the government’s wider policy towards Israel.
Häkkänen visited Lebanon and Israel from 13 to 18 September. According to the Ministry of Defence, he met Katz, reviewed the David’s Sling air defence system purchased for the Finnish Defence Forces, examined Israeli civil defence arrangements and visited defence companies supplying Finland.
In Lebanon, Häkkänen met President Joseph Aoun, Defence Minister Michel Menassa, UNIFIL commanders and Finnish peacekeepers.
The Israel part of the trip has since become the focus of a dispute in parliament.
Greens chair Sofia Virta said she plans to submit a no-confidence motion against Häkkänen. She has demanded an explanation of whether the government approved the meeting with Katz or whether Häkkänen made the decision himself.
Häkkänen told Finnish news agency STT that the decision to make the visit was his.
Virta has argued that a ministerial meeting carries political significance because of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Katz’s statements concerning Palestinians. She has also questioned whether the visit conflicts with Finland’s stated support for international law.
The Left Alliance has said it will support the Greens’ no-confidence initiative. Virta has called on the Social Democratic Party, which has been considering its position, to join the motion.
Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela has also submitted a written parliamentary question over the visit. Koskela said the government should explain whether it assessed the trip in relation to Finland’s campaign for a UN Security Council seat for 2029–30.
Greens MP Atte Harjanne has separately asked whether the meeting had the backing of the foreign minister, the government and the president. He said Finland’s existing defence purchases from Israel created practical ties but questioned the need for a ministerial meeting.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo defended Häkkänen on Tuesday and described the criticism from the opposition as disproportionate.
Orpo said the trip involved a normal ministerial duty linked to Finnish defence and Häkkänen’s visit to Finnish personnel serving with UNIFIL.
He also pointed to David’s Sling, which Finland agreed to purchase from Israel during the previous government’s term. Häkkänen has said developments to the system following Iranian missile attacks were among the reasons for his visit.
“He was there ensuring the delivery to Finland of the air defence system ordered by the previous government, meaning the current opposition parties,” Orpo told reporters in parliament, according to Yle.
Häkkänen has also stressed Iran’s role in regional conflicts. In comments to Ilta-Sanomat, he said Hamas and Hezbollah operate in practice as extensions of Iran’s armed forces.
Middle East researcher Timo R. Stewart of the University of Helsinki disputed parts of that framing in comments to Helsingin Sanomat. Stewart said Iran has maintained close links with Hezbollah and has supported Hamas, but argued that placing the emphasis on Iran follows a narrative favourable to Israel and leaves out factors connected to Israel’s own policies.
Stewart also told HS that the ministerial visit sent a signal of closer cooperation with Israel, questioning the need for a political-level visit after the defence purchases had already been agreed.
The dispute also comes as Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen has backed a joint statement with other countries concerning restrictions on products originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The controversy comes weeks after Finland’s defence cooperation with Israel drew criticism from opposition parties. Yle reported in August that the two countries had renewed a memorandum on defence materiel cooperation for 10 years, extending the arrangement until 2034, without a public announcement from the Ministry of Defence.
The Greens and Left Alliance criticised both the agreement and the way it was handled.

El Nino poses growing global health threat as temperatures rise: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:28:24 UTC
22:28:24 KST

El Nino is strengthening rapidly and is expected to have health impacts worldwide, with the most severe consequences likely in countries already facing weak health systems and humanitarian crises, UN agencies have warned.
"We've just lived through the two hottest months on record. Sea surface temperatures are at record levels," Armel Castellan, extreme heat adviser at the joint WHO-WMO climate and health program, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday.
Castellan said El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of 2026, but stressed that its impacts would continue beyond that point.
As the event peaks, much of the Southern Hemisphere, including southern Africa, South America and Australia, will move into its hottest season in early 2027, potentially increasing risks of drought, wildfires, smoke and air pollution, he said.
‘Public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon’
Teresa Zakaria, WHO's unit head for risk reduction, humanitarian operations and climate change, told reporters that El Nino is "a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon."
She said malnutrition and cholera are assessed as "very high" risks in both drought- and flood-affected settings.
More than 150 million people are already facing acute food insecurity globally, with that figure expected to increase as climate shocks disrupt food production and livelihoods, she said.
Warmer temperatures and changing rainfall could also increase transmission of mosquito-borne diseases including malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika, potentially spreading them into areas where they have not traditionally occurred.
"We have a window of opportunity to act now before these risks become crises," Zakaria said.

North Korea's Kim lauds test of apparent new hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

North Korea's Kim Jong Un lauds apparent hypersonic missile test, calls it "incurable headache" for foes
Hong Kong — With his teenage daughter and possible successor by his side, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un watched on Sunday as his country tested a purported new hypersonic weapon designed to evade missile defenses. North Korean state media said Kim had lauded the weapon as an "irresistible force" that would be an "incurable headache" for North Korea's adversaries.
The country's state-run KCNA news agency said the "new weapon" tested on Sunday was "of great significance."
The type of weapon was not specified by the reports, but photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, with his daughter Kim Ju Ae, inspecting a screen with a label reading, "Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory."
Analysts say the title suggests the test was of an upgraded version of an existing North Korean short-range ballistic missile that adds a retrofitted hypersonic glide vehicle. Hypersonic missiles can generally fly lower and faster than conventional rockets, making them more difficult to intercept. North Korea has tested various hypersonic weapons systems since 2021.
They are among the advanced weapons Kim has wanted his country to develop as he seeks to upgrade North Korea's nuclear capabilities.
The test launch on Sunday will come as a blow to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is expected to lay out plans to improve relations with Pyongyang at the U.N. General Assembly this week. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since fighting in the Korean War ended in 1953 with a ceasefire agreement rather than a full peace deal.
Lee has proposed dropping South Korea's longstanding demand for Pyongyang to give up its nuclear weapons as a precondition for talks, suggesting instead a freeze on further nuclear weapons testing or development by North Korea, at least initially.
President Trump has also repeatedly expressed interest in meeting with Kim, possibly around the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November. The White House has suggested that talks could be held "without any preconditions."
Mr. Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, but failed to make any progress on the issue of denuclearization. Since then, North Korea has continued to develop its nuclear and conventional weapons programs and is now believed to possess dozens of nuclear warheads.
South Korea's government claims Pyongyang has between 80 and 120 warheads. Mr. Trump recently said the North had 57 nuclear warheads.
The Kim regime has given no indication of interest in a new round of talks with Mr. Trump or with Lee, despite Mr. Trump's move last month to scale back annual military drills with South Korea, which he called "hostile" to Pyongyang.

Settlers storm Palestinian towns as Israeli forces raid W. Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:27:33 UTC
22:27:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Settlers storm Palestinian towns as Israeli forces raid West Bank
Israeli settlers backed by occupation forces attacked several Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank in the early hours of Tuesday, as settler violence and military raids continue at unprecedented levels across the territory.
Dozens of settlers, accompanied by a large Israeli military force, stormed the town of Silwad, east of Ramallah, and seized dozens of livestock belonging to three Palestinian residents.
Property was damaged during the attack before local residents confronted the settlers and forced them to withdraw.
Silwad Mayor Raed Hamed told The New Arab that "hundreds of settlers entered the town of Silwad in the early hours of Tuesday via an unpaved agricultural road near the Ayoun al-Haramiyah area."
He said Israeli forces accompanied the settlers and provided them with protection, while other troops entered the town through its main entrances.
In nearby al-Mazraa al-Sharqiya, Mohammed Malash, a volunteer with the town's ambulance service, told The New Arab that settlers attacked the outskirts of the town at around 2 a.m. as the assault on Silwad was under way, prompting confrontations with Palestinian residents.
Malash said live ammunition was fired at young Palestinian men, although no injuries were reported. Residents quickly reached the area and prevented the settlers from breaking into one of the homes.
He added that settlers smashed Palestinian-owned vehicles and attempted to attack a house before residents confronted them and forced them to withdraw.
Israeli forces raid Palestinian towns
The settler attacks came alongside a series of Israeli military raids across the occupied West Bank.
In Nablus, Israeli forces stormed several areas of the northern West Bank city, searched homes and detained 68-year-old Samir al-Asta from his home.
Israeli forces also raided several areas of the Bethlehem governorate, including Beit Sahour and Beit Jala, as well as the towns of al-Ubeidiya, al-Shawawra and Zaatara. No arrests were reported there.
In Tammun, southeast of Tubas, Israeli forces detained 86-year-old Burhan Rashid Bani Odeh and his 57-year-old daughter, Rashida, on Tuesday morning.
Kamal Bani Odeh, director of the Prisoners' Club in Tubas, said the pair were detained in an attempt to pressure Rashida's son to turn himself in, adding that other members of the family had previously been arrested for the same reason.
In Ramallah and al-Bireh, Israeli forces tightened movement restrictions and erected a checkpoint at the entrance to Ain Sinya, north of Ramallah, disrupting hundreds of vehicles, particularly those leaving the city.
Another checkpoint was erected between Silwad and Yabrud, east of Ramallah, restricting residents' movement, while Israeli forces established a further checkpoint at the entrance to Aboud, west of Ramallah, where soldiers searched Palestinian vehicles and checked residents' identification documents.
Late on Monday, Israeli forces withdrew from the town of Biddu in the central West Bank following a day-long military operation involving raids, arrests, field interrogations and assaults on Palestinians.
Biddu Mayor Nazmi Mansour told The New Arab that "Israeli forces withdrew from the town overnight, and institutions, schools and shops resumed operations this morning."
He said five Palestinians remained in detention after others were released following the field interrogation of hundreds of residents. Dozens of injuries were also reported during the raid.
Settler violence reaches unprecedented levels
The attacks come amid an unprecedented surge in Israeli settler violence against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank.
Since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition took office at the end of 2022, settler attacks have increased sharply alongside settlement expansion and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement.
The UN has said settler violence has reached unprecedented levels in 2026, documenting more than 1,430 incidents resulting in casualties or property damage by 10 August and affecting around 260 Palestinian communities.
UN officials have also documented Israeli settlers and security forces acting together in attacks on Palestinian communities, while UN experts have described the escalating violence as "settler terror" carried out with the support and acquiescence of the Israeli state.
Thousands of Palestinians have been displaced this year amid settler violence, demolitions and evictions, with entire communities forced from their land.
The violence has included killings and physical assaults, as well as attacks on Palestinian homes, livestock, farmland, vehicles, water infrastructure and other property.
The Israeli Institute for National Security Studies warned earlier this month that surging settler terrorism posed a threat to Israeli state institutions.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. The UK and several other European governments have also imposed sanctions targeting settlers and entities linked to violence and settlement activity.
Israeli settlements and settlers have recently faced UK measures amid mounting international pressure over settlement expansion and attacks on Palestinians.

It's been a great experience, an amazing experience, and we've really formed a bond in doing it by expanding America's footprint in the Arctic and North Atlantic. This deal also protects Europe, in addition to America, and greatly protects them," Trump said.
Trump calls for rebranding artificial intelligence as 'super intelligence'
Trump also called for rebranding artificial intelligence as "super intelligence."
"It's actually amazing, but we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports. From this point forward, all of the United States documents and, hopefully, the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term "super" as opposed to artificial. So it's super intelligence," the president said.
"In other words, welcome to the new world of superintelligence. SI. SI. Let's see if that goes. It sounds much better. It is much better, and it's much more accurate. Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't. We're going to find out pretty soon," he added.
"The United States leads the world in superintelligence, and we'll continue to do so safely and responsibly. Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge," Trump said.
France's Macron: 'So-called peace in Gaza is spectacle that shames us all'
In his address later on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron said that the "so-called peace in Gaza is a spectacle that shames us all."
Macron also said that the "so-called peace has not opened any humanitarian corridors" in the Gaza Strip.
Macron also took a swipe at increased settler violence in the West Bank, saying it was removing the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to exist.
Guterres condemns Hamas's Oct. 7 massacre, calls Israel's reaction a 'scale of death and destruction unlike anything I have seen'
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned Hamas's October 7 massacre, before immediately denouncing Israel's reaction as "unlike anything [he had] ever seen before" during the opening statements at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.
"We must not for a moment lose sight of the devastating situation in the occupied Palestinian territories," he said.
"Almost three years have passed since the heinous Hamas terror attack of October 7, but what followed was a large-scale offensive against Palestinians in Gaza, involving a scale of death and destruction unlike anything I have seen during my years as secretary-general," he stated.
" The International Court of Justice has issued legally binding provisional measures in the case titled, and I quote, ‘Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip,’” he continued.
“In an advisory opinion issued last year, the international court made clear that the UN must be allowed to fulfill its mandates in Gaza, and that our staff and humanitarian aid workers must be protected," Guterres said.
"All parties must comply with international law and the Court’s orders," he added.
"Meanwhile, violence, displacement, and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are trampling the path to peace and raising fears of ethnic cleansing," he said.
"We cannot allow the two-state solution to disappear before our eyes," Guterres added.
Israel's Ambassador to the UN Danny Danon denounced Guterres's statements on X, saying that the UN chief "chose to use the podium to deliver a political indictment of Israel, with outrageous insinuations of “ethnic cleansing.”
"This is not diplomacy. This is anti-Israel propaganda under the UN banner. You have turned your office into a tool for attacking Israel and shattered the organization’s credibility," Danon said.
"It is time for new leadership," he added.
Jordanian King Abdullah II denounces Israel's actions in Gaza, West Bank, settler violence
Jordanian King Abdullah II denounced Israel's actions in Gaza, the West Bank, and settler violence during his address.
"In Gaza, the evidence is overwhelming. In the first 300 days of the so-called ceasefire, at least 300 Palestinian children were killed. Field hospitals were also targeted. President Trump has pushed hard for peace and a path to end this, but the Israeli government keeps moving the goalposts," Abdullah said.
"These can no longer be dismissed as temporary measures. Accountability begins when we call things what they are: an attempt to erase Palestinian and impose a new territorial reality," he added.
"When the language is sanitized, the actions become normalized. Appropriated occupied land is not land registration; it is de facto annexation. Systematic attacks on Palestinian communities are not settler unrest," he continued.
"They assure us that Israel is a country governed by law, but the situation on the ground says otherwise. Israeli soldiers stand by as settlers attack, often protecting and joining in. Soldiers block ambulances from reaching the wounded. What is unfolding across the West Bank is not a series of isolated acts; it is an element of a single policy to compel an entire population to leave their land, and there is a name for that: forced displacement, and that is a war crime," the king said.
"The world must abandon the illusion that Gaza and the West Bank are separate stories. In both, Palestinians are being killed. In Gaza, through destruction; in the West Bank, through de facto annexation. The idea of Palestinian statehood is 'cemented on the ground,'" he added.
"The Arab peace initiative of 2002 offered Israel normalization with 57 Arab nations, including Iran and Iraq. The offer has stood for 20 years, with the absence of an Israeli government willing to take it," he said.
"When confronted with evidence of wrongdoing, israeli gov't distracts and discredits critics. has painted the conflict as a war of religion: Jews on one side, Islam on the other. But it is not. Distractions will not fly anymore. People across the world are paying attention," he continued.
"We have tools: sanctions, etc., yet with Israel, resolution ends where they begin, on paper. The Israeli government no longer asks, 'Can we get away with this?' That's why no one in the assembly should assume that its desires end with Palestine," he said.
"Step by step Israeli is testing how far it can go," Abdullah added, regarding Israeli-Syrian border buffer zones.
"Jordan will not look away. We will protect our water, our security, our people. If Israel continues its antagonistic approach in southern Syria, will the international community stand by? Through it all, we will continue to support Palestinian resilience," he stated.
Erdogan: 'Injustice against Palestinian brothers and sisters deeply offends humanity'
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan commented that the "injustice" allegedly caused by Israel "against Palestinian brothers and sisters deeply offends humanity."
"We will continue to be a voice for the state of Palestine. I call on all countries who do not recognize the state of Palestine to reconsider," he said.
"In Gaza alone, over the past 3 years, we have lost 74,000 of our brothers and sisters (most women and children) to what we regard as state acts of terror by Israel," Erdogan said.
"Innocent children who have lost their arms and legs in Gaza are trying to return to school with prosthetics made of wood. Hospitals in Gaza are having fuel shortages. Today, Gaza is not the world's largest child graveyard; it is also the place with the highest rate of child amputation in the world," he added.
"Gaza has become the most inhumane and shameful concentration camp of our time. The West Bank is experiencing the most severe period of 'settler violence.' In Jerusalem, Muslims and Christians are being denied access to holy sites. There is an initiative to destroy UNRWA. We are faced with a genocidal mindset that cannot get enough of killing. No one with a sense of humanity and compassion can possibly remain indifferent to this picture," he said.
"The UN has been rendered unable to fulfill its mission of maintaining worldwide peace," he added.
"Children in Gaza must be safe. When Palestinian children look up at the sky, they'll see kites, not fighter jets or drones. The UN Security Council must be reformed," Erdogan said.
"As for Gaza, we remain committed to the agreement signed in Sharm el-Sheikh a year ago. We must begin the reconstruction of Gaza immediately. Attempts to strangle the state of Palestine will fail. God willing, we will see an independent state of Palestine based on the 1967 borders, with east Jerusalem as its capital," he added.
Erdogan also commented that "We are witnessing Syria moving towards becoming a safe and peaceful country under [Ahmed] al-Sharaa."
Erdogan also condemned "xenophobia, cultural racism, Islamophobia, and antisemitism" as "toxic trends that must be combated with determination."

Qatari emir calls for reopening Strait of Hormuz, returning to negotiations

It's destruction of entire villages in southern Lebanon in broad daylight is reminiscent of its history in Palestine," he continued.
"Dealing with Israel, putting an end to the harm it causes, and training its unlawful conduct, constitute the true test of the international community's seriousness in upholding values and the rule of law," he added.
"The law must apply equally to all. When it binds the vulnerable but spares the powerful, it loses its meaning," he said.

UN Special Rapporteur "Francesca Albanese must not be persecuted for telling the truth," Lula added.

Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has condemned Israeli violence, displacement, settlement expansion in occupied West Bank as "bulldozing path to peace," raising "specter of ethnic cleansing."
"Violence, displacement, and settlement expansion by Israel in the occupied West Bank are bulldozing the path to peace and raising the specter of ethnic cleansing," Guterres said in his opening address to the 81st U.N. General Assembly in New York.

The Transitions Shaping Australia’s Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:25:00 UTC
22:25:00 KST

Every five years, the Australian Treasury releases its Intergenerational Report (IGR). The report is designed to look at the major structural changes and challenges the country faces to understand how Australia can best navigate the world in the coming decades. This week, the Treasury released its latest report. It argued that despite significant global changes, Australia remains relatively well placed to maintain its prosperity, but its major advantages cannot be taken for granted.
The report highlighted five transitions that will shape the coming decades: artificial intelligence, geopolitical fragmentation, the energy transition, an aging population, and the transformation of Australia’s industrial base. A sixth, overarching, issue is a continuation of intergenerational inequality, with older generations remaining better off than younger Australians. This affects the major structural components of people’s lives – affordable housing, what taxation younger generations will have to pay, and their overall access to opportunity.
The most significant new development to arise since the previous IGR is the ascent of AI. Here, the actual real world outcomes remain unknown, but the Treasury treats AI as a general-purpose technology capable of shifting the economic realities of a wide range of industries. AI is expected to automate some tasks while – hopefully – increasing demand for other forms of work, particularly where human judgment and relationships remain important. The question remains whether Australian businesses and institutions can adjust quickly enough to capture its potential gains, while being aware of and adaptable to any potential negative side effects.
The other major change since the last report has been the acceleration of change in the international environment. Australia’s primary security partner, the United States, is seemingly working hard to dismantle the network of allies that has maintained relative peace and stability over the past 80 years, and it cannot be assumed that this tendency in Washington will subside when President Donald Trump leaves office. China’s massive military build-up and flouting of international law in the South China Sea remains a potential major disruptive force in the Indo-Pacific, while Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has shifted Europe’s focus away from opportunity in the Indo-Pacific to security at home.
The 2026 IGR expects geopolitical fragmentation to make economic relationships increasingly dependent on security considerations, rather than efficiency alone. This creates significant tension for Australia as it has benefited from the openness of international trade, and in particular from trade with China. The report highlighted that Australia is a resource-rich country that has commodities that other countries need, but cannot simply rely on market demand to maintain this advantage in a world where other considerations need to be balanced.
This demand and geopolitical complexity, however, is also affected by the energy transition. Australia may lose advantages in coal and LNG exports, but gain greater energy security through renewables – with Australia currently being heavily dependent on foreign oil. The energy transition requires an enormous investment in generation, storage, and transmission, as well as a shift in consumer habits toward electric vehicles (and the charging infrastructure to support this shift). The growth in data centers – an issue highly controversial in Australia at present – adds another layer of complexity to how the country will manage its energy requirements.
Yet the potentially most consequential issue that the report addressed is Australia’s aging population. Lower fertility combined with an increasing public suspicion of immigration means that the country will grow more slowly, and by the 2060s deaths are projected to exceed births. Longer lives means that the number of Australians over 85 years old will triple in this period, creating increased demand for health care, aged care, and pensions, but with less working-age people to pay for these services.
These demographic changes feed directly into the report’s concerns about productivity. The Treasury projected that average annual economic growth will be about two-thirds of what it has been over the previous four decades. Therefore there is a need to focus on investment, greater skills acquisition, innovation, and regulatory reform to maintain the country’s prosperity. AI may help or hinder this.
It is here where intergenerational inequality becomes more pronounced. House prices have risen faster than incomes for the past two decades, substantially lowering rates of home ownership. Slower economic growth compounds this problem with less opportunity for younger people, less wage growth, and higher tax burdens to pay for government services for older generations. Each of those trends makes it more difficult to have more children.
Taken together, the Intergenerational Report is less a forecast than an account of the pressures Australia will have to manage simultaneously. Australia starts from a strong position as a wealthy, well-educated country, but the test of these assets will be how the population adapts to change.

Malta attorney general appeals blogger murder trial verdict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Malta attorney general appeals blogger murder trial verdict
VALLETTA, Sept 22 - Malta’s attorney general has filed an appeal against a jury verdict finding a businessman not guilty of charges of complicity and criminal association in the murder of prominent journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb placed in her car blew up as she drove out of her home in 2017.
While the men who planted the bomb and those who produced it are serving long jail terms, the man suspected of masterminding it, Yorgen Fenech, was acquitted by an 8-1 verdict earlier in September after a two-month trial.
The verdict shocked the country and sparked protests.
No details were immediately available on the grounds of the appeal, but an appeal in jury trials is limited to points of law.
The Criminal Code allows the Court of Criminal Appeal to order a retrial if it considers that the interests of justice require it.
Malta police last week confirmed that three jurors, a reserve juror and the husband of a juror involved in the trial had been arrested and questioned on the basis of social media posts they are alleged to have authored, along with suspicions that one juror had access to a phone while sequestered for the trial.
All four were released on police bail and no charges have been filed.
The killing of Caruana Galizia nine years ago shocked Europe and set off a political firestorm in Malta as well as focusing international attention on its police and judiciary.
Prosecutors alleged that Fenech, the heir to a property empire that includes hotels and casinos, wanted Caruana Galizia dead because she was about to reveal information about his business dealings. He denied the accusations against him. REUTERS

Romanian court grants former presidential candidate conditional release in fraud case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:23:26 UTC
22:23:26 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
A Romanian court on Tuesday ordered the conditional release of former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu in a fraud case, broadcaster Digi24 reported.
The Bucharest Tribunal rejected prosecutors’ request to keep Georgescu and co-defendant Ionel Rusen in custody for 30 days, placing both under judicial control.
Georgescu cannot leave Romania and must report regularly to police.
Prosecutors from Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) detained him for 24 hours on Monday in an investigation into organized crime and an alleged €1.1 million ($1.3 million) fraud.
Prosecutors allege that three people formed an organized criminal group in September 2021 and operated mainly in Romania and the UK as part of a scheme involving promises of foreign financing, according to DIICOT.
The investigation concerns a businessman who allegedly lost about €1.1 million after being promised access to financing.
Georgescu was detained after investigators carried out searches at five locations in Bucharest and nearby areas, including his home in Mogosoaia.
He exercised his right to remain silent during questioning, according to judicial sources cited by Romanian news agency Agerpres.
Dozens of supporters gathered outside the courthouse during Tuesday’s closed-door hearing, chanting “We do not give up!” Digi24 reported.
Georgescu, running as an independent, unexpectedly won the first round of Romania’s 2024 presidential election with about 23% of the vote.
However, the Constitutional Court later annulled the election following intelligence reports alleging campaign irregularities and foreign interference. Georgescu was subsequently barred from running in the repeat election in 2025.
The latest fraud case remains under investigation.

The UN General Assembly begins in New York with around 130 leaders taking part. Zelenskyy and Pezeshkian will speak on Wednesday.

Türkiye, 7 countries call on Israel to commit to Gaza peace plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:23:00 UTC
22:23:00 KST

Foreign ministers of Türkiye, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) issued a joint statement on the situation in Gaza and Israel’s actions. The ministers met Monday on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
In their statement, the ministers expressed “deep concern over the continued humanitarian suffering in Gaza” and called on Israel to “immediately fulfill its outstanding commitments under the First Phase of the Comprehensive Plan, including by ensuring the immediate, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance and Early Recovery supplies, and facilitating the rehabilitation of critical infrastructure.”
“They stress the imperative of preserving the ceasefire and ending all violations,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry announced Tuesday.
“The Ministers stress that the Road Map constitutes an integral part of the Comprehensive Plan and provides the implementation framework for advancing its Second Phase, including decommissioning alongside full Israeli withdrawal, the deployment of the International Stabilization Force (ISF), the assumption by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) of its responsibilities throughout the Gaza Strip, and the launch of Early Recovery and Reconstruction across Gaza. They call on all parties to fulfill their respective commitments in good faith and without delay,” the statement also said.
The top diplomats also condemned the expulsion or forced displacement of Palestinians from their homeland “or attempts to alter the territorial or demographic character of the Occupied Palestinian Territory.”
“They deplore in this context the illegal measures aimed at consolidating Israeli control and annexation, including the accelerating settlement expansion, land confiscation, demolition of Palestinian homes, settler violence and terrorism, and forced displacement, and called for their immediate reversal. They express grave concern over measures undermining the historical and legal status quo of the Muslim and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem,” the statement said.
The ministers, meanwhile, welcomed efforts by the United Kingdom and European efforts in response to illegal Israeli settlement activity, “including measures to halt trade with illegal Israeli settlements,” and called for further effective measures to end settlement expansion and ensure accountability for settler violence.
“Gaza must remain an integral part of the Palestinian territory,” the statement said, reaffirming that the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan must contribute to the reunification of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip, and to a credible and irreversible pathway toward the exercise of the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and the realization of a sovereign, viable and independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, through the implementation of the two-state solution.
Additionally, the ministers commended U.S. President Donald Trump and hailed the “indispensable role” of his country “in ensuring the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan.” They also called for “sustained and active U.S. engagement to ensure that all parties, including Israel, fulfill their commitments and obligations and to overcome obstacles to the implementation of the Road Map.”
“The tangible progress on the ground will strengthen the credibility of the Board of Peace and the authority of the plan and create deeply needed momentum,” the statement said.
The statement also reaffirmed the countries’ “readiness to continue working collectively with the United States, the Board of Peace, the Palestinian Authority and all relevant parties to advance the full implementation of the Comprehensive Plan and its Road Map, alleviate the suffering of the Palestinian people, fulfill their right to self-determination and independent statehood, and achieve just, lasting and comprehensive peace in the region.”

American fashion brand Gap enters the Estonian market and opens its first store at Ülemiste Centre  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:22:04 UTC
22:22:04 KST

On 15 October, international fashion brand Gap will open its first store in Estonia at Ülemiste Centre. Gap’s Estonian online store will go live on the same day, making the brand’s full range available to shoppers from opening day.
The new store will be located on the second floor of Ülemiste Centre and will cover almost 340 square metres of retail space. Both the store and the online store will be operated by Iconic Brands Nordic, the exclusive partner of Gap Inc. in the Nordic and Baltic countries, responsible for developing Gap’s retail, wholesale and digital sales in the region. Entering the Estonian market is part of Gap’s broader strategy to strengthen its position in the Baltics and expand its reach in Europe.
According to Facundo Ginobili, Senior Vice President of Franchise and Wholesale at Gap Inc., the company aims to connect with people through local stories and experiences. “We see great growth potential in the Nordic and Baltic countries, and our partnership with Iconic Brands Nordic helps us stay as close as possible to customers here,” he said. “We are bringing the Gap range to people in Estonia both online and in stores, to offer fashion lovers a shopping experience without borders.”
For now, the store at Ülemiste Centre will remain Gap’s only standalone store in the whole of Scandinavia and the Baltics – until now, the brand has been available in the region only through partner department stores and e-commerce sites.
“We believe that Gap’s simple, recognisable style and timeless basics will quickly find their way into Estonian customers’ wardrobes,” said Kristjan Rajando, CEO of Iconic Brands Nordic. He added that since the store and the online store are opening at the same time, shoppers will have access to the full Gap range from day one.
According to Guido Pärnits, Director of Ülemiste Centre, the arrival of a major international brand in Estonia confirms that the local market is still seen as attractive and as having room to grow. “Optimism is back in the economy, and that encourages big retailers to invest here. Confidence in the local market and the recovery of consumer spending is growing again,” he added.
He stressed that Gap’s arrival at Ülemiste Centre had been long awaited. “Our customers keep a close eye on global fashion trends, and international brands are highly valued here. Gap’s decision to choose Ülemiste Center for its first store in Estonia is an important recognition,” Pärnits explained.
Gap’s expansion plan got under way in August this year on the Scandinavian fashion platform Boozt, after which its collections arrived in Stockmann department stores in Estonia, Finland and Latvia.
Gap Inc. is one of the largest clothing retailers in the United States, with a brand portfolio that includes Old Navy, Gap, Banana Republic and Athleta. The brands’ clothing, accessories and lifestyle products are sold worldwide through the company’s own stores, franchise stores and online retailers.
Iconic Brands Nordic was founded in 2025 as a joint venture between Brandgate Group and Tristafan. It is the exclusive partner of Gap Inc. in the Nordic and Baltic countries and is responsible for developing Gap’s retail, wholesale and digital sales in the region.

22:21:44 KST

Imagine the prize pool is well over 5 million, and the outcome of the match depends on a single bullet. With stakes that high, some will try to exploit the system. Whether you are casually spectating the weekend main event or analyzing the latest 7bet odds, you want the certainty that the match is legitimate.
Nobody wants to see a rogue piece of code win the championship. We want to see split-second reactions, the result of a deep human dive. But how exactly do the event organizers prevent such disasters? Anti-cheat software is no longer enough to stop would-be hackers. These are under-the-hood security measures that make LAN tournaments the most trusted in the industry!
Hardware quarantines
As early as a few weeks before the event, each participant must prepare their input devices for inspection. This is a necessary step since modern-day cheat programs can sometimes be directly embedded into a device’s firmware. Hackers could modify a mouse’s internal memory so that a simple button press would trigger an aimbot.
To prevent such an exploit, the tournament’s security will inspect and potentially sanitize a player’s gear. Note that the peripherals are taken away from the participants until it is time to play. This is why you see the pros frantically scrambling before a match - they have to quickly reinstall their preferred DPI and button bindings.
Internet and rig lockdown
Your regular home PC is a far cry from what the professionals use. While you might have Discord and a browser open on your desktop, experts’ machines are stripped of every potential distraction. First, the organizers disconnect the internet. The PC has only one place to connect - the LAN (local area network), located inside the building, so the computer is not connected to the outside world. Such a setup makes it impossible for a hacker to remotely access the machine and inject malicious code.
The operating system is also heavily restricted - ports not needed for the LAN are closed off by the firewall. In some cases, the motherboard’s BIOS setting can also be used to disable USB ports, preventing unauthorized peripherals. In case a player wants to change their DPI or crosshair settings, they have to ask the tournament admins for permission.
White noise and referees
Software and hardware security are not enough to guarantee a fair competition. With 20,000 fans in the stadium, what can stop a competitor’s friend from holding up a sign with information about the enemy team’s positions? To avoid such exploits, the players are isolated from the outside world. They must wear special noise-canceling headphones that block out all outside sound.
Inside the headset, the players can hear the casters and their own teammates. The only way for an unscrupulous fan to leak information is if they get past the row of referees. These are not ordinary security guards - they are trained to watch the participants’ every move, making sure that they do not have any unauthorized devices!

On 22 September, Riga Airport begins a new phase in the development of the RIX Airport City project by launching the qualification stage of an international competitive dialogue for the construction of a hotel and office building within the Airport territory.
As part of the first phase of the RIX Airport City project, a hotel and an office building are planned to be developed adjacent to the Airport by 2030. The objective of the competitive dialogue is to identify the most suitable and economically advantageous development solution for the hotel and office complex, aligned with the Airport’s interests. The project will create new amenities and opportunities for passengers and businesses while also contributing to the growth of the Airport’s non-aviation revenue streams.
The land available for development under the tender has been divided into two lots. A 1.2-hectare site is allocated for the construction and operation of a hotel and its associated infrastructure, while a 0.9-hectare site is designated for an office building and related infrastructure. The successful bidder will be granted building rights for a period not exceeding 50 years.
The tender will be organised in two stages. During the first stage, applicants meeting the qualification requirements will be selected and invited to submit their proposals. During the second stage, discussions will be held with selected candidates to address issues necessary for the development of the final hotel and office infrastructure concepts and the preparation of final proposals.
Sustainability and environmentally friendly solutions are among the key requirements of the tender. In accordance with the tender terms of reference, the development of the sites must follow the principles of sustainable planning, promoting reductions in CO₂ emissions and energy consumption, evaluating opportunities for the use of alternative energy sources, and implementing other measures that support environmental protection.
Following the competitive dialogue process, Riga Airport will select one or more developers that submit the most suitable and economically advantageous proposals in line with the requirements and guidelines set out in the tender documentation.
Applications for participation in the qualification stage should be submitted by 30 October.
RIX Airport City is among Riga Airport’s most significant long-term development projects. Over the coming years, it will transform currently undeveloped land surrounding the Airport into a modern airport city featuring hotels, office buildings, retail and logistics facilities. Covering an area of more than 24 hectares, RIX Airport City will offer a diverse range of services for passengers, businesses, and local residents. It will also provide infrastructure and services tailored to the needs of the aviation sector and related industries. Through its connectivity, infrastructure and cargo capabilities, RIX Airport City is set to become a dynamic business hub for companies seeking to establish or expand their presence in the Baltic and Northern European markets.

'Military Schengen': Europe Needs Faster and Seamless Cross-Border Military Mobility  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:21:20 UTC
22:21:20 KST

Europe must be able to move troops, military equipment and supplies across national borders within days rather than weeks. Achieving this requires a form of “Military Schengen” – harmonised and digitalised cross-border procedures, fit-for-purpose dual-use infrastructure and close cooperation between EU Member States, NATO, and the defence and transport sectors. Amid sustained geopolitical tensions, military mobility is becoming an essential prerequisite for European security, participants concluded at the forum “Mobility in Europe 2030 – Serving Sustainability and Military Purposes” held in Riga.
Military mobility in Europe is currently constrained not only by insufficient capacity of individual roads, bridges, railway lines or ports. Significant obstacles also include differing national customs and administrative requirements, inadequate multimodal connections, shortages of transport assets and a lack of qualified personnel. Military mobility therefore requires an integrated system in which infrastructure, transport capacity, energy supply and cross-border procedures function as interconnected elements.
The forum in Riga brought together representatives of EU institutions, NATO, the European Defence Agency, national authorities, academia, and the transport, defence and energy sectors. Discussions focused on how Europe’s transport system can simultaneously adapt to the new security environment, economic needs and sustainability objectives.
The keynote session on the future of European mobility addressed the changing geopolitical environment and its implications for transport policy, infrastructure investment and regional cooperation. Speakers included Latvian Minister of Transport Rihards Kozlovskis, State Secretary of the Latvian Ministry of Defence Airis Rikveilis, Marcin Nowacki, President of the Section for Transport, Energy, Infrastructure and the Information Society at the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC), Riga City Council Chairman Viesturs Kleinbergs, Head of the European Commission Representation in Latvia Andris Kužnieks, and Sami Moisio, Professor of Spatial Planning and Policy and Vice-Dean of the Faculty of Science at the University of Helsinki.
Marcin Nowacki, President of the Section for Transport, Energy, Infrastructure and the Information Society of the European Economic and Social Committee, stressed at the forum that, in the current geopolitical context, mobility must be addressed from both a military and a civil protection perspective. He particularly emphasised the need to overcome the existing fragmentation across the European Union and move towards a more coordinated approach.
“The important message is that the geopolitical situation has changed. Everybody knows that. But it will be a long-lasting one,” Professor Sami Moisio stressed, arguing that infrastructure, investment and political action therefore need to be planned from the perspective of a fundamentally changed security environment. He also emphasised that military preparedness, sustainability and social cohesion should not be viewed separately, but as interconnected elements of European resilience.
Andris Kužnieks highlighted another dimension of Europe’s changing mobility environment – the need to combine climate objectives, technological development and economic competitiveness. Referring to Europe’s future priorities, he stressed that climate policy increasingly involves both mitigating risks and adapting to the reality of a changing climate, which will also have consequences for future transport demand and infrastructure.
Military mobility requires an integrated European system
The panel “Security, Infrastructure and European Mobility Policy” focused on military mobility, dual-use infrastructure, cross-border coordination, regulatory alignment and investment priorities.
A central conclusion was that military mobility should be understood as an integrated, end-to-end system rather than simply as the construction of individual roads, bridges, railway lines or ports. Effective movement depends on physical infrastructure, multimodal connections, available transport assets, energy supply, digital systems and, crucially, harmonised procedures across borders.
The discussion highlighted a significant change in thinking in recent years: military mobility is increasingly regarded as a whole-of-government and whole-of-society responsibility. Moving troops, heavy equipment and supplies depends extensively on civilian transport companies and infrastructure operators. Consequently, cooperation between defence authorities, transport ministries, EU institutions and the private sector is essential. Military mobility cannot be ensured at national level alone, as reinforcement and large-scale military movements are inherently cross-border operations.
Participants repeatedly stressed two key operational requirements – mass and speed. Giuseppe Dello Stritto, Head of Unit – Land and Logistics at the European Defence Agency, noted that critical bottlenecks arise when physical infrastructure limitations, weak multimodal connections, shortages of transport assets and fragmented procedures converge. Ports, railways and logistics hubs therefore need to function as interconnected elements of a single transport chain. Energy supply, including fuel, electricity and other support required at logistics hubs, is likewise an integral part of military mobility.
The NATO perspective also underlined the need for simpler and more consistent procedures. Current arrangements have developed through layers of differing national customs, safety, health and administrative requirements, making rapid, large-scale military movements more difficult. The discussion therefore repeatedly returned to the idea of a “Military Schengen” – a European system that would allow military personnel, equipment and supplies to cross national borders more rapidly through harmonised and digitalised procedures and fewer administrative obstacles.
A further objective is to significantly shorten the time required to obtain the necessary permissions. The discussion pointed to a future model in which standardised military transport permission requests would be submitted through a common EU digital system and processed within days rather than weeks, as can currently be the case.
The scale of the investment challenge is considerable. During the panel, it was noted that the current Connecting Europe Facility included EUR 1.7 billion dedicated to military mobility, while demand significantly exceeded the available funding. The European Commission has proposed increasing funding for military mobility to EUR 17.6 billion in the next Multiannual Financial Framework, with investment focused on dual-use infrastructure, military corridors and critical infrastructure bottlenecks.
Speakers nevertheless emphasised that funding alone will not solve the problem. Europe also needs common priorities, coordinated projects along entire military corridors, sufficient civilian and military transport capacity, qualified personnel and faster implementation. As the discussion highlighted, vehicles and equipment can be purchased comparatively quickly, while skilled drivers and other transport professionals cannot be trained overnight.
Defence can help accelerate alternative energy solutions
The forum also examined transport electrification, alternative fuels and the decarbonisation of transport. One of the main barriers identified by industry representatives was cost: some alternative fuels remain several times more expensive than conventional equivalents, making commercial deployment difficult without predictable policies, support mechanisms and long-term investment certainty.
At the same time, the defence sector could become an important early adopter of emerging energy technologies. As European governments significantly increase the resources allocated to security and defence, the deployment of military solutions is less constrained by the immediate commercial cost considerations faced by civilian transport operators.
Participants suggested that producing, testing and deploying alternative fuels for defence purposes could help increase production volumes, support the practical and engineering development of technologies and generate economies of scale. Defence demand alone cannot eliminate the price gap, but it could contribute to technological development and incremental efficiency gains that could eventually make alternative fuels more competitive in the wider transport market.
Military mobility is becoming a European strategic priority
The conclusions of the Riga forum closely reflect the European Economic and Social Committee’s 2026 opinion on Military Mobility (TEN/869). The EESC stresses that military mobility is vital to EU deterrence and defence, particularly for frontline and transit Member States on the EU’s eastern flank. It calls for simplified and harmonised logistics, customs and transport rules, stronger protection and involvement of civilian personnel, and prioritised EU investment in dual-use infrastructure and technologies, including railways, roads, data networks, satellite communications, drones and innovative propulsion systems. The opinion also calls for substantially greater dedicated funding for military mobility under the Connecting Europe Facility.
The Riga discussion was moderated by Baiba Miltoviča, President of the Permanent Group on Transport at the European Economic and Social Committee, who is actively involved in the EESC’s work on European transport and infrastructure policy. The forum brought together representatives of the EESC, EU institutions, national authorities, NATO, the European Defence Agency and industry, allowing the practical challenges of implementing Europe’s military mobility ambitions to be examined from both civilian and defence perspectives.
The message emerging from the Riga forum was clear: military mobility is no longer a specialised defence issue. It is a test of Europe’s ability to coordinate infrastructure, transport, energy, regulation, investment and human resources across national borders. In an era of sustained geopolitical tension, resilient dual-use infrastructure and the capacity to move rapidly across Europe are becoming essential prerequisites for both European security and the functioning of the continent’s transport system.
