EXPLAINER - Morocco heads to polls: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:58:21 UTC
21:58:21 KST

Serdar Dincel
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
- 7,288 candidacies have been registered nationwide, official data shows
- Main parliamentary forces are broadly divided between parties forming current government coalition and those in opposition
Morocco heads to the polls on Wednesday for a parliamentary election that will determine the makeup of the country’s 395-seat House of Representatives and shape the next government under King Mohammed VI.
Some 15.8 million registered voters are eligible to cast ballots in the North African kingdom, where political parties compete for control of parliament but the monarch retains significant powers over the state’s most important political and strategic decisions.
The vote will be Morocco’s sixth legislative election since Mohammed VI took the throne in 1999, and the fourth since constitutional reforms introduced after the 2011 Arab Spring expanded the powers of parliament and the prime minister while preserving the king’s central role.
Here is a look at Morocco’s political system, the main parties competing in the election, the groups boycotting the vote and how Moroccans living abroad can cast their ballots.
How does the election work?
Twenty-eight political parties are vying for 395 seats in the House of Representatives.
A total of 7,288 candidacies have been registered nationwide, averaging more than 18 candidates per seat.
Since Morocco is divided into local electoral constituencies, 305 seats are elected locally and 90 others are elected through regional constituencies.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), Istiqlal Party, Party of Progress and Socialism and Justice and Development Party each submitted 92 local lists, covering all 92 local constituencies, with 305 candidates each.
The National Rally of Independents (RNI) also submitted 92 local lists with 305 candidates, while other parties submitted fewer lists
Who are the main parties?
The main parliamentary forces are broadly divided between the parties forming the current government coalition and those in opposition.
The coalition consists of the National Rally of Independents, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, and the Istiqlal Party.
RNI, the largest party in the 2021 election, is seeking to maintain its position, while PAM is aiming to emerge as the leading party and head the government for the first time. Istiqlal is also seeking to expand its influence after joining the coalition in 2021.
The main opposition parties include the Socialist Union of Popular Forces, the Party of Progress and Socialism, the Popular Movement and the Justice and Development Party, which are seeking to increase their representation in parliament.
The election will determine the composition of the House and, under Morocco’s constitutional system, the party that emerges with the largest number of seats will be called upon to form the government.
Who is boycotting the election?
Not all political groups are taking part.
The Justice and Charity Association, Morocco’s largest religious movement, and the Democratic Labour Way Party, a left-wing group, are boycotting the election.
Both have criticized the political environment and argued that the conditions do not allow for what they consider free and fair political competition.
Can Moroccans living abroad vote?
The Interior Ministry has launched an online platform allowing Moroccans living abroad who are registered on the electoral rolls to arrange voting by proxy.
Under Moroccan law, eligible voters abroad can appoint a voter registered in Morocco to cast a ballot on their behalf.
The electronic platform allows them to complete the proxy procedure before election day.
Who oversees voting?
Morocco’s Central Election Monitoring Commission, supported by regional and provincial committees, oversees the electoral process.
A total of 3,006 accredited observers, including representatives of 20 international and regional organizations, will monitor the legislative elections on Sept. 23.
Independent and impartial election observation has been regulated by law since 2011.
Observers monitor the process independently and cannot intervene in electoral operations, while state monitoring committees can take action over violations.

Lockheed, Kongsberg test twin-Javelin setup on armored turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:55:18 UTC
21:55:18 KST

- The Javelin Joint Venture and Kongsberg completed a simulation demonstration in Norway using a Medium-Caliber Turret fitted with a prototype dual Javelin launcher assembly.
- The companies called it the first phase of an integration effort and have not disclosed a target vehicle platform or timeline for further testing.
The Javelin Joint Venture completed a simulation demonstration in Norway using a Kongsberg Medium-Caliber Turret fitted with a prototype dual launcher assembly for the Javelin anti-tank missile.
The companies described it as the first phase of an ongoing effort to integrate Javelin more closely with vehicle-mounted turret systems.
The Javelin Joint Venture is a partnership between Lockheed Martin and Raytheon, an RTX business, that builds and sells the Javelin missile system. Javelin is a shoulder-fired, fire-and-forget anti-tank weapon that has also been adapted for vehicle-mounted use over the past decade, most often paired with Kongsberg’s remote weapon stations rather than a full turret system like the Medium-Caliber Turret.
The Medium-Caliber Turret, built by Norway’s Kongsberg, is best known in U.S. service as the turret on the Army’s Stryker Dragoon vehicles, where it carries a 30 mm autocannon along with a coaxial machine gun. Kongsberg’s turret family already supports Javelin as an add-on weapon in some configurations, mounted either on a companion remote weapon station or alongside the turret’s main gun. A dual launcher assembly would let a single turret carry two ready-to-fire Javelin rounds rather than one.
Kongsberg and the Javelin Joint Venture have worked together on vehicle-mounted Javelin systems since at least 2012, when the two companies fired Javelin missiles from a Kongsberg Protector remote weapon station mounted on a Piranha V vehicle during winter trials in Norway. More recent demonstrations have shown Javelin firing from robotic and unmanned ground vehicles equipped with Kongsberg’s Common Remotely Operated Weapon Station, including a 2024 U.S. Army exercise in which Javelin fired from two different unmanned ground vehicles at once.
The U.S. Army remains the Javelin Joint Venture’s largest customer. The venture is operating under an indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity production contract with a ceiling of $7.2 billion covering fiscal years 2023 through 2026, and it delivered the first units of a new Lightweight Command Launch Unit to the Army in May. The Army has not said whether it is evaluating the Medium-Caliber Turret dual launcher configuration for its own vehicle fleet.

Digitex acquires a 90% stake in InfoStrategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:52:48 UTC
21:52:48 KST

Latvian information technology group Datlex continues to expand its expertise in business intelligence and data analytics. SIA Digitex, a software development company within the group, is acquiring a 90% stake in SIA InfoStrategy. An existing co-owner of InfoStrategy will retain a 10% stake and continue working at the company.
The transaction marks the next step in the growth of the Datlex Group following the 2025 acquisition of Visma Consulting by Codex, another IT company within the group. Following the acquisition, Visma Consulting continued its operations under the name Digitex. The latest transaction will expand the group’s expertise in developing business intelligence solutions and increase its capacity to deliver larger-scale projects across the Baltic states.
“We do not want to grow simply in terms of numbers—each transaction must bring new expertise and opportunities into the group. InfoStrategy is a small but highly professional team with strong experience in business intelligence and data analytics. By combining its expertise with the technological capabilities of Digitex and Codex, we will be able to undertake larger and more complex projects,” said Uldis Semeiks, Member of the Management Board of Datlex.
With InfoStrategy joining the group, Datlex gains the team’s expertise, accumulated project experience and portfolio of business intelligence solutions. InfoStrategy will continue working with its existing clients and contracts as before. Since its establishment in 2016, the company has specialised in business management and analytics solutions, including management planning, budgeting, cost calculation modelling and data analytics, serving clients throughout the Baltic states.
“Nothing will change in our clients’ day-to-day cooperation with us—they will continue working with the same people they have known for years. What will change is the scale of our capabilities: joining a larger group will give us access to broader technological expertise and capacity that a team of eight could not provide on its own. We will retain our specialisation in business intelligence while gaining the ability to undertake significantly larger projects,” said Romāns Kairovs, Member of the Management Board of InfoStrategy.
Following the transaction, InfoStrategy will continue operating under its existing name and brand. No change to the company’s name or visual identity is currently planned.
Datlex Strengthens Its Group Model Across the Baltic States
The acquisition of InfoStrategy forms part of the Datlex Group’s broader development strategy. The group’s operations are structured around two principal business areas: IT infrastructure solutions and software development.
In the infrastructure segment, the group operates across the Baltic states and Scandinavia. In Latvia, this business area is represented by Datakom, which provides the implementation and maintenance of IT infrastructure solutions, as well as related consulting services. Other companies within the group complement this offering with IT consulting and infrastructure management services. The group’s companies have more than 30 years of experience in this field.
The group’s software development segment comprises Codex, Digitex and InfoStrategy. Codex and Digitex primarily develop customised business information systems for public- and private-sector clients, while InfoStrategy strengthens the group’s expertise in business intelligence, data analytics and data-driven solutions.
“We are developing as a unified group rather than as a collection of separate companies. Our complementary areas of expertise allow us to cooperate freely and make effective use of the knowledge and experience available across the entire group. It is precisely this close cooperation between our software development and infrastructure teams that enables us to offer clients throughout the Baltic states and Scandinavia broader and more technologically sophisticated solutions,” Uldis Semeiks explained.
The Datlex Group will continue assessing opportunities for growth and the acquisition of new expertise in the Baltic market, combining organic development with the integration of professional teams.
The transaction was financed in cooperation with Swedbank, using a guarantee provided by the European Investment Fund under the European Union’s InvestEU programme.

Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to set foot on US soil since the start of the war, which began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
Reopening the strategic Strait of Hormuz remains central to negotiations to end the war.
Traffic in the vital maritime corridor, through which one-fifth of the world's oil and LNG passed before the war, has been severely disrupted, with Iran firing on commercial ships and demanding that they approve passage.
In response, the US is maintaining a counterblockade of Iranian ports while upping economic pressure on Tehran.
"We will not back down on the strait, and as long as the United States and other countries do not halt their actions, they will face expensive gasoline and oil, along with ongoing energy problems," Iranian Parliament Vice Speaker Ali Nikzad said on Tuesday.

Since taking office, the new Hungarian government has made numerous goodwill gestures toward Ukraine. Linell Raud: 43,000 Estonian companies may face tax risk in 187 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Linell Raud: 43,000 Estonian companies may face tax risk in 187 countries
Do we explain tax risks clearly enough to e‑residents, or do we only whisper about taxes because the topic is too complicated, asks Linell Raud.
For the past decade, Estonia's flagship on the international stage has been the e‑residency program. More and more, however, it has become clear that behind a simple program lie only complicated tax problems. Since Estonia has already had to acknowledge international reputational damage in the Danske Bank money‑laundering scandal and in recently uncovered shell‑round deals, it would be wise to prevent the next blow rather than provide the drama theater with material for another hit production.
The e‑residency program has been successfully marketed worldwide as an easy way to establish a company in Estonia within minutes, bring business profits here, and benefit from our tax system, where profits are taxed only upon distribution. But do we explain tax risks clearly enough to e‑residents both in Estonia and abroad, or do we only whisper about taxes because the topic is too complicated?
So far, 140,000 people from 187 countries have joined the program and established roughly 43,000 companies. In addition to contributing as owners, they participate actively and daily in Estonia's economy as taxpayers and consumers of various goods and services. The direct tax contribution of e‑residents over the lifetime of the program is estimated at about €433 million, and last year alone it was €125 million.
Where does the problem arise?
A more global world brings new problems both in Estonia and in the e‑residents' home countries. Many e‑resident companies operate as one‑person firms, where the owner, board member, and worker are all the same person. There are no employees, no office, clients are generally scattered around the world, and often there are no clients in Estonia at all. The owner does everything remotely, wherever they happen to be.
Like companies founded by Estonians, many e‑resident companies are registered in Estonia as value‑added tax payers. This allows them to freely invoice goods and services sold and purchased, and profit is taxed only upon distribution. But unlike companies operated in Estonia by Estonians, e‑residents face two "buts."
The VAT problem in Estonia
The first "but" is VAT registration. To be registered as a VAT payer in Estonia, a company must conduct business activity in Estonia. If it does not, the Tax and Customs Board (MTA) has the right to cancel the registration. And that is exactly what has happened to many e‑resident companies.
Over the past year, the MTA has focused on checking the VAT numbers of such companies and has requested information about the location of the board, employees, and office. The goal is to assess the companies' real ties to Estonia and the extent of those ties. If it is determined that a company is registered in Estonia and has a VAT number but no actual business activity takes place here, the VAT number is removed.
Once the VAT number is removed, any VAT paid on purchased goods and services becomes a simple expense that can no longer be deducted. The MTA's recommendation in such cases has been that an e‑resident living in another European Union country should explore the possibility of registering as a VAT payer there.
Without business activity in Estonia, the local VAT number will not be kept. Registration abroad may be possible, but unlike Estonia, in most countries it takes a long time.
The income‑tax problem abroad
In addition to VAT, an even more pressing "but" is income tax.
Under the general rule, if a company's activities are managed or carried out daily outside Estonia, the foreign country may have the right to tax the company's profit. The foreign country essentially treats the Estonian company's profit as its own and taxes it as if it had been earned by a local company.
E‑residents are exactly in this situation. They have Estonian private limited companies, but the board member and actual worker — often the same person — are located abroad. Foreign tax authorities are not asleep and are aggressively checking such companies and taxing their profits. Since most countries tax corporate profits annually, the tax obligation is determined for each year, including retroactively.
For example, if a French e‑resident established a company in Estonia in 2023 and earned about €500,000 in profit, the French tax authority has determined that because the board member is located in France, the Estonian company has had a permanent establishment there since its founding.
France has taxed all profits retroactively, and €150,000 in income tax must be paid. In addition, the company owes €100,000 in interest and penalties for not acting correctly from the start.
In some cases, the foreign tax authority has also fined the company's board member personally. In the French example, the personal tax risk was €250,000. So from roughly €500,000 in profit, the foreign tax risk became €500,000. Profit drops to zero, and stress, pressure, and administrative burden skyrocket.
E‑residents understandably ask where the promised tax advantage and simplicity went. The correct answer is that everything promised applies only if the company's board and actual business activity are in Estonia. If either is missing, a profit‑sized tax risk is a real possibility.
Can this risk be avoided?
Measure nine times, cut once applies here as well. Timely notification and reaction would help avoid unpleasant surprises that are indeed mentioned on the e‑residency website but have not reached e‑residents' awareness.
Although company finances are each person's own responsibility, the program could consider stronger communication about risk areas. The mentality of dealing with the problem only once it appears does not work in tax matters. If a company has entered a tax authority's field of interest, it may already be too late to show ties to Estonia or reduce foreign tax risk.
Although the e‑residency website includes an overview of both income‑tax and VAT risks and recommends consulting advisers, this does not seem to be enough. Perhaps it could include specific recommendations, coordinated with the MTA, on bringing the board to Estonia or hiring employees for an office here.
Although such recommendations may bring additional ongoing costs for e‑residents, they would actually create more jobs in Estonia, increase tax revenue, and reduce future misunderstandings with tax authorities on both sides of the border.
E‑residency as Estonia's flagship works only if people participate. To ensure the program continues to bring tax revenue to Estonia, we should speak honestly about both its strengths and weaknesses. If e‑residents feel they learn about real tax risks only through professional advisers or when the tax authority is already knocking, this could become a new ticking reputational bomb or inspiration for another hit stage production.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

Due to climate change, Tunisia sees 2026 summer as hottest on record
Tunisia's summer this year was its hottest on record, the country's weather authority said Tuesday, following multiple heatwaves, water shortages and power cuts.
"The summer of 2026 was ranked the hottest in Tunisia since 1950," the year temperature records began, the National Meteorological Institute said.
The average temperature was about 2.9 degrees Celsius higher than the previous record, it added.
Although accustomed to scorching heat, Tunisia experienced a particularly gruelling summer in 2026, with July and August marked by "intense and prolonged heatwaves", the authority said.
Scientists attribute these episodes to climate change.
This summer also saw persistently high nighttime temperatures, the agency added.
The highest temperature was recorded in the central city of Kairouan, which reached 49.7 degrees Celsius in mid-July.

Erdogan Says ‘The World Is Bigger Than Five’ as He Calls for UN Veto Abolition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:49:22 UTC
21:49:22 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for the abolition of the UN Security Council’s veto power and an end to permanent membership, arguing that the body’s structure no longer reflects the realities of the modern world.
“The tragedies of recent years, including pandemics, energy crises, disruptions to supply chains and regional conflicts, have demonstrated that leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world,” Erdogan wrote in an opinion piece published by Bloomberg ahead of the UN General Assembly’s annual session in New York.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The adaptation of global decision-making mechanisms to today’s circumstances can no longer be postponed.”
The Security Council has five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States – all of which have veto power.
The arrangement was established in the UN Charter in 1945, when the five countries, then including the Soviet Union rather than Russia, were given permanent seats because of their central roles in establishing the UN and maintaining international peace and security.
Russia later took over the Soviet Union’s seat.
The council also has 10 non-permanent members elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. A substantive resolution requires at least nine votes and cannot pass if one of the permanent members votes against it.
Ukraine, Russia, Hard to Reconcile on Black Sea, Turkish Minister Says
Erdogan said simply adding new permanent members would not address the concentration of power.
“Adding new privileged members to the Security Council would not resolve the problem of decision-making power being concentrated in the hands of a few states; rather, it would expand the scope of the privileged structure,” he wrote.
Instead, he proposed abolishing permanent membership altogether. Under his model, all Security Council members would be elected by the General Assembly on a rotating basis for fixed terms, with countries seeking another term required to win majority support again.
“The powers of the General Assembly should be strengthened, and the representativeness of the Security Council and its accountability to the General Assembly should be enhanced,” Erdogan wrote.
He framed the proposal as an extension of his long-standing slogan: “The world is bigger than five.”
“We must harness the experience, capacity and aspirations of different regions in efforts to address global and regional challenges,” Erdogan wrote. “In this respect, our call that ‘The world is bigger than five’ is a call for a broader understanding of responsibility.”
Reform has been discussed for years
The push for reform is not new, and the General Assembly has been discussing changes to the Security Council for years.
In September 2024, UN member states adopted the Pact for the Future, committing to reform the Security Council and make it “more representative, inclusive, transparent, efficient, effective, democratic and accountable.”
The agreement identified the underrepresentation of Africa as a priority and called for continued negotiations on the council’s membership and the future of the veto.
The General Assembly has continued intergovernmental negotiations on reform, but the council’s basic structure has not changed.
The reform process remains focused on questions including how many members the council should have, which regions should receive greater representation and whether the veto should be limited or otherwise changed.
How the veto can block the UN
The veto gives each of the five permanent members the ability to block a substantive Security Council resolution even if the measure has broad support among the other members.
Russia demonstrated that power in March 2024, when it vetoed a resolution that would have extended the mandate of a UN panel monitoring North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs, with Moscow and Pyongyang having fostered closer defense ties since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
The other Security Council members did not block the measure, but Russia’s veto was sufficient to prevent its adoption.
The mechanism has also been central to the Security Council’s response to major international conflicts, including Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, where Moscow’s status as a permanent member has prevented the council from adopting resolutions opposed by Russia.
Erdogan argues that such a system allows a small number of capitals to determine whether the UN can act on major international crises.
“We cannot build the international order of the future by preserving the hierarchies of the past,” he wrote.
“The developments of the last quarter century – a relatively brief period in world history – have demonstrated that no balance of power and no international order are permanent.”
Ankara says it will support efforts to abolish the veto, strengthen the role of elected Security Council members and give the General Assembly greater weight in international decision-making.
“Such a change requires international will on a broad scale,” Erdogan wrote.

Swedish prosecutors probe election fraud allegation casting shadow over vote

Swedish prosecutors probe election fraud allegation casting shadow over vote
STOCKHOLM, Sept 22 - Swedish prosecutors are investigating possible election fraud that could lead to a re-run of the vote in one county, potentially putting 11 parliamentary seats in play and raising uncertainty about the final result of the September 13 vote.
Sweden's parliamentary election saw the opposition narrowly defeat the incumbent right-wing government in a vote widely seen as a referendum on whether the far-right Sweden Democrats should be part of the next administration.
However, the prosecution service has started a preliminary investigation into potential election fraud in Borlange, a town in the largely rural county of Dalarna, central Sweden, that might still affect the final result.
The preliminary investigation was initially closed for lack of evidence, but was reopened this week, prosecutor Oskar Edvardsson said. "New information came in that gave reason to look at this further," he told Reuters.
Swedish media reported that the prosecutor's investigation centred on the election of Mohamed Abdukardir Ali, a Left Party candidate for parliament, who unexpectedly overtook other representatives on the ballot for the party.
In Sweden, voters choose a party but can also pick an individual candidate from a party list. The probe related to the several hundred voters who had checked his name amid reports of pre-marked ballots, Swedish media reported.
Ali told Swedish TV that the allegations were false. "It's completely, completely wrong," he said.
Reuters was not immediately able to reach Ali for comment.
ELECTION RE-RUN WOULD BE A FIRST FOR SWEDEN
The investigation, which was opened on September 1, two weeks before the election, is at an early stage and no suspects have been identified, Edvardsson said. He declined to give further details.
Sweden's Election Review Board could decide on a re-run or recount of the vote in Dalarna, which elects 11 members of parliament, if it decides the result is suspect.
An election re-run would be "a blank slate," said Niklas Bolin, professor of political science at Mid Sweden University.
Sweden has never before re-run a parliamentary vote, he said.
Even if there were a re-run, however, the balance between the two blocs at the national level would be unlikely to change, he said. Voters were more likely to move between parties in the same bloc than across blocs.
"But there is the potential for a different result," he added.
In the September 13 election, the centre-left opposition won 176 seats to 173 seats for the right. In Dalarna, the centre-left bloc won six seats and the right-wing bloc five.
The Election Review Board said it was too early to comment.
A re-run would have to take place within three months of the original election. REUTERS

Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
Nine people were acquitted, while another defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, the court said.
Sri Lanka’s High Court has convicted 15 of the 24 men accused of being involved in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings, which killed 279 people, including 45 foreigners, and injured more than 500.
After a five-year trial, the three-judge bench on Tuesday found that 14 of the accused were guilty on all charges, which included murder, conspiracy to commit “terrorism” and possessing firearms and explosives under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
A 15th defendant was found guilty of only some of the charges, while nine others were acquitted.
All of the accused are from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community. Twenty-five men were originally charged, but one defendant died in custody.
Among those convicted on all charges was Mohamed Naufar, whom prosecutors identified as the ringleader who provided support to the eight-member squad that carried out the bombings.
The presiding judge told a packed courtroom that sentencing would take place later on Tuesday. Dozens of police commandos provided security outside as the verdicts were read.
Sri Lanka’s Roman Catholic Church welcomed the convictions. “Finally, we have justice,” Catholic priest Jude Fernando told the AFP news agency. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”
Teresa Fernando, a survivor who suffered head injuries, said no one should have to endure what she had gone through. “We came here today as victims of this attack to receive justice,” she said. “Whatever the court says… we will bow our heads and accept it.”
Attack on hotels, churches
The coordinated bombings in April 2019 were carried out at three luxury hotels and three churches – two of them Catholic and one Protestant.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks.
Two Sri Lanka-based armed groups were accused of carrying out the bombings.
Sri Lanka’s Catholic Church has claimed, without providing evidence, that those identified so far as perpetrators are not the masterminds behind the bombings, and that there was a bigger conspiracy behind the attacks.
In July, a former police chief and a former senior Defence Ministry official were also sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.

Royan Institute findings highlight MSCs’ potential for cell-based ASD therapy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:45:34 UTC
21:45:34 KST

Royan Institute findings highlight MSCs’ potential for cell-based ASD therapy
TEHRAN – Researchers from Royan Institute, in a study, have managed to lower the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) scores and certain inflammatory biomarkers in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) using allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly.
The study was conducted as part of the ongoing research by Royan researchers in the field of regenerative medicine and in the investigation of the potential applications of MSCs for cell-based therapeutic approaches across a range of diseases.
According to the Public Relations Department of Royan Institute, five children with Level 2 ASD participated in the study and received three intrathecal administrations of MSCs derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly. Each administration consisted of 20 million cells, with a one-month interval between administrations, royan.org reported.
The preliminary findings of a Phase I clinical trial evaluated the safety and tolerability of three intrathecal administrations of allogeneic MSCs derived from umbilical cord Wharton’s jelly in children with ASD. No serious adverse events or Grade 3 or higher adverse events were reported during the study period, and the intervention was considered acceptable in terms of safety and tolerability.
These findings are of particular relevance from the perspective of Phase I study design, as a primary objective of such early-phase trials is to assess the safety and tolerability of an investigational intervention and to determine whether further clinical investigation is warranted.
The researchers assessed the severity of autism-related symptoms using the CARS and reported a reduction in CARS scores in all participants. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) also demonstrated reductions in certain inflammatory biomarkers, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Changes in patterns of cerebral electrical activity were additionally reported based on electroencephalographic (EEG) assessments.
These observations may provide a basis for further investigation into the potential relationships among cellular and molecular alterations, neurophysiological parameters, and selected clinical manifestations of autism spectrum disorder in future studies.
According to the investigators, rigorous evaluation of the potential efficacy of this approach, the durability of the observed effects, and its benefit–risk profile will require further clinical trials involving larger numbers of participants, randomized study designs, and appropriate control groups.
The findings of this study, published in the international journal ‘Stem Cell Research & Therapy’, should not be interpreted as evidence that autism has been treated or cured through cell therapy. Rather, the findings provide preliminary data regarding safety and certain clinical and biological changes observed following the intervention, which may inform the design and scientific rationale of future studies.

Poland's Auschwitz Museum faces US lawsuit over art by Holocaust victim
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:44:16 CEST
21:44:16 KST

Poland's Auschwitz Museum faces US lawsuit over art by Holocaust victim
Heirs of a Jewish prisoner at the former Nazi German concentration camp in Auschwitz have filed a lawsuit with a US court over works created during her imprisonment and kept at the Auschwitz Museum in Poland, US media outlet CBS News reported on Saturday.
Daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor, demand the return of watercolour portraits of fellow prisoners at Auschwitz that Babbitt was forced to paint for notorious Nazi doctor Josef Mengele.
According to CBS News, the lawsuit is among the first two filed after the US state of California and the Congress passed laws which strengthened the ability to claim artworks forcibly taken from Jews during World War Two. The other one regards the return of two 16th-century paintings stolen by Nazi commander Hermann Goering from the collection of a prominent Dutch-Jewish art dealer, currently held at the prominent Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.
Representatives of both museums maintain they hold legal titles to the artworks and intend to keep them on public display.
Auschwitz Memorial spokesman Pawel Sawicki told CBS News that the portraits of Roma victims must remain at the memorial site to document Mengele's murderous medical experiments on camp prisoners. In Sawicki's view, the watercolours should not be categorised as "Nazi-stolen art" in the traditional sense, as they were created by a prisoner under camp orders and are among the few surviving testimonies of Mengele's crimes.
Spokesman for the Auschwitz Memorial Pawel Sawicki told CBS News that the portraits of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint must remain at Auschwitz to document Mengele's horrendous medical experiments on camp prisoners. In Sawicki's view, the artworks should not be labelled "Nazi-stolen art" as the painter created them as a prisoner and therefore had no ownership over them. He said that the watercolours were among the few remaining testimonies of Mengele's crimes.
"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," Sawicki said as quoted by CBS News. "...The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz," he said.
According to CBS News, in the period of 1933-1945, the Nazi regime seized over 600,000 works of art from Jewish families, collectors and museums across Europe. Many of those pieces are held today by prominent institutions around the world. (PAP)

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Establishing a unified framework for "cognitive sovereignty" requires joint efforts to counter those who deliberately weaponize falsehoods, Andrey Kondrashov, Director General of TASS and President of the Organization of Asia-Pacific News Agencies (OANA), said at the Dialogue on Fakes 4.0 forum.
"To achieve this, we need common verification standards, the sharing of technologies and methodologies, educational programs for journalists, and unified approaches to labeling AI-generated content," he said.
Kondrashov said TASS was working to build an international information security system spanning the region from the CIS to Africa and Asia. He added that, as part of its OANA presidency, the agency was implementing a program to share expertise and best practices in combating fake news.
"We invite everyone who shares our values to collaborate. Together, we can transform fragmented projects into a unified system for protecting the truth," he concluded.
The Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum is a global platform for discussing methods to combat disinformation and develop fact-checking technologies. The event is taking place at the Russia National Center with the participation of over 2,000 journalists, experts and businesspeople from 80 countries. It is organized by the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), established in 2025 by the TASS news agency, the autonomous nonprofit organization "Dialogue Regions," and the New Media Workshop. TASS is the forum’s strategic media partner.

Brazilian police capture suspected serial killer disguised as woman with toddler
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:42:48 UTC
21:42:48 KST

Brazilian police have arrested alleged serial killer Jorlan Lopes da Silva, who is accused of murdering 16 people over the past three months and is suspected of killing dozens more over the past 20 years.
Police revealed that, during the manhunt, da Silva hid in camps he built in the forest and was eventually found disguised as a woman while carrying a small child who was not related to him.
Da Silva, 33, operated in the isolated area of Mulungu in Paraiba state in northeastern Brazil, where locals nicknamed him “the mosquito” because of his thin build.
Douglas Garcia, the investigator who led the two-day operation that ended with da Silva’s capture on September 13, said his slight build had helped him evade arrest for years and hide in makeshift camps in dense vegetation.
“Jorlan lived mainly in the forests, which is why it was so difficult to locate him and connect him to crimes that initially did not appear to be related,” Garcia said.
Garcia said police were able to link da Silva to other crimes after he shot and killed an 18-year-old in a square in Mulungu. According to the investigator, the suspected serial killer claims he attacked only criminals, but evidence gathered so far suggests otherwise.
Garcia also said da Silva has provided evidence indicating that he committed additional crimes beyond those for which he is currently facing charges. According to the investigator, da Silva himself said he had killed about 80 people over the course of his life, the first when he was just 13 years old.
Garcia stressed that he could not provide further details about the additional crimes because some investigations are still underway, while others involving unsolved cases are now being reopened. The identities of the victims and details of the circumstances of their deaths are also being kept confidential to allow prosecutors to carry out their work.
Da Silva was captured wearing a black dress with white stripes, a wig and nail polish. He also was wearing sunglasses and carrying a 2-year-old child whom authorities confirmed was not a relative, though they did not provide further details.
“We caught him because he was unable to reach his tent in the forest, so out of desperation he obtained this disguise, took this baby who was not his and was eventually arrested,” Garcia said.
Police had previously said da Silva was a member of a criminal gang that murdered dozens of people in the area.
He denies any connection to local gangs and told investigators at the time of his arrest that he had been waging a “personal war.”

Which Dutch city actually fits your budget and lifestyle in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:42:28 UTC
21:42:28 KST

Partner content
Which Dutch city actually fits your budget and lifestyle in 2026
Moving to the Netherlands means picking not just a country but also a city, and in 2026 that choice matters more than it used to. Rents in the unregulated sector rose 7.3% nationally over the past year, according to the latest Pararius Huurmonitor, pushing the average to roughly €21 per square metre. But that average hides a lot of variation. Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Utrecht, The Hague, and Eindhoven, the so-called G5, each behave quite differently right now, and the gap between them is worth understanding before you commit to a lease.
Here’s how the five compare.
Amsterdam is still the most expensive place to rent in the country by a wide margin, at €28.53 per square metre after a further 5.1% rise this year. That premium buys you the strongest job market for tech, finance, and creative roles, plus the density of international life that draws people here in the first place. An 80m² apartment typically runs €2,300 to €2,500 a month before utilities. If your work is anchored in the city, it’s worth starting your search among the apartments in Amsterdam currently listed.
Rotterdam had one of the sharpest price increases of any G5 city this year, up 10.4% to €22.78 per square metre, and it’s still noticeably cheaper than Amsterdam for comparable space. The city’s pull comes from its modern skyline, its logistics and maritime industry, and an international business culture that doesn’t feel like a smaller copy of the capital. You’ll generally get more square metres for your budget here. Current listings for apartments in Rotterdam are a reasonable place to gauge what that looks like in practice.
The Hague rose 6.5% in price this year to €22.42 per square metre and remains a common choice for people working at the international courts, embassies, or corporate headquarters based there. It has a slower pace than Rotterdam or Amsterdam, more green space, and the coastline is a short cycle away. Neighbourhoods range from the stately Statenkwartier to livelier, more central pockets, so it’s worth browsing a spread of apartments in The Hague before narrowing down an area.
Utrecht climbed 5.9% to €21.61 per square metre and sits at the literal centre of the country’s rail network, which matters more than it might sound. The city has the Netherlands’ largest university, a well-preserved medieval core, and a train commute of 30 minutes or less to nearly any other major Dutch city. That combination of culture and connectivity keeps competition for listings tight. Have a look through apartments in Utrecht to see what’s currently on the market.
Eindhoven posted the second-largest increase in the G5 this year, up 10.0% to €19.55 per square metre, still the most affordable of the five despite that jump. The city runs on ASML, Philips, and a wider “Brainport” ecosystem of tech and engineering firms, which explains why it draws a heavily specialised international workforce. If that’s your field, apartments in Eindhoven are where to start looking.
What this means for your search: In a market this tight, landlords generally expect a gross income of three to four times the monthly rent, and they’ll want to see it upfront. Have your employment contract, recent payslips, and a short summary of your rental history ready before you start applying, since properties in demand can be gone within days. Pararius only lists properties from verified, professional agents, which at least removes one layer of risk from an already competitive process. You can view all listings here.

Economic Watch: Chinese companies willing to prosper together with their global partners
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:41:13 CST
21:41:13 KST

HEFEI, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition area, a bright green SUV with a boxy shape and sturdy-looking lines attracts crowds of visitors. Inside the car, visitors marvel at the spacious interior and intelligent driving systems.
The vehicle, present at the ongoing World Manufacturing Convention in Hefei, capital of east China's Anhui Province, is the outcome of a collaboration between British automaker Jaguar Land Rover and China's Chery Automobile, with the two sides bringing together their respective strengths in vehicle design, manufacturing and intelligent technologies.
Decades ago, China's auto industry largely looked overseas for advanced vehicle models, technologies and production systems. Today, Chinese automakers are bringing their own strengths in electrification and intelligent vehicles into joint ventures and other partnerships, working with global partners to develop products for markets around the world.
"We want to build mutual advantage and look at ways in which our trade and investment can really help each other," said Peter Wilson, British ambassador to China. He said the two countries can do more research and development together, with their advanced technologies being highly complementary.
The goal, Wilson said, is to build "more of a genuine partnership" rather than simply having each side sell products to the other, adding that there is significant potential for further cooperation.
The United Kingdom is the guest country of honor in this year's convention. Along with Chinese companies, more than 40 foreign enterprises from the United States, France, Russia and other countries are exhibiting in the event.
"There are many possibilities for partnerships," said Jonathan Zeidler, personal assistant to the CEO of Kling PM GmbH, a German management company for energy, grid infrastructure and battery storage.
The company is already cooperating with Chinese partners, Zeidler said, adding that it is interesting to see Chinese companies invest in Germany, cooperate with local businesses and bring skilled employees to the country.
In the first quarter of 2026, Anhui, a manufacturing powerhouse in emerging sectors, registered 82 overseas investment projects filed by local companies, up 41.4 percent year on year and 3.2 times that of 2021, official data showed.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian recently said at a media conference that China stands ready to work with countries around the world to continue dialogue and cooperation in frontier fields such as artificial intelligence and embodied intelligence, turning Chinese innovation and manufacturing into a genuine driving force for common development.
Cooperation potential can be unlocked through technological connectivity, joint standard-setting and market sharing, and innovation dividends can be better delivered to humanity, he added.
Li Zhen, chairman of Hefei-based leading lithium battery maker Gotion High-tech Co., Ltd., said the company has established 10 industrial bases across Europe and Africa, the Asia-Pacific region and the Americas.
"Gotion follows one principle in expanding its global footprint: to pursue localized development by establishing factories, R&D, jobs and supply chains in local markets and growing together with local partners," Li said.
Overseas business now accounts for about 30 percent of its total business, and the company plans to achieve a 1:1 ratio between overseas and domestic production capacity in the future.
"We have always believed that helping others succeed is the key to achieving our own success," Li said. ■

Death toll rises to 6 following typhoon-induced downpours in Japan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:41:04 CST
21:41:04 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The death toll rose to six on Tuesday, with six others still missing, after heavy rain from a large typhoon battered the Kanto region in eastern Japan and triggered landslides and flooding a day earlier, local media reported.
Among the deaths, five were confirmed in Chiba Prefecture, east of Tokyo, including a man in his 50s who died after falling into a bamboo grove while operating heavy machinery to clear mud and debris from a landslide. The others were in their 70s and 80s, according to Kyodo News.
Another death was confirmed in Yokosuka, Kanagawa Prefecture, also near Tokyo, where a woman in her 60s died on Monday after a landslide struck her home and sent mud pouring into the house.
Police and firefighters are continuing to search for the missing people.
Typhoon Dujuan, which approached Japan's eastern Pacific coast on Monday and is now moving away, brought record rainfall to the Kanto region and the Izu Islands, triggering a series of landslides and river flooding.
Rainfall in Oshima Town in the Izu Island chain over the 48 hours to 8 p.m. local time on Monday reached 832 mm, more than 2.4 times the town's average rainfall for the entire month of September and the highest since records began, according to public broadcaster NHK. A top-level landslide warning was temporarily issued for the town on Monday.
The typhoon, coming in the middle of the country's Silver Week holidays, was particularly problematic for Chiba, where intense rain inundated houses and roads and temporarily cut off electricity to about 58,000 households early Tuesday, Kyodo News said.
The typhoon also disrupted transportation, forcing All Nippon Airways and Japan Airlines to cancel more than 270 flights, mainly those to and from Tokyo's Haneda airport, affecting about 40,000 people in total. ■

Swimming roundup: China collects another Asian record, four more titles at Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:40:59 CST
21:40:59 KST

TOKYO, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- China had four more gold medals in its swimming haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Tuesday, with Zhang Zhanshuo claiming his second title here, Peng Xuwei setting an Asian record in women's 200m backstroke and Li Bingjie successfully defending her title in women's 400m free.
China also secured the men's 4x100m medley relay victory.
Zhang, 19, stormed to victory in the men's 1,500m freestyle in 14 minutes 42.42 seconds, finishing ahead of Japan's Tabuchi Kaito in 14:45.99 and teammate Imafuku Kazushi in 14:54.37.
It was Zhang's second gold of the Games. A day earlier, he anchored China's men's 4x200m freestyle relay team to victory, producing a 1:42.92 split and overtaking Japan in the final 50 meters as China clocked an Asian record of 7:00.17.
"I just don't want to lose," Zhang said after completing what he called the toughest challenge of the Games. "I think that will give me more motivation and make me look forward to the races ahead."
Peng defended her women's 200m backstroke title in 2:05.77 to refresh the previous 16-year Asian record set in Guangzhou Games. Teammate Sun Mingxia took silver in 2:08.65, while Japan's Rio Shirai claimed bronze in 2:08.70.
"2:06.46 (the previous record) has always been a guiding light for me, encouraging me to keep improving and serving as a goal I have pursued," Peng said. "I hope this new record can inspire more Asian backstroke swimmers to challenge me and push each other forward."
China added another gold in the women's 400m freestyle, where Li Bingjie retained her Asian Games title in 4:02.71. Li said she believed there was still room for improvement.
"I think my potential lies in my ability to finish strong. When I raced against Katie Ledecky and other strong swimmers, I felt I could really tap into my potential when I had someone to chase down in the latter stage of the race," she said.
In the women's 100m freestyle, 200m free winner Siobhan Haughey of Hong Kong, China claimed her second gold in 52.45, while China's Yu Yiting secured silver in 53.21 and teammate Cheng Yujie took bronze in 53.47.
Japan grabbed the sole swimming gold in the men's 400m individual medley, as Kojima Yumeki touched first in a new Games record of 4:07.02, followed by compatriot Matsushita Tomoyuki in 4:09.64. China's Wang Shun took bronze in 4:14.59.
For Wang, a five-time Asian Games veteran, the bronze added another medal to his durable career. "Every Games have left me with many wonderful memories," Wang said, adding that he hoped more young Chinese athletes would compete on the world stage and achieve better results.
The night ended with a relay gold for China. In the men's 4x100m medley relay, China held off a late challenge from Japan to win in 3:27.89. Japan cut the gap to just 0.29 seconds with 350 meters to go, but the Chinese quartet of Xu Jiayu, Dong Zhihao, Xu Fang and Pan Zhanle held firm through the final turn to touch first. South Korea took the bronze.
Asked about the pressure as Japan closed in, backstroke veteran Xu said he never lost faith in his teammates. "Although we have young swimmers on the team, we've been working together for four years. So we trust each other," he said.
Looking ahead to his next relay on Thursday, 100m freestyle winner Pan acknowledged that it would be "a big challenge," with South Korea expected to pose a strong challenge. ■

Players of China celebrate victory after the final match of Women's Volleyball between China and Japan at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026 in Komaki, Japan, Sept. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng)
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Defending champion China claimed its 10th Asian Games women's volleyball gold medal with a 3-0 victory over Japan in the final here Tuesday.
The teams traded points early in the first set. Midway through the set, China gradually pulled ahead and sealed a 25-19 win.
China maintained a narrow lead throughout the second set. Both sides ramped up their intensity, staging several long rallies before China closed out the set 25-20.
Japan cranked up its attack at the start of the third set, jumping out to a 7-1 lead, forcing China to call a timeout. China then reset its rhythm and leveraged its serving and blocking strengths to tie the score at 19-19. After four deuces, China sealed the set 25-23 to claim the match.
China edged Thailand 3-2 in Monday's semifinal, avenging their loss in last month's Asian Women's Volleyball Championship final and advancing to the gold-medal match against Japan. In the day's other semifinal, Japan beat South Korea 3-0.

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Japan's Aiko Sugihara claimed gold in the women's artistic gymnastics all-around at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Tuesday, ending China's run of 13 consecutive Asian Games titles.
In the women's qualification competition largely contested between gymnasts from China and Japan, Sugihara won the all-around title with 55.599 points, edging China's Ke Qinqin by 0.4 points. Japan's Misa Nishiyama took bronze with 55.032, while China's Zhang Qingying finished fourth.
Sugihara made a slow start, placing eighth on the uneven bars in the opening rotation. Her Japanese teammates, however, made a strong impression on the apparatus, with Nishiyama scoring 14.533 and Mana Okamura 14.066.
China's gymnasts, all making their Asian Games debuts, had mixed results on the uneven bars. Zhang and Ke finished second and third in the rotation, while Qiu Qiyuan fell from the high bar and Du Siyu made a heavy landing on her dismount.
Qiu bounced back on the balance beam, posting the highest score of 14.833, while Sugihara also recovered with 14.266 for fourth place on the apparatus.
Sugihara then delivered a strong floor exercise routine to score 13.700, the highest mark of the competition despite a 0.2-point penalty. She closed out the competition with 14.100 on the vault, the second-highest score among the gymnasts competing in the event.
Ke still had a chance to overtake Sugihara on the floor exercise, but despite earning 8.166 for execution, her difficulty score of 5.2 left her short of the Japanese gymnast. The 16-year-old Chinese gymnast eventually settled for silver.
"I didn't make any major mistakes today, which I'm happy about. My main goal was always the team event, so I'm very happy to win the individual all-around gold," Sugihara said in the post-game press conference.
"I didn't know I was in first place until after the vault, so I was quite surprised. I need to improve my floor exercise, and I'll keep my focus on tomorrow's team competition," she added.
Ke said she hoped to put the result behind her and perform closer to her training level in the upcoming team and individual events.
"This is my first Asian Games. I hope to work hard and have the chance to compete at the Asian Games again in the future, and stand on the higher step of the podium in this event," the silver medalist said.
Japan topped the women's qualification with a total score of 166.363, followed by China in second place with 165.697, marching into the women's team final. The other teams advancing to the final are the DPR Korea, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and Chinese Taipei, with Kazakhstan named as the reserve team. ■

Global multiple sclerosis prevalence reaches 3.1 mln: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
20:40:23 CST
21:40:23 KST

MELBOURNE, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- About 3.1 million people worldwide are estimated to be living with multiple sclerosis (MS), a 54-percent increase over the past decade, an international study involving scientists in Australia has revealed.
The study, based on data from 133 countries and regions representing 93 percent of the world's population, provides the latest update of the Britain-based MS International Federation's Atlas of MS, the leading source of global data on the prevalence and impact of the disease, according to a statement released Tuesday by Australia's University of Tasmania (UTAS).
The findings, published in Multiple Sclerosis Journal, also reflect trends in Australia, where an estimated 37,756 people were living with MS in 2024, up 77 percent from 2010.
Professor Ingrid van der Mei, a study co-author from the Menzies Institute for Medical Research at UTAS, said the findings highlighted the growing global burden of MS and the importance of reliable data for healthcare planning and research.
The rise in prevalence did not necessarily mean MS was becoming more common, with earlier and more accurate diagnosis, improved data collection and longer life expectancy among people with MS likely contributing to the increase, researchers noted.
The findings also showed that women accounted for about 70 percent of cases globally, while more than 40,000 children and adolescents were reported to be living with MS. ■

====================================================================================================

Pentagon: laser defense needs hardware, not more demos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:40:03 UTC
21:40:03 KST

- Assistant Secretary of War Michael Dodd said Sept. 22 that high-energy laser programs must move from demonstrations to ruggedized, fielded systems for air and missile defense.
- The U.S. Army has already committed to a Joint Laser Weapon System program and a $464.8 million laser contract with AeroVironment, while the Navy and Air Force have not.
Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies Michael Dodd said the Department of War needs to move directed energy weapons out of testing and into the field, arguing in a Sept. 22 post on X that high-energy laser programs have proven the technology works and now need ruggedized, deployable systems for air and missile defense.
Dodd did not announce a new program or contract in the post. His comments add to a public campaign he has run for months, pushing the military services to commit money and timelines to fielding lasers and high-power microwave weapons rather than running further demonstrations.
The Army has already made that commitment. It awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract this year for the Enduring-High Energy Laser program, a 30-kilowatt system the company has called the first production contract for a directed energy weapon in U.S. history. The Army has also agreed to transition its Joint Laser Weapon System into a formal program of record. Dodd has said his office funds prototypes and early, small-scale deployments, but expects the individual services to buy directed energy systems by the dozens or hundreds once a design proves itself.
The Navy and Air Force have not made comparable commitments. Dodd said in August he is pressing both services to follow the Army’s lead, with the Navy interested in much higher-powered systems, in the hundreds of kilowatts to a megawatt range, to defend ships against cruise missiles, a heavier requirement than the counter-drone systems the Army is pursuing.
Cost is central to the Pentagon’s argument for lasers. Officials have said a single laser shot can cost around $3.50, compared to millions of dollars for a Patriot interceptor missile, against drones that can cost tens of thousands of dollars apiece. Dodd has pointed to that mismatch as the reason directed energy needs to scale quickly, saying in March that the department aims to field directed energy weapons broadly within 36 months.
The technology still faces real constraints. Laser and microwave systems draw on rare earth elements and other critical minerals largely processed in China, and Dodd has acknowledged that per-system costs remain high because production has not scaled up. He has also pushed industry to shrink the size, weight and power demands of these weapons so they can fly on aircraft, telling contractors in August to bring “hardware we can put on a range and stress” rather than further concept presentations.
The Air Force has tested high-power microwave systems for counter-drone use, including the trailer-mounted THOR system, though its most recent publicly disclosed test dates to 2023. The Air Force Research Laboratory has said it is developing a follow-on system.

Türkiye's economy remains resilient despite global, regional challenges: Simsek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:39:03 UTC
21:39:03 KST

Türkiye’s Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek has said that the country’s economy remained resilient despite challenging global conditions and conflicts in the region.
He was speaking at a meeting in New York organised in cooperation with Citi as part of a three-day conference, organised by the Foreign Economic Relations Board (DEIK) and its Türkiye-US Business Council (TAIK).
The conference began on Monday and is running from September 21-23.
The opening day brought US direct investors together with Simsek, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan and Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir for discussions on Türkiye’s economic outlook, investment opportunities, industrial development and high technology.
“Solid foundations support our economy’s resilience against shocks,” Simsek said at the meeting, pointing to relatively high fixed capital investment, recent productivity gains, low overall indebtedness, fiscal space, reduced external vulnerabilities, rising international reserves and the continued exit from the foreign exchange-protected deposit scheme.
He said Türkiye offered investors opportunities through its large domestic market, strategic location, manufacturing and services sectors, infrastructure and skilled workforce.
Simsek also highlighted opportunities in defence, tourism, health tourism and digital services, including television series and mobile games.
He said Türkiye was accelerating its green and digital transformation, industrial transformation and productive infrastructure investments, while new tax incentives were strengthening the investment and export environment.
Karahan also provided assessments of monetary policy and the macroeconomic outlook at the meeting, while the participants discussed the government's three-year roadmap under the Medium-Term Programme announced earlier this month.
The discussions also focused on price stability, fiscal discipline, medium- and long-term growth prospects and Türkiye’s efforts to improve productivity and competitiveness.
Türkiye’s manufacturing infrastructure, transport and logistics links and access to regional markets were also highlighted, alongside investment opportunities in advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, healthcare, logistics, transport and digital technologies.
Türkiye seeks US cooperation in high technology
A separate roundtable organised with Concordia focused on industrial and high-technology cooperation between Türkiye and the US.
Kacir told US companies that Türkiye was building the industrial capacity, energy infrastructure, digital networks and physical connectivity needed for future technologies.
“Türkiye connects production with markets, technology with industry and Asia with Europe,” Kacir said.
“We invite American companies to produce, innovate and grow together with us in Türkiye.”
The meeting examined Türkiye’s potential to become a global hub for high-technology production and innovation, with discussions covering semiconductors, mobility, green energy, advanced manufacturing, healthcare, digital technologies, communications and space.
Participants also discussed opportunities for complementary investments across different parts of global value chains and were briefed on Türkiye’s HIT30 Investment Incentive Programme.
DEIK Chairman Nail Olpak said there were significant opportunities for joint work in industry and technology, particularly by combining Türkiye’s industrial capabilities with US strengths in artificial intelligence, semiconductors and software.
He said predictability remained one of the business community’s key expectations amid growing uncertainty in the global economy.
Murat Ozyegin, chairman of DEIK’s Türkiye-US Business Council, said maintaining the direction of Türkiye’s disinflation programme remained important despite increasingly difficult geopolitical and economic conditions.
He said attracting long-term foreign direct investment that brings technology transfer and skilled employment was among the business community’s priorities for the coming period.
Business leaders gather at New York Public Library
The conference’s first day ended with an evening reception at the historic New York Public Library, bringing together Trade Minister Omer Bolat, Kacir, Karahan, and senior representatives from the Turkish and US business communities.
The reception, organised by TAIK in cooperation with the American Turkish Business Roundtable, provided a platform for networking and discussions on investment and business opportunities between the two countries.
The conference is sponsored by Borusan Holding, Calık Holding, Fiba Holding, Kibar Holding, Koc Holding, Limak Holding, Sabancı Holding, Sahibinden, Turkish Airlines and Türk Telekom.

Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on Tuesday chaired a meeting of the State-Level Vigilance and Monitoring Committee constituted for the effective implementation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
DEHRADUN: Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami on tuesday chaired a meeting of the State-Level Vigilance and Monitoring Committee constituted for the effective implementation of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and directed officials to ensure time-bound disposal of pending cases.Reviewing cases registered under the Act since 2024 where investigations are still pending, Dhami directed officials to examine the reasons for delays and take action on priority. He also called for close coordination among the police, administration and prosecution departments in long-pending and serious cases.The chief minister directed regular review of cases pending before special courts and asked officials to ensure the availability of special public prosecutors wherever required for effective prosecution.Dhami stressed that there should be no delay in disbursing prescribed relief to victims. He directed officials to separately review cases where relief payments have been delayed and said assistance to affected families should also extend, wherever required, to healthcare, education, security, rehabilitation and other eligible government schemes.The chief minister also directed officials to accord the highest priority to the safety of victims and their families in serious and sensitive cases.
He said the education of children from affected families should not be disrupted and that eligible children should be linked with scholarships and other educational assistance schemes.According to the Social Welfare Department, the state has provisions for financial assistance to victims of atrocities under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, with assistance provided at different stages depending on the nature of the offence.Dhami further directed senior-level accountability in every district for monitoring cases under the Act and called for regular training of police personnel on its provisions, investigation of sensitive cases and appropriate conduct towards victims.He also instructed the Social Welfare, Police and Prosecution departments to jointly organise refresher training programmes and directed officials to work towards developing a digital monitoring system to track investigations, court proceedings, relief payments and other assistance.Districts where progress in investigation, disposal of cases or distribution of relief is unsatisfactory should be reviewed separately, Dhami said, adding that effective practices followed by better-performing districts should be shared with others.
The chief minister also called for extensive awareness campaigns in rural and remote areas about the provisions of the Act, legal rights and assistance available to victims. He stressed that decisions taken during the meeting should not remain confined to official records and that responsibility and timelines should be fixed for every decision.The meeting was informed that 189 cases were registered under the Act in 2024 and 157 in 2025. In 2026, 116 cases had been registered up to September 15, of which 25 were under investigation.It was further informed that during 2024-25, financial assistance of Rs 228.71 lakh was provided to 205 victims; during 2025-26, Rs 143.16 lakh was provided to 127 victims; and during 2026-27, Rs 99.528 lakh had been provided to 104 victims as of September 18.Regular meetings have also been held at the state level under the chairmanship of the chief secretary and at the district level under the chairmanship of district magistrates.

El Nino strengthening rapidly, health impacts expected worldwide: UN agencies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:37:03 UTC
21:37:03 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
El Nino is strengthening rapidly and is expected to have health impacts worldwide, with the most severe consequences likely in countries already facing weak health systems and humanitarian crises, UN agencies warned Tuesday.
"We've just lived through the two hottest months on record. Sea surface temperatures are at record levels," Armel Castellan, extreme heat adviser at the joint WHO-WMO climate and health program, told reporters in Geneva.
Castellan said El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of 2026, but stressed that its impacts would continue beyond that point.
As the event peaks, much of the Southern Hemisphere, including southern Africa, South America and Australia, will move into its hottest season in early 2027, potentially increasing risks of drought, wildfires, smoke and air pollution, he said.
Teresa Zakaria, WHO's unit head for risk reduction, humanitarian operations and climate change, told reporters that El Nino is "a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon."
She said malnutrition and cholera are assessed as "very high" risks in both drought- and flood-affected settings.
More than 150 million people are already facing acute food insecurity globally, with that figure expected to increase as climate shocks disrupt food production and livelihoods, she said.
Warmer temperatures and changing rainfall could also increase transmission of mosquito-borne diseases including malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika, potentially spreading them into areas where they have not traditionally occurred.
"We have a window of opportunity to act now before these risks become crises," Zakaria said.

After floods, Nepal minister demands 'climate justice'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:37:00 UTC
21:37:00 KST

After floods, Nepal minister demands 'climate justice'
September 22, 2026
Nepal is seeking $20 million (just under €17.5 million) from the international Loss and Damage Fund, the UN-backed mechanism designed to support countries suffering irreversible climate-related losses, Environment Minister Geeta Chaudhary said in an exclusive DW interview.
The move comes after floods and landslides killed more than 1,400 people in August and left thousands missing.
"We have already issued the official letter for the fund for the loss and damage," Chaudhary told DW. "Most of the countries have sent us a positive response."
The flash flooding caused widespread destruction across large swathes of Nepal, damaging homes, agricultural land and infrastructure. Rescue and recovery efforts are still ongoing in several areas, while authorities continue to assess the full scale of the losses.
In the Himalayan nation, the tragedy has become a powerful symbol of what developing countries describe as the unfair climate burden of contributing little to global emissions while facing disproportionate consequences.
'Sympathy alone will not work for us'
Talking to DW, Chaudhary repeatedly framed Nepal's response through the lens of climate justice, a concept that has become increasingly prominent in global climate negotiations.
"Sympathy alone will not work for us," she said. "We don't need sympathy. We need justice. It's high time. If you're not able to give us justice, then we also don't need the words."
"Those countries who are emitting the most and are able to contribute the funds, they need to pay for the climatic disasters like what we are facing," she said.
Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Its geography, however, makes it extremely vulnerable to climate-related risks. Rising temperatures in the Himalayas have accelerated glacial retreat and increased concerns about glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and extreme weather events across the region.
In the wake of the most recent disaster, the government has intensified calls for more adaptation financing, direct access to climate funds and stronger international commitments to fight consequences of climate change.
'The world is watching'
Chaudhary pointed to melting glaciers, warming temperatures and changes in mountain environments as factors behind the deadly floods.
"Our evidence is showing that this catastrophic event is because of climate change," Chaudhary said.
While many scientists agree that climate change increases the likelihood and severity of such events, establishing a causal relationship between a specific disaster and global warming typically requires detailed attribution studies.
Researchers are more likely to point to a combination of factors, including glacier and permafrost degradation, extreme weather conditions and geological vulnerabilities.
The Nepali government, however, insists that the connection is clear.
"We are the real example and the world is watching us," Chaudhary told DW.
Building support ahead of COP31
The minister's comments come as Nepal seeks to build momentum for COP31, the UN's annual climate conference set to be held in Turkey this November.
When asked about her government's plans for the conference, Chaudhary said "Nepal will no longer negotiate on vague promises or slow-moving traditional and development aid."
According to the minister, Nepal intends to push for greater recognition of the specific challenges facing mountainous countries, arguing that global climate discussions often overlook the risks confronting Himalayan regions.
"Mountain issues need to be addressed," she said. "The world needs to see us, that we are victimized countries. We are paying the price."
Chaudhary also pointed out that Nepal received strong backing from fellow vulnerable nations at the recent gathering of Least Developed Countries (LDCs) in Timor-Leste.
"All the LDCs stood with us," she said. "They are very concerned."
The government plans to bring climate concerns to the UN General Assembly, highlighting the recent disaster and calling for concrete support from the international community.
Nepal to improve its early warning systems
The scale of the disaster has also prompted scrutiny inside Nepal, particularly of the country's warning systems and its disaster response.
Residents in some affected areas have complained that warnings came too late or did not adequately reflect the scale of the danger.
Chaudhary defended the government's response but conceded that existing systems were overwhelmed by the sheer scale of the event.
"We had sent them messages and information," she said. "But the situation was beyond imagination."
She acknowledged that Nepal's early warning systems must improve and said authorities are now reviewing and strengthening existing monitoring mechanisms.
"Our hydrology and meteorology departments are working on that," she said.
The floods also highlighted the importance of cooperation between Nepal and its neighbors, particularly China, in monitoring river systems and glacial hazards that cut through national borders.
"We are working closely," Chaudhary said, adding that technical teams from both countries are sharing information and examining future risks.
Himalayan catastrophe as a warning for the world
For Chaudhary, the disaster is not only a national tragedy but a warning about the future.
"Our snow is melting, our lakes are in danger," the minister said.
She warned that, unless global warming is limited in line with the Paris climate agreement of 2015, vulnerable countries could face increasingly severe disasters.
Asked whether the world is acting fast enough, the minister responded: "I don't think so."
Edited by: Darko Janjevic
