What will UK's Ed Miliband focus on at his first UNGA?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:13:34 UTC
21:13:34 KST

Breadcrumb
What will UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband focus on at his first UNGA?
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is attending his first United Nations General Assembly high-level week since taking office, arriving in New York with the Middle East and Sudan among the major crises confronting world leaders.
In his first nine weeks as foreign secretary, Miliband has already taken a tougher stance on Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, announcing plans to ban imports from settlements and impose sanctions on individuals and companies involved in settlement activity.
But how will Britain's new foreign secretary approach these issues on the world stage? And where does he stand on other major questions facing this year's gathering, including the US-Israel war on Iran, Sudan's devastating civil war and nuclear disarmament?
Will Miliband discuss Israel and Palestine?
Israel and Palestine are expected to feature prominently in Miliband's diplomacy in New York.
Earlier this month, the UK announced plans to prohibit imports of goods from illegal Israeli settlements and introduce sanctions against individuals and companies supporting, facilitating or benefiting from settlement activity.
The measures followed Miliband's condemnation of settlement expansion and settler violence in the occupied West Bank. He has also repeatedly backed a two-state solution and said Israeli settlements are a "flagrant breach of international law".
However, Miliband has rejected the wider Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, drawing a distinction between measures targeting illegal settlements and a broader boycott of Israel.
Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group's Head of UN Affairs, told The New Arab that Miliband "will be closely involved in discussions around Palestine and the Two State Solution, where UN-backed diplomacy has fallen by the wayside at the expense of the Board of Peace".
"States will watch closely to see how UK officials defend their sanctions on Israel for expanding settlements in the West Bank, and how fiery a response they receive from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu."
Netanyahu is also expected to attend this week's gathering in New York. He responded angrily to Britain's settlement measures, while the Israeli government has strongly rejected international pressure over its policies in the West Bank.
What about Sudan?
Sudan is also emerging as a significant part of Miliband's first UNGA agenda.
Britain is the UN Security Council penholder on Sudan and has pushed for stronger international action as the country's civil war and humanitarian crisis continue.
Speaking in New York on Monday, Miliband described Sudan as "the worst humanitarian crisis this century" and set out three priorities for international action: diplomacy aimed at securing a ceasefire and eventual civilian government, improved humanitarian access, and greater protection for civilians.
He also called for stronger scrutiny of countries and networks supplying weapons and other support that are fuelling the conflict.
Forti said Miliband would use his time in New York to raise the profile of the war.
"Miliband will also hope to use his time in New York [to] raise the profile of the on-going war in Sudan. The UK leads the Security Council's discussions on the country but has been unable to rally its members around a common strategy to back various diplomatic efforts," he said.
"The UK will likely use a range of side events during UNGA to remind world leaders of the war's horrific toll and the urgent need to bring the warring parties back to the negotiating table."
What has Miliband said about the war on Iran?
Miliband's response to the US-Israel-led war on Iran has combined calls for diplomacy with a focus on the conflict's economic impact on Britain.
Following talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Miliband said Britain would work towards a ceasefire, while repeatedly highlighting the consequences of instability in the Middle East and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz for energy prices and the cost of living in the UK.
He has also maintained Britain's longstanding position that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
In a foreign policy speech earlier this year, Miliband said the objective should be to move "from conflict to containment", using coordinated international action and diplomacy to prevent Iran from rebuilding capabilities that threaten regional states and international shipping.
Iran will also be represented at this week's meetings in New York, potentially making diplomacy surrounding the conflict another important issue on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
What is Miliband's stance on nuclear weapons?
Nuclear weapons will also be on the UN agenda this week, with a high-level meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
The meeting is intended to give UN member states an opportunity to reaffirm their commitment to nuclear disarmament.
Miliband has historically supported maintaining Britain's nuclear deterrent and voted in favour of replacing the UK's Trident nuclear weapons system while serving as an MP.
Since becoming foreign secretary, his comments on nuclear proliferation have focused primarily on Iran, repeatedly stressing that Tehran must not acquire a nuclear weapon.
It remains unclear whether Miliband will attend the UN nuclear disarmament meeting. His participation, or absence, could nevertheless draw attention to the tension between Britain's support for international nuclear non-proliferation and its continued maintenance of its own nuclear deterrent.

Ground broken for Makkoran’s history and culture museum in Chabahar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:12:43 UTC
21:12:43 KST

Ground broken for Makkoran’s history and culture museum in Chabahar
TEHRAN - Ground was broken for the Makkoran’s history and culture museum in the Chabahar Free Zone on Tuesday, marking the start of a project aimed at documenting and showcasing the ancient history and cultural heritage of Iran’s Makkoran coast.
The ceremony was attended by Hossein Forouzan, secretary of Iran’s High Council of Free and Special Economic Zones; Mohammad-Saeid Arbabi, chief executive of the Chabahar Free Zone Organization; Alireza Noura, governor of Chabahar; and a number of provincial and regional officials.
Hamidreza Soleimani, CEO of the Dafineh Museums of the Mostazafan Foundation, said the museum was designed to provide a comprehensive and documented account of the ancient history and rich cultural heritage of the Makkoran coast.
The museum will be built on three floors, Soleimani said.
The ground floor will serve as the entrance and introductory area, where visitors will be introduced to the region through interactive touchscreens, sensory displays and other digital technologies.
The first floor will house archaeological artifacts and present the history of navigation and maritime trade in Makkoran, while the second floor will focus on the region’s development, infrastructure, industrial potential and contemporary transformations.
The museum will occupy a site of about 10,000 square meters, with a built-up area of approximately 2,500 square meters, according to Soleimani.
Under an earlier memorandum of understanding between the Chabahar Free Zone Organization and the Dafineh Museums Institute, the institute will oversee and provide specialist expertise for the museum’s design, content development and launch.
The Makkoran coast, also known as Makran or Mokran, is a largely semi-desert coastal strip along the Sea of Oman, extending across southeastern Iran and southwestern Pakistan. In Iran, the coast lies mainly in Sistan-Baluchestan province and includes Chabahar, a major port and commercial center on the Sea of Oman.

Taiwan removes low-value exemption for illegal e-cigarette imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:08:30 UTC
21:08:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Finance on Tuesday removed a low-value exemption from customs penalties for illegal imports of e-cigarettes and related products.
CNA reported that e-cigarettes, e-liquids, cartridges, and related components are no longer covered by an exemption from penalties for imported goods valued at NT$5,000 (US$158) or less. Customs authorities are also preparing guidelines that would increase fines for smuggling, false declarations, and other attempts to evade import restrictions.
Customs Administration Deputy Director-General Chao Tai-an (趙台安) said e-cigarette products have been used to consume new types of illegal drugs. He said authorities are strengthening border enforcement because of the risks to public safety.
Customs recorded 1,346 e-cigarette cases last year involving about 120,000 devices and 33,000 containers of e-liquid or cartridges. In the first eight months of this year, authorities recorded 726 cases involving about 35,000 devices and 40,000 containers of e-liquid or cartridges, per UDN.
Under the planned guidelines, violations such as smuggling or falsely declaring e-cigarette products would carry fines equal to 1.5 times the value of the goods. The higher penalties are intended to strengthen enforcement against prohibited vaping products entering Taiwan.
Travelers caught bringing prohibited e-cigarette products into Taiwan can have the goods confiscated. Cases may also be referred to local health authorities, with violations of tobacco control laws carrying fines starting at NT$50,000.
Customs said it will continue inspections to stop illegal e-cigarette products at the border. It also warned travelers not to bring them into Taiwan for personal use, as gifts, or on behalf of others.

Signs of a secret corridor and chambers discovered near Tutankhamun’s tomb
Kyiv • UNN
Researchers recorded new underground anomalies near KV62, including a possible corridor two meters wide. The discovery supports the hypothesis of a Nefertiti complex.
Researchers have found new signs of unknown corridors and chambers near Tutankhamun’s tomb, KV62, in the Valley of the Kings. To do so, they conducted more than 1,200 measurements across an area of about 35 square meters, Daily Star reports, according to UNN.
Details
The most mysterious find was dubbed “anomaly 7.” The measurements indicate an area of reduced density containing an almost square object with higher density. Ballard suggests that it could be a chamber containing burial objects.
Of particular interest is a possible corridor about two meters wide branching off from Tutankhamun’s burial chamber. According to geophysicist George Ballard, it may be filled with debris, which could explain why previous studies failed to detect it.
The new results have once again revived the hypothesis of British Egyptologist Nicholas Reeves, who has suggested since 2015 that a larger complex associated with Nefertiti may be hidden behind Tutankhamun’s tomb.
Additionally
Pharaoh Tutankhamun ruled Egypt approximately from 1332 to 1323 BC. Ascending the throne at the age of about 8–9, he became one of the youngest rulers in history, which is why he is often called the “boy pharaoh.”
Queen Nefertiti ruled approximately from 1353 to 1336 BC as the principal (Great) Wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV).
It will be recalled
In Egypt, archaeologists discovered the intact tomb of an official named Sekhentiu-Ptah, containing ritual objects.

Taiwan institute uses AI to sharpen drone thermal images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:08:17 UTC
21:08:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Institute for Information Industry said Tuesday that it had developed an AI system to improve the clarity of thermal images captured by drones, according to a press release.
Thermal imaging allows drones to operate at night and in other low-visibility conditions. However, high-end thermal sensors are expensive and vulnerable to supply-chain disruptions, making widespread deployment difficult.
The institute uses an AI super-resolution algorithm and edge computing to sharpen low-resolution thermal images captured with more affordable sensors. The algorithm reconstructs edges and contours to produce clearer images without requiring more expensive equipment.
Running the algorithm on an edge-computing chip allows images to be processed locally in real time. The resulting low latency makes the technology suitable for drone operations, the institute said.
The system is designed for nighttime patrols, search-and-rescue missions, and inspections in low-visibility environments. Clearer images can help operators locate heat sources more quickly.
The institute said it had also integrated domestically sourced chips, thermal cameras, and edge-computing modules to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers. It aims to offer the integrated system to businesses and other users.

Missouri airbase adds weapons storage building for incoming B-21s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:08:09 UTC
21:08:09 KST

- The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded K & K Industries $13.6 million to build a B-21 weapons release system storage facility at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri.
- The project is due for completion by March 31, 2028, part of roughly $900 million in planned B-21 construction work across Whiteman.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers awarded K & K Industries a $13.6 million contract to build a weapons release system storage facility at Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, part of the base’s preparation to host the B-21 Raider stealth bomber. The Windsor, Missouri-based company’s firm-fixed-price award brings the project’s total value to $14,993,485.
Three companies bid on the project. Work will be done in Knob Noster, Missouri, the town adjacent to Whiteman, with an estimated completion date of March 31, 2028. The Army obligated $13,649,923 in fiscal 2026 military construction funds at the time of the award. The Kansas City District of the Army Corps of Engineers is managing the contract.
The facility will give Whiteman dedicated space to store and support armament-related equipment for the B-21, according to Air Force documentation on the project. It includes a new weapons and release-system shop covering about 1,580 square meters (17,000 square feet), along with alterations to roughly 674 square meters (7,250 square feet) of existing space, plus utilities, communications, access routes and site preparation work. Air Force documents describing the project say Whiteman currently lacks enough room to handle the munitions-related parts and equipment expected to arrive with the bomber.
Whiteman is home to the Air Force’s current B-2 Spirit fleet and is set to become the second operational base for the B-21, after Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota. The Air Force has said the new facility will let the base keep running B-2 operations without competing for existing infrastructure as B-21 support work ramps up.
This is one of roughly 30 military construction projects planned at Whiteman for the B-21 program, together valued at about $900 million, according to slides the Army Corps of Engineers presented at an industry day in September. Those projects include a dormitory and a radio-frequency hangar in addition to the weapons storage facility, with a weapons load trainer facility and a sustainment complex planned for awards in fiscal 2027.
The Army Corps separately awarded Conti Federal Services $74.8 million this month to build a radio-frequency and measurements hangar at Whiteman, a facility designed to check whether the B-21’s low-observable coatings and stealth characteristics hold up after maintenance or repairs. That hangar is scheduled for completion in September 2029.

Xi Jinping will demand an end to arms sales to Taiwan during his meeting with Trump - Reuters

China may demand an end to new and already ordered arms deliveries to Taiwan. Xi Jinping and Trump's talks will take place in Washington.
Chinese leader Xi Jinping may call on Washington to stop selling weapons to Taiwan during his upcoming meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump. Reuters was told this by sources familiar with the matter, reports UNN.
Details
It is noted that China will likely raise the issue of the third joint communiqué between the two countries, signed in 1982.
In the document, the United States stated its intention to gradually reduce arms sales to Taiwan and not pursue long-term arms deliveries to the island.
At the same time, then-U.S. President Ronald Reagan noted in an accompanying memorandum that Washington’s willingness to reduce arms sales depended on China’s continued commitment to a peaceful resolution of its differences with Taiwan.
China considers Taiwan its territory and regularly calls the island issue one of the most sensitive matters in relations with the United States. Beijing has repeatedly called on Washington to stop selling weapons to Taiwan.
China wants to stop deliveries that have already been ordered
According to the sources, China may call on the United States not only to halt new arms sales to Taiwan but also to stop supplying weapons that the island has already ordered.
One source said Xi Jinping may tell Trump that Taiwan itself is the source of instability in U.S.-China relations and is allegedly changing the status quo.
According to Reuters, China is instead offering to help the United States exert pressure on Iran in connection with the war in the Middle East.
The United States adheres to a “one China” policy, under which it does not officially determine Taiwan’s sovereignty but does not support Beijing’s position that the island is part of China.
In December, the Trump administration approved an $11 billion arms sales package for Taiwan — the largest in history. Another package worth approximately $14 billion has remained suspended for several months. After meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing in May, Trump called this package “a very good bargaining chip.”
What they are saying in the United States
A White House representative said that Trump plans to make a decision on a new arms sales package for Taiwan fairly quickly.
During his first presidential term, Trump approved more arms sales to Taiwan than any other U.S. president. According to the White House representative, in the first year of his second term he has already approved more such sales than Joe Biden’s administration did over all four years.
Taiwan said it is closely monitoring high-level contacts between the United States and China and continues to maintain close communication with Washington.
Xi Jinping will arrive in Washington on Wednesday. Official talks with Trump are scheduled for Thursday, while the Chinese leader’s visit to the U.S. National Archives is scheduled for Friday.
At the same time, Senator Pete Ricketts Matt Pottinger said that he does not expect significant agreements on Taiwan during this week’s meetings.

Energy, defense sectors most attractive for investment in Ukraine despite war risks - survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:06:18 EEST
21:06:18 KST

The energy sector and defense industry top the list of the most promising areas for investment in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian and international business representatives.
That's according to a Business Ombudsman Council (BOC) survey, "Current Challenges to Business and Ukraine's Investment Attractiveness," in which 60% of respondents named energy as promising and 53.2% named the defense industry. The IT sector (42.5%), construction (38.1%) and agriculture (35.4%) also ranked among the top industries.
Despite the ongoing war, international interest in the Ukrainian market remains: none of the foreign business representatives surveyed said they had no interest at all in investing in Ukraine. More than a third of foreign companies (35%) rated their familiarity with the local business climate as high. Foreign investors consider direct investment in already-operating enterprises and forming joint business partnerships with Ukrainian companies to be the most common ways of entering the market.
War-related risks remain the main obstacle to opening or expanding foreign business, cited by 75% of respondents.
At the same time, institutional factors play a decisive role: to improve the investment climate, 90% of foreign investors point to the need to reduce corruption, 75% to simplifying administrative procedures, and 65% to ensuring access to justice. Tax incentives or the creation of special economic zones, by contrast, rank as much lower priorities for investors.
Ukraine's course toward EU integration has a strong positive effect on investment decisions for 94.9% of international companies, serving as a signal of long-term stability and regulatory alignment. Among Ukrainian businesses, meanwhile, 61.1% already actively export to EU countries, and another 9.9% plan to start exporting soon. Businesses cite high financial costs (45.5%), stiff competition (38.9%) and the difficulty of certifying products to European standards (36.2%) as the main barriers to entering the EU market.
The survey covered 319 Ukrainian companies from 20 regions. Fieldwork ran from May 14 to June 4, 2026.

"Hannibal Holiday"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:03:48 UTC
21:03:48 KST

"Hannibal Holiday"
« previous post |
Today's Frazz:
Caulfield substitutes day for way, in the English translation of the Latin phrase "Aut inveniam viam aut faciam", which Wikipedia tells us "has been spuriously attributed to Carthaginian General Hannibal, in response to his generals statement that it was impossible to cross the Alps by elephant, during the Second Punic War in 218 BC". The fact that Caulfield frames the pun, and Frazz recognizes the reference, is a tribute to their shared erudition.
When I first learned this phrase many years ago, I wondered why the Romans would immortalize their enemy Hannibal. Perhaps it was like the British fascination with Napoleon? But apparently the only classical source for the phrase is Seneca's Hecules Furens, where it's used in the 3rd person singular to describe Hercules' return from the underworld. First-person versions appear as mottos in 16th-century England, and presumably the attribution to Hannibal started at some point after that.
I frequently walk past a first-person-plural version of the motto, over the Class of 1893 Memorial Gate on Spruce St. just west of 34th St.
In addition Penn's class of 1893, English-language Wikipedia lists several other British and American "social, educational and military organizations" who have adopted it as a motto. Italian Wikipedia gives a couple of Italian ones. And there's the fictional University of American Samoa.

====================================================================================================

GM Defense lands nearly $700 million for ISV design changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:02:09 UTC
21:02:09 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded GM Defense a $697.7 million contract modification on Sept. 21 for Infantry Squad Vehicle Utility engineering changes, bringing the deal's total value to $915.6 million.
- GM Defense has received several follow-on Infantry Squad Vehicle orders since its original $214.3 million contract in 2020, with the Army planning to field more Utility-variant vehicles over time.
GM Defense won a $697.7 million modification to its Infantry Squad Vehicle contract with the U.S. Army, funding engineering changes to the vehicle’s five-seat cargo variant, the Department of War announced Sept. 21. The modification, designated P00053, brings the total value of the underlying contract to $915.6 million.
The Warren, Michigan-based company was the only bidder on the modification. The Army Contracting Command-Detroit Arsenal in Michigan managed the award. Work locations and funding will be set order by order, with an estimated completion date of June 25, 2028. The Army has not disclosed how many vehicles or kits the engineering work covers, or whether the changes apply to vehicles already fielded, future production, or both.
The Infantry Squad Vehicle entered Army service in 2020 as a nine-seat troop carrier built to move an infantry squad quickly across rough terrain. It is based on the Chevrolet Colorado ZR2 midsize truck and uses roughly 90 percent commercial off-the-shelf parts, including Multimatic dampers and other Chevrolet Performance components. The vehicle weighs about 4,930 pounds (2,236 kg), carries a payload of 3,200 pounds (1,451 kg), and runs on a 2.8-liter Duramax turbo-diesel engine paired with a six-speed automatic transmission. It is light enough to be sling-loaded under a UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter and compact enough to fit inside a CH-47 Chinook.
This modification covers the Infantry Squad Vehicle Utility, a newer five-seat version with a rear cargo bed in place of extra passenger seats. GM Defense has said the Army intends to eventually field more Utility-variant vehicles than the original nine-seat troop carrier, a shift the company has attributed to feedback from the Army’s Transforming in Contact initiative. The Utility variant is built to support logistics runs, fire support, command-and-control posts, electronic warfare equipment, and counter-drone systems.
GM Defense first won the Infantry Squad Vehicle production contract in June 2020, beating competing bids from Oshkosh Defense and a Science Applications International Corporation and Polaris team. That initial award was worth $214.3 million for 649 vehicles, part of an Army objective covering up to 2,065 Infantry Squad Vehicles across variants. The Army approved full-rate production for the program in April 2023.
Orders under the contract have continued since then. The Army awarded GM Defense roughly $44.8 million in February 2025 for additional vehicles. In March 2026, the company received an order worth about $458.4 million covering 121 Utility-variant vehicles along with anti-lock brake and electronic stability control kits. A separate contract announced in June 2026 added $142,985,392 for more Infantry Squad Vehicles and winch kits, bringing that agreement’s cumulative value to $623,769,043.
General Motors CEO Mary Barra told investors during the company’s second-quarter 2026 earnings call that GM Defense’s revenue is on pace to approach $700 million for the year and that the unit expects Infantry Squad Vehicle awards in 2026 to exceed $1 billion. GM Defense, relaunched by General Motors in 2017, has built its military vehicle business almost entirely around the Infantry Squad Vehicle family since winning the original Army contract.
The vehicle family now includes several configurations beyond the original troop carrier and the Utility variant covered by this week’s modification, among them a two-seat cargo version with a larger flatbed and a heavy gun carrier fitted with a turret ring for a machine gun.

Religious women are more receptive to potential partners on dating apps, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:00:26 UTC
21:00:26 KST

A recent study suggests that a woman’s level of religious belief influences how she evaluates potential partners on swipe-based dating apps like Tinder. When navigating these platforms, women often face a trade-off between evaluating a potential partner’s genetic fitness and their willingness to invest in a relationship. The findings indicate that more religious women show a broader initial receptivity to men’s profiles, while overall, women tend to prefer softer facial features but surprisingly favor exaggerated, unverifiable profile biographies. The research was published in Psychology & Sexuality.
Swipe-based dating applications require users to make split-second decisions about potential partners based on a single photograph and a brief biography. These platforms compress mate selection into rapid, low-consequence choices, forcing users to rely heavily on highly visible cues. When evaluating a photograph, people often pick up on facial sexual dimorphism, which refers to how physically masculinized or feminized a face appears.
Earlier research discovered that women often prefer softer, feminized male faces over hyper-masculine ones. For instance, a 1998 study showed that women routinely find feminized male faces more attractive than strictly masculine alternatives. This preference exists partly because rugged features are linked to lower trustworthiness, with a 2012 study indicating that women view more masculine men as more likely to engage in unfaithful behavior.
Religious norms often emphasize long-term relational stability and sexual restraint. Supporting this, a study covered by PsyPost in 2017 indicated that higher religious commitment is associated with a greater preference for long-term mating strategies and fewer sexual partners. Because of this association, researchers expected that religious women might be more cautious when evaluating potential partners online.
The new study builds on this concept by examining how initial visual judgments interact with written profile details and a woman’s own religiosity on modern dating apps. The research was conducted by Katherine L. Sheetz, a Ph.D. candidate, and Lisa L. M. Welling, a professor of psychology, both at Oakland University.
“Online dating has changed the way people make initial judgments about potential partners, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic forced the majority of dating online,” Welling, who directs the Welling Research Lab, told PsyPost. “Swipe-based platforms reduce initial mate choice selections to very rapid decisions based on relatively limited visual and textual information, yet we know relatively little about how individual differences, such as religiosity, shape those early decisions.”
“With this study, we were particularly interested in religiosity because it is associated with sexual restraint, restricted sociosexuality (meaning lower openness to casual sex), and long-term relationship motivations on average,” Welling explained. “We therefore wanted to test whether more religious women would be more selective when evaluating potential male partners in an online context, particularly when profiles contained cues that could be relevant to apparent trustworthiness and relationship intentions.”
The study included 439 single cisgender women between the ages of 18 and 38 who were primarily attracted to men. The participants completed an online survey that began with questionnaires assessing their religious beliefs and their motivations for using dating applications. Afterward, they completed a simulated Tinder task where they viewed 20 distinct male dating profiles. Each profile featured a photograph of a smiling man and a short, 500-character biography.
The researchers manipulated the photographs using computer software so that the faces appeared either 50 percent more masculinized or 50 percent more feminized, while keeping skin tone and identity the same. The profile biographies were also written to be either trustworthy or untrustworthy.
Trustworthy biographies included verifiable, specific information regarding education or employment and avoided grand claims. Untrustworthy biographies featured exaggerated personal achievements and vague job descriptions, a tactic known as selective self-presentation. The participants had to either accept each profile, mimicking a right swipe, or reject the profile, mimicking a left swipe.
The researchers found that facial features strongly guided the women’s choices. Profiles featuring masculinized faces had approximately 56 percent lower odds of being accepted compared to profiles with feminized faces. However, the biographic text yielded unexpected results. Instead of favoring honest profiles, women showed a preference for the exaggerated text. Profiles with untrustworthy biographies had about 24 percent higher odds of acceptance compared to those with straightforward, trustworthy biographies.
“We were also surprised that profiles containing our ‘untrustworthy’ biographies were accepted more often than profiles containing the ‘trustworthy’ biographies,” Welling said. “The manipulation successfully changed perceptions of trustworthiness in the intended direction, so the finding suggests that participants may have been responding to other characteristics conveyed by those biographies, rather than simply preferring less trustworthy partners. We think it might have been something like perceived confidence in the untrustworthy bios because they tended to be more boastful.”
A woman’s level of religious belief also played a role in her swiping behavior, but not in the direction the researchers originally predicted. Higher religiosity predicted higher overall profile acceptance across the board. For each one-unit increase on the study’s seven-point religiosity scale, the odds of a profile being accepted increased by roughly 38 percent.
“The main takeaway is that religiosity was associated with greater initial receptivity to potential partners in our simulated online-dating task, rather than greater selectivity, which is the opposite of what we originally predicted,” Welling noted.
She cautioned that while the association was statistically reliable, it was not necessarily a massive shift in real-world behavior. “An odds ratio is not the same thing as saying that someone was 30% or 38% more likely to date someone,” Welling clarified. “The outcome in our study was simply whether a participant accepted a profile in a controlled, simulated swiping task. In other words, our findings suggest that religious women are more likely to be open to dating men with a greater range of characteristics, but not that they necessarily would accept more men after that initial swipe.”
In exploratory analyses, the researchers looked at why the women used dating apps in the first place. Women who used the apps with the goal of finding a relationship accepted fewer profiles overall, showing a 38 percent reduction in acceptance odds for each one-unit increase in relational motivation. Entertainment or exploratory motives for using the app had no statistical effect on acceptance rates.
The preference for exaggerated biographies is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2016, which found that dating profiles featuring heavy bragging reduced viewers’ intentions to contact the owner. This difference might be explained by how the new study was designed, as the simulated Tinder task measured immediate profile acceptance during rapid swiping rather than a deliberate intention to date the profile owner.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The simulated paradigm was not a fully interactive dating application, meaning real-world swiping behavior might differ. The acceptance of a profile in this specific task might reflect a general openness to new experiences or basic social interaction, rather than true romantic intent.
“The biggest caveat is that accepting a dating profile is not the same thing as choosing a partner, having sex with someone, entering a relationship, or taking a real-world interpersonal risk,” Welling emphasized. “Our measure captured an early-stage decision about whether a profile was sufficiently appealing to remain in consideration for potential further contact.”
She also warned against misinterpreting the biography finding as evidence that women prefer dishonest men. “Our biographies combined different aspects of self-presentation, including the extent to which information could theoretically be externally verified and the degree of selective self-presentation,” Welling explained. “Although they produced the intended differences in perceived trustworthiness, they may also have conveyed other characteristics, such as confidence… or like social status, that then influenced profile acceptance.”
The religiosity measure used in the study combined social elements, like attending religious services, with intrinsic elements, like personal beliefs. Social religiosity is often linked to higher interpersonal trust, which might explain the unexpectedly high acceptance rates among religious women. The study sample was also limited to young college-aged women in the United States, meaning the results might not automatically apply to other demographics.
Future research could use eye-tracking technology to see exactly which parts of a dating profile women pay the most attention to. Researchers might also separate different types of religious belief to better understand how they affect romantic risk-taking online. This would provide a better picture of how individuals navigate trust and uncertainty in the digital dating world.
“A major next step is to make the dating environment more realistic and to see how these findings translate into the in-person dating world,” Welling told PsyPost. “Our task captured the rapid decision-making aspect of swipe-based dating similar to dating apps like Tinder, but it was still a controlled simulation and results from face-to-face dating may differ.”
“I think the broader point is that online dating is an interesting setting for studying human decision-making because it makes the initial stages of mate evaluation unusually visible,” Welling concluded. “People are making rapid judgments from photographs, short biographies, and other limited cues, and those judgments reflect both characteristics of the profile and characteristics of the person doing the judging. Our findings suggest that we should be cautious about assuming that a characteristic associated with one aspect of mating psychology will necessarily predict behavior in another context.”
The study, “Holy swipes: the influence of religiosity on mate choice in online dating,” was authored by Katherine L. Sheetz and Lisa L. M. Welling.

Who Should Get a Blood Test for Alzheimer's Disease?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

For decades, the only way to confirm that someone had Alzheimer’s disease was by autopsy after death, when pathologists could confirm amyloid plaques, which are hallmarks of the disease, in the brain. Doctors now use a combination of factors to diagnose Alzheimer’s, including reports from patients and their caregivers about changes in memory or other cognitive functions, performance on cognitive tests, brain imaging, and tests of spinal fluid. But some of these measures can be subjective, invasive, expensive, or hard to assess.
Enter the blood tests. There are now four blood tests cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to detect the earliest signs of the neurodegenerative disease: an important advance in helping to diagnose Alzheimer’s in more people, as well as detecting it earlier in the disease course.
“This is a very exciting time for the field,” says Dr. Eric Reiman, CEO emeritus and lead researcher at the Banner Alzheimer’s Institute in Phoenix. “We’re going to start personalizing Alzheimer’s care similar to cancer, where we can inform diagnosis, prognosis, and staging to further inform disease severity.”
The two newest blood tests cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August make blood tests for Alzheimer's disease more widely available for doctors to prescribe—and in a younger population of people—for the first time. But that doesn't mean everyone should get one. Here's what to know about the available blood tests for Alzheimer's disease and when experts recommend taking them.
The first two blood tests for Alzheimer's disease
The first blood test for the disease, made by Fujirebio, was cleared by the FDA in May 2025. It determines the ratio of two key Alzheimer’s proteins—a form of beta amyloid and a form of tau—which reflects whether amyloid plaques are accumulating in the brain. But the test can only be run on specialized equipment and therefore isn't widely available in commercial labs.
The second test, made by Roche and FDA-cleared in October 2025, detects levels of a version of tau that correlates with the buildup of amyloid plaques. It's the first Alzheimer’s blood test that primary care physicians can prescribe to rule out the disease.
The newest Alzheimer's blood tests
The latest two tests, cleared in August, are intended to make diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease easier and more accurate.
PrecivityAD2, a new blood test from the diagnostics company C2N, is based on an earlier version of the company's test that was available only via certified labs. It uses a technology called mass spectrometry that is a more sophisticated way of picking up amyloid and tau compared to traditional assays. It provides a probability score that reflects how likely a person is to have amyloid plaques in the brain. Major laboratories as well as specific clinic and health system labs are able to perform it, so it is more widely available for doctors to prescribe.
Because PrecivityAD2 was studied in younger populations with a higher family risk of developing Alzheimer’s, it is also the first test cleared to use in people as young as 40 who show signs of cognitive problems. (The other blood tests are generally for people in their mid-50s or older.) "Because of the ability to go after individuals who represent the earliest stages of the disease process, we now have the opportunity to provide early diagnosis and then think about what should come next in managing that patient,” says Dr. Joel Braunstein, cofounder and CEO of C2N.
The other newly cleared test, from Roche, is called the Elecsys ptau217 plasma test and looks specifically for a changed version of tau—called ptau217—that appears when amyloid starts to accumulate in the brain. For people with memory issues or other cognitive complaints, the test can help them and their doctors to determine if the cause is likely due to Alzheimer’s disease or not. “It’s the most useful [test] and has the highest sensitivity and specificity,” says Dr. Thomas Wisniewski, professor of neurology, pathology and psychiatry and director of the Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center at NYU Langone Health. “We’ve been using these blood tests on the research side for a decade or so, so we have long experience knowing their utility.”
Who should be getting these blood tests?
All of the tests are designed for people who are showing signs or symptoms of brain lapses or memory issues. While blood tests are relatively easy to administer and are generally used to screen for other conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol, in this case, they're not meant to be used as screening tools for otherwise healthy people with no cognitive symptoms to identify those who might be at higher risk of Alzheimer’s.
Once people or their loved ones start noticing changes in cognitive function, the blood tests can be a useful way to determine if the reason for those changes is related to Alzheimer’s or something else.
“I worry about them being used inappropriately, especially in patients without symptoms,” says Dr. Lawren VandeVrede, assistant professor of neurology at University of California San Francisco. “One of the clear bright lines we have is that these tests are intended to identify the cause of cognitive symptoms in the context of an appropriate workup in which we look at medications, mood problems, and think of potential contributors to cognitive changes.” He says that these considerations have historically contributed to a diagnostic accuracy, without using blood tests, of about 85% for Alzheimer’s disease. Adding blood tests could increase that accuracy.
“These blood tests don’t provide definitive answers; they provide information about risk,” says Wisniewski. “So they are really for evaluating people with some sort of cognitive symptoms.”
Why can’t I take a blood test to know if I’m at risk for Alzheimer’s disease?
The main reason that these blood tests aren’t being used in people without cognitive problems is that they haven’t been studied in this group. That means that the data don’t support whether the tests would have unacceptably high rates of false positive or false negatives to be useful. Already, scientists know that looking for the Alzheimer’s proteins in people at lower risk of the disease tends to lead to more false readings.
However, that could change in a year or so when two large studies conclude. Both are studying people who do not have cognitive symptoms but do have signs of abnormal brain proteins. The trials test whether using either of the currently approved Alzheimer’s drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, in people without memory problems can reduce or clear the buildup of abnormal proteins in their brains and slow the progression of the disease. If those trials show that these drugs can slow Alzheimer's, then these blood tests may become a critical part of identifying people at the earliest stages of the disease, well before they show memory or other problems.
“Published research suggests that a third of people who are cognitively intact above a certain age will show positive biomarkers for Alzheimer’s disease, including on blood tests,” says Dr. Jason Hinman, professor of neurology and director of the Mary S. Easton Center for Alzheimer’s Research and Care at the University of California Los Angeles. That means that the blood tests could become an important part of evaluating brain health and Alzheimer's risk well before symptoms start. They could also open the door for treating people at earlier stages of the disease—if the studies support it—to protect them from advancing more quickly.
For people who start the Alzheimer’s medications, the blood tests could also play an important role in tracking how well the drugs work in reducing or clearing the plaques from the brain. In a recent study published in Alzheimer’s & Dementia, scientists in Korea reported that patients taking lecanemab showed a drop in levels of ptau217 three to six months after beginning the drug, and that drop was linked to slower cognitive decline as measured in cognitive tests.
What are the differences between the tests?
All of the blood tests look for one or both of the hallmark proteins associated with Alzheimer’s, but with different levels of sensitivity and specificity. Most experts agree that levels of ptau217 provide the most reliable sign of Alzheimer’s disease so far. “The ptau217 test was a real surprise,” says VandeVrede. “We didn’t know how good it would be, how accurate it was.”
PrecivityAD2, because it was studied in younger people, might be useful for people who have a family history of the disease and are starting to show signs of cognitive problems or memory loss.
The blood tests also put more information in the hands of primary care doctors, who are often the first to confront cognitive changes in patients. Recent studies showed that primary care physicians—not just specialists—are able to interpret and manage Alzheimer’s diagnoses using blood tests. Having blood tests to confirm a potential Alzheimer’s diagnosis also helps primary care physicians triage which patients might need to be referred to specialists for further confirmatory testing, such as an amyloid PET scan or a spinal fluid test. “Blood biomarker [tests] are democratizing the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease," says VandeVrede. "I am seeing patients show up much earlier than they used to, because I think these tests are helping more people to take the symptoms seriously.”
To help primary care doctors interpret the blood tests, the Alzheimer’s Association created guidelines by which doctors should first establish that the patient shows signs or symptoms of cognitive issues, and secondly rule out other potential causes of those problems, including depression, medications, vitamin deficiencies, and even sleep disorders. “We know that a lot more people will be asking for these blood tests,” says Maria Carrillo, chief science officer at the Alzheimer’s Association. “So the upshot of our guidance is triaging patients. A lot has to be done before patients should be getting a blood test for Alzheimer’s.”

Trump defends military action against Iran, Venezuela, and calls for rebrand of AI

Trump defends military action against Iran, Venezuela, and calls for rebrand of AI
US President Donald Trump used his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday to defend recent military action against Iran, urging countries to maintain economic pressure on Tehran – and declaring that he now faces a choice between making a deal, or taking far more drastic steps.
Calling Iran “the number one sponsor of terror,” the President devoted much of his speech to the Islamic Republic, arguing that his Administration had confronted a threat that previous leaders – in the US and abroad – had failed to address.
He told world leaders gathered in the Assembly Hall for the annual General Debate that for 51 years, “the fanatical Iranian regime” had spread “carnage and chaos” across the entire Middle East and beyond.
Nuclear weapons ban
“I will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
Mr. Trump said his administration had offered Iran economic cooperation in exchange for ending its nuclear programme and support for terrorism, but that Tehran had rejected the proposal.
“Then in Operation Midnight Hammer, the US military obliterated their nuclear programme beneath mountains of rubble,” he said.
The President went on to claim that subsequent military operations had severely weakened Iran’s military capabilities, citing the destruction of naval assets, air defences and missile production facilities.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” he asked.
But he also described a binary choice, over whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and “drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness.”
Mr. Trump predicted an agreement would eventually be reached. “I believe we’ll make a deal," he said.
Calling for continued international unity, he urged countries to support the “complete economic isolation of Iran” until it ended attacks on commercial shipping and support for terrorism.
Wars settled, conflicts addressed
Turning to broader foreign policy, Mr. Trump said he had helped bring an end to eight conflicts since returning to office.
Among those he listed were disputes involving Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as the war in Gaza.
The President also said efforts were continuing to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
“It's time to stop the killing,” he said.
Pressure in the Americas
Mr. Trump highlighted a series of developments across the Western Hemisphere, including what he described as a US military operation in Venezuela that resulted in the arrest of President Nicolás Maduro.
He said the US was now working with Venezuelan leaders toward what he called “a much better future for the Venezuelan people” and announced a major oil agreement between the two countries.
On Mexico, the President focused on efforts against transnational crime, saying drug cartels had been designated as foreign terrorist organizations and calling on the country to “reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity.”
He also cited ongoing negotiations with Cuba, saying his administration sought "a fundamental change in the situation” there.
The President also lauded the new agreement due to be signed with Greenland, describing the Arctic territory as strategically important to regional and international security.
Mr. Trump said the arrangement with Denmark and Greenland would give the United States "permanent control over security and all other needs" on the territory and would support NATO's security posture in the Arctic and North Atlantic regions.
From AI to ‘superintelligence’
A significant portion of the address also focused on artificial intelligence (AI), which Mr. Trump argued should instead be called “superintelligence.”
“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake,” he said. “It is not fake. It's actually amazing.”
President Trump said technological leadership would be central to economic and geopolitical competition in the years ahead.
“Whoever wins superintelligence wins,” he declared, adding that the US would encourage development of the technology while monitoring potential risks.
‘Evil people’
Mr. Trump also renewed criticism of several international bodies.
He described the International Criminal Court (ICC) as an institution “full of evil people” with no jurisdiction over the United States and called on nations to withdraw from it.
The President was similarly critical of the Geneva-based UN Human Rights Council, accusing it of focusing excessively on the US while overlooking abuses elsewhere.
He criticized the education, culture and science agency, UNESCO and the International Maritime Organization, arguing that international bodies should not advance what he characterized as global governance initiatives.
Concluding his address, Mr. Trump called on countries to confront global challenges with “courage and resolve,” saying cooperation among nations could create “a future for our people that is brighter, more hopeful, and more magnificent than ever before.”

Diplomacy is the way to address global challenges, Brazil tells General Assembly
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva told the General Assembly on Tuesday that the UN needs to become a “temple of peace” once again, as it confronts one of the most critical periods in its 80-year history.
Opening this year’s General Debate, the President – known to all as Lula – expressed his indignation at the widespread attacks taking place on multilateralism worldwide.
According to the Brazilian leader, more effective diplomacy is the only way for collective challenges to be successfully addressed.
He said the organization's credibility has been weakened due to paralysis of the Security Council, the use of veto powers and growing geopolitical tensions.
“We are all held hostage by the inaction of the Security Council” he said, stressing that Brazil has spoken out against the use of veto power by permanent members in the chamber since the first general assembly meeting in 1946.
World of conflict
The Brazilian leader recalled that the previous year had seen the highest number of armed conflicts registered since the Second World War.
He called for regional conflicts to be contained before they escalate into “tragedies of global proportions”.
Turning to the conflict in the Middle East, Lula said that “generations of Palestinians” will now carry “the pain and trauma left by the genocide of women and children,” criticising the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank – all making a two-State solution increasingly difficult to achieve.
Lula also addressed the war between Russia and Ukraine, saying the conflict had continued to claim lives and that there would be “no winners on the battlefield”.
Brazil’s path
He also highlighted key policies at home, noting that Brazil has once again made inroads against hunger and adopted a new law to combat corruption and organised crime – which has led to a record level of seizures of drugs, assets and illicit funds.
“The fight against corruption shall remain relentless," Lula said. "No matter who it hurts. No one is above the law.”
Trusting science
On climate change, President Lula said that, in an era of disinformation, those who reject scientific evidence are denying reality.
He said economic development should always go hand in hand with environmental protection.
The president also called for greater regulation of large technology companies and artificial intelligence (AI), warning against a technological race without ethical safeguards.
In his closing remarks, Lula highlighted the UN's historic role in decolonisation, human rights, sustainable development and the protection of migrants and refugees.
He called on Member States to find the political will to once again make the UN a “temple of peace”

Displacement on the rise in Yemen as fighting continues

Displacement on the rise in Yemen as fighting continues
As hostilities worsen in Yemen, more people have been fleeing their homes, further intensifying the humanitarian crisis within the region, the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) warned on Tuesday.
“Fighting in Yemen is expanding across multiple front lines, triggering a rapidly growing displacement crisis and driving more than 130,000 people to flee their homes since the beginning of September,” UNHCR spokesperson Babar Baloch told reporters in Geneva.
The mass displacement follows the Iran-backed Houthi fighters’ rapid advance down Yemen’s western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in recent weeks and clashes with Saudi-backed Yemeni Government forces.
The city of Taiz in south-western Yemen remains the epicentre of the crisis, Mr. Baloch said, accounting for more than 60 per cent of overall displacement.
No safe place
“Many families remaining within the governorate itself [are] unable to move to safer locations due to fighting, blocked roads or lack of transportation fuel,” he said.
Displacement is also being reported from Al Jawf, Marib and Hudaydah governorates. According to UNHCR, the vast majority of those displaced are women and children, and many have already been forced to flee several times.
Before the recent escalation, more than 5.2 million people were already internally displaced inside Yemen, which has seen more than a decade of conflict and economic collapse. The UNHCR spokesperson said at least 22 million people – over half of the country’s population – are estimated to require humanitarian assistance. Yemen has also been hosting some 65,000 refugees and asylum seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.
Mr. Baloch stressed that more Yemenis are now becoming refugees, as civilians fleeing clashes across the Gulf of Aden continue toarrive in Djibouti. More than 3,000 have arrived so far, while hundreds more have landed in neighbouring Somaliland and Puntland. The number of new refugee arrivals in Djibouti has already surpassed the total number of Yemenis arriving in recent years.
More than 10,000 arrivals are expected in Djibouti, Mr. Baloch explained, as sea conditions are forecasted to improve by mid-October, which could enable further crossings.
UNHCR’s Djibouti operation is only 15 per cent funded, while in Yemen in 2026, the agency has received only $34 million of the $194 million required even before the latest escalation.

Time to accept ‘hard truths’ so trust can be rebuilt: General Assembly president
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Time to accept ‘hard truths’ so trust can be rebuilt: General Assembly President
The UN’s survival for 80 years is not, by itself, proof of success, and now, the institution must confront painful truths if it hopes to rebuild public trust, said Khalilur Rahman, president of the General Assembly’s 81st session on Tuesday.
Key points:
- The UN has grown from 50 Member States in 1945 to 193 today, but survival alone is not evidence of success
- Global military spending has climbed toward $3 trillion while development assistance fell 23 per cent year-on-year even as progress has stalled for a third of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets
- Africa remains without a permanent Security Council seat after eight decades, which must change as a matter of “fairness, justice” and credibility
“Outside these walls, people are not asking whether the United Nations still exists. They are asking whether it works,” said Khalilur Rahman.
Acknowledging the UN’s failures – including the unresolved Palestinian question and ongoing wars in Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar and across the Middle East – Mr. Rahman balanced this with lesser-known successes.
He cited the return of nearly five million people to their homes in Iraq, ongoing delivery of aid in Haiti despite security challenges and the work of peacekeepers described by one war-torn nation’s representative as builders of “roads and communities”, not just “Blue Helmets”.
Three paths towards trust
“Trust is not given,” Mr. Rahman said. “It is earned. Passive ownership is not enough. If we do not claim proactive ownership of this place, we cannot expect it to heal.”
He outlined three paths:
- Honest acknowledgment of institutional shortcomings
- Deep structural reform beyond cosmetic budget changes
- Greater inclusion of businesses, scientists and civil society in UN decision-making, particularly on artificial intelligence (AI)
On Security Council reform, Mr. Rahman renewed calls for fairer representation.
“When the Security Council works, the United Nations works,” he said.
After eight decades without a permanent African seat despite the continent’s central role in peacekeeping operations, Mr. Rahman called for action.
“Africa needs a seat at the table, not to be on the menu,” he said,
Watch the full general debate on UN Web TV:
Military spending spikes
He flagged a stark funding imbalance: development assistance fell 23 per cent year-on-year to roughly $175 billion, even as global military spending approached $3 trillion – marking 11 consecutive years of growth.
Despite this, Mr. Rahman pointed to genuine progress:
- Nearly a billion people gained access to safe drinking water over the past decade
- Electricity now reaches 92 per cent of the world’s population
- Internet access has risen from 40 to 74 per cent
AI guardrails
On artificial intelligence, Mr. Rahman urged the UN not to fall further behind.
He warned that AI is already embedded in critical systems worldwide and called for “prudent and reliable guardrails” developed with scientific input from outside government.
“We cannot allow an arms race for control of AI to carry us over the precipice,” he said.
Fighting hate
Hateful narratives are spreading like wildfire across borders and into homes at unprecedented speed and scale, targeting women and girls, minorities, migrants, refugees and persons with disabilities, often for political gain, Mr. Rahman said.
“We must choose dialogue and tolerance and foster a culture in which human rights are respected not only in law, but in our daily interactions, and we must stop the cherry picking of those rights that fit our respective cultures or the politics of the day,” he said.
In addition, new and emerging technologies are used to amplify lies, manipulate public debate, spread hatred and give incitement to violence faster and farther than ever before.
“Whether it is islamophobia, antisemitism, homophobia, or misogyny, it's all the same... hatred, repackaged and relabelled,” he said. “Let us use the tools of our age not to deepen fear, but to widen understanding and advance human dignity, for everyone, everywhere.”
Transformation time
Mr. Rahman said it was time to address those concerns.
“We cannot continue treating a chronic ailment with temporary painkillers when what we need is a deeper diagnosis and a more profound plan for transformation,” he said.
“The task is not easy, nor can it be done overnight. Let us dedicate ourselves to the task of rebuilding trust and confidence in the United Nations so that it lives up to that incredible potential for many decades to come.”

Guterres: ‘Cracks have become canyons’ as world faces four tests of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Guterres: ‘Cracks have become canyons’ as world faces four tests of power
Humanity faces four defining “tests of power” – around war or peace, inequality, climate change and AI – that will determine whether the world moves towards a new era of cooperation or deeper division, the UN chief warned the General Assembly on Tuesday.
Key points
- UN chief urges binding international cooperation on AI governance, warning that life-and-death decisions must never be handed to machines
- Calls for Security Council reform, highlighting the continued “indefensible” absence of permanent African representation
- For the first time in its history, UN has achieved full gender parity across senior leadership and staff
With roughly 100 days remaining in his term as UN Secretary-General, António Guterres delivered a wide-ranging speech that framed the world’s most pressing crises not as isolated problems, but as different expressions of the same underlying struggle over how power is exercised and by whom.
“The greatest power is not the power to dominate. It is the power to build a future that works for everyone,” he said, presenting his annual report of the Organization.
Describing a decade of eroding international norms – from civilians targeted in war, and humanitarian workers killed, to international law “cast aside” and fraying trust between nations – he said power itself is being fundamentally reshaped in three ways:
- Emergence of new State powers
- Significant transfer of authority from governments to private corporations and individuals
- Growing role of AI and autonomous weapons in decisions once reserved for humans
“The faultlines in our world are widening,” he said. “Cracks have become canyons.”
Rather than accepting fragmentation as inevitable, he called for galvanizing cooperation and a truly global network built on interdependence and shared rules while warning against sliding into rival blocs with separate economic and security systems, a scenario he has termed in recent years the Great Fracture.
No real ceasefire in sight
Pointing to cascading crises across the Middle East, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar, Mr. Guterres argued that so-called ceasefires have often amounted to little more than “lesser fires”, with civilians continuing to pay the price.
He renewed calls for compliance with International Court of Justice (ICJ) orders regarding Gaza and warned that settlement expansion in the Israeli-occupied West Bank threatens to extinguish the two-State solution.
He also condemned Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a clear violation of the UN Charter.
Renewing longstanding calls for Security Council reform, he singled out the continued absence of permanent African representation as “unjust and indefensible” given the 15-member organ’s founding in a starkly different geopolitical era.
‘Equality is not a dream; it is a decision’
Highlighting the gap between record global wealth and the billions still lacking access to food, clean water, education and healthcare, he said inequality is not merely an economic issue but a question of power over opportunity, resources and self-determination.
He reiterated his long-held view that the international financial system leaves developing nations crushed by debt while facing climate disasters they did little to cause.
In this vein, he called for faster debt relief, bolder multilateral development banks and fairer access to Special Drawing Rights created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Devoting particular attention to gender inequality, he announced that the UN has achieved full gender parity across senior leadership, headquarters staff, and professional roles for the first time in its history.
“Equality is not a dream; it is a decision,” he said, citing progress at the UN as proof that entrenched power structures can change.
Twin challenges: Climate and AI
On climate change, Mr. Guterres said the crisis is the “most profound intergenerational power imbalance”, warning of a near-certain breach of the 1.5°C threshold.
Calling for polluters to “pay” and for developed nations to triple adaptation funding, he pointed out that major oil companies are reaping substantial profits since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine while global adaptation finance for developing countries remains a fraction of that sum.
Turning to AI, the Secretary-General warned that power is increasingly concentrated in data, computing capacity and algorithms, advancing faster than humanity’s capacity to govern it.
“The danger is not technology,” he said. “The danger is technology without accountability.”
Outlaw killer robots
Guard rails on AI must be built, the UN chief said, adding that children must never become the test-subjects for unregulated systems.
“Life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines,” he warned. “Killer robots must have no place in our future.”
To address this, he called for a multilateral AI risk management framework with independent oversight, stating firmly that children must never become test subjects for unregulated systems and that life-and-death decisions must never be surrendered to machines.
Stronger, not weaker
Mr. Guterres reaffirmed that peace, development and human rights are inseparable pillars of the UN Charter, rejecting any notion that dignity and rights can be divorced from security and opportunity.
In the face of global catastrophe more than 80 years ago on the battlefields of World War Two, the United Nations was created as an act of defiance of hope, of people who refuse to surrender the future to fear and of countries that know their futures are bound together.
Pledging to carry the “spirit of resolve” through his remaining time in office, he vowed to continue championing the UN Charter’s values, even after leaving his post as Secretary-General.
“The world does not need a weaker United Nations,” he said. “It needs a UN strong enough to face the world as it is and determined enough to build the world as it should be.”

Millions of children return to schools that still can’t provide clean water or a working toilet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Millions of children return to schools that still can’t provide clean water or a working toilet
A new academic year is underway in many countries across the world, yet millions of children still attend schools where the water is unsafe to drink, toilets are unusable and there is nowhere to properly wash their hands.
That’s according to a report by the World Health Organization (WHO) and child rights agency UNICEF that reviews progress on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) in schools from 2015 to 2025.
WASH services are critical at schools as they can impact learning, health, and dignity, particularly for girls.
During this period, the proportion of schools with basic drinking water services rose from 67 per cent to 78 per cent. Global coverage of basic sanitation also increased, up from 67 per cent to 77 per cent, as did basic hygiene, from 59 per cent to 72 per cent.
Progress in danger
Despite these improvements, the report warns that the world remains off track in ensuring universal access by 2030, as stipulated under the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
It reveals that in 2025:
- 429 million school-age children lacked drinking water services at school
- 460 million lacked a basic sanitation service
- 545 million lacked a basic hygiene service, with water and soap for handwashing
Inequalities among countries
Significant inequalities persist, with the largest gaps reported in low-income and fragile settings, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.
For example, only 54 per cent of schools in low-income countries had basic drinking water services, while 50 per cent had basic sanitation services and 35 per cent had basic hygiene services.
By comparison, coverage of all three services exceeded 99 per cent in richer countries.
Challenge in sub-Saharan Africa
Sub-Saharan Africa had the lowest levels of coverage. Fewer than half of schools there had basic drinking water services, 46 per cent, or basic sanitation services, 43 per cent. Only 39 per cent had basic hygiene services.
Nearly three in five children globally who lack basic drinking water at school, around 250 million, live in the region, which is also home to some 264 million children who lack basic sanitation and 282 million lacking basic hygiene.
Achieving universal access for both basic drinking water and hygiene services in schools over the next five years would require a fourfold increase in the current rate of progress, and a fivefold increase for sanitation services.
UNICEF stressed that “without faster action, hundreds of millions of children will still lack these essential services at school in 2030.”

The goal is to get Iraq to rein in the Iranian-backed militias, many of which are designated terrorist groups by the US. Zaidi has now said he wants to see the arms under state control by June 2027, according to an interview with The New York Times.
“Militia groups have largely pushed back against the deadline to disarm. Two prominent pro-Tehran armed groups, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib Imam Ali, alongside cleric Muqtada al-Sadr’s Saraya al-Salam faction, claim they have placed their weapons under state authority. But hardline factions – mainly Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba – have said they will not disarm until foreign troops leave,” The National added.
Zaidi’s US meetings aimed at getting support for Iraq
Zaidi’s meetings in the US, with Rubio and others, are aimed at getting support for Iraq. He wants to see more investment and hopes for a new partnership with America after its forces leave.
Both Iraq and Syria are at a crossroads. The meetings at the UN indicate that they are seeking a new future in the region. If they succeed, that will stabilize a large swath of the Middle East between Turkey, Iran, and Saudi Arabia. If they are unable to bring home the investment they need, there will be difficult times ahead.

New rare diseases identified in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

New rare diseases identified in Iran
TEHRAN – Eighteen more rare diseases have been identified in the country, bringing the total number of rare diseases to 531, according to the Rare Disease Foundation.
Idiopathic camptocormia, Intellectual disability, eye abnormalities, microcephaly, peripheral spasticity syndrome, Riboflavin transporter deficiency (Brown-Vialetto-van Laere syndrome (BVVL)), Mantle cell lymphoma, Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, combined immunodeficiency due to IL21R deficiency, Isolated tibial hemimelia, Phyllodes tumor of the breast, and 3MC syndrome are among rare diseases that have been identified in the country, Mehr news agency reported.
According to WHO, rare diseases are often serious, chronic, and life-threatening. The European Union (EU) definition of a rare disease affects fewer than 5 in 10,000 people. Around 80 percent of rare diseases are genetic disorders, and half of them occur during childhood.
Rare diseases affect millions of people globally and are often complex, involving multiple organ groups and resulting in disabilities and premature death. Many people living with a rare disease frequently experience diagnostic delays, fragmented care, limited access to effective interventions, financial hardship, stigma and social exclusion.
The incidence of rare diseases is very low to the extent that maybe one or two people with a certain rare disease are present in the country. Some rare diseases such as ‘butterfly skin or EB’, ‘Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)’, ‘Metabolic diseases’, ‘Autism’, and ‘Dystrophies’ are among the most common cases in the country.
Among rare diseases, cancers are the most expensive ones covered by the Rare Disease Foundation so that 70 percent of the funds is allocated to cancer-related medicines. The rise in cancers highlights the need for the development of preventive programs, early detection, targeted screening, and fair access to health services.
The budget allocated to rare and hard-to-treat diseases has increased over the past few years, rising from 50 trillion rials (about 21.7 million dollars) in the first year to 120 trillion rials (about 52.17 million dollars) this year.
Health insurance provided for some 2m patients
In May, Sajjad Razavi, an official with the health ministry stated that about two million patients with rare and hard-to-treat diseases are covered by the Health Insurance Organization.
The Rare Disease Foundation also covers the patients, IRNA quoted Razavi as saying.
The official made the remarks on the occasion of the national day of rare and hard-to-treat diseases observed annually on the 18th of Ordibehesht, the second Iranian calendar month, which falls on May 8.
 
 The day is a good opportunity to rethink the health system’s responsibilities toward patients who need ongoing, multidimensional care and comprehensive support because of the complex, chronic, and mainly hard-to-treat nature of their diseases.  
To safeguard the patients’ health and lower financial burden on households, tens of specialized healthcare service packages have been defined for them, with some more being continuously developed.
The packages include diagnostic, therapeutic, pharmaceutical, rehabilitation, and dental services, whether in the form of outpatient or inpatient services, which are provided with minimal deductibles or free of charge.
Despite lower prevalence, rare and hard-to-treat diseases are among the top health priorities due to difficulties in their diagnosis and treatment.
There are no cures for rare diseases, and patients with rare diseases need supportive care and rehabilitation services throughout their lives. Hence, the day highlights the need for coherent planning, the development of recurrent specialized services, genetic counselling, the expansion of insurance coverage, and social support.
Promoting health literacy, strengthening the referral system, and expanding preventive services are key factors to lower mortality among patients.
