After brutal cuts, can this NASA center still build multibillion-dollar space telescopes?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:17:35 UTC
20:17:35 KST

After a successful late-August launch, the $4.3-billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is cruising to its final orbit about a million miles from Earth. If all goes well, NASA’s latest “flagship” observatory will be sending back unprecedented cosmic panoramas and revolutionary images of exoplanets by the end of the year.
Like its predecessor, the James Webb Space Telescope, Roman was designed and built primarily at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md., just outside Washington, D.C. But some current and former Goddard workers say NASA would not be able to build another telescope like Roman today. There aren’t enough people or pieces of equipment left.
Budget cuts and workforce reductions by the Trump administration have arguably hit Goddard the hardest out of NASA’s 10 research centers. From March 2020 to January 2025, a period that included U.S. DOGE Service layoffs and several rounds of early retirements in 2025, Goddard lost 40 percent of its personnel, shrinking from 10,000 federal workers and contractors down to 6,000. Since then managers have hired back 600 workers. In addition, NASA shut down several testing and technology development labs and broke up engineering teams, making work more difficult for those who remain.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Goddard’s diminution is part of a broader pivot at NASA as the White House redirects the space agency to put American astronauts on the moon by 2028. Budget proposals for the past two years have slashed NASA’s science funding, and some of the nation’s best and brightest minds have now left the space agency because of uncertainty about their role in its future. According to a July 23 report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), NASA lost a fifth of its civil servant workforce in the past year, with impacts to more than two dozen major projects. “The civil servant departures have left NASA’s workforce out of balance with NASA’s programmatic needs,” the report said.
NASA’s hardest hit centers were Goddard, its Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Ala., and its Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif. Combined, the three had 14 space exploration missions that were proposed to be canceled or delayed, the report stated.
NASA administrator Jared Isaacman has dismissed the GAO report: “I would not read too much into dated news designed to needlessly elevate people’s blood pressure,” he wrote on X.
Congress has rejected most of the White House’s proposed science funding cuts, but many of the space agency’s remaining scientists and engineers still worry that NASA’s ability to build ambitious interplanetary missions and astrophysical observatories has been so damaged that any recovery, if it occurs at all, will take decades. Based on interviews with 10current and former Goddard workers, as well as several independent space policy experts, Goddard is ground zero for these sweeping changes.
“I really like doing hands-on work and in-house building of spacecraft,” says one engineer who left Goddard in April after being at the center for seven years, during which they mostly worked on Roman. According to this former employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of reprisal, what once was a robust “pipeline” of future spacecraft has now dwindled. The engineer says their work on Roman ended when their lab was abruptly closed in November 2025 and adds that Goddard’s leadership has failed to adequately explain the research center’s apparent shift in status under the Trump administration.
“It’s hard to fathom how management can be so out of touch with what the workforce wants and needs,” says the engineer, who began their NASA career as an intern. “How can they make so many decisions that seem only meant to drive people away?”
NASA officials dispute that Goddard won’t be able to build space telescopes like Roman now or in the future.
“Conceiving, designing, developing, integrating and operating flagship missions of discovery are core capabilities of the Goddard Space Flight Center,” a NASA Goddard spokesperson tells Scientific American. “Goddard has a long history of delivering complex spaceflight hardware and engineering solutions that have enabled some of NASA’s most consequential missions, delivering game-changing scientific discoveries, and that responsibility and capability remains unchanged.”
A separate review released in June by NASA’s Office of Inspector General found that NASA officials broke no laws or rules during the rapid closures and layoffs of 2025. But, as described in its summary at the office’s website, the report agreed with Goddard employees’ complaints that “communication failures throughout the process resulted in confusion related to the efforts and increased challenges to the Center’s workforce.”
During the federal shutdown last fall, NASA officials closed labs at Goddard that manufactured advanced optical detectors for spacecraft, a unique test facility called an anechoic chamber that simulated the quietness of space and machine shops that built parts for scientific instruments that are scheduled to land on the moon in the next two years. The detector labs were later reopened.
Last November NASA also shut down the Goddard propulsion lab that built the fuel tanks, valves and thrusters for Roman and other spacecraft; the center’s propulsion engineering team dropped from 30 people to just seven. And inJanuary space agency officials closed the building that housed Goddard’s library—NASA’s largest—which stored thousands of historical journals and spaceflight documents and was used as a meeting place for Goddard employees.
NASA said the closure was part of a 2022 master plan for the campus, but the employees’ union has sued over the issue. The library remains closed for now, employees have said.
The agency spokesperson says that the anechoic chamber hadn’t been upgraded since 1997 and that its microwave-absorbing foam spires were crumbling. Future tests will be conducted at NASA Langley Research Center’s Experimental Test Range in Hampton, Va., within a similar chamber that was used to test the antenna for the space agency’s Europa Clipper mission before its 2024 launch.
The Goddard propulsion lab was closed because “propulsion fabrication is now readily and more efficiently available from the private sector,” the spokesperson says, adding that Goddard will continue to design and integrate future spacecraft propulsion units.
Despite such justifications, these cuts, closures and layoffs have caused morale to plummet at Goddard, some current workers say, and have left management increasingly disconnected from the research center’s day-to-day operations.
“The real value of Goddard is not just the facility itself but that there was a huge amount of expertise there,” says Margaret Samuels, a materials scientist and research engineer at the research center. Samuels, who is also an officer of the union that represents Goddard workers, says that the loss of expertise will take a long time to replace. “We are an ecosystem, and we rely on each other’s capabilities.”
For their part, NASA officials have said that last year’s layoffs and lab closures are making Goddard more efficient and competitiveand that the consolidation of buildings was part of a 2022 master plan.
But a skeptical Congress has directed the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) to form an investigative panel on whether Goddard still has the equipment, personnel and infrastructure to ensure “future cutting-edge scientific discovery and crewed space exploration.” The panel’s report is expected in December.
Goddard’s director, Jamie Dunn, was promoted to the role in May, after delivering Roman under budget and ahead of schedule as the telescope’s project manager since 2018. “The mood is good” at Goddard, Dunn told the NASEM panel during an August meeting. “There is work that needs to be done,” he added, but “people can see that we’re starting to come on an upswing.”
“I acknowledge we’ve been through a turbulent time,” Dunn also said at the meeting. “There’s a confluence of events. It wasn’t just one thing, and it didn’t all just start last year. It’s been a number of things that have been piling up over the years.”
The research center’s funding and staffing have always fluctuated, Dunn said, depending on the missions being built there and budgetary battles between U.S. policymakers. He cited Roman as an example, noting that the Trump administration had repeatedly proposed defunding the telescope, only for Congress to rescue the project each time by keeping the money flowing. In the future, he told the panel, “I am hopeful I can find more money” for Goddard.
At present there are no major flagship missions being built at Goddard, although planning is underway for the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), a space telescope that could launch a decade or more from now to image and study potentially Earth-like exoplanets. More immediately, Goddard engineers are building a mass spectrometer for the upcoming Dragonfly drone copter, which is set to launch to Saturn’s largest moon, Titan, in July 2028. The center has also been charged with developing DAVINCI (Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble Gases, Chemistry, and Imaging), a Venus probe that has faced funding and schedule delays but is presently set to launch sometime in the early 2030s.
Besides the high-level federal investigations into Goddard’s situation, smaller, more grassroots efforts are also seeking to raise the alarm.
The NASEM committee asked for a review of Goddard’s current capabilities by the Goddard Retirees and Alumni Association (GRAA). It revealed that the center faces a crisis in several areas. The findings, which came from a survey of 10 current workers and 27 former ones who left recently, stated that the safety and mission assurance team had lost half its staff as of July 2026. That means there are fewer people left to make sure labs and clean rooms pass all the required safety checks during tests that involve extreme temperatures, pressures and electrical discharges.
NASA officials say, however, that safety has not been compromised and that Goddard has one of the lowest mishap rates of any NASA center.
GRAA also found the center has lost expertise for coordinating robotic lunar spaceflights and questioned Goddard’s ability to “formulate and execute” large space telescopes such as HWO, as well as to perform other “complex research and operational missions, including maintaining world-class science, system engineering and project management.”
Carl Stahle, the report’s author and a retired Goddard engineer, tells Scientific American that the biggest loss was the people. “Many of the key skills and experience were lost in engineering,” he says.
The cuts to Goddard and NASA’s overall science and exploration mission will have implications for decades to come, according to Casey Dreier, chief of space policy at the Planetary Society.
“There’s no market to replace what we’re losing as a public investment in scientific exploration,” Dreier says. “Ironically, the current public policy is to throw more money at the area where private money is already flowing and to cut money where there is no private money supporting it and to just stop doing it.”
Speaking anonymously, a senior Goddard astrophysicist who has worked on several spacecraft missions says rebuilding the renowned campus, which was established in 1959, will be difficult.
“We can’t do another Roman from Goddard because lots of essential things are gone,” the engineer says, citing the staggering attrition of the center’s personnel and the damage or destruction of mission-critical assets. “There were instances of people grabbing a friend’s pickup truck to save essential parts of their equipment before it was thrown away,” the engineer says. “This is not how you treat unique hardware that costs the taxpayer millions of dollars. It was basically a rapid, unplanned disassembly.”
Despite the disruptions, closures and changes at Goddard, the scientist isn’t ready to quit NASA.
“Being able to dream and to reach space and to make measurements to the end of the universe or the beginning of the universe,” they say, “I mean, it’s hard to give that up.”

Mathematicians use AI to find mysterious symmetries, solving decades-old problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:16:57 UTC
20:16:57 KST

This past May mathematicians headed into a room near the top of the California Institute of Technology’s tallest building to prep for a sprint. The American Institute of Mathematics was soliciting questions of a particular kind: ones ripe for harnessing artificial intelligence’s unique ability to sift through larger-than-human-scale possibilities. Rachel Pries, a mathematician at Colorado State University, took to the podium to present a particularly strong candidate. “This problem had been open for a very, very long time,” she said.
Her challenge focused on the deep connections between polynomial equations such as 4x2 – 1 = 0 and the symmetries buried in their solutions. Within a few short months of the conference, by intertwining human insight with AI scale, the decades-old mystery would collapse.
Pries’s suggestion, known as the inverse Galois problem, was inspired by the work of the 19th-century French mathematician Évariste Galois, who perished after he was wounded in a gun duel at age 20. He had been studying patterns of symmetries that arise in polynomial equations with rational coefficients (numbers that can be written as fractions, such as 3 or 1⁄2). Mathematicians have long known that some polynomial equations have only rational solutions, while others have irrational solutions (such as ). But Galois’s work classified polynomials far more finely. By studying their solutions, he isolated symmetries that were peculiar to each equation, defining what eventually came to be known as “Galois groups.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Consider the equation x2 + 1 = 0, which has imaginary solutions—called roots—of +i and –i, where i = .
Imagine sneaking into a math library and combing through every mathematical text ever written. You secretly replace every i with –i and every –i with i. In the end your prank fails because the swap is a genuine symmetry, so all the equations in each book are still true. Pair that with the “do nothing” identity symmetry, and you have the two elements of the x2 + 1’s Galois group.
The more complicated a polynomial is, the more ways there are to shuffle its roots without anyone noticing the difference, leading to a richness of symmetries.
For any polynomial, known algorithms tease out its Galois group. But the reverse direction is opaque: Given a particular Galois group of symmetries, can you always find an associated polynomial? The quandary became known as the inverse Galois problem.
Most Galois groups come in orderly families. Shuffle three polynomial roots, and you get one group, shuffle four, and you get the next group; and so on up a ladder. But 26 different groups refuse to fall in line. The “sporadic” groups belong to no family and follow no pattern, with no simple explanation for why they exist at all. The first five sporadic groups to be discovered were the Mathieu groups: M11, M12, M22, M23 and M24.
In the 1980s teams of mathematicians around the world unearthed the polynomials corresponding to 25 of the 26 sporadic groups—but not M23. “There’s this one last holdout,” says Bjorn Poonen, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “I think some people were even wondering whether there might be no polynomial giving M23.”
After the Caltech talks concluded, the organizers asked participants to bid on problems they wanted to attack. The inverse Galois problem quickly racked up bids. In the end, six participants who had never worked together soon found themselves part of a mathematical dream team. Pries and Poonen were joined by Xiaoyu Huang of Temple University, Blake Jackson of the Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics, Kyu-Hwan Lee of the University of Connecticut and Shaowu Zhang, a Ph.D. student at Caltech.
And before three months had passed, M23’s mysteries fell apart.
“We could do it very efficiently,” Kyu-Hwan Lee says. “That wasn’t really possible five years ago.”
The team used AI to comb through M23 for combinations of symmetries. Of the results, they took the smallest collection—a set of seven surfaces—and asked the AI to numerically approximate their equations. Perhaps one could be pinned to exact numbers? But the decimals didn’t resolve into anything recognizable. The AI kept suggesting more precision, but by the time they hit 90 digits, they had maxed out the computer’s memory. The project halted. Huang posted a suspicion in the team’s chat that the choice of coordinates was to blame. “I think Bjorn pointed out that we could try some other way,” she said.
The group set a raft of AI agents to work on new, more harmonious coordinates. The group described what happened next as “miraculous” in a paper posted on the preprint server arXiv.org. Huang says most of the agents failed, but one came back excited about one of the seven surfaces. “This might work!” the agent wrote.
With just a few more steps, the group turned the approximation of the surface into an explicit equation and, ultimately, a family of polynomials with degree-23 (meaning the variable climbs to x23 and there are 23 roots to shuffle around). Here’s one whose symmetries form M23:
x23 – 184x21 – 1150x20 + 26151x19 + 18400x18 – 1808490x17 + 1545462x16 + 67672923x15 – 42732528x14 – 1333395744x13 + 290615166x12 + 10550424369x11 + 3700476348x10 + 35123826654x9 – 194398310718x8 – 1023887308293x7 + 3961650395556x6 + 1949980486716x5 – 28142323927002x4 + 53599151839311x3 – 46185312415788x2 + 19169943578802x – 3150159884154
The M23 solution is one small-but-mighty piece of an enormous puzzle. Mathematicians suspect there is a master group, the “absolute Galois group,” that describes the symmetries of all possible polynomials at once. Because groups and polynomials turn up everywhere in number theory, mapping this all-encompassing group is one of the field’s biggest ambitions. Each new group arising from a polynomial inches mathematicians closer to the absolute Galois group’s structure.
In an adjacent development, a crowdsourced competition—open to amateurs and professional mathematicians alike—launched with the goal of finding polynomials for every group acting on 24 roots; the largest such group is the symmetric group S24 containing all permutations. While M23 had been a mystery, examples of S24 mapping to polynomials were already plentiful, so the competition was more about constructing unknown, elegant solutions. Each such pattern illuminates a fragment of the absolute Galois group’s structure. The competition’s host, the Foundation for Science and AI Research (SAIR), was founded by top scientists, including Fields Medalist Terence Tao, an advocate for ethical AI use in math.
“If you just pick one [polynomial] arbitrarily,” says Jen Paulhus, a mathematician at Mount Holyoke College and one of the SAIR competition’s organizers, “its [Galois group is] likely going to be part of the big symmetric group. The interesting groups are the small, rigid ones, and random searches almost never land on them.”
Participants would need a strategy.
Submissions soon began pouring in from around the world, including everyone from career number theorists to hobbyists who may have had to look up what a Galois group was, with work powered by everything from AI to stubborn human brainpower. The first phase of the competition concluded in late August, with all 25,000 relationships between polynomials and symmetry groups realized. “I was a little surprised that we got all the groups that we were looking for in the first pass,” Paulhus says.
Emerging as the final winners were a pair of German mathematicians. And despite the pervasive use of AI as a tool throughout the competition, its only contribution to the winning team was to write an upload script. “It was open to AI, and it was still these folks who did the best,” Paulhus says. “As a working mathematician, that heartened me.”

UNGA 2026: What to know as world leaders gather in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:15:15 UTC
20:15:15 KST

Breadcrumb
UNGA 2026: What to know as world leaders gather in New York
Almost 130 heads of state and government are gathering in New York this week as the high-level general debate of the UN General Assembly gets underway.
The general debate is the centrepiece of the UNGA's annual High-level Week, giving world leaders a platform to set out their positions and priorities on major international issues.
The 81st session of the General Assembly formally opened on 8 September, with Bangladesh's Khalilur Rahman taking over as its president.
When is the general debate taking place?
The general debate opens at 0900 local time (1300 GMT) on Tuesday 22 September and runs through to Saturday 26 September. It will resume for a final day on Monday 28 September, with no session held on Sunday.
The debate is divided into two daily sessions, with the morning session running from 0900 to 1445 (1300 to 1845 GMT) and the afternoon session from 1500 to 2100 (1900 to 0100 GMT the following day).
Speakers are asked to observe a voluntary 15-minute limit, although statements frequently run longer and sessions continue until all scheduled speakers have delivered their addresses.
Who is speaking and when?
Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will open proceedings on Tuesday by presenting his annual report and is expected to deliver his final address to the general debate before leaving office at the end of the year.
He will be followed by General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman, who will formally open the debate.
The first two countries to speak will follow a long-running UN tradition. Brazil has opened the country statements since 1955, while the United States, as the host country, traditionally speaks second.
US President Donald Trump is expected to take the podium after Brazil on Tuesday morning.
Jordan's King Abdullah II, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani are also due to address the assembly during Tuesday's morning session.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa will open Wednesday's morning session, followed shortly afterwards by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Mohammed al-Menfi, chairman of Libya's Presidential Council, is also due to speak during the morning session.
The State of Palestine, the Holy See and the European Union are also invited to participate despite not being UN member states.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is expected to address the assembly by prerecorded video after the United States denied visas to Palestinian officials. UN member states voted to allow his remote participation.
What is on the agenda?
The 81st General Assembly is being held under the theme "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Alongside the general debate, High-level Week features a series of meetings on some of the major challenges facing the international community.
These include high-level events on climate action and a just transition and the 40th anniversary of the Declaration on the Right to Development on 23 September, sea-level rise on 24 September, pandemic prevention, preparedness and response on 25 September, and the 25th anniversary of the Durban Declaration against racism on 28 September.
A high-level meeting on the total elimination of nuclear weapons will follow on 29 September.
Many leaders' speeches are also expected to focus on the wars and conflicts across the Middle East and Ukraine, the global economy, artificial intelligence and the UN's growing funding pressures.
The week comes against a backdrop of mounting geopolitical divisions and growing pressure on the multilateral system, with the UN also facing questions over how to make the organisation more efficient and effective.
Who will replace Guterres as UN chief?
The race to succeed Guterres as the UN's next secretary-general is not expected to conclude this week.
While the General Assembly formally appoints the secretary-general, the 15-member Security Council must first agree on and recommend a candidate.
Seven candidates remain in the running, including former Senegalese president Macky Sall, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi and UN trade agency chief Rebeca Grynspan.
The other declared candidates are Guyana's UN ambassador and former foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Ecuadorian diplomat and former minister Ivonne Baki, former General Assembly president Maria Fernanda Espinosa of Ecuador and former Ugandan foreign minister and UN undersecretary-general Olara Otunnu.
Former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet withdrew from the race on Saturday.
Several Security Council members have said they want a woman to become UN secretary-general for the first time. Since the organisation was founded in 1945, all nine people to hold the post have been men.
Guterres's second and final term will end on 31 December.

Türkiye’s crackdown on LGBTI groups and activists is part of an escalating rights crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:13:55 UTC
20:13:55 KST

On 13 September, I woke in southwest Türkiye to news of a large-scale operation targeting LGBTI organizations and human rights defenders across the country. Since then, police have arrested at least 116 people across 15 provinces following raids on homes, venues and the offices of LGBTI rights organizations. At least 83 people have been placed in pretrial detention and criminal investigations have been launched against more than 160 people. LGBTI rights organisations have reported allegations of intrusive strip searches, insults and humiliation as well as HRDs being held in isolation in violation of their rights. Hundreds of social media accounts belonging to LGBTI organizations and activists, journalists, media outlets and others have so far been blocked or restricted alongside a number of websites. Those affected include Amnesty International Türkiye’s X account.
As protest within Türkiye builds and international condemnation mounts, it is clear that the Turkish authorities have every intention of intensifying the crackdown
Milena Buyum, Amnesty International
The authorities have named this operation “Ailem Güvende” (“My Family Is Safe”) under the spurious guise of ‘protecting the family’. Yet as LGBTI activists and many others rightly point out, families in Türkiye are suffering poverty, insecurity and increased repression of their civil and political rights, while violence against women and girls is rife, including inside their homes. Far from protecting anyone, this sweeping crackdown has nothing to do with protecting families and everything to do with further harming and stigmatizing people who have battled decades of discrimination and intimidation.
As protest within Türkiye builds and international condemnation mounts, it is clear that the Turkish authorities have every intention of intensifying the crackdown. The Ministry of Justice has sent a circular to 175 chief public prosecutors in all of Türkiye’s 81 provinces, regarding content and activities deemed in their view contrary to “public morality” and harmful to families, children and young people. It instructs prosecutors to promptly assess complaints and reports, take immediate investigative steps, preserve digital evidence and, where necessary, seek the removal or blocking of online content on the vague grounds of ‘obscenity’.
Police reportedly used pepper spray against peaceful protesters in İzmir and more than 100 people were reportedly detained when they peacefully gathered outside the İstanbul Courthouse in Çağlayan. With countrywide protests expected in the coming days and weeks, there are fears of more arrests to come.
The crackdown is part of a wider ongoing attack on the rights of LGBTI people and those who advocate for LGBTI rights. Pride marches including Istanbul Pride have been banned since 2015. In the last two years, proposals to introduce penalties to criminalize expressions of LGBTI identities or consensual same-sex sexual activity have been repeatedly leaked into the public domain. They were withdrawn after huge public uproar and resistance from civil society. While these government efforts to legislate failed, ‘My Family is Safe’ is a further attempt to exclude LGBTI people.
July marked the tenth anniversary of the failed coup attempt that ushered in state of emergency provisions which were in place for two years. These provisions morphed into a raft of repressive legislation targeting civil society, with the independence of the judiciary hollowed out, domestic courts weaponized, international courts ignored, and treaties and standards trampled on. Over the last decade, Türkiye has been subjected to an ongoing authoritarian bonfire of rights which has impacted every aspect of Turkish society, silencing dissent, stoking divisions, and spreading fear.
Whilst thousands of people in Türkiye have been impacted by baseless prosecutions and convictions, there have been several emblematic cases. Prisoner of conscience Osman Kavala, who remains in prison despite two binding European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) judgments (in 2019 and 2026) ordering his release and infringement proceedings against Türkiye initiated by the Council of Europe in 2022. Selahattin Demirtaş and Figen Yüksekdağ, former leaders of the People’s Democratic Party, also remain in prison despite ECtHR rulings ordering their immediate release. Taner Kılıç, Amnesty Turkey’s Honorary Chair, was tried alongside İdil Eser, the organization’s former Turkey director and nine other human rights defenders, known as the Istanbul 10, on baseless allegations of “membership of a terrorist organisation”. They were all eventually acquitted, with Taner Kılıç’s acquittal coming almost eight years after his imprisonment for over 14 months in 2017.
The rights to freedom of peaceful assembly, association and expression have come under sustained attack with arbitrary restrictions and blanket bans. Peaceful protesters have been subjected to police violence and allegedly tortured in police custody.
Women’s Day marches have also faced bans at a time when the rights of women and girls are facing serious erosion. In 2021, Türkiye withdrew from the Istanbul Convention, the landmark treaty on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence. In so doing, Türkiye not only became the first Council of Europe member to withdraw from an international human rights convention but removed key protections in a country where gender-based violence remains widespread.
It is time to stand together against the repression of LGBTI people in Türkiye
Milena Buyum, Amnesty International
Ten years after the failed coup attempt, the distance that Türkiye has travelled along the authoritarian path is starkly clear, but this trajectory is still reversable. The targeting of LGBTI communities must end immediately and Turkish authorities must ensure the immediate release of all those detained solely for their human rights work. LGBTI defenders and associations must be allowed to operate and carry out their vital work without discrimination, criminalization, intimidation or reprisals.
On Friday, people took to the streets in more than 50 cities around the world to demand an end to the crackdown. It is time to stand together against the repression of LGBTI people in Türkiye, to raise our voices and to make our solidarity even more visible. Leaders around the world must publicly condemn the crackdown, raise concerns with the highest level of the Turkish government, and provide support to LGBTI organisations and defenders. We must all demand a reversal in this deepening human rights crisis.
Milena Buyum is Senior Campaigner on Europe for Amnesty International

Why does Netanyahu's Likud fear Israeli expats voting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:11:41 UTC
20:11:41 KST

Breadcrumb
Why does Netanyahu's Likud fear Israeli expats voting in the upcoming election?
Ahead of every Israeli general election, the question of Israelis living abroad resurfaces. Some return to Israel to cast their ballots, while others choose not to make the journey.
But the upcoming Knesset election on 27 October has given the issue particular significance. It will be the first general election since 7 October 2023 and comes amid deep political polarisation in Israel and polls indicating a close contest between the coalition and opposition blocs.
Some estimates put the number of Israelis living abroad at around one million, with the largest proportion in the United States.
Israeli citizens eligible to vote generally cannot cast ballots from their countries of residence, with the exception of diplomats, official representatives and several thousand other eligible Israelis working at Israeli missions abroad.
So why has the prospect of Israelis returning from overseas to vote become such a contentious election issue?
What is Likud trying to stop?
The debate returned to the forefront after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party petitioned Israel's Central Elections Committee to block initiatives helping Israelis living abroad return to vote.
Likud, which raised similar objections in August, targeted the America–Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition and its FLY&AID project, as well as the Israeli Camp organisation and the Democrats party.
The party argues that the initiative amounts to an illegal electoral benefit and violates campaign finance laws, claiming it is intended to help Israelis abroad for political purposes and has links to elements of the Israeli left.
AID Coalition denies the allegations and has accused Likud of trying to prevent Israelis from exercising their right to vote. It says it operates independently of political parties and provides bureaucratic assistance rather than financial support, with voters covering their own travel costs.
The organisation says its services are open to all eligible Israelis regardless of how they intend to vote. More than 30,000 Israelis have registered with the initiative, while organisers have said they hope to help between 50,000 and 70,000 voters reach Israel.
Why could overseas voters matter?
The political significance lies in who these Israelis might vote for.
A review by The New Arab of several Israeli media outlets found that the political preferences of Israelis returning from abroad have varied between elections.
However, some Israeli assessments based on previous elections suggest that those living overseas, particularly in Europe and North America, who make the journey back specifically to vote have tended to favour centrist, left-wing or opposition parties.
Likud could view large-scale initiatives making it easier for these voters to return as potentially benefiting its political rivals.
Previous Israeli research and data have also indicated that many long-term Israeli residents abroad are concentrated in major North American cities, including New York, cities in California and Toronto, as well as London and Berlin in Europe.
These populations have been described as tending towards secular and liberal views and sharing socioeconomic characteristics with groups inside Israel that have historically voted in higher proportions for centrist and left-wing parties.
How many could actually return to vote?
The exact number remains unknown. A Haaretz report in July said thousands of Israelis living overseas were planning to travel to Israel shortly before the election, with estimates that tens of thousands could eventually return.
The newspaper cited assessments that an overwhelming majority of those voters could support parties that would not back Netanyahu.
People have also posted images on social media showing airline tickets they had bought, while entire charter aircraft were reportedly being hired to transport groups of voters.
AID Coalition estimates that between 800,000 and one million Israelis living abroad are eligible to vote. Its chairman has said around 35,000 people have registered with the initiative.
Could flights be restricted?
The controversy has also extended to whether the government could make it more difficult for overseas Israelis to return.
Transport Minister Miri Regev, a Likud member, has denied reports that her ministry was examining ways to restrict non-scheduled flights ahead of the election. She said Israel's skies would remain open and noted that right-wing voters were also planning to return to cast ballots.
The Association for Civil Rights in Israel has meanwhile warned against attempts to restrict voters' ability to return.
In July, it approached the Central Elections Committee, the transport minister and the attorney general, asking them to prevent any measures that could impede Israeli citizens from travelling to vote.
The organisation acted following reports that senior Transport Ministry officials were considering measures to prevent Israelis abroad from arriving on charter flights ahead of the election for what it described as illegitimate political reasons.
How many Israelis live abroad?
There is no definitive figure, as estimates vary depending on how long someone has lived abroad and how Israeli emigrants are defined.
A recent Tel Aviv University study found that 90,922 Israelis left the country for at least three consecutive months in 2025, broadly similar to the 91,499 recorded in 2024 and slightly above the 86,509 in 2023.
Data from Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics also indicate negative migration, meaning more Israelis have been leaving than returning.
The United States, Canada, Britain and Germany are among the main destinations. Several Israeli sources estimate that around half of Israeli emigrants live in the United States, rising to roughly 60% when Canada is included.
Research published by the UK-based Institute for Jewish Policy Research in 2025 estimated that, when Israeli emigrants and their children are counted together, around one million people of Israeli origin live abroad.
The institute estimated that around 630,000 Israelis lived outside the country between 2021 and 2023. This included 328,000 people born in Israel and around 302,000 born elsewhere who obtained Israeli citizenship and lived in Israel at some point.

West using fake news against Global South – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:11:18 UTC
20:11:18 KST

West training own public to swallow lies – Lavrov
Fake news has become a routine Western tool for undermining competitors, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said. He argued that Western media have conditioned their audiences to believe negative reporting about countries portrayed as adversaries.
Russia’s top diplomat made the remarks during the opening ceremony of an international forum in Moscow dedicated to combating fake news.
RT has collected the highlights from Lavrov’s speech.
West abuses new technology to ‘derail multipolar world’
Modern information technology allows “any piece of news, even unverified or obviously fake, to be disseminated to millions, if not billions of people,” Lavrov warned. Western officials exploit this environment to “derail the creation of a just multipolar world order,” he added.
According to Lavrov, fake news is part of a broader set of tools the West uses against nations of the Global South.
Western efforts to obfuscate and distort the truth reflect a broader trend: its fear to compete honestly in virtually every sphere of human activity.
Unilateral economic sanctions, tariffs, and accusations of “industrial overcapacity” are being used against China, Lavrov said. Meanwhile, diplomatic pressure and blackmail in international organizations serve to obscure the fact that “on many key issues of modern development the West would have been left in absolute minority, should the voting be conducted fairly.”
Russia became a target after rejecting ‘neocolonialist cooperation’
Lavrov said Western pressure against Russia intensified in the early 2000s, when the country “began to liberate itself from neocolonial forms of cooperation with our Western colleagues.” That shift prompted the West to pursue a policy of containing Russia, he argued.
The minister cited several cases in which serious accusations were leveled against Moscow while, according to Lavrov, Russian requests for supporting evidence were rejected. He focused in particular on the so-called “Bucha massacre” – alleged mass killings of civilians near Kiev in 2022 that Moscow maintains were a Western-backed fabrication.
Lavrov criticized UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres for lending credence to the accusations and urged the public to examine a recent Russian investigation. He said researchers used publicly available Ukrainian sources, including obituaries and government databases, to trace people whose names Kiev placed on a memorial to alleged Russian victims in Bucha.
According to Lavrov, the list includes “dozens of names” of Ukrainian military personnel, members of the Security Service of Ukraine, territorial defense forces, police, and the national guard.
“Over 70 names have no digital footprint whatsoever, which is nearly impossible in today’s world,” Lavrov said, adding that “these facts disprove the claim that hundreds of civilians were killed in Bucha.”
West has ‘trained’ its citizens to swallow lies about Russia
Lavrov said Western media have for years deliberately “trained their public to trust any, even the most crazy anti-Russian tropes and fantasies.” Western governments take advantage of the rapid modern news cycle to make such messaging effective, he argued.
The essence of Western media policy: cook up some fake news, blow it up to the scale of a cosmic disaster for a day or three, and shut down access to any alternative views.
Lavrov cited a recent drone incident at an airport in Leipzig, Germany, which Berlin blamed on Russia while moving to close Russian diplomatic venues, as an example of that approach.
The West also simply ignores inconvenient facts, Lavrov said, pointing to Ukraine’s deadly drone attack on a vocational college dormitory in Starobelsk in May.
The incident killed dozens of students but “prompted no condemnation from Western governments and international organizations controlled by the West, and unfortunately barely made a ripple in the Western media,” he said.

6-year-old girl sets Rubik's Cube speed record, Chinese state media say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:10:05 UTC
20:10:05 KST

6-year-old Chinese girl reportedly sets Rubik's Cube world record, completing puzzle in just over 4 seconds
A 6-year-old Chinese girl has set a new women's world record for solving a 3x3 Rubik's Cube in just over 4 seconds, state media reported Tuesday.
Young speedcuber Lian Yunzhi broke the women's 3x3 average world record twice in three days at two World Cube Association certified competitions in Wuhan and Guangzhou, according to state broadcaster CCTV on Monday.
She posted averages of 4.52 and 4.27 seconds after solving the Rubik's Cube five times.
Lian, who is from Chengdu, in China's southern Sichuan province, is "the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds," CCTV added.
A video CCTV posted showed the small girl wearing a red gingham bow on her head as she deftly turned and twisted a Rubik's Cube.
After solving the puzzle, she placed the cube on the table, clapped her hands and fist pumped the air.
Nicknamed "Zhizhi," Lian was first introduced to the Rubik's Cube after being enrolled into a class as a child — one of various extracurriculars alongside dance and music lessons, her mother Lin Yangxi told local media outlets, according to the AFP news agency.
Lin "gradually realized" that cubing was an "excellent activity for fostering a child's comprehensive abilities" and shifted her focus toward it, she told Chengdu's Red Star News.
Her daughter has now mastered over 1,300 Rubik's Cube solving algorithms, practicing daily for 2 to 3 hours, Lin said.
Photos from Red Star News showed Lian's trophies displayed on a shelf in her home.
"Solving a Rubik's Cube improves focus, memory, logical thinking, spatial awareness, and helps develop a healthy mindset toward winning and losing," Lin said.
"It's not just about blindly memorizing formulas, but using logical reasoning to find optimal solutions," she added.

Three in four Americans say AI firms not doing enough to prevent disaster, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Three in four Americans say AI firms not doing enough to prevent disaster, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
- Three-quarters of Americans worry AI companies are not doing enough to prevent serious harm from AI, with 73% prioritising safe and responsible development over global competition.
- 39% believe AI negatively impacts society, the highest since March, while 55% support slowing AI development for better oversight and safety.
- Concerns include AI's cybersecurity risks and potential existential threats, highlighted by experts quitting and calls for stronger federal regulation amid political delays.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Three-quarters of Americans, some 73 per cent, worry that AI companies have not gone far enough to prevent AI from causing serious harm to society, as concerns grow about where the technology may lead, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.
The four-day poll, which concluded on Sept 20, found that 39 per cent of respondents think that artificial intelligence is having a negative impact on society, up from 36 per cent in August and the highest share since Reuters/Ipsos began asking the question in March. Only 11 per cent said the new technology was a positive thing. The rest were not sure or did not answer the question.
The poll found many Americans lacked confidence in AI companies’ ability to regulate themselves, with most respondents saying federal officials should play a major role in setting safety standards.
While high-profile leaders ranging from US Senator Bernie Sanders – a progressive independent who caucuses with Democrats – to Steve Bannon – a close ally of US President Donald Trump – have called for federal action, little has come so far. Trump himself backs fast development of the technology and the Republican-led House of Representatives is on recess until November, leaving little chance for quick action.
The technology is upending how computer programmers work but it remains to be seen how much disruption it will cause in labour markets. The technology appears to pose significant risks to cybersecurity, with OpenAI revealing over the summer that its AI agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into another company’s systems without either company’s initial knowledge.
AI researchers quit over fears
Earlier in September, a researcher at Anthropic, another leading AI company, publicly quit his job over concerns that AI could be on a path to wipe out humanity. Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger echoed the warning, saying there was a more than 10 per cent chance of such an event within the next decade.
Most Americans – some 69 per cent of respondents – said they had followed the news that major AI companies were calling for a slowdown in AI development as well as greater oversight and safety standards.
Some 55 per cent of people in the Reuters/Ipsos poll said it would be a good thing to slow down AI development, compared with 13 per cent who said it would be a bad thing. The rest were not sure or did not answer the question.
Artificial intelligence burst onto the national stage in 2022 when OpenAI launched ChatGPT, a consumer-facing product that could answer user questions much as a human might and offered a new way to search the internet.
Supporters of the technology say AI has the potential to boost productivity, accelerate scientific discovery and transform industries ranging from healthcare to finance.
Heavy investment in the construction of data centres – vast collections of computers that power the technology – is boosting the economy but also creating enough noise to anger neighbours and put pressure on politicians ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Some 73 per cent of respondents in the poll said it was more important for the US to ensure AI is developed safely and responsibly, compared to 23 per cent who said it was more important for the US to stay ahead of the rest of the world on AI development.
The poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,277 US adults nationwide. Its results had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction. REUTERS

Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, whose country retains sovereignty over Greenland, had previously rejected Trump’s stated intention to gain control of the territory.
Trump has repeatedly argued that bringing Greenland under US control is necessary for national security. During his first presidential term, he proposed purchasing the island. In March 2025, he said he was confident that Greenland could ultimately become part of the United States and threatened Copenhagen with tariffs if Denmark refused.
Following a visit to Washington in January by Greenland’s Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt and Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen, a working group involving representatives of all three parties was established to discuss issues related to Greenland.

The human brain clears fluid directly into the skull, and poor sleep slows the process down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:21 UTC
20:00:21 KST

Brain fluid drains directly into the spongy marrow of the human skull, establishing a physical connection between the nervous system and the immune system. A recent imaging study reveals that this drainage process is slower in older individuals and those experiencing poor sleep or cognitive decline. The research was published in the journal eLife.
Historically, biologists thought the central nervous system was entirely isolated from the rest of the body. A specialized cellular boundary called the blood-brain barrier supposedly prevented immune cells and other substances from entering or leaving the brain. This isolation was thought to protect delicate neural tissue from damaging inflammation. Recent discoveries have challenged this view of the nervous system, revealing that the brain communicates directly with the surrounding bone.
Studies in mice and human tissue have identified tiny physical channels connecting the brain’s outer protective layers directly to the bone marrow inside the skull. The bone marrow is a spongy tissue inside bones that produces blood cells and immune cells. These microscopic channels allow cerebrospinal fluid to exit the brain and interact with the immune cells residing in the skull. Cerebrospinal fluid is the colorless liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord, acting as a waste removal system for the nervous system.
To better understand how this fluid moves in living humans, researchers at Zhejiang University in China organized an imaging study. The research team, led by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, and Min Lou, wanted to map exactly where and how fast the fluid travels into the skull. They also wanted to see if medical conditions, sleep quality, and memory might relate to how well this fluid system functions.
The researchers enrolled 87 patients who were already scheduled to receive a spinal tap for various neurological conditions. The medical team injected a contrast agent called gadolinium into the cerebrospinal fluid in the lower back of each patient. Gadolinium shows up brightly on magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, allowing researchers to track the fluid as it travels up the spine and into the head.
The patients underwent MRI scans before the injection and at three later time points. These follow-up scans occurred at 4.5 hours, 15 hours, and 39 hours after the initial injection. The research team focused their analysis on the bone marrow in three specific areas of the skull. They looked at the top of the head near a major vein called the superior sagittal sinus, the sides of the skull near the lateral fissure, and the base of the skull near the cisterna magna.
To measure the concentration of the contrast agent, the researchers compared the signal in the skull marrow against a reference point in the eyeball. The fluid inside the eye does not absorb the contrast agent, providing a stable baseline. By calculating the ratio between the skull signal and the eye signal, the team could track how much fluid had reached the bone marrow at each time point.
To evaluate health and lifestyle factors, the researchers also administered questionnaires to the participants. They used a standard survey to assess sleep quality over the previous month, looking at factors like sleep duration and nighttime disturbances. One month after the patients left the hospital, researchers evaluated their cognitive performance using a telephone-based test that measures attention, language, memory, and orientation.
The MRI scans showed the contrast agent moving from the cerebrospinal fluid directly into the skull bone marrow. The speed of this fluid movement varied depending on the anatomical region. Fluid reached the bone marrow at the top of the head the fastest. For a majority of the patients, the contrast agent peaked in this top region at the 4.5-hour mark.
Fluid movement into the bone marrow at the base of the skull was much slower. In half of the patients, the contrast agent did not peak in this lower region until 15 hours after the injection. The researchers hypothesize that fluid might travel through alternative pathways between the skull and the brain, speeding up delivery to the top of the head while bypassing other areas.
The researchers then analyzed what biological factors might influence the speed of fluid drainage near the top of the head. They found that older age, high blood pressure, and diabetes all correlated with slower fluid movement into the skull bone marrow. Female patients also showed slower drainage compared to male patients.
The drainage patterns were also linked to signs of systemic inflammation. Patients with slower fluid drainage had higher percentages of neutrophils, but lower percentages of monocytes and lymphocytes, in their blood. Neutrophils and monocytes are types of white blood cells that respond to infections and injuries. This suggests that higher levels of inflammation in the body might restrict the flow of cerebrospinal fluid into the skull marrow.
The patient questionnaires revealed a link between fluid drainage, sleep, and memory. Patients who reported worse sleep quality had slower drainage into the skull bone marrow at the top of the head. Slower drainage also correlated with lower scores on the cognitive telephone test.
Through statistical analysis, the researchers explored whether this drainage system might bridge the known gap between poor sleep and memory problems. Their calculations showed that the speed of fluid drainage accounted for roughly 38 percent of the statistical association between poor sleep and lower cognitive scores. The research team proposed that sleep disturbances might worsen inflammation, which in turn slows down fluid drainage and contributes to cognitive decline.
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot prove that slow fluid drainage causes cognitive decline or sleep problems. The statistical links only show that these variables change in tandem. Additionally, the patients in the study all had existing neurological conditions, such as peripheral neuropathy or encephalitis. Without a comparison group of healthy individuals, it remains unknown if these fluid dynamics operate the same way in the general public.
The methods used to measure sleep and cognition also present limitations. The researchers relied on self-reported questionnaires and telephone interviews rather than objective physiological measurements. A clinical sleep study measuring brain waves would provide a more accurate picture of how specific sleep stages relate to fluid movement.
The interpretation of the imaging timeline requires caution. The researchers classified the highest MRI signal at 4.5 hours as an indicator of drainage efficiency. This early time frame might just represent the fluid entering the bone marrow, while the later scans might better reflect the fluid actually washing out of the tissue. Future imaging studies with more frequent scanning intervals will be required to map the exact timeline of fluid entering and exiting the skull.
The study, “Skull Bone Marrow Drainage and Its Associations with Inflammation, Sleep Quality, and Cognitive Performance,” was authored by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, Xiao Zhu, Yifei Li, Ziyu Zhou, Xin Huang, Huihong Ke, Mengmeng Fang, Jianzhong Sun, and Min Lou.

McDonald's is hosting an investor day as its U.S. business struggles. Here are 4 things to expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

McDonald's is expected to share more details about its new strategy to win back diners at its investor day on Wednesday in Chicago.
The company unveiled its new global growth plan, called McDonald's > NEXT, in June at its biennial worldwide convention for franchisees. Pillars of the strategy include a new restaurant design, better-tasting food and drinks and consumer-led innovation. But executives have otherwise offered few details, holding back until Wednesday's event.
Nearly three years after McDonald's previous investor day, the presentation comes after McDonald's U.S. business disappointed in its most recent quarter. The chain's same-store sales increased just 0.8%, and traffic to its restaurants fell.
CEO Chris Kempczinski said that the problems were due to shortcomings in execution, like a mixed implementation of its value offerings, rather than issues with the chain's overall strategy. Skye Anderson, who was tapped as president of McDonald's U.S. business in the wake of the weak quarter, will likely speak on Wednesday.
Kempczinski, Anderson and the rest of the McDonald's executive team will have to win over investors, who are increasingly skeptical that the fast-food giant can win over diners in the near term.
Over the past 12 months, the stock has fallen 18%, dragging McDonald's market value down to about $175 billion. The S&P 500 has climbed 16% in the same period, as optimism about artificial intelligence has offset concerns about the financial health of consumers.
Loading chart...
Here's what McDonald's presentation is expected to cover:
1) Value strategy
Over the past two years, value has become all-important to restaurants, which are competing over a smaller pool of customers who care about both price and experience. While chains like Taco Bell and Chili's have thrived, McDonald's has struggled recently as its value offerings got lost among its other promotional messages.
Plus, its franchisees have pushed back against discounts, which grow sales but eat into operators' profits, especially as high beef prices raise expenses. Only about two-thirds of McDonald's U.S. franchisees implemented its recent "under $3 menu," executives said in August. For its part, McDonald's lets franchisees set their own prices, but the company assesses how operators' menu prices help deliver value.
Analysts expect that McDonald's will continue to emphasize value, and franchisees' cooperation will be key to its success.
"We expect MCD to use this event to make it clear to franchisees that adherence to pricing recommendations will be a key factor in evaluating agreement renewals," Citi Research analyst Jon Tower wrote in a note to clients with his investor day predictions.
Tower also cut his price target for the company to $310 per share from $345 a share, citing investor concerns about franchisees' buy-in for the company's overall strategy.
2) Menu updates
Besides value, McDonald's is also looking to attract diners through menu offerings with elevated taste and quality.
In recent years, McDonald's has shifted its menu to include more chicken options, as beef prices have risen and rivals like Chick-fil-A threaten its sales. At the franchisee convention, executives shared that the next evolution of its chicken offerings will be hand-breaded. Chick-fil-A, Raising Cane's and Popeyes all hand bread or batter their chicken rather than using a machine. The technique usually results in a crispier exterior, but it takes more time and labor.
In addition to chicken, McDonald's has also leaned into expanded beverage options recently. After winding down CosMc's, its drink-focused spinoff, McDonald's has rolled out a variety of beverage options in the U.S., including crafted sodas, refreshers and energy drinks. A handful of international markets, like Germany, have also been rolling out more drink offerings.
"What's important — we'll talk a lot more about this at investor day — is beverages," Chief Financial Officer Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call in August.
3) Restaurant remodels
Roughly every decade, McDonald's mandates that franchisees remodel their restaurants to fit new aesthetic guidelines and improve their technology and equipment.
And it looks like another round of restaurant renovations is coming as part of the growth strategy. At the convention, franchisees got the first look at the new restaurant design.
Typically, McDonald's chips in some support for franchisees who are remodeling their restaurants. While upgraded locations usually generate higher sales, operators have to fund the remodels at a time when borrowing costs are elevated. And thanks to tariffs and high energy prices, construction costs are increasing, too.
As a result of the remodel program, McDonald's capital expenditures could increase by $600 million to $900 million in 2027 and 2028 from its projected spending in 2026, according to a research note from BMO Capital Markets analyst Andrew Strelzik. But executives are expected to share the company's own projected costs for the remodel program at investor day.
4) Cost cuts
While McDonald's will likely spend more on capital expenditures over the next two years, the company will likely try to cut costs elsewhere.
McDonald's will share its outlook for general and administrative spending during investor day, Borden said in August.
McDonald's could target G&A spending to be less than 2% of its systemwide sales, down from its current goal of 2.2%, Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo wrote in a note to clients. In recent years, the company's workforce has shrunk as part of a reorganization effort.
Indirectly, McDonald's will also cut costs by refranchising some of its company-owned restaurants.
Selling locations to franchisees means that McDonald's will not be responsible for the operational costs or capital expenditures required to run a restaurant successfully. The company will also share more details about those plans at the investor day, according to Borden.

Everything You Know About Political Violence Is Probably Wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.
In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”
Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.
But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”
What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.
What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.
Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?
America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.
Although uncertainty remains at the margins, the evidence strongly suggests that since roughly 2016, political violence on both the right and the left has reached levels unseen in the United States since the upheavals of the 1960s. These patterns reflect not a single ideology but the deeper forces of violent populism: hardened identities, perceived existential threats, collapsing institutional trust, and elite rhetoric that frames politics as a struggle between enemies rather than fellow citizens.
Much of the public disagreement about whether political violence is rising and who is responsible for it stems not from ideology alone but from competing definitions about what should be counted.
In scholarly literature, political violence is generally defined as the use or credible threat of physical force for political ends. Those ends may include coercion, intimidation, punishment, or symbolic signaling intended to influence public behavior, political outcomes, or institutional authority. Under this definition fall assassination attempts, armed assaults on public officials, bombings, arson attacks, violent intimidation, riots against buildings with explicit political aims, and organized plots to use force against political targets.
Just as important are the exclusions. Political violence does not include ordinary criminal activity lacking political motivation, interpersonal violence driven by private disputes, or lawful protest—even when protests are disruptive, angry, or unlawful. Nor does it include harsh rhetoric alone, however inflammatory, unless it is paired with a credible threat of force. These boundaries matter, because collapsing political violence into crime or protest obscures its distinct causes and consequences.
The hardest problem is determining intent. Political violence is defined not only by what happens but by why it happens—and intent is often ambiguous. When a crowd burns a police precinct, is the act political rebellion, criminal opportunism, or both? When a gunman attacks a synagogue, is the motive ideological antisemitism, personal grievance, or mental illness layered atop political belief? When an individual sends a death threat to a lawmaker, is it expressive rage, partisan trolling, or preparation for real-world violence?
Reasonable scholars answer these questions differently, often using dissimilar evidentiary thresholds. Some datasets require explicit ideological statements; others infer political intent from targets, symbols, or timing. Some classify riots as political violence only when their organizers articulate political goals; others focus on behavior rather than rhetoric. None of these choices is neutral, and each shapes the resulting picture.
These definitional choices explain why prominent datasets sometimes appear to disagree. Federal law enforcement datasets emphasize lethality, capability, and threats to national institutions. Protest-oriented datasets capture frequency and geographic spread. Terrorism databases prioritize ideological framing and tactical similarity to global movements. Each captures something real—and each misses something important.
For this reason, no single dataset can settle the debate. Accordingly, my work triangulates across several sources, combining federal threat assessments, incident-level databases, congressional security data, and survey research. The goal is not to produce a definitive body count but to identify patterns that recur across independent measures: who is targeted, how violence is carried out, how lethal it is, and how those patterns have changed since 2016.
This approach does not eliminate uncertainty. But it does attempt to move beyond partisan narratives and toward a more accurate understanding of how political violence in America has evolved—and why arguments over its meaning have become almost as intense as the violence itself.
The most authoritative window into political violence in the United States comes not from media tallies or advocacy groups but from the federal agencies charged with tracking national security threats—above all, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Yet even here, readers encounter a fundamental problem: There is no single, formal US government definition of “political violence.” Instead, federal agencies operate with overlapping categories—domestic terrorism, domestic violent extremism, hate crimes, threats against officials, and antigovernment violence—each shaped by legal constraints, investigative mandates, and statutory language rather than a unified conceptual framework.
This definitional fragmentation matters. Unlike many countries, the United States does not criminalize “domestic terrorism” as a stand-alone offense; the relevant statute (18 U.S.C., § 2331) defines “international terrorism” and “domestic terrorism” descriptively but does not by itself create a prosecutable offense. As a result, the FBI does not report a simple annual count of domestic terrorism incidents. Instead, the statistics reflect investigations, disrupted plots, arrests, and threat assessments organized around ideological motivation, such as racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism, antigovernment or antiauthority extremism, and hostile acts against government structures. The absence of a single metric has fueled public confusion and partisan cherry-picking, with critics on all sides accusing the FBI of either exaggerating or minimizing particular threats.
Despite these constraints, a consistent picture emerges from FBI testimony, annual threat assessments, and congressional reporting since 2016. Across political administrations, FBI directors have warned that domestic violent extremism is a persistent and elevated threat, with particular emphasis on right-wing ideologies—especially white supremacist and ethno-nationalist violence—as the most lethal category among domestic violent threats. This assessment is grounded not in ideology per se but in outcomes: The majority of fatal attacks tied to political or ideological motives in recent years have originated in right-wing ecosystems, often carried out by lone actors inspired by online propaganda rather than formal organizations.
At the same time, federal reporting makes clear that political violence is not monopolized by the right. The FBI and DHS have also documented significant spikes in violence associated with mass protest movements, assaults on law enforcement, arson, and attacks on government facilities during periods of intense unrest—most notably in 2020, when protests following the killing of George Floyd were accompanied by substantial violent confrontations in many cities. These events are more commonly linked to left-wing or anti-authority contexts, tend to cluster geographically, and are far less likely to result in mass casualties. The distinction federal agencies draw is therefore not between “violent” and “nonviolent” sides but between forms of violence that differ in frequency, lethality, and strategic orientation.
A further frustration is temporal. Much of the FBI’s publicly accessible data lags behind current events. Detailed breakdowns often stop several years short of the present, while ongoing investigations limit transparency about more recent trends. As a result, scholars and policymakers must rely on testimony, qualitative assessments, and partial datasets to infer patterns after 2021—a gap that has widened in the wake of intensified threats against public officials and institutions. This delay has created a disconnect between the lived experience of escalating threats—particularly against elected officials—and the statistical record available to the public.
These limitations should not be mistaken for insignificance. On the contrary, the persistence of the same core warnings across multiple administrations, political contexts, and leadership teams suggests institutional continuity rather than partisan distortion. While the FBI cannot provide a clean annual count of “political violence,” its threat assessments provide something arguably more important: a comparative judgment about which forms of violence are most likely to kill, destabilize institutions, and undermine democratic governance.
When federal threat assessments are read alongside terrorism databases, incident-level coding, congressional security data, and survey research, the contours of political violence since 2016 come into focus—even if the exact numbers remain contested. The challenge is not the absence of evidence but the difficulty of integrating imperfect sources into an honest and comprehensive account.
Excerpted from Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism. Copyright © 2026 by Robert A. Pape. Used with permission of the publisher, The New Press. All rights reserved.

Top TV networks – including Fox – revolt in solidarity with media banned by Trump
