‘Revitalize UN authority’: China’s vice president to address General Assembly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:43:35 UTC
17:43:35 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
China’s Vice President Han Zheng will address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, Beijing announced Tuesday, saying he will stress revitalizing the authority of the world body.
Han will be in New York on Sept. 24-26 to attend the general debate of the General Assembly, China’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The General Assembly will hear the address from the Chinese representative on Saturday.
During his visit, 72-year-old Han will also attend the high-level dialogue on the 5th anniversary of the Global Development Initiative hosted by China, and meet with the UN secretary-general, the president of the 81st UN General Assembly, and leaders of relevant countries, the statement added.
The General Assembly is set to begin the high-level debate on Tuesday, ahead of a summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, who will fly to Washington on Wednesday for a three-day state visit.
The international situation is faced with “intertwined challenges and turbulence and confronted with mounting risks and challenges,” China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing.
He said the UN “serves as the core platform for global governance, and the General Debate provides a vital opportunity for countries to build political consensus and coordinate multilateral actions.”
“This year marks the 55th anniversary of the restoration of China's lawful seat in the UN,” he noted.
China was granted its seat in the UN on Oct. 25, 1971, when the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758.
Guo said that during the General Debate, Han will “present China's views and positions on the current international landscape, major international and regional issues, and the work of the UN.”
Han “will outline China's concrete actions to practice true multilateralism and promote world peace and development, and call on the world to revitalize the authority and role of the UN, build greater synergy for reforming and improving global governance, and work together in the right direction of building a community with a shared future for humanity,” Guo added.

Beijing slammed the threats on Tuesday, calling such measures "illegal".

The criticism comes on the eve of a summit between President Xi Jinping and his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
The United States and Iran have been at war since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic Republic's supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a broad offensive.
Tehran countered by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for energy transit, causing global oil prices to surge as the conflict spread in the Middle East.
The United States imposed sanctions this month on "all remaining Iranian airlines" that had yet to face such penalties.
The US Treasury Department also took aim at targets for supporting Iran's aviation sector, including firms based outside Iran.
"If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," Bessent said in the interview.
He had previously vowed the United States would declare "economic D-Day" on Iran and pledged to choke off Tehran financially.
Bessent's comments came a day after he met with Vice Premier He Lifeng for economic talks, laying the groundwork for the meeting between the two countries' leaders this week. (AFP)

Details

On Monday, more than $920 million in bearish bets were liquidated amid the price surge. The ongoing closing of short positions could trigger a squeeze as traders rush to buy back assets to close losing trades, creating additional upward pressure on prices. However, open interest continued to rise, indicating that new leveraged positions were entering the market even as shorts were being forced out.
A squeeze usually destroys open interest. This one did not, which means positions are immediately being replaced. Traders are chasing the move rather than reducing risk. That is why the next 5% in either direction will be faster than expected

Peace in southern Lebanon remains ‘elusive’: UN mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:42:47 UTC
17:42:47 KST

Wassim Samih Seifeddine and Lina Altawell
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said Tuesday that peace in southern Lebanon remains "elusive," stressing that permanently ending the conflict requires political will from the parties.
The remarks came in a statement marking the International Day of Peace, observed annually on Sept. 21, which UNIFIL commemorated Monday evening with a ceremony at its headquarters in the southern Lebanese town of Naqoura.
“Today, peace in south Lebanon remains elusive, but the hope for peace endures,” UNIFIL said, stressing that lasting peace requires “political commitments and solutions from the parties themselves.”
“Peacekeepers can help restore stability, avoid misunderstandings, and reduce the risk of escalation -- but they cannot replace the political will and decisions needed to end the conflict permanently,” it said.
"Peace is not something we address once a year; it is an enduring responsibility," UNIFIL Head of Mission and Force Commander Major General Diodato Abagnara said.
“We patrol, we keep channels of communication open with the parties to reduce the risk of misunderstanding and escalation. We work with the Lebanese Armed Forces as they assume greater responsibilities in the south,” Abagnara said.
He stressed that responsibility for reaching a political solution rests with the parties, while “UNIFIL will continue to do its part, keeping communication open, reducing the risk of escalation, and supporting diplomatic efforts.”
The full implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1701 "remains the objective and the basis for lasting peace and stability in south Lebanon," Abagnara added.
“Continued cooperation between the Lebanese Armed Forces and peacekeepers remains central to maintaining stability and supporting the extension of state authority in the south,” he added.
The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 in August 2006 following a 33-day war between the Israeli army and Hezbollah.
The resolution calls for a complete cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River in southern Lebanon to be free of weapons and armed personnel except those of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL.
 
Disrupted livelihoods
UNIFIL said the current conflict has forced thousands of people from their homes, with many remaining displaced.
“It has disrupted livelihoods, caused widespread damage to homes and infrastructure, and resulted in civilian deaths and injuries,” it added.
This year's International Day of Peace is the last UNIFIL will observe before its mandate expires at the end of 2026, following a UN Security Council decision in 2025 to end the mission.
The UN General Assembly established the International Day of Peace in 1981 to promote ceasefires, nonviolence, tolerance, justice and human rights.
Israeli attacks on Lebanon since March 2 have killed at least 4,386 people, injured 12,407 others and displaced more than 1 million, according to Lebanese authorities.
The attacks have continued despite the two countries signing a US-brokered framework agreement on June 26 providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of Hezbollah.
Israel occupies areas in southern Lebanon, some for decades and others since the 2023-2024 war, while Israeli forces have advanced more than 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) during the current offensive.

Historic Kawabata Bridge reopens between Taipei and New Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:40:14 UTC
17:40:14 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The historic Kawabata Bridge, built in 1937 and one of the few substantially preserved large bridges from the Japanese colonial period, reopened Monday as a pedestrian and bicycle route connecting Taipei and New Taipei.
The bridge crosses the Xindian River. Following the completion of the new Zhongzheng Bridge, the old structure was restored and repurposed to connect surrounding riverside parks and provide views of the river, per a press release.
New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) attended the evening reopening ceremony and walked across the restored bridge.
The project included structural reinforcement, restoration of the bridge’s steel beams, and improvements to the surrounding area. The bridge retains its distinctive double-column arched piers and steel-beam structure from the Japanese colonial period. Railings modeled on its original design were also installed.
Hou said the bridge represented the longstanding connection between Taipei and New Taipei and praised cooperation between the two municipalities in preserving it. He also credited Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), who served as deputy mayor in New Taipei, Kaohsiung, and Taipei, for his role in the project, per CNA.
Chiang said the restoration demonstrated the two cities’ commitment to preserving historic structures while giving them new functions. “Today we witnessed the rebirth of the Kawabata Bridge,” Chiang said, noting that the cities had worked together to preserve the historic piers, Japanese-era steel beams, and original-style railings.
New Taipei’s Public Works Department said the restoration team discovered extensive corrosion in parts of the old bridge’s steel beams. The project therefore included reinforcement and restoration of the original paintwork while retaining the historic structural elements.
The bridge was expanded in 1962 and again in 1972 as traffic increased. After the new Zhongzheng Bridge was completed, the historic structure was retained rather than demolished.

Türkiye set for rainy autumn despite above-normal temperatures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:39:58 UTC
17:39:58 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye is expected to experience a warmer-than-normal autumn but receive above-average rainfall across much of the country, according to a climate scientist, who said the outlook marks a departure from last year’s drier autumn.
Murat Türkeş, a member of the executive board of Boğaziçi University’s Center for Climate Change and Policy Research, said temperatures are likely to remain above seasonal averages in October, November and December, meaning Türkiye is expected to enter winter under warmer-than-normal conditions.
“Unlike last year, I expect this autumn to be rainy,” Türkeş said, forecasting above-normal precipitation across a large part of the country during the three-month period. He said rainfall in western and northwestern Türkiye is expected to remain around or below seasonal averages, while most other regions are likely to receive more precipitation than normal.
Türkeş attributed the outlook to the expected influence of frontal low-pressure systems originating from the North Atlantic and, at times, the Mediterranean over the northern Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, the Balkans and Türkiye.
However, he cautioned that higher temperatures could still intensify the effects of drought by increasing evaporation from ecosystems, soil and water resources and reducing soil moisture. Warmer conditions can also contribute to agricultural drought even when rainfall is adequate.
Türkeş noted that above-normal precipitation from last autumn through the summer had already eased hydrological and agricultural drought across much of Türkiye. Prolonged drought remains a concern in parts of the northwest, the Marmara and northern Aegean regions, as well as central parts of southeastern Türkiye.
Despite the expected rise in temperatures, he said rainfall could limit the severity of drought conditions during the coming season.

"For us, anyone who comes to Italy and wants to build their future here must learn our language, understand our culture, and respect our rules," she said to a standing ovation at the Gioventu Nazionale national festival in Rome. "It is the only serious way to welcome them."

Meloni, who has political roots in the far-right, has consistently been hawkish on migration. But she has evolved politically over her tenure as prime minister, shifting from a nationalist outlier to an establishment figure among European Union politicians.

Earlier this month, Meloni’s conservative administration became Italy’s longest-serving uninterrupted government since World War II.

The end of humanity? What would happen if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:32:08 UTC
17:32:08 KST

The end of humanity? What would happen if the Yellowstone supervolcano erupted now
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- A Yellowstone super-eruption would begin not with a sudden surprise, but with weeks of increasingly alarming warning signs such as migrating earthquake swarms, rapid ground uplift, changing geysers, and rising volcanic gases. In a worst-case scenario, those signals could culminate in a VEI 8 eruption that blasts ash tens of kilometers into the atmosphere, unleashes deadly pyroclastic flows, buries parts of the western United States in ash, and cripples transportation, electricity, water systems, agriculture, and communications across much of North America.
- Share:
Around 631,000 years ago — a geological blink of an eye — catastrophe unfolded in what is now north-western Wyoming, US. During what is thought to have been a series of immense volcanic eruptions, life within hundreds of kilometers of the blasts was shattered. Ash was dispersed across much of North America and the effects were felt worldwide. This was a super-eruption of the massive volcanic system located in what is now the Yellowstone National Park.
Despite the scale, no known human witnessed the cataclysm. As far as we know, early humans had not yet reached the continent. Across oceans, perhaps early humans did wonder at the hazier skies and unusually vivid sunsets. Volcanic particles circulating in the sky cooled their climate and likely affected their weather patterns and lives. Whether they noted these changes – or connected them to any distant event – is unknowable.
Today, humanity would certainly notice. We already know that a super-eruption on this scale would be a threat civilization as we know it. So what exactly would we experience if Yellowstone erupted? We are experts in disasters and volcanoes and what follows is a thought experiment into what might happen in the worst case scenario. We’ve based our hypothesis on research and by examining how countries have dealt with disasters in recent years.
T-2 months
Shortly after 6am, an analyst at the University of Utah Seismograph Stations sees a series of sharp spikes interrupting the usually quiet wavy lines recorded by Yellowstone’s earthquake monitors. The measurements represent earthquakes detected beneath Yellowstone overnight. The scientist raises an eyebrow and takes a deep breath – these observations don’t fit with Yellowstone’s usual behavior.
People often imagine Yellowstone as a sleeping “supervolcano.” It may sleep, but its geological processes never do. An array of instruments monitors its activity – and any changes in it. A dense network of seismometers records earthquakes in the region. Around the clock, data feeds in from GPS stations, strainmeters (instruments which measure deformations and changes in the shape of the Earth’s crust) and sensors positioned within its active geyser areas. Satellite observations, gas sampling and field surveys add plenty more information.
Scientists look at the number of earthquakes along with their location, depth and size. Earthquake “swarms” warrant particular attention, especially when they appear to be migrating through the crust (Earth’s solid, outermost rocky shell) or becoming progressively shallower. Such patterns can indicate that magma or pressurized hydrothermal fluids (hot, mineral-rich water) is moving upwards.
Our scientist is relieved to discover that most of the unusual tremors are tiny — too weak to have been felt. But together, they form an unusually concentrated swarm. The analyst checks the signals against neighboring seismometers and, more out of curiosity than concern, contacts colleagues at several partner organizations comprising the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory (YVO) in order to follow YVO’s response plan.
They deduce that, overnight, instruments have recorded a tightening cluster of earthquakes beneath Yellowstone’s vast caldera, which is roughly 55–70 kilometers across. Yellowstone experiences thousands of earthquakes each year, and swarms are not unusual. But this one appears to be migrating ever so slightly upwards. Still, an earthquake swarm by itself doesn’t mean Yellowstone is preparing to erupt, nor does ground deformation, changing temperatures or gas emissions. Scientists are more concerned about several such changes happening together.
The team of scientists decides to wait and see what happens next.
T−1 month
Four weeks later, the swarm has continued to migrate upwards. New events are also appearing along a narrow zone beneath the caldera, notes the analyst, who has now lost their appetite for both food and caution and is writing reports designed to be alarming. GPS stations above the swarm have begun moving apart. Measurements of strain have increased and satellite radar reveals the cause: there’s a broad area of accelerating uplift of the ground.
Together, the observations are consistent with magma forcing its way into the crust – as seen in places like Hawai'i prior to eruptions. Reassuringly for YVO staff, Yellowstone has produced similarly alarming combinations of signals before with no subsequent eruptions. Between 2013 and 2014, parts of the caldera began rising at rates of more than 15 centimeters a year and earthquake activity increased.
This culminated in a magnitude 4.8 earthquake, the largest recorded at Yellowstone since 1975. Shortly after, the uplift changed to subsidence (the ground moving downward) and scientists concluded that the episode was associated with hydrothermal fluid movements rather than magma.
Mindful of the need to keep the public informed without causing unnecessary alarm, YVO responds cautiously. A duty scientist assumes responsibility for assessing the incoming data. Additional, temporary seismometers and GPS units are deployed to provide more precise data, and gas and water are sampled more frequently.
YVO begins closer coordination with the National Park Service and emergency management authorities, reviewing road closures, public communications and evacuation plans. Perhaps ominously, but to err on the side of caution, Yellowstone’s Volcano Alert Level is raised from “normal” to “advisory,” indicating that unrest is above its established background level.
These developments are worrisome enough that scientists start speculating about a major eruption’s impacts. The media take an interest, but the volcanologists have learned how damaging it can be when volcanic uncertainties morph into a full-blown dispute, played out in public.
Scientists privately discuss differences in interpretations, agreeing on regular updates for the public via media briefings and social media postings. As the volcano’s activity continues to ramp up, high-level decision-makers are alerted that this situation could become a major catastrophe. The probability of it happening within three months increases from 6-9% to 21-27%.
Due to the uncertainties, the politicians make no specific declaration. The US’s Federal Emergency Management Agency nevertheless starts drawing up plans for a large-scale evacuation. They express confidence in public while perhaps fearing in private that a worst-case scenario could make it hopeless to try to save everyone.
Over the following fortnight, the unrest escalates dramatically. Earthquakes become more frequent and shallower. Long-period seismicity (much gentler earthquakes, usually caused by fluid movement rather than faults shifting and known to occur at Yellowstone) and sustained volcanic tremors suggest magma and pressurized fluids are forcing open fractures in the ground.
The uplift accelerates and GPS stations move centimeters in days. Geyser activity becomes increasingly erratic. Even the Old Faithful geyser becomes less faithful: its usually regular eruptions become harder to predict. Meanwhile, gas measurements and changes in spring water chemistry indicate an increased input of carbon dioxide and sulfurous gases into Yellowstone’s hydrothermal system. Taken together with the shallow earthquakes and rapid uplift, the concern is that magma may be moving upwards.
T-2 weeks: ‘It’s gonna blow!’
These new observations lead to a press conference describing an 85-92% probability of a cataclysmic eruption within three weeks. At this point, the YVO raises Yellowstone warning to “watch,” and the USGS raises the Aviation Color Code to orange, with aircraft rerouted around the region.
An evacuation zone extending 100 kilometers beyond Yellowstone National Park is announced, affecting roughly 200,000 residents, as well as thousands of visitors in the region. The topic now dominates both traditional and social media. The attention likely spawns detractors as well as conspiracists. The former claim that nothing will happen. The latter spread the disinformation that YVO is being paid by foreign shadow billionaires to bring down the US so that other countries can control the world’s economy.
Now that a super-eruption appears imminent with high confidence, world leaders swing into action. They must make a choice: help each other as a global village or repeat COVID-19 style global shuttering.
If they choose collaboration, then they start evacuations, moving people as far as needed – including across international borders. This would involve supporting them with adequate homes, water, food, electricity and community through schools, jobs, transport and safety. Achieving all this seems unlikely, since most of the world’s population has always lacked it. Nonetheless, the US has the money, skills and goods to evacuate and resettle the huge numbers, if leaders cooperate and use everything available.
More likely, many countries could be reticent to accept “volcano refugees,” making excuses – perhaps legitimate ones – that they don’t have the money, resources or space to safely settle so many people so swiftly. They are further stretched by those who self-evacuate through having more than one passport, along with the wealth or the social network to start afresh.
Charities step in to help some people leave on chartered planes, as well as via long, excruciating journeys on overcrowded trains and buses. The most marginalized and poorest may have no option but to stay behind. Some might join the minorities who do not believe the eruption will happen, who think their well-stocked underground bunkers will protect them (an overly optimistic belief), or who would rather die at home than live in a foreign land with a devastated world.
T=0
In an instant, seismic instruments are overwhelmed by an intense burst of shallow earthquakes. Expanding clouds of steam rise from newly opened cracks. The YVO and USGS have no choice but to raise the warning level and Aviation Color Codes to red: a dangerous eruption is imminent.
The eruption does not begin with the entire caldera exploding at once. Instead, rising magma intrudes into Yellowstone’s shallow hydrothermal system, rapidly vaporising immense volumes of water. At atmospheric pressure, water can expand in volume around 1,700 times when converted to steam. Trapped beneath the surface, this rapid expansion triggers violent so-called phreatomagmatic explosions that send superheated steam, mud and shattered blocks of rock kilometers into the air.
There are no human casualties yet, thanks to the wide exclusion zones on land and in the air. Wildlife, livestock and vegetation are not as fortunate. Within roughly 4–6 kilometers of the initial eruption sites, the landscape is battered by falling rock, ash and mud. Beyond the exclusion zone, people watch an impressive two kilometer-high plume rise into the sky – but it rapidly grows larger, and any sense of relief is short-lived.
A few hours later, gas-rich magma, 650-800°C in temperature – well above the melting points of lead and zinc – breaks through the fractured surface. As the confining pressure falls, dissolved gases separate into distinct components from the melt and expand violently. The magma fragments into pumice (porous rock) and ash while tearing away huge fragments of the surrounding rock from the walls of the erupting vent.
Expanding gases and intense heat drive this material upwards, creating a vast eruption column rising 30–50 kilometers into the atmosphere – far above commercial passenger aircraft, which usually cruise at up to about 13 kilometers. On this clear morning, its upper reaches are visible from Denver, some 800 kilometers away.
As the eruption continues and the volume of material expelled mounts, scientists realize it might be the opening stages of a VEI 8 super-eruption (magnitude 8 or greater) – the highest formal notch on a scale used to measure the size of explosive volcanic eruptions. It was 74,000 years ago that humanity last witnessed this scale of eruption with Toba in Indonesia.
The immense umbrella cloud that forms does not behave like a normal ash plume that simply drifts with the prevailing wind. Its momentum initially drives ash outwards in every direction – spreading hundreds of kilometers before high-altitude winds take over and carry fine ash thousands of kilometers downwind within a day.
After a few hours of continuous eruption, parts of the column collapse, generating scorching pyroclastic density currents (extremely hot, fast-moving mixtures of gas, ash and rock fragments). These surge for tens of kilometers, splintering trees, igniting forests and burying the remnants beneath hot ash and pumice.
Anyone within this zone is pulverized by the blasts, crisped by the heat, or asphyxiated by the ash. There may be up to 1,000 immediate human deaths, including people who refused to move. It is too dangerous to recover most bodies. And even if it were possible, many bodies no longer exist to be recovered.
Outside the main pyroclastic density current zone, casualties mount from vehicle crashes as drivers lose visibility or skid due to ash, from heart and breathing difficulties and from suicide. Vegetation fires spreading beyond the immediate burn zone add perhaps hundreds of fatalities from burning, smoke inhalation and vehicle crashes.
As the magma continues to escape, sections of the unsupported ground subside, opening new fractures and vents while feeding further eruptive columns and pyroclastic density currents. Hundreds of kilometers away – in Denver and along the Canadian border – heavy ashfall darkens the sky, obstructs roads and disrupts power, water supplies and communications. This ash devastates farmland across at least eight states.
Further immediate deaths could result from loss of power disrupting traffic and street lights; curtailing health services including surgery and obtaining prescriptions; and electrocution, fire and carbon monoxide poisoning from trying to set up and operate home electricity generators. Looting and increasing crime during disasters is typically rare, but it could happen in a more desperate worst-case scenario, adding to the casualty toll.
Over the coming days, the eruption continues in pulses as sections of the caldera collapse and new vents open. Successive column collapses generate pyroclastic density currents with the resulting deposits reaching several hundred meters in thickness, as they did in the last super-eruption.
Nearby infrastructure is shattered and entombed beneath the deposits. Airports close because ash interferes with aircraft and other transport networks falter. Communities across all states bordering Wyoming face darkness, breathing difficulties and roofs collapsing under accumulated ash. As the eruption eventually begins to weaken, sulphur dioxide high in the atmosphere forms sunlight-reflecting sulfate aerosols that spread around the northern hemisphere to influence the world’s climate for several years.
T+3 days
Three days into the eruption, much of North America is living in the shadow of Yellowstone. Each successive powerful eruptive pulse sends another column tens of kilometers upwards, from where it spreads into a new umbrella cloud.
Within Wyoming and neighboring states, conditions are catastrophic. Billings, Montana, the nearest large city, is disappearing beneath what will eventually exceed a meter of ash (one published model of a Yellowstone supereruption predicts the city as receiving up to 1.8 meters of ash). Salt Lake City, Utah, and Boise, Idaho, receive tens of centimeters. For southern Canada, much of the US and northern Mexico, day becomes twilight and breathing outdoors without masks becomes increasingly difficult. People on other continents watch in trepidation under vivid, red-orange sunrises and sunsets.
Back in the US, electricity networks begin failing. Warnings had not been heeded that damp ash conducts electricity, short circuiting power lines and substations. Ash clogs machinery and generator intakes. Its weight damages cables and weaker structures.
As electricity fails, so do water pumps, sewage treatment, heating systems, fuel stations and mobile phone and internet networks. People are scared and supermarket shelves empty nationwide as regional and national supply chains begin to break down.
T+2 weeks
Over the following weeks, the crisis becomes one of survival. Repeated ashfall blocks roads, overwhelms drainage systems and damages roofs. During rain, dry ash turns into a dense slurry that makes clearance work harder. Airports remain closed or severely disrupted across much of North America, while railways, freight depots and farms struggle to operate. Livestock and crops die where pasture and water supplies are buried or contaminated by ash.
Large areas close to Yellowstone remain evacuated, while across the US, shelter, fuel, food and clean water become increasingly scarce. Some countries airlift or airdrop humanitarian relief supplies, but are also concerned about stockpiling for themselves. Losses to agriculture, transport and insurance – with many other businesses and services closed – could lead Canada, Mexico and most Caribbean and Central American countries to declare states of emergency. This is partly due to direct impacts on those countries and partly due disruption across the USA and people fleeing from it.
T+4 months
Several months later, eruptions have weakened to intermittent explosions, but the threat of renewed activity remains. For millions, the disaster is far from over. Dry, windy days lift ash back into the air, while rain and snow turn it into a heavy deposit blocking drains and damaging infrastructure. Eye and throat irritation are widespread. People with asthma and other respiratory conditions face serious health risks under reduced and overworked health services.
Water treatment and power plants struggle with ash contamination, equipment failures, lack of spare parts and overwhelming demand, disrupting essential medical and industrial processes. Crops across the most heavily affected regions have been buried. The loss of American and Canadian grain, maize and soya exports drives global food prices upwards.
Flights gradually resume in less affected areas, but airports across North America repeatedly close whenever winds remobilize the ash. The unreliable airspace and transport networks – coupled with agricultural losses, business disruption and reconstruction costs – trigger banking and insurance crises, producing a global recession.
Meanwhile, the atmospheric effects become global. Most volcanic ash has fallen out, but sulfur dioxide injected into the stratosphere produces sulfate aerosols which reflect a significant proportion of the Sun’s energy. Scientists call it a “volcanic cooling episode,” avoiding the term “a new ice age”. Modeling suggests it’s unlikely to cool the global average by more than about 1.5°C, although particular regions and seasons could experience much larger changes. Notably, central North America remains far cooler than before the eruption.
T+10 years
In the years following the eruption, the world moves into long-term recovery and rebuilding. People across the world adapt to a more agrarian lifestyle, learning to fill the land with root vegetables, grains and legumes. With far less leisure time and diminished income, recreational facilities are turned over to food production, notably small-scale greenhouses and vertical farming for producing varied fruits, vegetables, nuts and legumes.
Livestock decreases due to lack of land and feed, opening up more space for crops. People still eating meat typically either hunt big game or trap smaller birds and mammals. Insect farming tends to dominate the re-establishment of bird or mammal farms. People living near coasts, rivers and lakes ramp up fishing, depleting stocks rapidly until controls are enacted in some locations, along with increased farming for seaweed. Where rules are not agreed or enforced, starvation and migration are rampant.
Freshwater availability varies. The world’s climate has changed, providing ample rainfall in some places while drying out others. Large-scale water treatment technology remains known and used, but supply lines for chemicals and spare parts are unreliable. Many people develop local approaches and manage while others suffer contaminated water and disease, including cholera, dengue fever and malaria, just as billions did before the eruption.
Before the eruption, around 4.4 billion people from the world’s population of 8.3 billion lacked full, safe freshwater access. A decade after the eruption, it’s possible that 4.8 billion people lack such freshwater, while the world’s population may have declined to 7.9 billion due to spikes in elderly and infant mortality.
For the eruption’s survivors, disease and death are still rising. The eruption may well provide substantive, long-term evidence for the carcinogenic level of silica in the ash. A small but statistically significant increase in diagnoses of both silicosis (an irreversible lung disease) and lung cancer appears from exposure to ash, with similar results for cardiovascular disease in people breathing in ash particles.
Rates are likely higher than measured, because health systems across a continent were knocked out by the eruption and struggling to recover ten years later. The worst part is that the lack of health systems means that many who are diagnosed cannot be treated properly. Survivable diagnoses become lethal.
Inside the eruption zone, two decades follow of a grey landscape. It appears almost lifeless, with the ash transformed into raging mudflows called lahars in every storm. But vegetation, starting with grasslands and shifting to forests, creeps back into the swathes wiped out in the explosion and people follow. These new pioneers coax the landscape into fertile framing, helping to feed hungry populations.
The dispersed ash eventually settles out of the atmosphere, permitting the Sun’s rays to shine fully on the surface again – reviving agriculture and ecosystems. It also revives fears of human-caused climate change, despite the volcano-induced reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. Scientists work hard to determine whether the global climate has been knocked onto a new trajectory – which might be better or worse for human beings – or whether the heat stored in the atmosphere and oceans from humanity’s greenhouse gas burning will once again force a rapidly heating globe.
Additionally, scientists want to calculate deaths, injuries and loss to quality of life. Excess mortality analyses could suggest 0.7-1.3 billion premature deaths due to the eruption and its impacts. Perhaps double that number experienced temporary or permanent health effects but survived, although some will say that 100% of humanity was directly affected.
The good news, at least for our species, is that this unstoppable power of volcanism changed the planet, but did not end humanity – or come close to doing so.
T+1 million years
A creature descends to Earth from a sleek spacecraft, still humanoid but far removed from its ancestor species Homo sapiens sapiens. Tjjze (the pronoun used) has absorbed all the scant information available about ancient “Earth” and is curious to learn more.
The most notable material is the rise of its first technological civilization just over a million years ago. This was followed by the species abandoning the planet as it changed 140,000-160,000 years ago – becoming taller, sleeker, with longer limbs, and with larger hands, heads and brains – having already established itself around the galaxy. In the remaining lore, myths recur of episodes of runaway planetary temperature changes, hot and cold, as well as a series of volcanic blasts that changed the globe.
Tjjze observes that the vegetation is lush and the H2O is plentiful, providing ample food and water for the bizarre animals and ecosystems. A rapid scan reveals much below the surface. In fact, a large roughly ellipse-shaped ridge made of rock appears prominently underneath the top layers. Yes, this particular region, about 24.3 cqurzots in radius, is definitely lower than the vast plains outside the depression. This seems to indicate an ancient volcanic eruption. And to leave a scar this big, it must have been gigantic.
Tjjze warps the equivalent of the face into the equivalent of a frown as more data are revealed. Indeed, this definitely looks like a caldera. And the age is coming in at around a million years (plus/minus).
Could it have erupted during the time of the technological civilization? Or were they lucky to have just missed it? It is impossible to really know.

South African firm unveils V-Raven unmanned aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:30:15 UTC
17:30:15 KST

- Paramount unveiled V-Raven, a reusable vertical-takeoff drone, at the Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition in South Africa on Sept. 19.
- The petrol-powered version can fly up to eight hours and 1,200 km, while a planned armed variant will carry precision-guided glide munitions.
South African defense company Paramount unveiled a new reusable drone called V-Raven at the Africa Aerospace and Defence exhibition in South Africa on Sept. 19, replacing an earlier catapult-launched design with an aircraft that takes off and lands vertically without a runway.
V-Raven grew out of Paramount’s earlier N-Raven program, a swarming drone the company first showed in 2021. That version launched from a catapult and weighed 41 kg, cruised at about 180 km/h and could fly for roughly two hours. V-Raven drops the catapult in favor of vertical takeoff and landing, which Paramount says lets forces launch and recover the aircraft from remote locations without fixed infrastructure.
“The V-Raven has been developed for the realities of the modern African battlefield,” said Sello Ntshiele of Paramount. “Vast operating areas, remote terrain, dispersed threats and the increasing use of drones mean that forces need to be able to see further and stay on station longer. V-Raven brings those capabilities together in a highly flexible, reusable unmanned system.”
The drone comes in two power configurations. The petrol-powered version can fly for up to eight hours, cover a range of up to 1,200 km and cruise at about 140 km/h, with a communications range of up to 150 km from its ground station. An electric version trades range and endurance for a smaller footprint, flying for up to two hours over a maximum range of 250 km. Both share the same airframe: a 3.6-meter wingspan, a 2.1-meter fuselage and a maximum takeoff weight of 65 kg.
Unlike a one-way loitering munition, V-Raven is built to fly a mission and land for reuse. The base ISR version carries an electro-optical sensor for day and night surveillance, with automatic target tracking and support for interchangeable electro-optical and infrared sensors. Paramount is also developing a second configuration that adds precision-guided glide munitions for strikes on selected targets; DefenceWeb reported the weapon under development is Paramount’s LongClaw glide bomb. That armed version will go through further systems integration, ground testing and flight trials before it is ready to field.
“What we are unveiling at AAD is the next stage of the V-Raven journey,” Ntshiele said. “It is a common aircraft architecture that can evolve as operational requirements develop. The immediate focus is a highly capable ISR platform, while the family architecture provides a pathway towards additional mission configurations, including light attack.”
Paramount pointed to security challenges in the Sahel and northern Mozambique as examples of the kind of terrain V-Raven is meant to cover, where forces often lack conventional airfields to operate from. AAD 2026 drew 287 companies and 33 countries to Waterkloof Air Force Base near Pretoria, South Africa’s defense minister, Angelina Motshekga, said at the show’s opening.

Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts

Hong Kong lacks a climate narrative to unify its efforts
Hong Kong does not mention ‘climate change’ in its five-year plan, yet it already has many ingredients of climate leadership
Hong Kong deserves credit for its first five-year plan, accompanied by a detailed policy address. The plan establishes a useful framework beyond the annual policy cycle. Precisely because this is an important first effort, it is worth asking what could make the framework even stronger.
One striking omission is that the five-year plan never explicitly mentions climate change. This does not mean Hong Kong is failing to act.
Consider the binding indicators. They include the long-standing reduction in carbon emissions per unit of gross domestic product and increasing the proportion of zero-carbon energy in electricity generation. The plan also addresses cleaner power, electric vehicles, green maritime fuels, sustainable aviation fuel, energy efficiency, hydrogen, waste reduction and carbon trading.

Israeli sentenced to 55 months in prison for spying for Iran, photographing Gallant's house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:29:49 UTC
17:29:49 KST

An Israeli citizen was convicted of contact with an Iranian foreign agent on Tuesday, with the tasks he carried out including hiding phones in Haifa and Kiryat Haim and photographing streets near the home of former defense minister Yoav Gallant.
The Haifa District Court sentenced Fares Abu al-Hija, 32, of Kaukab Abu al-Hija, to 55 months in prison after he was convicted as part of a plea agreement, which did not include an agreement regarding sentencing, for contact with a foreign agent.
According to the amended indictment, to which he confessed, Hija carried out a series of tasks for an individual identified by the Shin Bet (Israeli Security Agency) as an Iranian intelligence operative, including photographing streets near Gallant's home.
According to the indictment, between October 2025 and January 2026, Hija was in contact via Telegram with a person who called himself "Martin," and carried out a series of tasks for him in exchange for payments transferred through the Binance app.
During his interrogation, it emerged that Hija had begun to suspect that the individual was connected to Iranian intelligence. The Shin Bet identified the person he had been in contact with as an Iranian intelligence operative.
Hija hid cell phones, delivered cryptocurrency account information
As part of the assignments, Hija purchased cellphones and a charger and hid them at several locations in Haifa and Kiryat Haim. He activated the devices, installed communications applications on them, documented the locations where they had been hidden, and sent the documentation to his handler.
He was later asked to deliver an envelope containing an access code to a cryptocurrency account to a location in Zichron Yaakov, and to photograph a cafe in Tel Aviv.
In January 2026, Hija was asked to travel to the community of Amikam and photograph streets near Gallant's home. He took the photographs and sent them to his handler, after which he was arrested in an operation by the Shin Bet and the Menashe District Central Unit of the Israel Police's Coastal District.
Judge weighs Hija's confession, life circumstances over deterrence
In his sentencing decision, Judge Avi Levy noted that Hija's confession, acceptance of responsibility, expression of remorse, and the judicial time saved weighed in his favor. The court also took into account his family circumstances, including his father's serious medical condition and the impact of his arrest on his family.
At the same time, the court emphasized the severity of the offenses and the need for deterrence. The judge said the court must take into account "in light of the defendant's dangerous conduct," and added that general deterrence should be included among the considerations determining the sentencing range, given the growing prevalence of the phenomenon.
The court ultimately sentenced Abu al-Hija to 55 months in prison, with time already served in detention deducted from the sentence, as well as a 24-month suspended sentence for three years and a NIS 10,000 fine.

Defense officials push to expand Israel's submarine fleet as Turkey continues naval buildup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:29:13 UTC
17:29:13 KST

Israel will hold a ceremony on Thursday displaying the final of six submarines manufactured by Germany as part of a deal signed a considerable time ago.
On September 1, the IDF and the Defense Ministry announced that this final submarine, the “Dragon,” had left Germany on its way to Israel.
Israeli Navy chief V.-Adm. Eyal Harel and German Naval chief Jan Christian Kaack, as well as other top Israeli and German officials, attended a send-off ceremony for the submarine on September 1, and top Israeli officials are expected at Thursday’s ceremony.
In February, Elbit Systems put out a strikingly vague statement about the beginning of joint work in Israel with the German maritime vessel manufacturing giant TKMS (the successor company to an expanded ThyssenKrupp and producer of this submarine) to produce “structural components” for future submarines.
As part of the cooperation, Elbit said at the time that it would establish a new manufacturing facility for underwater Glass Reinforced Polyester (GRP) components for submarines.
Elbit: Cooperation will expand manufacturing capabilities
Yoram Shmuely, general manager of the Aerospace Division at Elbit Systems, said, “This cooperation will expand local manufacturing capabilities and serve as an anchor for global activity in the underwater domain.”
In December 2025, with Germany about to deploy its Arrow air defense system bought from Israel for the first time, the Israeli Defense Ministry made new progress regarding the German-built submarines in Berlin, The Jerusalem Post reported at the time.
According to foreign reports, the submarines are able to deliver nuclear weapons. Multiple foreign publications have reported that Israeli submarines are part of a triad of nuclear deterrence that Israel possesses, along with land-based and air-based weapons
During their stay in Germany, Defense Ministry Director-General Amir Baram and other senior defense officials made new progress regarding the ongoing submarine deals, which have unique offensive and also defensive capabilities.
Though Israel has never publicly admitted to possessing nuclear weapons, former prime ministers, such as Ehud Olmert and others, have, at times, slipped up and alluded to the weapons program.
Besides the offensive dimensions, the IDF made unusual disclosures during the Israel-Hamas War about the involvement of submarines in operations against Iran, Yemen, and Syria, including operations that assisted with Israel’s defense against aerial threats.
Movement on both the submarines and the Arrow, along with new levels of Israeli and German cooperation in other cutting-edge technologies, such as artificial intelligence, signaled in December 2025 that the special relationship between Berlin and Jerusalem remained despite disagreements over the war in Gaza.
Germany acquires Israel's Iron Dome system
Earlier this month, Germany also moved forward in acquiring Israel’s Iron Dome system for shooting down shorter-range threats, notably drones.
In November 2024, then-IDF naval chief Adm. David Saar Salame named the new Dragon submarine at a ceremony in Germany.
At the time, it was thought that Israel would receive the submarine in late 2025.
The navy has carried out surveillance and struck Hezbollah targets in a number of areas that are deeper in Lebanon than where IDF ground forces have progressed, given that those forces are limited to southern Lebanon.
In addition, the navy has provided constant defense to Israel’s maritime borders and to its strategic sites, such as its natural gas rigs.
This has included clandestine operations which can reveal Hezbollah and other countries’ plans to threaten or prepare to fire on Israel before they actually fire, in order to enable the air force to preemptively strike such enemy locations.
One area which has been especially challenging has been defending against Houthi attacks on Eilat, given that when the navy helps shoot down threats, it must contend with an extremely small zone of defense to avoid invading Egyptian or Jordanian airspace – or it would need to coordinate with those countries if necessary.
The six-submarine deal dates back many years and has been part of the navy’s strategic modernization effort.
Earlier on Tuesday, Army Radio reported that the Israeli defense establishment is beginning to push for the government to sign a deal for a seventh submarine in the near future, followed by an eighth at a later date.
The idea would be to keep up with Turkey, which has 14 submarines and is moving toward 18 submarines.
On the other hand, a single submarine can cost around €1 billion, and the Defense Ministry and Finance Ministry are already at loggerheads about a delayed NIS 15b. payment due to the IDF some time ago.
The military has threatened that if the payment is not made soon, it will cut back on ground force drills, reservists’ call-ups, and upkeep of certain vehicles; and it may eventually cut back on purchases of military vehicles of strategic value.

Canadian police have yet to formally determine the motive behind the shooting outside Congregation Beth Jacob in Belleville, Canada, which occured as worshipers gathered for Yom Kippur prayers on Sunday.

Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said during a briefing that the shooter was 29-year-old Sean Ward of nearby Quinte West, about 18 kilometers from Belleville. He remains hospitalized with life-threatening injuries.
Meeks identified the wounded officer as Jeff Smith, a veteran police officer who has served for 13 years. She said Smith was hospitalized in intensive care and faces a significant recovery, but that his condition had stabilized.
Kristy Denette, a spokeswoman for Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which is investigating the incident, said in response to a question that logic pointed toward a terrorist incident targeting the Jewish community. She stressed, however, that the SIU's investigation was focused on the actions of the police officer.
Denette said the scene was complex and that forensic investigators would need several days to complete their work there.
Belleville Mayor Neil Ellis said it was "too early to determine that this was a hate crime," but noted that the location and timing, outside a synagogue on the eve of Yom Kippur, "point in that direction."
None of synagogue's 24 worshippers injured in attack

Following the incident, police increased their presence across the city, including around houses of worship.
Israel's Foreign Ministry in Jerusalem said the terror attack against Congregation Beth Jacob in Belleville on the eve of Yom Kippur marked a further escalation in Canada's antisemitism crisis.
"Our thoughts are with the police officer who acted with extraordinary courage and was wounded in the line of duty. We pray for his full and speedy recovery," the Israeli Foreign Ministry said. "Israel stands in solidarity with the Jewish community in Canada, which is confronting an increasingly threatening reality."
The ministry added that "open incitement that goes untreated in the public sphere, together with anti-Israel policies, fuels antisemitism. A change is needed."
Denette said Belleville Police were conducting a parallel investigation that included examining the suspect's motive. She declined to say whether others directed or activated the suspect, repeatedly saying the question fell outside the scope of the SIU's investigation.
On-duty police officer guarding synagogue was first target of shooting
According to Denette, the suspect arrived in his vehicle, believed to have been a pickup truck, at around 7 p.m. while armed with a shotgun. He fired first, initially targeting the on-duty police officer who was securing the synagogue.
The officer returned fire, and a second officer later arrived and also opened fire. The suspect and the first officer were both struck.
The scene extended for roughly half a block. Witness accounts and the preliminary investigation indicated that as many as 30 rounds were fired. A police cruiser, other vehicles, and nearby homes were hit.
A team of four investigators and two forensic investigators was assigned to the case. They collected evidence, reviewed security footage, police body-camera recordings, and vehicle-camera footage, and took witness statements.

The Seoul High Court handed down the lighter sentence, acquitting her of some counts. The court ordered the confiscation of gifts offered to her, along with a forfeiture fine of 24.4 million won (about 18,000 U.S. dollars).
The team of Min Joong-ki, an independent counsel who led investigations into corruption allegations involving the former presidential couple, demanded a seven-year sentence for Kim for selling public offices in exchange for high-priced jewelry and luxury goods.
The court overturned a conviction regarding a luxury wristwatch, which Kim received from a robot dog entrepreneur in September 2022 in return for business favors.
The court also acquitted her of charges that she received a replica of a famous painting in exchange for personnel solicitation, citing a failure to prove the charges.
However, the court upheld all other corruption charges from the initial trial.
Kim was found guilty of accepting luxury jewelry, including a necklace, a brooch and earrings, from a businessman between March and May 2022 in return for the appointment of his eldest son-in-law to a government post.
She was convicted of receiving a designer bag and other luxury goods from a pastor between June and September 2022 in exchange for favors, and a gold turtle from a former chief of the national education commission in exchange for an appointment favor in April of the same year.
The court upheld the finding that Kim received a painting from a former prosecutor in February 2023 in return for political nomination favors.
Kim, who was indicted under detention in August 2025, became the first wife of a former South Korean president to be tried under detention. ■

Details

The products of both refineries, it is emphasized, are used to meet the needs of the russian army.
"The striking of such facilities is Ukraine’s exercise of its inherent right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the russian federation. Around 40 industrial parks currently operational in Ukraine – MP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

Around 40 industrial parks currently operational in Ukraine – MP
Deputy Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Economic Development Dmytro Kysylevskyi said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"There are currently slightly more than 120 industrial parks registered in the industrial parks register. At the same time, the number of parks is not an indicative figure – it is like counting the number of individual entrepreneurs or limited liability companies. Much more important is the dynamics of active industrial parks – those where industrial infrastructure and industrial enterprises are being built or have already been built. If there were only two such parks in 2021, there are now almost 40," the MP said.
For the third year in a row, the government has been allocating around UAH 1 billion for the development of industrial infrastructure in industrial parks. The funds are provided on a 50/50 co-financing basis. In addition to contributing its share of the financing, the applicant undertakes to commission at least 5,000 square meters of industrial real estate within three years and attract at least two industrial enterprises to the industrial park. Thus, for every UAH 1 of state investment, the recipient undertakes to attract UAH 5-6 in private investment.
"By the end of last year, 37 plants had been built or were under construction at these industrial sites. Construction of most of them began during the full-scale invasion. We now have more than 300 MW of substation capacity in industrial parks, as well as more than one million square meters of industrial real estate. Overall, nearly UAH 46 billion in investment had already been made in industrial parks by the beginning of 2026," Kysylevskyi said.
According to him, the number of such plants is expected to reach around 50 by the end of 2026.
Under the program to stimulate the development of industrial infrastructure in industrial parks, an average of 15-17 applications are currently considered each year. The first assessment of how the state funds have been used will take place in 2027, when the three-year period for the provision of the funds expires.
"The first funds were disbursed at the end of 2024, which means that the first assessment will take place at the end of 2027. In other words, the parks that received funds in 2024 will have to report on the fulfillment of their commitments," the MP said.
Recently, the Verkhovna Rada adopted Law No. 12117, aimed at creating clearer and more effective conditions for attracting industrial investment through industrial parks. Kysylevskyi said the law does not contain any revolutionary solutions, but instead technically improves legislation governing the operation of industrial parks and addresses 20 issues, each of which helps remove a specific local obstacle to attracting investment.
"For example, we have regulated the procedure for adding and removing land plots from an industrial park. We allowed the status of management company and industrial park initiator to be held by the same entity. We granted management companies the right to take out loans under the '5-7-9%' program, among other things," he said.
The amendments are expected to accelerate investment processes, simplify the work of management companies, which serve as ambassadors for attracting industrial investment to Ukraine, and encourage communities to more actively develop industrial infrastructure.
As reported, Ukraine has launched a program to stimulate industrial parks that have been damaged by Russian shelling. Under the program, the state covers up to 80% of the cost of restoring infrastructure, but no more than UAH 200 million per park. For the construction of new infrastructure, the co-financing rate is 50%, with funding of up to UAH 150 million.
Photo: Ministry of Economy

Istat said Tuesday that Italy's deficit-to-GDP ratio for 2025 was 3.1%, confirming the provisional figure it gave in April. The government had been hoping the final figure would be revised down to bring it within the 3% threshold laid down in the EU budget rules to enable Italy to emerge from its excessive-deficit infringement procedure. - War in Ukraine
Russia Delays Civilian Spending as Soaring War Costs Widen Budget Deficit
The Russian Finance Ministry was forced to delay a portion of scheduled government expenditures to later periods to maintain its "everything for the front" priority and keep the budget balanced.
Finance Minister Anton Siluanov announced these measures during the Moscow Financial Forum, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 21.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The most important thing for us right now is defense tasks, the tasks of the front," the minister stated, adding that resolving budget challenges this year required "digging around somewhere" and adjusting both expenditures and the resource base.
From January through August, the federal budget deficit expanded to 5.8 trillion rubles ($72.5 billion), representing 2.5% of GDP. Siluanov noted that this deficit will continue to grow, explaining: "During the execution of the budget, additional needs for financing and expenditures arose.
Additional sources of funding for these costs will also be provided for this purpose. We expect the deficit to be larger than planned, but it will remain within 3% of GDP." He added that the government intends to cover the shortfall using accumulated account balances and borrowing on the debt market, according to The Moscow Times.
In the 2026 budget law, the Russian government originally allocated 12.9 trillion rubles ($161.25 billion) under the "national defense" item.
However, actual spending related to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, including adjacent budget categories, reached 10.687 trillion rubles ($133.58 billion) in the first half of the year alone, according to calculations by Janis Kluge from the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, The Moscow Times reports.
Compared to the same period last year, military and arms production expenditures grew by another 30%. They rose by 65% compared to January–June 2024, and have increased more than fivefold compared to pre-war 2021. Cumulative spending on the military since the beginning of 2022 has exceeded 57 trillion rubles ($712.5 billion).
This stagnation aligns with a previous report, which warned that severe labor shortages and intense military spending have pushed Russia to its absolute productive limits.
It notes that the Kremlin is rapidly exhausting its current human and financial resources, leaving Putin with a fundamental choice: either scale back his military ambitions in Ukraine or implement deeply unpopular domestic measures, such as forced conscription and a Soviet-style command economy, to sustain the invasion.

Red Cat’s maritime arm hits a one-year milestone in Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:17:27 UTC
17:17:27 KST

- Blue Ops, the maritime arm of Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since opening its uncrewed surface vessel plant in Valdosta, Georgia.
- The company built its first prototypes with Hodgdon Shipbuilding in Maine before shifting production to the 155,000-square-foot Valdosta facility.
Blue Ops, the maritime division of drone maker Red Cat Holdings, marked one year since it opened a manufacturing plant in Valdosta, Georgia, the company said. The state of Georgia recognized Sept. 21 as the inaugural Blue Ops Day in the city, according to a company statement.
Blue Ops builds uncrewed surface vessels, small autonomous boats used for military and national security missions. The company leased a 155,000-square-foot former boat factory at 601 Gil Harbin Industrial Boulevard in Valdosta, the site of an earlier Regal Boats plant, and announced the move in April with plans to invest about $30 million and create more than 200 jobs. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp announced the facility in April, and state officials said the company planned to hire up to 100 workers in 2026, with more roles to follow as production increased.
Blue Ops president Barry Hinckley said at the time the investment was meant to build “a modern, scalable, and domestic USV manufacturing base from the ground up.”
The company built its first prototype vessels elsewhere. Blue Ops partnered with Hodgdon Shipbuilding, a Maine boatbuilder founded in 1816, to construct its first five uncrewed surface vessel prototypes at facilities in Boothbay and Damariscotta, Maine, before shifting full-rate production to Valdosta.
In April, Blue Ops also partnered with HADDY, a robotic 3D printing company, to add large-scale 3D printing and robotic production systems to the Valdosta plant. The companies said the partnership would roughly double the facility’s manufacturing capacity by using robotic systems to build vessel hulls before workers complete final assembly.
Red Cat Holdings, based in Salt Lake City and traded on Nasdaq under the ticker RCAT, also makes small drones through its Teal Drones and FlightWave Aerospace subsidiaries. The company has positioned Blue Ops as its expansion into uncrewed maritime systems, alongside its existing air-domain drone business.
Blue Ops has not disclosed how many vessels it has built at the Valdosta facility over the past year or named specific government customers for its USV line. The company said in its anniversary statement that it intends to keep expanding production capacity at the site.

Libya’s NOC says armed group shuts oil pipeline valve, sharply reducing main field output
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:13:28 UTC
17:13:28 KST

Muetaz Wannes and Mohammad Sio
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
An armed group has shut a valve on a crude oil pipeline linking Libya’s Sharara field to the western port of Zawiya, causing a sharp drop in production at the country’s main oil field, the National Oil Corporation (NOC) said late Monday.
The NOC said the armed group closed Valve No. 7, halting the flow of crude from the Sharara field, operated by Akakus Oil Operations, to Zawiya Port in western Libya.
The closure caused pressure to build up in the crude pipeline, resulting in a “significant reduction” in production at Sharara, it added.
Located in the Murzuq Desert, around 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of Tripoli, Sharara is Libya’s largest oil field, with production capacity of around 340,000 barrels per day.
The NOC said it contacted the southwestern branch of the Petroleum Facilities Guard and urged it to carry out its duties, but the appeals “had produced no results.” Technical teams had also been unable to reach the area around Valves 6 and 7.
The corporation warned that the continued shutdown would halt production at the Sharara field as well as oil transport and export operations, directly harming Libya’s economy by causing a decline in state revenues.
It also warned that the oil transport system and its facilities will be exposed to technical and operational risks, anticipating that the shutdown will cause the Zawiya oil refinery to cease operations, thereby further increasing the cost of importing fuel from abroad.
It called for the immediate reopening of the pipeline and demanded the relevant authorities secure oil installations and keep them away from protests and other disruptions.
The corporation said it “may be compelled to declare force majeure” if the closure continues.
Force majeure is a contractual provision that suspends liability when extraordinary circumstances prevent parties from meeting their obligations.
The NOC did not identify the armed group responsible for shutting the valve.
The incident comes a week after members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed the main Hamada-Zawiya oil pipeline on Sept. 15, causing production and operations to stop at the Hamada and Al-Tahara fields and Station NC5. The NOC also warned at the time that it could declare force majeure if the closure persisted.
The Hamada field is located in the Hamada al-Hamra area of the Ghadames Basin in western Libya, about 400 kilometers (250 miles) south of Tripoli. It is considered one of the key oil and natural gas fields in western Libya and produces around 700 barrels per day.
Members of the Petroleum Facilities Guard have been demanding higher salaries amid a broader wave of labor protests in Libya.

U.S. Army orders more M270A2 launcher upgrades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:09:31 UTC
17:09:31 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million in September to rebuild more M270 rocket launchers to the M270A2 standard.
- The upgrade adds a new engine, an armored cab and a fire-control system shared with HIMARS, letting both launchers fire the same precision munitions.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin $200 million to rebuild more M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System launchers to the M270A2 standard, the company said. The September award is the latest in a series of contracts that began in 2019 to modernize the tracked rocket launcher.
The recapitalization strips down existing M270 launchers and rebuilds them as close to new, with a new engine, an armored cab and the Common Fire Control System, the same fire-control system used on the wheeled HIMARS launcher. That shared system lets the two launchers fire the same family of precision munitions, including GMLRS, Extended-Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile, and lets crews trained on one system move more easily to the other.
The Army has awarded similar M270A2 recapitalization contracts nearly every year since 2019, including a $362 million award in 2019, a $226 million award in 2020, a $451 million award in 2024 and a $214 million award last year. Lockheed Martin has said the goal is to keep the M270 fleet in service through 2050. The Army’s fleet includes 225 M270A1 launchers being upgraded to the A2 standard, along with about 160 older, decommissioned M270A0 launchers slated for the same overhaul.
The M270A2 is a tracked launcher that carries more armor and cargo capacity than the wheeled HIMARS, while HIMARS offers greater mobility on roads. Both can fire the Extended-Range GMLRS, which reaches out to 150 km (93 miles), and the Precision Strike Missile, a longer-range weapon still being fielded across the Army. Lockheed Martin has said only the M270A2 and HIMARS can fire those newer munitions, which older, unmodernized M270 launchers cannot use.
The recapitalization work is split among Lockheed Martin’s Camden, Arkansas, plant and facilities in Grand Prairie and New Boston, Texas, with the Army’s Red River Army Depot handling part of the overhaul. Recent contracts have carried completion dates stretching into 2027 and 2030, reflecting the scale of the work needed to rebuild dozens of launchers at a time.
The Army has fielded more than 220 M270-series launchers, and international partners that operate the M270 or HIMARS, including NATO members, are also eligible for the upgraded fire-control system under foreign military sales.

U.S. Army laser weapon shown defeating drones at border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:05:04 UTC
17:05:04 KST

- Newly released footage shows an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with AeroVironment technology, defeating drones at the southern border.
- The system engaged and defeated three hostile drones over two nights in late August under Joint Task Force Southern Border.
The U.S. Department of War has released new footage showing an Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, built with directed-energy technology from AeroVironment (AV), defeating drones along the U.S. southern border, according to a report by Army Verification Alliance (AV).
The laser is deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, a U.S. Northern Command unit that supports U.S. Customs and Border Protection. In late August, task force personnel used the system, known as AMP-HEL, to engage and defeat three drones over two nights, Aug. 25 and 26, near the border. The U.S. Army said the aircraft were judged hostile based on their use in direct support of activity that threatened U.S. military personnel and CBP partners.
“Cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human-smuggling and actively spy on our personnel and law enforcement partners,” said Army Maj. Gen. Curtis Taylor, commander of Joint Task Force Southern Border. “By integrating layered countermeasures alongside advanced directed-energy capabilities like this laser system, we have made it clear that we will not tolerate hostile surveillance.”
The Army has not disclosed exactly where the drones were engaged or confirmed who was flying them, though officials have linked similar incursions to cartel surveillance. AV told Breaking Defense the system used is the product of the Army’s AMP-HEL program but did not say which specific configuration was deployed or whether it was vehicle-mounted.
AMP-HEL is a 20-kilowatt-class laser weapon built to defeat Group 1 and Group 2 drones, the U.S. military’s category for smaller, slower unmanned aircraft. AV delivered the first two prototypes, mounted on Joint Light Tactical Vehicles, to the Army in December 2025 as part of the AMP-HEL prototyping effort. The company markets the underlying laser weapon system as LOCUST, which it says pairs an electro-optical tracking system, a laser rangefinder and a targeting laser with the high-energy laser itself. AeroVironment says the system uses a common gaming controller for weapon control and is designed to plug into a range of sensor types and radio-frequency bands, as well as existing command-and-control networks.
About 8,000 service members are currently deployed under Joint Task Force Southern Border, the Army said. Officials have said hundreds of drones fly near the border each day, and Northern Command leaders have described the border as a proving ground for technology meant to counter them. Weeks after the August engagements, the Army awarded AV a production contract for the laser under a separate program called Enduring High Energy Laser; DefenseScoop reported the deal is worth $464.8 million and covers dozens of additional LOCUST-based systems over the next several years.

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
08:04:59 UTC
17:04:59 KST

Four Corners episodes breached ABC's editorial standards, ombudsman's investigation finds
In short
The ABC breached four editorial standards in stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal, its ombudsman found.
The episodes involved have already been withdrawn by ABC News.
What's next
The ABC has said it accepts the report's seven recommendations and has started to implement them.
The ABC's Four Corners program had insufficient verification and fact-checking and a culture of "limiting knowledge" about anonymous sources, its independent ombudsman has found, identifying breaches of editorial standards in two stories by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal .
The ombudsman's report, released this afternoon, found two episodes failed to meet editorial standards for accuracy, fair and honest dealing, and independence.
"Audiences were given a misleading impression of who key contributors were, the basis on which the ABC was relying on them and the level of confidence that could reasonably be placed in their claims," the report said.
The ombudsman made seven recommendations, which include amending the ABC's editorial standard on anonymity, further legal and editorial training for the Four Corners team and more support for less experienced reporters.
The ABC says it accepts the recommendations in full and has begun implementing them.
ABC News had already removed the two episodes covered by the ombudsman's review — Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway — after its own investigation into the anonymous interviewees.
In total, three episodes of Four Corners and two of Background Briefing by Fazal have already been withdrawn by the ABC, with a short segment edited out of another Four Corners episode.
Last month, the ABC said its own review found verification policies on anonymous interviewees were "not followed to a level that meets our editorial standards".
"The ABC is committed to journalism of the highest standard. Maintaining the trust of Australians depends on upholding those standards and we take any concerns about our journalism seriously," it said.
Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, had his employment terminated in May after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year.
He had launched an unfair dismissal claim in the Fair Work Commission, but his hearing was removed from the schedule. The ABC said it was aware Fazal was no longer pursuing his claim.
In a social media video post last month, Fazal said he felt like the ABC was "trying everything in their power to stop me from ever working again".
"Even though all my work was approved across different teams and departments, cross-checked and met the standards before broadcast, they've decided there's now different standards that are retrospectively being applied to all of my stories," he said.
"They want to make me a scapegoat? Don't give a s***. I won't stop."
He has previously said he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources, but that proximity had then been used against him.
Previously, Fazal's reporting appeared in VICE, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.
Last month, the ABC announced its head of investigations and current affairs, Jo Puccini, was leaving the public broadcaster after a 25-year career.
She had oversight of Four Corners and Background Briefing.
Other senior managers at the ABC at the time of Fazal's reporting, including news director Justin Stevens, have already left the broadcaster. The ABC's incoming news director Simon Robinson started in the role on September 14.
Last week, ABC managing director Hugh Marks rejected an Australian Communications and Media Authority finding that the public broadcaster breached impartiality obligations in an unrelated Four Corners program about the redevelopment of the Australian War Memorial.
ACMA said on Thursday it had found the program's March 2025 episode, Sacrifice, had "unduly favoured one perspective".
The ABC says it "stands behind the team" that created the episode.
"If this interpretation of the code is applied, including more widely across the industry, it could have a chilling effect on the body of investigative journalism that delivers the important stories that serve the public interest," Marks said in a statement.
