====================================================================================================

Negative religious coping is linked to a mind-body disconnect during acute stress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
22:00:23 UTC
07:00:23 KST

A new study suggests that when facing a challenging situation, people who feel punished by or angry with God report feeling more stressed, yet their bodies show a smaller increase in blood pressure than expected. The findings provide evidence that psychological and physical responses to stress do not always match, especially when spiritual struggles are involved. The research was published in Psychology of Religion and Spirituality.
Religious coping refers to how people use their faith to understand and deal with difficult life events. While some individuals rely on positive strategies, such as seeking comfort from a higher power, others experience negative religious coping. This involves spiritual struggles, such as feeling abandoned by God, questioning divine intentions, or viewing hardships as a spiritual punishment. In daily life, this negative coping style is often linked to poorer mental health and a harder time managing emotions.
“Religion is often viewed as a source of comfort and support during stressful times, but not all forms of religious coping are beneficial,” lead author Ailbhe Dempsey, a researcher at the Study of Anxiety, Stress and Health Laboratory in the Department of Psychology at the University of Limerick, told PsyPost. “Negative religious coping, such as feeling punished or abandoned by God or questioning one’s faith, is consistently associated with poorer psychological well-being, yet we know relatively little about how it relates to the body’s response to acute stress.”
When a person faces a sudden psychological challenge, the body’s cardiovascular system naturally responds. Heart rate and blood pressure typically rise to supply the body with energy to meet the demands of the situation. This process is known as cardiovascular stress reactivity. Some research indicates that certain religious behaviors can influence this physical response. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that frequent private religious practices are associated with smaller spikes in blood pressure during stressful tasks.
While extremely large spikes in blood pressure can increase the risk of heart disease over time, unusually low or blunted responses are not necessarily healthy. A 2011 study indicated that people who report high levels of stress in their daily lives tend to have blunted heart rate reactions to new stressful situations. Similarly, a 2020 study demonstrated that diminished physical stress responses are linked to higher levels of behavioral disengagement, meaning individuals are more likely to give up when faced with a challenge.
Scientists theorize that chronic emotional struggles might exhaust or downregulate the body’s stress systems, leading to these blunted physical reactions. To explore this complex relationship, Dempsey and her colleagues aimed to examine how negative religious coping affects both how stressed someone feels and how their heart and blood vessels physically react during a challenging moment.
“Most previous research has focused on general life stress rather than responses to a standardized stressor in a controlled setting,” Dempsey said. “We therefore wanted to examine both the psychological and cardiovascular responses associated with negative religious coping in young adults.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 81 healthy young adults with an average age of 19 from a Christian university in the southern United States. The participants completed questionnaires assessing their typical use of negative religious coping, rating how often they felt abandoned by God or questioned their faith during hard times. They also answered questions about their general religiosity, symptoms of depression, and personality traits.
During the laboratory session, participants sat quietly for a ten-minute resting period to establish a baseline for their heart rate and blood pressure. Then, they completed a stress-inducing task called the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task. This involved listening to a fast-paced series of numbers and adding consecutive digits together out loud. To make the task more stressful, researchers included elements of social evaluation. Participants were told they were competing against peers on a fictional leaderboard, recorded on video, and asked to look at themselves in a mirror during the test. For every incorrect or missed answer, they were warned that points would be deducted.
Blood pressure and heart rate were continuously monitored while the participants completed the mental math challenge. Immediately after the task was over, the participants rated how stressed they felt on a scale from one to seven. The researchers then analyzed the data to see if typical religious coping styles were associated with the participants’ reactions in the lab.
The mental math task successfully triggered a stress response across the group, raising both average heart rates and blood pressures. However, the researchers found a divergence between the participants’ mental and physical reactions based on their religious coping styles. Individuals who reported higher levels of negative religious coping felt more stressed during the mental math task. Yet, these same individuals displayed a blunted physical response.
Specifically, they had a smaller increase in their diastolic blood pressure, which is the pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats. Negative religious coping accounted for an additional eight percent of the variance in this blunted blood pressure response and six percent of the variance in self-reported stress levels. These associations held true even after the researchers accounted for other factors that might influence stress, such as resting blood pressure, biological sex, overall religiosity, neuroticism, and symptoms of depression.
The researchers did not find a statistically significant association between negative religious coping and changes in heart rate or systolic blood pressure, which is the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats. While the physical measures were mixed, the psychological aspect of these results is consistent with research covered by PsyPost in 2022. That study, which examined self-reported mental health during the pandemic rather than immediate responses to a laboratory stress task, similarly found that negative religious coping was linked to heightened psychological distress.
“The main takeaway is that the way people engage with religion during difficult times may matter for how they experience stress,” Dempsey explained. “Importantly, psychological and physiological responses to stress did not necessarily move in the same direction, highlighting that feeling highly stressed does not always mean showing a larger cardiovascular response.”
“These findings add to evidence that struggles involving religion or faith can be an important aspect of how some people experience and cope with stress,” she added.
There are a few things to keep in mind regarding the current study. The research was observational and cross-sectional, meaning it can only highlight associations at a single point in time. “It is important not to interpret these findings as showing that negative religious coping causes blunted cardiovascular responses or greater stress, as the study was observational and cannot establish causation,” Dempsey cautioned. It is possible that individuals prone to heavy stress and emotion regulation difficulties naturally develop both a cynical view of their faith and a fatigued cardiovascular response.
The study also focused on a specific demographic. “In addition, our sample consisted of predominantly female undergraduate students at a private Christian university in the United States, which may limit how broadly the findings generalize,” Dempsey noted. Because religion might be more culturally embedded in this specific environment, struggles with faith could exert a stronger influence on stress than they would in other settings. The results might not perfectly translate to older adults or individuals in more secular or religiously diverse environments.
The researchers also noted that blood pressure was recorded semi-automatically. This required a researcher to push a button at specific times to take a reading, which introduces a slight possibility of human error, even when monitoring a stopwatch. Fully automated equipment might provide more precise measurements in future studies.
“Larger and more diverse studies are needed to better understand the relationship between negative religious coping, stress responses, and health,” Dempsey concluded. Including measures of how well people regulate their emotions could also help explain why spiritual struggles seem to disconnect the mind’s experience of stress from the body’s physical reaction.
The study, “Negative Religious Coping Is Associated With Blunted Cardiovascular Reactivity and Higher Self-Reported Stress in Response to Acute Psychological Stress,” was authored by Ailbhe Dempsey, Thomas A. Fergus, Siobhán Howard, Stephen Gallagher, and Annie T. Ginty.

VILNIUS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Lithuania has secured natural gas supplies from the United States for 10 years, covering about 40 percent of the country's household gas demand, Lithuania's Ministry of Energy announced Monday.

According to a statement released by the Ministry of Energy, under the agreement, Ignitis will purchase 10 liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargoes from EQT between 2027 and 2036, with one cargo, equivalent to about 1 terawatt-hour (TWh) of gas, to be delivered each year.

"This long-term agreement is an important step toward strengthening the security and flexibility of natural gas supplies for Lithuanian household customers. It will diversify supply sources, enable more effective management of price fluctuation risks and ensure more stable supply conditions over the longer term," Ignitis CEO Andrius Kavaliauskas said.
The country's Energy Minister Lukas Savickas said the agreement would help reduce Lithuania's vulnerability to gas price fluctuations in the European market and mitigate their impact on household bills. ■

Sardine mortality subsides as South Africa maintains precautionary fishing measure

CAPE TOWN, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's environment department said Monday that widespread sardine mortality is subsiding as the government maintains a precautionary fishing measure.
In a statement, the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment said no renewed widespread mortality had been reported. "The only new report during the past week was an isolated fresh sardine stranding near Mbotyi on the northern Wild Coast on Sept. 11."
The department said the available evidence did not indicate that the mortality had reduced the sardine population sufficiently to warrant a complete closure of the fishery. The current measure is precautionary and time-limited and can be reviewed sooner if conditions deteriorate.
Industry reported that strong winds had prevented recent fishing west of Cape Agulhas, while fishing opportunities in Algoa Bay were also limited by weather. Only one sardine catch, amounting to 26 tonnes, has been taken since the beginning of September.
Pilchard herpesvirus (PHV) remains the strongest identified biological factor associated with the mortality and has been confirmed in affected sardines from the Western Cape and Algoa Bay, the department said.
"Monitoring, sampling and laboratory investigations are continuing," it said.
Earlier samples from KwaZulu-Natal (KZN) Province tested negative for PHV, but only a small number were tested. Additional samples are expected to help determine whether the result is consistent across a broader sample.
"If these also test negative, this will support, but not prove, that the event did not extend into KZN, consistent with the reported mortality front ending before it reached the province," the department said.
No effects on sardine-dependent seabirds or marine mammals have been confirmed.
The Small Pelagic Scientific Working Group will meet on Sept. 29 to review the available evidence and reconsider management of the fishery before the temporary measure ends.
A hydroacoustic survey planned for October and November will provide the first fisheries-independent estimate of sardine biomass and distribution following the event. ■

Roundup: Zimbabwean farmers adopt drought-tolerant crops for resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:43 CST
06:52:43 KST

A farmer displays samples of beans at the Good Seed and Food Festival in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Sept. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tafara Mugwara/Xinhua)
HARARE, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Faced with recurring droughts, Zimbabwean smallholder farmers who largely rely on rain-fed agriculture are turning to drought-tolerant traditional crops to safeguard food supplies and strengthen resilience.
The shift was reflected at the Good Seed and Food Festival in Harare, Zimbabwe's capital, on Saturday, where farmers showcased and exchanged seeds such as cowpeas, sorghum and millet.
Traditional crops have sustained communities for generations and are valued for their ability to perform under dry conditions, said Delmah Ndlovu, national chairperson of the Zimbabwe Smallholder Organic Farmers' Forum, an organization that seeks to improve smallholder livelihoods through sustainable ecological agriculture.
Crop diversification should be viewed as an integrated farming system that enables farmers to become more self-sufficient, he said, encouraging farmers to diversify their crops to build resilience.
"Having different crops gives the farmer protection. When one fails, the other does well," said Ndlovu, adding that growing a variety of beans and legumes helps farmers hedge against unpredictable weather conditions.
"We have traditional crops that provide farmers with leaves for relish, seeds for food and oil crops such as groundnuts and sunflowers for cooking oil and peanut butter. Some varieties mature quickly, while others take longer, giving farmers different options to meet their food and nutritional needs," he said.
Early-maturing seed varieties can help farmers cope with low rainfall, while late-maturing varieties are better suited to seasons with adequate rainfall, reducing the risk of total crop failure, Ndlovu added.
Zimbabwe's 2026/2027 rainfall season is forecast to be influenced by El Nino, which will increase the likelihood of a below-normal rainfall season.
"We learnt that if we grow traditional seeds and practice water harvesting, we can make the most of the little water available. We will continue doing the same so that we can still harvest enough grain even when we do not receive much rainfall," said Jenny Dube, a farmer from Chimanimani District, Manicaland Province.
Smallholder farmers account for 89 percent of agricultural producers, serving as the backbone of Zimbabwe's food security, according to a United Nations Development Program report.
As key drivers of food production, smallholder farmers play a crucial role in national development, said Melamiseli Ncube, a farmer from Nkayi District in Matabeleland North Province.
The farmer said adequate preparation, including the use of drought-resistant seed varieties, can help farmers mitigate the effects of drought, even in worst-case scenarios.
"Last season, we had a good harvest. After hearing about the El Nino, we set aside pest-resistant grain such as millet and sorghum. These reserves can sustain our household for two seasons without getting grain from other areas," he said. ■
A farmer displays harvested sorghum heads at the Good Seed and Food Festival in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Sept. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tafara Mugwara/Xinhua)
Visitors gather around an exhibition table to examine seeds at the Good Seed and Food Festival in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Sept. 19, 2026. (Photo by Tafara Mugwara/Xinhua)

Russia zeroes out grain export tariffs through late 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:38 CST
06:52:38 KST

MOSCOW, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Russia has zeroed out export duties on grain crops through the end of 2026, the Russian Agriculture Ministry announced Monday.
According to a new decree, the "floating" export tariff on wheat, barley, and corn has been scrapped until Dec. 31, 2026. Meanwhile, duties on sunflower oil and sunflower meal will be capped at the levels set for August 2026: 7,748 rubles (about 92.13 U.S. dollars) per metric tonne for sunflower oil and 312 rubles (about 3.71 dollars) per metric tonne for sunflower meal.
The decision aims to support domestic producers and exporters of grain and oilseed crops amid the ongoing restructuring of export logistics, the Agriculture Ministry said in a statement.
"These measures will reduce costs for market participants, make sales conditions more predictable, and support the industry's export potential," the ministry said.
"We expect the temporary adjustment of export duties to lower market players' costs, sustain production economics and ensure stable supplies of Russian agricultural goods," Maxim Borovoy, deputy minister of the Agriculture Ministry said earlier.
Russia introduced export duty mechanisms for grain, sunflower oil, and sunflower meal in 2021. The rates are calculated based on the difference between the base price and the indicative price. ■

Unknown Publisher

05:52:35 CST
06:52:35 KST

OSLO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Norway and Canada plan to strengthen defense cooperation, including more joint training exercises and operations in the Arctic, the Norwegian government said on Monday.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store met with his Canadian counterpart, Mark Carney, in Ottawa on Sunday to discuss closer bilateral cooperation.
In a press release, Store said: "Arctic security is important to the national security of both our countries."
According to the press release, the two countries issued a joint statement saying that they intend to pursue an enhanced defense cooperation agreement after negotiations are concluded on Canada's submarine procurement project. The agreement would build on a defense memorandum of understanding signed in 2023.
Canada decided in July to procure the same type of submarines as Norway and Germany, paving the way for defense, industrial and technical cooperation among the three countries.
Store said the submarine partnership would strengthen Norway's and NATO's ability to monitor northern sea areas and create opportunities for Norway's defense industry.
The leaders also reaffirmed their support for Ukraine. Other areas of cooperation include closer collaboration between their polar research institutions and the safe use of artificial intelligence to improve public services.
The talks followed Carney's visit to Norway in March, when the two countries agreed on a broader strategic partnership that included Arctic security. ■

California declares state of emergency to prepare for historic El Nino season
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:24 CST
06:52:24 KST

LOS ANGELES, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. state of California on Monday proclaimed a state of emergency to prepare for what is shaping up to be a potentially historic El Nino season.
The proclamation will mobilize state resources and accelerate preparations ahead of potential winter storms, coastal flooding and other impacts, according to a statement from the governor's office.
"The emerging El Nino event is already breaking records, and forecasters expect it to continue to strengthen, potentially becoming the strongest in recorded history," the statement said.
The proclamation directs state agencies to protect vulnerable communities, prepare roads and critical infrastructure, stockpile emergency supplies, and help local partners reduce the risk of flooding, landslide and coastal hazards.
El Nino is a natural climate pattern marked by warmer-than-average ocean temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific. It can alter weather patterns and bring wetter, more intense winters to California, according to the governor's office.
The office urged Californians to sign up for emergency alerts and make evacuation plans. ■

SANAA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi warned Türkiye and Pakistan against involvement in the group's escalating confrontation with Saudi Arabia.
In a televised speech broadcast by the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV channel, al-Houthi accused Saudi Arabia of seeking military support from Türkiye and Pakistan as the conflict intensifies both inside Yemen and across the Saudi-Yemeni border.
He urged the two countries not to become "entangled" in the conflict in pursuit of political or economic interests with Riyadh.
Al-Houthi also alleged that Saudi Arabia was seeking to bring fighters from Syria into the conflict, without providing evidence to support the claim.
On the possibility of de-escalation, the Houthi leader said his group was not demanding "impossible conditions," reiterating its call for an end to Saudi military operations and what the Houthis describe as a blockade.
He called on his supporters to maintain mobilization and continue strengthening the group's military and security capabilities amid the escalating confrontation.
The warning comes as the Houthi-Saudi confrontation spills increasingly across the border, with Saudi airstrikes in Yemen met by Houthi missile and drone attacks deep inside the kingdom. Al-Houthi said Monday that Saudi Arabia had launched 760 airstrikes since the latest escalation began.
There was no immediate response from Saudi Arabia, Türkiye or Pakistan to al-Houthi's remarks.
The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement on Aug. 7 in the Saudi city of Mecca, stipulating that an attack on any signatory will be considered an attack on all. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said last Saturday that Türkiye would keep its promise under the agreement and could provide technical assistance to Saudi Arabia. ■

Displaced families in Yemen need urgent food, shelter support: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:23 CST
06:52:23 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Families displaced by hostilities in Yemen urgently need food and shelter support, while supplies are running thin as the violence and needs increase, UN humanitarians said Monday.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that, with its partners, it scaled up support for displaced families and all those in need. But the response faces ongoing funding shortfalls and access constraints.
Over the weekend, OCHA said that 21,000 households were displaced across Yemen since Aug. 1, most of them in the governorates of Taiz and Lahj, a figure expected to rise as registration continues.
Since Aug. 1, the UN Human Rights Office verified 125 civilian casualties in 36 incidents, with 32 people killed and 93 others injured. This month, more than 80 percent of casualties were women and children. The actual toll is likely much higher.
OCHA said that ambulances were attacked in Lahj governorate on Friday, killing a driver and an emergency medical responder. Nine health facilities or locations in Taiz and Lahj governorates and in the city of Al Hodeidah were damaged, closed or directly attacked. Hospitals receiving the wounded are running short of blood, anesthetics and surgical supplies.
The office said that women and girls have historically faced high levels of risk in Yemen, particularly pregnant women, who have extremely limited access to health care. Three women die every day in Yemen due to pregnancy complications or during childbirth. The latest escalation in conflict has amplified these risks.
The UN Population Fund estimated that more than 2,700 pregnant women are among the displaced, including 300 expected to give birth in the next two weeks and at least 500 in need of emergency obstetric or newborn care. However, key emergency obstetric facilities have been closed in Taiz, forcing displaced women to give birth in the open without skilled medical care.
OCHA said that humanitarian partners have reached nearly 13,000 displaced households with rapid response kits and other urgently needed assistance. The World Health Organization has delivered surgical supplies and antibiotics to four hospitals in the cities of Aden and Marib.
OCHA called on the parties to protect civilians, including health workers, and ambulances and to facilitate the unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid. ■

Slovakia sees surge in car ownership, growth in green mobility
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:13 CST
06:52:13 KST

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The number of cars in Slovakia has doubled over the past two decades to 3.8 million, while the country is seeing a shift toward greener transport, according to data released by the Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic on Monday.
An average of about 105,000 cars have been added to Slovakia's roads each year, the office said in a statement marking European Mobility Week which was held from Sept. 16 to 22. This year's European Mobility Week will culminate in Car-Free Day on Tuesday, which promotes walking, cycling and public transport as alternatives to private cars.
Electric mobility is contributing to greener transport. More than 111,800 electric vehicles were produced in Slovakia last year. Slovak manufacturers accounted for about 5 percent of the 2.2 million electric vehicles sold by manufacturers in EU countries.
Public transport is also gaining importance, particularly in major cities. Slovaks made 502 million public transport journeys in 2025, nearly one-third more than that of 2019. On average, each resident made 93 public transport journeys, covering a total distance of 346 km.
Rail transport is one of the most environmentally friendly ways of travelling, enjoying growing interest. According to the Statistics Office data, Slovaks made 74 million rail journeys last year, meaning an average of 14 journeys and 701 km per resident.
In addition, cycling infrastructure has expanded significantly in recent years. The total length of cycling routes in Slovakia's regional capitals reached 624 km in 2025, an increase of two-thirds over the past six years. ■

3 U.S. media outlets file lawsuit after being barred from entering White House
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:09 CST
06:52:09 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Three U.S. news organizations -- CNN, MSNOW and Politico -- said Monday that they are suing U.S. President Donald Trump and several White House officials after being barred from entering the White House.
"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three news organizations said in a joint statement.
"Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference," the statement continued.
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, also listed Steven Cheung, assistant to the president for communications, Sean Curran, director of the Secret Service, and Susan Wiles, White House chief of staff, as defendants.
The latest lawsuit came after Trump said on social media Friday that CNN, MSNOW and Politico were banned from the White House "effective immediately," citing what he called constant "fake news."
On Saturday, reporters from the three media outlets were denied entry to the White House, and their press credentials were confiscated.
In a social media post, Trump reacted to the latest lawsuit on Monday. "As expected, Fake News CNN, Politico (Pay back the 8 Million Dollar contribution made by the U.S. Government to keep them afloat!), and MSNOW (formerly known as MSDNC!), have brought suit to gain access to the White House, and your President, ME!" Trump said in a post on his social media platform Truth Social.
"Almost without question and, as usual, we'll go for appeal," Trump continued, arguing that "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World."
Since the beginning of Trump's second term, his relationship with U.S. news organizations has remained tense, with the president frequently criticizing media outlets over what he calls "fake news" and taking legal action against some of them.
In February 2025, reporters from The Associated Press (AP) were barred from access to the White House Oval Office, Mar-a-Lago and Air Force One after the AP declined to adopt the Trump administration's renaming of the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."
Trump has also filed lawsuits against media organizations including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and CBS, accusing them of defamation or misleading reporting. ■

Libya's Sharara oil field output falls after pipeline valve closure
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:09 CST
06:52:09 KST

TRIPOLI, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Monday that crude oil production at the Sharara oil field in southwestern Libya had fallen significantly after an armed group shut a main valve on the pipeline transporting crude to the Zawiya terminal.
The NOC said in a statement that the group closed valve No. 7 on Monday morning on a pipeline operated by Akakus Oil Operations Company, causing increased pressure in the pipeline and a sharp decline in production.
The corporation said it had contacted the Petroleum Facilities Guard in the southwestern region to secure the pipeline, but its appeals yielded no results. Its technical teams were also unable to reach valves No. 6 and 7 to address the problem.
The NOC warned that continued closure could completely halt production at the field, disrupt oil transportation and exports, and threaten operations at the Zawiya refinery, potentially increasing fuel import costs.
The corporation urged the relevant authorities to secure oil facilities and reopen the pipeline, warning that it "may be forced to declare force majeure" if the closure continues.
The Sharara oil field, located in the Murzuq Basin, is one of Libya's largest oil fields, with a normal production capacity of about 300,000 barrels per day. ■

Uganda urges coffee farmers to remain resilient amid market, weather headwinds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:08 CST
06:52:08 KST

KAMPALA, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Ugandan government has urged coffee farmers not to lose heart amid volatility in the global market and adverse weather conditions affecting production.
Frank Tumwebaze, minister of agriculture, animal industry and fisheries, said in a statement dated Sunday that the international coffee market had recently come under downward pressure amid increased supplies from major producing countries, particularly Brazil and Vietnam.
"Our price analysts attributed the immediate pressure partly to increased Brazilian exports as that country's harvest approached completion. This tells us that the current price movement is not unique to Uganda. It is part of a wider international market adjustment," Tumwebaze said.
Besides, Uganda is facing domestic supply challenges following a prolonged period of drought and unusually high temperatures in several coffee-growing areas, he said.
The resulting water stress has affected coffee flowering, cherry development, bean filling and, ultimately, processing yields and quality, according to the minister.
"The impact of this drought on coffee production at farm level has been felt at the national level," Tumwebaze said, noting that Uganda exported 846,376 60-kg bags of coffee in July 2026, down from 997,105 bags in the same month a year earlier.
Coffee export earnings also fell to 204.1 million U.S. dollars in July 2026 from 250.7 million dollars in July 2025, according to the minister.
Despite the challenges, farmers are not necessarily facing losses, Tumwebaze said, stressing that a decline in prices does not automatically mean farmers are operating at a loss.
He urged farmers and other players in the coffee value chain not to lose confidence, saying the resilience of Uganda's coffee industry continues to make coffee production and related activities profitable.
He added that the government was implementing measures to help farmers recover from the effects of adverse weather, mitigate future climate risks, and raise productivity and incomes.
Coffee remains a key commodity in Uganda's economic agenda, with about 1.7 million households depending on the crop, according to the ministry. ■

Denmark, Greenland, U.S. to sign Arctic security agreement
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
05:52:06 CST
06:52:06 KST

OSLO, Sept. 21 (Xinhua) -- Denmark, its autonomous territory of Greenland and the United States will sign an agreement in New York on Tuesday to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic region, the Danish Prime Minister's Office said on Monday.
The agreement will be signed by Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and U.S. President Donald Trump, according to the office's statement.
The signing ceremony is expected to take place at United Nations headquarters at 10:30 a.m. local time (1430 GMT), on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, the statement said, but did not disclose the agreement's specific terms.
Trump announced on social media on Friday that the three sides had reached a deal, saying it would give the United States "permanent control" over Greenland's security.
In response, Frederiksen said on the same day that the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark's sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.
Under a defense agreement signed by Denmark and the United States in 1951 and amended in 2004, the U.S. military already has broad authorization to maintain personnel and facilities in Greenland, including the Pituffik Space Base. ■

EU foreign policy chief calls for protection of ICC amid 'immense pressure'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:27:40 UTC
06:27:40 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas called Monday for the International Criminal Court (ICC) to be protected, saying it is under “immense pressure” and warning that pressure on the court and its judges raises questions about commitment to the international legal order.
“First, we defend the mechanisms we already have to uphold International Humanitarian Law, domestic courts as well as international courts, the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court, the ICC,” she said at a UN General Assembly side event on humanitarian diplomacy and international humanitarian law.
Kallas said accountability was a key part of upholding international humanitarian law.
“Contrary to what should be happening, the ICC is now under immense pressure,” Kallas said.
She said pressure on the ICC and its judges was not only about the institution itself, but also raised questions about commitment to the international legal order established in the aftermath of World War II.
“And let us not forget, the ICC is the world's promise that victims of the gravest international crimes will not be forgotten because accountability has become politically inconvenient. We must protect it,” she said.
Kallas said international law was not the main problem, arguing that “impunity breeds impunity.”
She outlined three ways to strengthen accountability: defending existing judicial mechanisms, creating new ones where existing mechanisms fall short, and ensuring that legal cases can be properly built.
Kallas cited the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials, as well as tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine as examples of mechanisms established to pursue accountability.
She also highlighted EU-backed efforts to document alleged war crimes in Syria and a UN-led investigation into Afghanistan.
In Gaza, Kallas said it was essential to preserve evidence of potential war crimes as efforts to clear rubble begin.
“Be it in Syria, Afghanistan, Gaza, or anywhere in conflict, accountability cannot be selective or else the entire system is called into question,” she said.

Typhoon Dujuan lashes Tokyo, over 1M urged to evacuate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:23:00 UTC
06:23:00 KST

Typhoon Dujuan battered the Tokyo region with torrential rain early Tuesday, prompting evacuation advisories for more than 1 million people and hundreds of flight cancellations as flooding and landslides threatened parts of Japan.
Two people have been confirmed dead as heavy rainfall triggered landslides in Chiba and Kanagawa prefectures near Tokyo, local governments reported according to Japanese media including the Kyodo news agency.
Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn, and other storms have already disrupted some events at the Asian Games being hosted in the country.
Dujuan was bringing winds of some 144 kilometres (89 miles) per hour Monday as it moved to around 130 kilometres south of Katsuura City near Tokyo.
By early Tuesday the storm had shifted away from the coast and was heading northeast out to sea, with slightly diminished winds, the Japanese Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.
Japan Airlines cancelled 135 flights and All Nippon Airways scrapped 140, while more than 9,000 households near Tokyo were without power.
More than 1.6 million residents in and around the capital were urged to evacuate Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations are not mandatory.
Landslide warnings were issued for Tokyo as well as for Chiba, Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures. Railway operators in Tokyo and neighbouring regions suspended services on some lines.
In areas where warnings have been issued, "there's a risk the rain will continue as the typhoon moves north", the JMA's Takuya Hosomi told reporters.
The JMA warned on Sunday that rain and winds were expected to intensify even before the typhoon's arrival.
"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the agency said.
Dujuan forced the early closure of the Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video-game trade fairs, on Monday, its final day.
A major outdoor music festival and a baseball match both scheduled to be held in Chiba were also cancelled.
Social media posts showed images of roads in front of Kamakura station, a popular sightseeing spot, were flooded.
"There is flooding in various parts of the city, so travelling by car is dangerous," Kamakura City Mayor Takashi Matsuo said on X.
Flooding also inundated parts of Ichikawa city east of Tokyo.

“The “I” that considers is very different from the “I” that has fears. To have fears, to have, specifically, the fears on which Keats dwells, is to be immersed in acute sensation. The fear that one will cease to be is unlike the state of chronic fearfulness we call timidity. This fear halts and overtakes, it carries intimations of change or closure or collapse, it threatens to cancel the future. It is primal, unwilled, democratic, urgent; in its presence, all other function is suspended.”

====================================================================================================

Putin’s United Russia remains in power. What should concern the West is how it got there - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:12:48 UTC
06:12:48 KST

Unsurprisingly, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party won a vast majority of seats in the State Duma elections.
Preliminary results released on Monday indicated that United Russia won 355 of 450 seats in the state’s lower house of the legislature, or approximately 57.8% of the vote, Russia’s Central Election Commission announced.
Notably, at least 86 veterans of the war in Ukraine are expected to take seats in the Duma, The Moscow Times reported.
This does not include the hundreds of regional officials elected across the world’s largest landmass. The CEC said it will release the final results no later than October 5.
United Russia’s victory was an unfortunate but obvious conclusion. It is concerning that this election maintains Putin’s hold on power and could lay the groundwork to further escalate the war in Ukraine, especially as many fear another round of draft orders.
However, it is vital to understand why this election turned out this way in the first place.
How does Russia manipulate election results?
Some analysts and exiled journalists called this election Russia’s most uncompetitive election in its modern history, not only because of the way politicians campaigned, but also because of how easily the Kremlin manipulated the results
First, the way Russia conducts its elections already makes the results easier to distort.
Russia offered electronic voting in 33 of its 89 federally recognized regions. The election also spanned three days. Both factors made it much easier to tamper with results in an already rigged election.
Secondly, Putin manipulated the fact that Russians even have elections in the first place as proof that his citizens support his increasingly authoritarian actions.
In several appearances before the elections, he pointed to the fact that Russia is having elections despite the conflict in Ukraine as proof of three different things.
His primary unspoken claim is that Russia is still democratic, or at least a “managed” democracy. His second claim is that Russians are supportive of the “special military operation” in Ukraine (Putin’s government does not call the war a war in an effort to delegitimize Kyiv and control the domestic narrative within Russia). Finally, he uses the fact that Ukraine has not had an election since it declared martial law over four years ago as proof that Zelensky runs a fascist regime.
“We have to stand for election, not be afraid to run for office,” Putin said in June. “And I would advise everyone to do the same. Especially in Ukraine.”
This is Russia’s first parliamentary election since it began the war in Ukraine. Over the course of election season, Putin also framed elections as a way to show support for the war.
“Your choice and resolve will show once again that millions of people stand behind our fighters,” Putin said last week. “Participating in the elections is our shared contribution to Russia’s victory.”
United Russia’s public approval rating was at a notable low of 33% before Friday
However, United Russia’s public approval rating was at a notable low of 33% before ballots were cast on Friday, according to Russia’s Public Opinion Foundation, which is regarded as Kremlin-friendly.
Still, Kremlin-friendly paper Kommersant claimed that this year had the highest voter turnout since the early 2000s, at about 60%.
This is part of the reason why, if the claims are true, it is so interesting that there was also notably little campaigning in this year’s State Duma race.
In more than one instance, Russian state TV channels were set to moderate a debate between candidates, but none showed up.
"Good evening, and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," one Russian state TV News anchor said in one clip circulating online. The camera then cuts to six empty podiums.
"The candidates haven't turned up. So, it's goodbye from me."
It’s worth noting that Putin has never participated in a televised electoral debate during his nearly 20 years in office. It’s fair to assume that other members of his party have since followed suit.
However, the fact that this happened more than once shows that Russian politicians know that there is little competition. United Russia will take most of the seats in the federal government as well as state and local elections, and a few opposition candidates will make the cut to maintain a veneer of democracy.
Only four other parties cleared the electoral threshold
In the 2026 election, only four other parties cleared the electoral threshold: the Communist Party, the Liberal Democratic Party, New People, and A Just Russia.
Put together, they have 89 seats.
It can be hard to distinguish between these parties. Some obviously tilt more to the right or left, but on the “special military operation,” they all vote the same way and therefore function as systemic opposition.
Under Putin, the Kremlin has eliminated dissenting parties from the ballot. Russians now have only 17 registered political parties that can run in elections, down from around 100 in the 1980s.
A prime example is Yabloko, a left-leaning party that explicitly called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and was eliminated from the ballot this summer.
Some individual candidates have run, but 29 of at least 36 opposition candidates barred from the elections were Yabloko candidates, according to reporting by the Moscow Times and the independent Russian-language outlet Vyorstka.
Notably, some Yabloko candidates were fined for interacting with materials involving slain Russian activist Alexei Navalny. While they have denied the charges, they were still disqualified, fined thousands of rubles, and in some cases were declared “foreign agents”, the Kremlin’s label to brand someone a traitor with foreign influence.
This election in Russia has not changed anything. Because there is no way to see the real breakdown of the data, there’s no way to know how Russians actually feel about their government. That, in and of itself, is the biggest indicator of how rotted Russia’s political system is.
So United Russia will take another supermajority in the State Duma, the so-called opposition will continue to play by the Kremlin’s rules, and ordinary Russians will continue to live under a “managed” democracy.
No one ever thought the Kremlin would lose in this election. But it has shamefully signaled to its citizens and to the world that it’s not going anywhere.

Trump approval drops to career-low 32% as GOP support erodes over Iran war, inflation - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:12:13 UTC
06:12:13 KST

US President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to 32% - the lowest of his political career - as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living amid the unpopular Iran war, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
The poll, completed on Sunday, was conducted over a four-day period that saw Trump throw three major news organizations out of the White House and muse that Washington's iconic Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts - named after slain President John F. Kennedy - could be torn down if Trump's own name could not be added to it.
It found voters leaning away from supporting Trump's fellow Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
Trump's overall approval was down from a reading of 35% in last week's Reuters/Ipsos poll, with support among his own Republicans down to 73% from 82% a week earlier.
Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 on promises to tame inflation and end foreign wars. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted in the hours after he was sworn in, he enjoyed a 47% approval rating.
Just 17% of respondents in the new poll approved of his handling of the cost of living - the top issue Americans say will determine how they vote in November.
Iran takes a toll
Dissatisfaction among Republicans on inflation has been growing since Trump launched the war on Iran in February, which has pushed gasoline and diesel prices sharply higher. Now for the first time, Republicans who disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living outnumber those who give him a thumbs up - 51% to 44%.
Trump's approval rating is lower than any recorded for his Democratic predecessor, Joe Biden, whose presidency was also marked by surging inflation and who ultimately ended his reelection bid after a poor debate performance heightened concerns about his age. Biden's low was 35%, reached in late October 2024.
Only 34% of the most recent poll respondents approve of the strikes on Iran. The conflict has cut the world off from a significant slice of the oil and gas produced in the Middle East, and threatens to stoke higher inflation in the US and elsewhere as businesses pass on higher fuel costs to consumers.
Trump initially said the conflict would last a few weeks and that Iran needed to be bombed to stop it from developing nuclear weapons. Earlier this month, the Republican leader pledged the war would end "immediately after" the election. But Iran has shown no sign of giving up, and in recent weeks Tehran and its allies have threatened further disruptions to oil markets.
Some 82% of poll respondents - including nine in ten Democrats and three-quarters of Republicans - said the conflict would likely go on for an "extended period of time."
Democrats trump Republicans in midterm polls
The Reuters/Ipsos poll showed registered voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans - 43% to 35% - when asked how they would vote in the midterms. The 8-point gap was the biggest lead for Democrats in Reuters/Ipsos polling this year. For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.
The poll results on congressional voting plans provide an overall view of which party Americans nationwide want to see in charge in Congress, though the results don't capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House of Representatives.
Trump remains popular among Republicans on the issue of immigration - with 79% of his party backing him - but only 36% of Americans overall support his approach to the matter, and 55% disapprove. Some Republican allies in Congress have warned that his aggressive campaign to deport people in the country illegally risks alienating voters with family who recently immigrated to America, like some Hispanics.
Some 35% of poll respondents approve of Trump's approach to fighting crime, compared to 50% who disapprove.
The Reuters/Ipsos poll was conducted online and gathered 1,277 responses from US adults nationwide. It had a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

NDIS fraud crackdown working, government says
The work of a NDIS integrity taskforce has resulted in $2.1 billion in savings and benefits since 2022, the federal government says.
The Fraud Fusion Taskforce, a partnership between multiple government agencies to find and stop fraud in government programs, was set up in November 2022.
NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister says, since then, $1.2 billion in fraudulent and non-compliant payments have been prevented, while $900 million has been directed away from bad actors and towards participants.
The government expects the taskforce, as well as newer initiatives including a dedicated online portal for scrutinising payment claims made by providers, to save a further $2 billion by mid-2029.
A parliamentary inquiry into the extent of fraud in the $50 billion NDIS reported in July, making 12 recommendations, after hearing concerns not enough safeguards had been built into the scheme’s original design.
Fraud has been a constant talking point in recent years, with the Albanese government citing it, alongside overall scheme sustainability, as justification for cuts to the scheme expected to save about $38 billion over four years.
The agency that runs the NDIS commissioned research in 2023 that found people were more "amenable" to support an overhaul of the scheme if "rorts, fraud and unreasonable pricing" were posed as an existential threat to it.

New ten year post-service commitment for new ADF recruits
Defence has quietly doubled the post-service commitment for new recruits, meaning they can be called back to serve for ten years after leaving the ADF.
Existing ADF members already have a five year commitment. In effect, it means anyone leaving the ADF (unless they are at retirement age) can be called upon in a time of conflict.
It doesn't require former members to continue training or maintain skills, but they remain 'on the books' in case the need to boost numbers arises.
From October 1, anyone who enlists will have a ten-year obligation.
The change was a recommendation from a 2024 review of Australia's reserve forces, which warned the number of reservists who could be called upon was too low.
Key Event
Taylor not keen to weigh in on Bragg's super debate
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has declined to weigh in on a debate his own shadow housing minister has started on superannuation.
Andrew Bragg, the shadow housing minister, re-ignited the fight over retirement savings this morning when he floated potentially using super as collateral for a mortgage or to increase a person's borrowing capacity.
When asked about Bragg's proposal, Taylor didn't engage with the idea but said people should have "choices".
"Superannuation is Australians' money. It's Australians', but they should have a choice. And that's why we strongly support self-managed super funds," he says.
"But the policy you're talking about there is not Coalition policy."
Bragg also stressed in an interview with ABC News Radio earlier that the idea was not Coalition policy and rather it was him trying to spark debate.
Taylor says the Coalition will have more to say on housing policy "over the next little while," and has pointed to the opposition's plan to link migration to housing supply.
Marles doubles down on plans to sell off defence sites
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles is not backing down over a plan to sell off the high-profile Victoria Barracks in Sydney.
The base is one of 67 defence sites the government has identified for potential sale. The Daily Telegraph this morning reported Marles had issued an eviction notice for the barracks, requiring all military and civilian staff to be gone by December 19.
Marles refused to be drawn on the timeframe but pushed back at the Coalition's call for a pause on the sale of the sites it says as both strategically and historically important.
"We are the largest landowner in the country ... and so much of what we own, we don't use and that is a function of years of neglect under the former Coalition government.
"The most significant aspect of having a defence estate which is not fit for purpose is that we're not spending hundreds of thousands of dollars maintaining sites that we don't use.
"It matters that we have a government which is willing to make difficult decisions. It does not matter that we happen to have the oldest wine cellar in Sydney ... that is not a core capability."

Defence Minister Richard Marles says the F-35 fighter jet parts mistakenly diverted to Hong Kong were not technologically "sensitive".
Politico reported over the weekend that a shipment of F-35 parts, including a canopy with radar-resistant technology, was unexpectedly sent to Hong Kong after leaving Australia.
That sparked concerns that China might have accessed militarily sensitive technology from the US fighter jet program, used by a host of US allies, including Australia.

"We are obviously working with the United States and obviously its prime contractor here, Lockheed Martin, in respect of this," he said.

Dating app harms fuel calls to extend digital duty of care to platforms
Women are being forced to act as their own safety system on dating apps where experiences of sexual harassment, manipulation and controlling behaviours are widespread, a study has found.
Australian researchers found 99 per cent of heterosexual women surveyed had encountered at least one harmful behaviour on a dating app in the previous three months.
Unsolicited explicit messages, attempts to monitor activity, love bombing, negging and gaslighting are common experiences on dating apps, according to the study released on Tuesday by the Minderoo Foundation-funded Behaviour Insights Team (BIT).
Women reported routinely screening profiles for warning signs, withholding identifying information and carefully managing interactions to protect themselves from potential harm.
These accounts have fuelled calls to ensure a proposed digital duty of care was implemented to require online services to tackle systemic risks.

Artificial intelligence was described by Treasurer Jim Chalmers as the "biggest economic transformation of our lifetime" as he released the intergenerational report yesterday.

Asked if the figure was overly optimistic, Chalmers defended Treasury's assumption, insisting it struck the "best balance".

You know, the US assumes 1.4 per cent, the UK assumes 1.5 per cent, and so we've assumed a much more conservative number than they have," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

UK PM Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
LONDON – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Sept 21 he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time period, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region.
Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
“We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling,” he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.
“Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request,” he said.
Britain and Saudi Arabia have been close military allies for decades, with Britain serving as one of the kingdom’s largest arms suppliers.
Earlier in 2026, Britain deployed its Sky Sabre air defence system to Saudi Arabia to help protect it from Iranian missile attacks during the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
For the new air-to-air refuelling support, Britain will deploy one Voyager plane in the coming days.
“That is a time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review,” he said, adding that Britain was “playing our part” in the Middle East also by supporting efforts to keep the Strait of Hormuz open. REUTERS

Ed Sheeran hit by viral false claims after Macklemore controversy
Unknown

Ed Sheeran hit by viral false claims after Macklemore controversy
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Ed Sheeran's controversial US tour has sparked a wave of viral rumours. A false claim that his music was removed from Spotify racked up more than 3 million views on X, despite his music remaining available. Another video, viewed over 14 million times, falsely suggested Sheeran was now defiantly performing solo after all his support acts withdrew. But not only is the footage dated, Sheeran has in fact replaced the backing musicians. Vedika Bahl fact-checks in Truth or Fake.
Sheeran's tour has become engulfed in controversy, ever since US rapper Macklemore was removed from the line-up over his pro-Palestinian comments on stage, triggering an avalanche of all the support acts to pull out in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
The dispute has also fuelled a wave of claims online, including two viral posts falsely portraying developments around Sheeran’s shows.
One claim suggested Sheeran’s music had been removed from Spotify following the backlash. The post, shared by an account called HoopsCrave, amassed more than 3 million views on X. But there is no evidence that Spotify has removed Sheeran’s music. His songs remain available on the streaming platform, and there has been no announcement from Spotify confirming any such decision.
The account behind the claim is labelled "Parody and Satire" on its X profile, an important detail that was missed by many users who shared the post.
The only legitimate online result regarding the removal of Sheeran's music involves a decision by Irish radio station Classic Hits Radio, which said it had removed his songs from its playlist “for the foreseeable future" following listener feedback.
A second viral claim focused on Sheeran’s performances following the withdrawal of several support acts.
Viewed more than 14 million times, a video was shared with a caption suggesting Sheeran was defiantly continuing the tour alone after his opening acts cancelled and his band quit.
But the footage is not from the current Loop Tour.
The clip shows Sheeran performing with his loop pedal at London’s Wembley Stadium in 2022, during his Mathematics Tour. The same footage was published online years before the current controversy, including in connection with Sheeran’s documentary.
The suggestion that Sheeran has been performing entirely alone is also misleading.
At his Philadelphia show, Sheeran did begin the concert without any opening act. But he later performed with other musicians, after his backing band, Beoga, withdrew from the tour in support of Macklemore. Sheeran addressed the change on stage, explaining that he had brought in musicians he had worked with previously.
The supporting acts that have withdrawn include Danish band Lukas Graham, Irish singer Aaron Rowe and Finneas, the brother of Billie Eilish, who was due to perform during the South American leg. The artists have cited support for Macklemore and Palestinians as reasons for exiting the tour.

Ukraine Breaches Bunkers at Russian Droneport Built to Store and Launch Strike UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:02:19 UTC
06:02:19 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Breaches Bunkers at Russian Droneport Built to Store and Launch Strike UAVs
Satellite imagery published on September 21 indicates that Ukrainian drones pierced protective bunkers and damaged hangars at Russia’s Tsymbulova droneport in the Oryol region.
Militarnyi reported the damage on September 21, citing satellite imagery published by the Telegram channel Absolutely Reliable.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Tsymbulova site, near the village of the same name in Russia’s Oryol region, is a dedicated base for storing, preparing, and launching Russian strike drones.
Construction of the facility began in August 2024, and investigators believe the first drone launches may have taken place as early as that autumn.
By 2026, the complex had expanded substantially. Satellite imagery reviewed by Militarnyi showed new launch positions, storage facilities, and support infrastructure for several types of Russian strike UAVs.
By August, the site had 10 launchers for Geran-5 jet-powered drones, 6 for Geran-4 UAVs, 4 for Geran-3 drones, and 3 for standard Geran-2s.
The droneport has repeatedly come under Ukrainian attack.
On the night of August 30, Ukrainian Defense Forces struck storage and launch facilities at the same complex, damaging a Geran launch position and a storage facility for strike UAVs.
The expansion of Tsymbulova coincides with Russia’s broader expansion of its drone production infrastructure.
At its Alabuga complex in Tatarstan, Russia's largest drone-manufacturing operation, construction crews have been excavating underground production halls, with roughly 42,000 square meters of subterranean space already built for planned Geran lines.

What is the White House press pool and why does it matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:01:26 UTC
06:01:26 KST

The White House press pool covers and travels with the U.S. president every day, providing news outlets and the public with a near-constant stream of information on the leader's activities.
With the television pool suspending coverage of President Donald Trump after he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, the public could be deprived of critical information about the president's activities.
The five networks that have made up the White House television pool — ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and NBC News — rotate each day by having one network that covers the president's daily movements in Washington and around the world and remarks he makes. They feed video to other news organizations, and it airs on television stations while also being used by journalists who are not in those spaces to report in real time what the president says.
The pool covers events that are widely open to the press and is in more limited spaces like awaiting the president underneath the wing of Air Force One and travelling with him aboard the plane. The pool also allows the press to be present — and therefore the public to have access to information — in spaces like the Oval Office, which does not have enough room to accommodate all of the hundreds of reporters covering the White House.
"The press pool serves as the public's eyes and ears inside the White House, since not all journalists, let alone all Americans, can be there themselves," said Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation. "[T]he public is entitled to hear how the president handles difficult questions, even if the answer is by berating those who ask. All of that becomes far more difficult, if not impossible, without a functioning press pool."
"The president's handpicked journalists don't need a First Amendment — its whole purpose is to protect the reporters the government doesn't want around," Stern said by email.
The pool has chronicled U.S. presidents every day for nearly a century, since the presidency of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, according to the White House Correspondents' Association, which represents journalists who cover the White House and advocates for access to the president. Pool reporters brought the nation live coverage of events including the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.
Broadcast, still photographers, print or digital and radio reporters cover the president at the White House and when he travels, from each day's initial "call time" to when a "lid" is called — the time when staff alerts reporters that the White House says the president will not be seen again for the day.
For most of the press pool's history, the White House Correspondents' Association controlled which outlets covered the president on any given day. In recent years, this typically included a TV crew — a slot that rotated between ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — a rotating "print" newspaper slot, a radio slot, and dedicated slots for still photographers and "wire" services like The Associated Press, Reuters and Bloomberg.
Trump's White House, however, has taken a heavier hand in pool coverage. 
In February 2025, the White House press office announced it would take control of determining the press pool that covered Trump. The administration has since made several changes to the composition of the pool that covers Trump, including the additions of secondary TV and print reporters and the elimination of the "wire" slot. The White House also added a "new media" seat, for which outlets not typically included in the press pool can apply to be chosen for by the White House press office. Outlets in the new media seat have ranged from right-wing influencers to startup media outlets. 
According to a 2025 analysis from the Poynter Institute, the White House's selection of the secondary TV and new media slot reporters has skewed towards conservative outlets.
The Trump administration also tried to suspend a CNN reporter's press credential in 2018 — although the attempt was unsuccessful and the reporter's credential was soon restored. In 2009, the Obama administration's Treasury Department attempted to exclude Fox News from a series of TV pool interviews with executive-pay czar Kenneth R. Feinberg amid tension between the Obama administration and the network. The administration, however, reversed course after pushback from the included TV outlets.
The pool gives the public extensive access to the president's activity and lets the president quickly summon reporters when the White House wants to widely disseminate information. The pool, which is coordinated by the White House Correspondents' Association, includes rotating representatives from participating news outlets, which pay for their journalists' travel with the president.
CNN was scheduled to be the TV network pool representative for the president's trip to the United Nations General Assembly on Monday.
The rest of the TV pool said they would not replace CNN in a backup capacity, effectively depriving live video footage from independent news media of the president's activity in New York.
Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

Why Older Americans Are Drinking More Alcohol—Not Less
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
21:00:04 UTC
06:00:04 KST

The U.S. is in the midst of a temperance boom. Drinking rates have been steadily declining nationwide, with an August Gallup poll showing that only 54% of Americans ever consume alcohol—sharply down from 67% as recently as 2010.
Now, a study in the Annals of Internal Medicine takes those findings a step further, reporting that younger adults in the Millennial and Gen Z cohorts—people born from 1981 to 2012—are driving that trend. Meanwhile, older Americans, aged 50-64, are actually consuming more alcohol than they used to, with rates increasing by more than one third since 2018.
“It’s encouraging to see alcohol use decline for the first time since the start of the pandemic,” said lead author Dr. Brian Lee, a hepatologist and liver transplant specialist with Keck Medicine of USC, in a statement that accompanied the release of the report. “However, use remains above pre-pandemic levels and certain groups continue to have concerning trends.”
Lee and his collaborators conducted their work by sifting through the responses from more than 114,000 U.S. adults who, from 2018 to 2024, participated in the National Health Interview Survey—an annual study conducted by the U.S. Centers of Disease Control and Prevention. The survey consists of several face-to-face interviews throughout the year. In the current study, researchers looked at whether and how much respondents drink; heavy drinking, for instance, is defined as five or more drinks per day or 16 or more per week for males, and four or more drinks per day or eight or more drinks per week for females.
Americans saw a 2% drop in overall drinking and 8% in heavy drinking in just the 2022 to 2024 window. Total drinking dropped most dramatically among Gen Z, with rates falling nearly 6% from 2022 to 2024, compared with about 2% for Millennials. Heavy drinking fell by roughly a fifth in both generations.
Older Americans, however, went in the opposite direction, with those in the 50 to 64 age group seeing an increase of 4% in overall drinking, and a 36% spike in heavy drinking from 2018 to 2024.
The reasons for the changes are not clear, but greater public awareness of the health risks of drinking may play a role in alcohol’s overall decline. Alcohol has been linked to 62 different diseases, according to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, especially liver disease, cardiovascular disease, and various forms of cancer. But not all Americans are equally aware of alcohol’s health harms. Past Research from 2024 found that far more younger people know that alcohol negatively affects health compared to older adults.
Some of that knowledge may track back to the COVID-19 pandemic. “There was a lot of messaging around young adults who were dying more from alcohol-related harm during the pandemic,” says Lee. “So they could have been targeted for this.”
It’s seniors, however, who could most use the same kind of public information, especially as their drinking rates go up—because the older people get, whether they drink or not, the more likely they are to contract most diseases. “This age group faces some of the greatest risks of harm from alcohol, including cirrhosis and alcohol-related cancers,” Lee said in the statement.
Public information campaigns are just one of the possible causes of the drop in drinking among young people. It’s also possible that Gen Z and Millennials are simply swapping one intoxicant for another. “The idea of substitution is a leading theory,” says Lee. “With the legalization of cannabis, are people using that rather than alcohol?”
And sometimes, it might simply come down to money—which most older folks have in relative abundance compared to younger people. “Younger adults in general have less disposable income [to spend on alcohol] than middle-aged or older adults,” says Lee.
Reducing drinking—or cutting it out altogether—may ultimately be a self-reinforcing habit, as social expectations shift in a newly temperate demographic. “When fewer people around you drink, there is less and less societal pressure,” says Lee. “Older adults grew up in an era where everyone was drinking heavily around them and it was acceptable, whereas that's no longer the case among Gen Z or Millennials.”
Whatever the causes of our society’s new sobriety, the less alcohol anyone consumes, the better. Young people may have tumbled to that truth first, but the older age groups among us would benefit from doing the same.

Former ‘death squad’ leader appears in military trial in The Gambia
Sanna Manjang faces a military court for deserting the country’s army in 2017 after the end of Yahya Jammeh’s 20-year rule.
The former head of the Gambian paramilitary unit known as the “Junglers” has appeared in a military court to face charges of desertion.
Sanna Manjang is accused of deserting the armed forces when the lieutenant colonel fled the country in 2017 after the end of the 20-year rule of President Yahya Jammeh.
The case in the capital, Banjul, marks another official bid at accountability for killings which happened when Jammeh was in power, after a murder case against Manjang was dropped in July.
He is facing trial for an absence of “a continuous period of nine years with the intention of deserting”. Manjang was arrested in Senegal last November and was repatriated to The Gambia a month later.
The Junglers armed group, which operated independently from the Gambian army, has long been accused by the United Nations of extrajudicial killings and torture.
Longtime leader Jammeh was forced into exile after losing power in 2016 to Adama Barrow, then opposition leader and now president.
Following Jammeh’s departure, the country established the Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC). It investigated alleged crimes under his rule and found that between 240 and 250 people were killed by the state. It also found evidence of widespread extrajudicial killings, torture, kidnappings, witch hunts and other abuses.
Several of Jammeh’s accomplices, including Junglers, have been detained and sentenced abroad in Germany, Switzerland and the United States.
Murder charges dropped
Manjang was previously charged with four counts of murder, including that of AFP journalist Deyda Hydara in 2004, but the charges were dropped in July as The Gambia struggled to summon witnesses, some allegedly members of the death squad.
In addition to Hydara’s shooting, Manjang was accused of killing three other men, including one he personally decapitated.
After the charges were dropped, Manjang was charged separately for the assault of two other men in an ongoing trial.
