WASHINGTON – Thousands of flights across the US were snarled on Sept 21, with incoming flights halted for hours at major East Coast airports, before the Federal Aviation Administration resolved a telecommunications problem late in the afternoon.
The issue started around 9.45am when workers accidentally cut a telecom line in New Jersey used by the FAA.
This forced a halt to incoming flights at major airports on the day that 130 world leaders and dozens of ministers were arriving in New York for the annual high-level meeting of the United Nations General Assembly.
The FAA stopped arrivals at all three major New York-area airports as well as Philadelphia and Boston and two smaller airports in the New York area. The problems were not fully resolved for eight hours.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X late in the afternoon that telecom lines had been repaired and normal operations throughout the North-east were resuming.
He said it would take time to resolve existing delays and urged passengers to check the status of flights they were waiting for.
FlightAware, a flight-tracking website, said about 7,000 flights were delayed or cancelled, including 1,400 flights at the three major New York-area airports.
More than half of all flights were canceled at Newark, a major United Airlines hub. United said it issued a travel waiver to help impacted passengers.
The issue also forced the diversion of more than 100 flights to other airports.
The incident demonstrated the fragility of the ageing US air traffic control system, which Congress awarded US$12.5 billion (S$15.9 billion) for upgrades in 2025.
New Jersey Transit said a crew had been digging at one of its work sites 3m away from the utility markings and it was still trying to determine if Verizon or the contractor made the markings.
Duffy initially blamed an Amtrak construction crew, which he said accidentally cut into a fibre line in New Jersey near New Brunswick, causing a telecom outage and forcing FAA to pause flights in the North-east. Amtrak said it was not responsible.
Around 5.30pm, New Jersey Transit said most of the fibre cables had been repaired and should be coming back online shortly.
Newark Airport reopened for arriving flights after eight hours and LaGuardia also reopened after being shuttered for flights for much of the afternoon.
Verizon said it was working to repair the damaged cable near the Amtrak rail line and to restore connectivity as quickly as possible.
Flights at Philadelphia had again resumed late in the afternoon after a second ground stop was lifted. Reagan Washington National Airport also halted flights for more than an hour because of volume issues.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said a replacement circuit had failed at Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control, which was the primary communications for the centre.
A ground stop at Boston, which stopped accepting flights because of spillover volume, was also lifted.
“The timing is absolutely horrible and I’m very sorry for the delays and cancellations,” Bedford told reporters.
He stressed that safety was the top priority.
“We’re going to do what is necessary to make sure the airspace is safe.”
The loss of communications was tied to a failed circuit at a Philadelphia air traffic control facility that handles air traffic for the airports, Bedford said. Then authorities discovered that the construction crew had accidentally cut a backup fiber line.
“When it went to flip into the backup, we discovered that the backup fiber had a break, and that fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It’s massive, I’m told. Meanwhile, we’ve got the new circuit ready to install now,” Bedford said.
Philadelphia is an American Airlines hub.
In May 2025, the facility that guides air traffic in and out of Newark airport suffered a series of significant communications outages.
The FAA said in 2025 a telecommunications outage impacted communications and radar displays at Philadelphia TRACON.
In 2025, Congress approved US$12.5 billion to address the ageing air traffic control system, and boost controller hiring following decades of complaints over airport congestion and flight delays and a series of technology issues in recent years.
Duffy said Congress needed to approve another US$17.5 billion to finish the job.
“This is unacceptable in America,” Duffy said. REUTERS

It is noted that polls still indicate strong international public support for the organization, with the public blaming world leaders at least as much as the UN itself for its recent failures.
A poll conducted by GeoPoll for the UN Foundation and published last week found that six in ten people trust the UN to address issues that matter to them, but 85% of respondents said they had heard nothing or almost nothing about the process of electing a new secretary-general.
The election winner must secure the support of nine sitting members of the 15-member Security Council, with none of the Council's five permanent members—France, the United Kingdom, China, Russia and the United States—casting a veto.
Reaching consensus among the five permanent members is a difficult task, given the depth of the political divisions. Guterres's term ends on December 31.
Among the names mentioned as potential late-stage candidates are Lana Nusseibeh, a UAE minister of state and former UAE ambassador to the UN, as well as Sigrid Kaag, a former UN under-secretary-general and Dutch centrist politician. She briefly served as the senior humanitarian and reconstruction coordinator in the Gaza Strip before joining the advisory committee to Donald Trump's Board of Peace.
Other candidates mentioned include Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, the president of Kazakhstan, as well as Viktor Orbán, the former prime minister of Hungary, whom Trump still greatly respects but whom many European leaders condemn as a destructive populist.
Vuk Jeremić, the former Serbian president of the UN General Assembly, who came second to Guterres in the 2016 election, was also mentioned.
The publication also notes that much may in fact depend on political bargaining between the US president and China's leader Xi Jinping, as well as on whether Trump recognizes that the UN's future matters more to China than it does to him; this could mean agreeing to a candidate who suits China and is acceptable to the United States.
It appears that during Mike Waltz's tenure as US ambassador to the UN, the Trump administration somewhat softened its skeptical attitude toward the organization. The United States not only allocated an additional $1.8 billion for humanitarian needs in March, but also recently paid $827 million toward its membership dues—although this amount is less than a quarter of the total arrears owed to the organization, which is facing an acute shortage of funds.

Russian dictator Vladimir Putin and his Belarusian ally Alexander Lukashenko welcomed Grossi's willingness to nominate himself for the post of secretary-general of the United Nations.
U.S. President Donald Trump wants FIFA President Gianni Infantino to become the next Secretary-General of the United Nations.

Mapping the relay stations of human consciousness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:00:22 UTC
05:00:22 KST

Researchers have mapped deep brain regions that act as central communication hubs for the brain’s outer surface, identifying potential targets to help restore awareness in patients with severe brain injuries. The results reveal how specific areas in the brainstem and thalamus connect to multiple cognitive networks to maintain human wakefulness. The findings were published in Human Brain Mapping.
Human consciousness relies on a constant exchange of information between two main parts of the brain. The subcortex, which consists of deep structures near the brainstem, regulates basic arousal and wakefulness. The cerebral cortex, the wrinkled outer layer of the brain, handles higher-level awareness and conscious thought.
When a severe injury damages the pathways between these two areas, patients can fall into a coma or experience other disorders of consciousness. Medical therapies sometimes attempt to restart these dormant communication lines using electrical pulses, ultrasound waves, or targeted medications.
To make these treatments effective, scientists need to know exactly which deep brain regions to stimulate. The goal is to find central relay stations that connect to wide swathes of the cerebral cortex at once.
Morgan K. Cambareri, a researcher at Massachusetts General Hospital and Boston University, led a team to map these connections in healthy brains. Along with co-senior authors Jian Li and Brian L. Edlow and their colleagues, Cambareri sought to identify the specific deep brain nodes that are most integrated with surface-level cognitive networks.
The researchers analyzed brain scans from 168 healthy subjects. These scans were originally collected as part of the Human Connectome Project, a massive initiative designed to map the human brain.
The team used a specific type of imaging called 7 Tesla resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, tracks blood flow in the brain to measure which areas are active at any given moment. A 7 Tesla scanner uses an extremely powerful magnet, providing highly detailed images of brain structures. The resting-state designation means the subjects simply lay awake in the scanner without performing any specific mental tasks, allowing researchers to observe the brain’s natural baseline activity.
The researchers focused on six major networks located in the cerebral cortex. These included the default mode network (active during daydreaming and rest), the executive control network (involved in decision making), and the salience network (which detects urgent things in the environment). They also mapped the dorsal attention network, the visual network, and the somatomotor network, which handles movement and touch.
To trace how these cortical networks link back to the deep brain, the team used a mathematical tool called a tensor decomposition method. Traditional brain mapping tools often force different networks into rigid, non-overlapping boundaries. The method used in this study allows different functional networks to overlap in both space and time, providing a more realistic representation of human biology.
The researchers isolated the signals coming from the deep subcortex. They then superimposed the maps of the six cortical networks over the deep brain regions to see where they intersected. By doing this, they identified subcortical hubs. They defined a hub as a single physical location in the deep brain that synchronized with multiple different networks on the brain’s surface.
The team found highly connected hubs in regions that doctors have historically targeted to treat disorders of consciousness. For example, the ventral tegmental area in the midbrain was strongly linked to four different cortical networks.
They observed similar connectivity in the central lateral and parafascicular nuclei, which are specific clusters of nerve cells in the thalamus. The thalamus sits near the center of the brain and acts as a major relay station for sensory and motor signals.
Another major hub was located in the pontomesencephalic tegmentum, a region of the brainstem. This specific hub perfectly overlaps with areas that, when damaged by physical trauma, are known to cause comas in humans. This anatomical overlap provides strong evidence that this region is essential for maintaining consciousness.
The brainstem and thalamic hubs shared strong functional connections with both the default mode network and the salience network. This suggests these specific networks play a major role in how the deep brain signals the rest of the brain to wake up and pay attention.
The researchers also mapped whether the deep brain hubs were acting in sync with the surface networks (a positive correlation) or if they acted in opposition (an anticorrelation, where one area activates while the other quietens down). They found that many hubs had mixed relationships. For instance, a small region might activate in sync with the visual and attention networks but suppress activity in the default mode network.
In addition to the wakefulness centers, the team found widely connected hubs in regions typically associated with memory, emotion, and movement. These included the amygdala, the hippocampus, and parts of the basal ganglia like the putamen and caudate head.
One structure, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, was uniquely connected to all six of the studied cortical networks. It shared a positive correlation with four networks and an anticorrelation with two, acting as a highly integrated junction box.
While the study maps the functional relationships between brain regions, there are several caveats to consider. Functional MRI detects correlations in blood flow, but it does not track the actual direction of electrical signals. The researchers cannot tell if a deep brain hub is sending commands up to the cortex or if it is receiving instructions from the cortex.
A high level of connectivity does not inherently mean a brain region controls consciousness. The caudate head, for example, is widely connected to multiple cortical networks, but medical literature links it to behavior and cognition rather than basic wakefulness. The anatomical maps must be interpreted alongside previous clinical data to determine a region’s actual function.
The study also excluded the limbic network, a brain system heavily involved in emotion and memory. Excluding this network means the researchers might have missed additional hubs or underestimated the connectivity of certain regions.
Aligning the exact boundaries of tiny deep brain structures across 168 unique individuals is mathematically difficult. The researchers noted that small distortions can occur during data processing, especially in the brainstem, so the exact anatomical borders of these hubs carry a small margin of error.
Future research will need to combine functional imaging with direct electrical recordings of brain activity. Tracking electrical signals in real-time will allow scientists to see the exact millisecond a deep brain hub fires and determine whether that signal physically causes the rest of the brain to wake up.
The study, “Subcortical Hubs of Brain Networks Sustaining Human Consciousness,” was authored by Morgan K. Cambareri, Andreas Horn, Laura D. Lewis, Jian Li, and Brian L. Edlow.

When Xi Visits Washington, Trump Must Raise China’s ‘Ethnic Unity’ Law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on September 24, the agenda will be crowded: trade, technology, fentanyl, Taiwan, and global security. But there is another issue that the United States cannot afford to leave out: China’s newly adopted Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress.
U.S. President Donald Trump should raise a question that goes to the heart of American sovereignty: Why are Uyghur Americans being forced to choose between exercising their freedoms here and protecting their relatives from retaliation in China?
The Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress was passed by China’s National People’s Congress in March and took effect July 1. Beijing presents it as a measure to promote harmony among China’s ethnic groups. Uyghurs, Tibetans, Southern Mongolians, and others know better. The law does not protect unity; it codifies the forced assimilation campaigns our communities have long experienced.
Since 2017, the Chinese government has waged a systematic campaign to extinguish Uyghur national identity, religion, and cultural life. With the ethnic unity law, Beijing has codified and expanded this assault.
Americans must pay particular attention to the law’s reach beyond China’s borders. Article 63 of the law says organizations and individuals outside China can be held legally responsible for actions deemed to “undermine ethnic unity and progress or create ethnic division.” China’s vice justice minister openly defended this overseas provision as “legitimate, lawful, necessary, and feasible.”
Article 10 asserts that foreign entities “using excuses such as ethnicity, religion, or human rights to insult and disparage, contain and suppress, or infiltrate and undermine the PRC are to be resolutely opposed.”
That is an unmistakable message to Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, and other communities: Beijing claims the right to police our identities even outside its borders.
But it is also a threat to all Americans, even those without family ties in China. Any person who expresses a view China deems as contrary to ethnic unity can be targeted under the new law.
These risks are not hypothetical. As I wrote last month, Uyghurs abroad already feel its impact. Since the law went into effect, families have stopped sending their children to Uyghur language schools out of fear of retaliation by Chinese authorities. People who live thousands of miles from China are asking whether a speech, a social media post, a cultural event, or even a private act of faith could put family members back home in danger.
This is how transnational repression works. The Chinese government does not need to arrest every Uyghur activist living in the United States or Europe. It only needs to create an atmosphere of fear. It only needs people to believe that what they do abroad may have consequences for themselves or their loved ones.
That is why this law is not only a human rights issue, it is an immediate challenge to U.S. sovereignty.
Other governments have spoken out. Australia reportedly raised concerns with Beijing. Members of the European Parliament called for the law’s repeal. U.N. experts warned that it risks entrenching forced assimilation and expanding transnational repression. But the United States, which formally recognized China’s treatment of Uyghurs as genocide and is home to several prominent Uyghur civil society organizations, has not clearly condemned the law.
Trump should raise the ethnic unity law directly with Xi and make clear that attempts to enforce it against people in the United States will not be tolerated.
No foreign government has the right to determine what people living in America or in any democratic societies say, believe, teach their children, or advocate for. Washington should say clearly that China’s “ethnic unity” law stops at America’s borders.

Emine Erdogan calls for changes in consumption habits to tackle climate crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:52:30 UTC
04:52:30 KST

Turkish First Lady Emine Erdogan, who chairs the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste, has called for changes in consumption habits and stronger international cooperation to address the climate crisis.
Speaking at the opening of New York Climate Week on Monday, Erdogan said the Zero Waste movement had turned individuals from “helpless observers” into actors in tackling climate change.
She said small behavioural changes could develop into broader social practices when widely adopted and supported by sound policies.
Erdogan attended the event in New York alongside Family and Social Services Minister Mahinur Ozdemir Goktas. The Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry and the Zero Waste Foundation were among the main sponsors.
She said climate change was a consequence of the burden human activity had placed on the planet, pointing to fossil fuels, industrial processes, high emissions and excessive consumption.
‘Rebuild our relationship with nature’
Erdogan said humanity had created a system based on short product lifespans and growing waste, citing estimates that 9.2 billion tonnes of plastic have been produced since the 1950s, with 7 billion tonnes becoming waste.
She said the environmental costs of high consumption were often borne by vulnerable societies and future generations that contributed least to it.
“We must therefore begin by reducing excess in our habits alongside our waste, changing our mindset alongside our systems, and rebuilding our relationship with nature on the principles of balance and justice,” she said.
Erdogan described Zero Waste as a moral approach that promotes limits and responsibility as consumption and waste become increasingly normalised.
She said the programme launched at the Turkish presidential complex in 2017 had since spread to schools, hospitals, municipalities, public institutions and households.
“Our recovery rate, which stood at 13 percent at the time, has now surpassed 37 percent,” she said.
‘Shared responsibilities’
Erdogan said Zero Waste did not reduce the responsibilities of governments and companies, but instead expanded them.
She called for infrastructure that helps people make sustainable choices, more durable and reusable products, circular production technologies and stronger international cooperation.
She also recalled that Türkiye's Zero Waste resolution was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2022, while March 30 was designated International Zero Waste Day and the UN High-Level Advisory Board on Zero Waste was established.
Erdogan said she hoped Zero Waste would be recognised as a tool for climate action at COP31, which Türkiye will host in November.
She warned that continuing habits that cause today's environmental problems would undermine future solutions.
“No target will be sufficient on its own, and no technology will be a solution on its own,” she said.
Erdogan said the success of New York Climate Week would ultimately depend on actions taken after the event, expressing hope it would lead to new habits and collective action.
Following her speech, Erdogan watched a live performance by contemporary marbling artist Garip Ay. Editors-in-chief of newspapers and television channels, along with other guests, attended the event.

What Russia’s Parliamentary Election Results Mean for Putin and the War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:50:43 UTC
04:50:43 KST

Russia's electoral commission on Monday said that United Russia, the ruling party aligned with President Vladimir Putin, is projected to win the parliamentary election that has been widely criticized as a “sham.” The Central Election Commission (CEC) reported that 95% of the votes have been counted after a three-day election that began last Friday and ended Sunday.
While the final counts are not expected to be certified until later this week, preliminary figures show that the pro-Kremlin party is projected to win a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma, the lower house of parliament, giving United Russia an even larger supermajority than its 2016 record high of 343 seats.
Voter turnout was high at just over 59%, according to a briefing from the CEC.
The election is the first parliamentary poll since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the Kremlin has cast it as a referendum on support for what it calls a “special military operation” rather than a war. It was also, therefore, the first parliamentary election to include voters from four partly occupied regions of Ukraine—Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia—which Moscow claimed to annex illegally in 2022 but does not fully control. Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed in 2014.
Despite the vote being framed as an opportunity for citizens to express sentiments about the war, it is widely considered an illusion of choice: Russia’s supreme court last month banned the federal candidate list of the one registered antiwar party, Yabloko, from participating in the State Duma.
“I would be very careful to kind of unpack the distribution of votes as something indicative of what people think of the war,” David Szakonyi, a professor at George Washington University whose research focuses on Putin-era Russia, tells TIME. “They were not given the choice to vote against it.”
“This playing field was tilted before the votes were even counted, and this was not by any means a free and fair election,” he adds.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told members of the press Monday that the election showed how Russians support the country’s leader and “point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state.”
Experts believe that the election will allow the Kremlin to continue justifying its war with Ukraine—and it could further consolidate Putin’s power.
How the results could shape Russia’s war against Ukraine
United Russia’s supermajority could embolden parliament to pass “drastic legislation” with regard to future war efforts, Szakonyi says. Although United Russia already held a constitutional supermajority in the outgoing Duma, the larger margin could embolden lawmakers to pursue more severe measures.
“They have every resource available to them to change the political system as Putin directs,” Szakonyi says, “and the propaganda in the next week or two is going to heavily emphasize the fact that United Russia improved its performance.”
Parliament could specifically use the election to request more sacrifices from citizens for the war effort, according to Szakonyi. He says, for example, that the party could support legislation expanding military recruitment or defending “greater investment in the war effort, at the expense of healthcare, education, and domestic spending in general.”
“It is highly possible that they will at least kind of build on these electoral results when they demand more from voters and citizens in the next couple months in order to win the war,” he continues.
Olena Lennon, a practitioner in residence of National Security at the University of New Haven, agrees that Putin did not necessarily need any more legislative power to exact his objectives. Instead, the election was “more about creating an image of national unity and demonstrating to various audiences that Putin has total political control," she says, adding that hosting an election offers the “optics of popular legitimacy, institutional strength, and political stability.”
“That potentially gives Putin greater political cover and legitimacy for unpopular measures in the future—such as putting the economy in wartime production mode and potentially full mobilization," Lennon says.
A new mobilization campaign could inject new momentum into Russia’s offensive campaign and replenish battlefield losses. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last month that he believes Russia is planning to draft an additional 300,000 troops for the war effort.
“We are confident that following the elections, they will carry out a mobilization. We believe this will not take place in the major cities,” Zelenskyy said on Aug. 23. “They’ll lose all 300,000 of these newly mobilized Russians there; we’ll wipe them out.”
Putin has denied that a new mobilization campaign is planned, calling the rumors “utter nonsense” on Sept. 1. Two days later, at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin emphasized that there “is no scenario today that would require mobilization.”
More than four years into the war, Russians are facing rising living costs amid inflation that some economists attribute partly to military spending, with the prices of several food staples in rising this year. The country is also experiencing fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to strategically target its oil refineries and depots.
U.S. President Donald Trump has criticized the tactic in recent weeks, arguing that it is impacting global fuel prices. Energy-market data over the past six months, however, shows that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and subsequent constrictions of major oil passageways like the Strait of Hormuz is the much larger disruption to global oil and diesel supplies.
Trump’s latest comments on the matter came Monday.
“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine. A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission,” Trump said on Truth Social on Sept. 21. “This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended.”
Beginning Saturday, as Russia entered its last day of voting, the government said it intercepted more than 1,600 Ukrainian drones, including 450 directed toward Moscow. The figures, attributed to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin and reported by state media TASS, have not been independently verified.
According to a statement by Sobyanin on Telegram, this was the largest ever drone attack on the Russian capital, damaging the city's oil refinery.
How the world reacted to the preliminary election results
European powers have largely condemned the results. That includes France's foreign ministry, which released a statement on Monday saying that the vote did not meet the conditions for “free, pluralistic, democratic elections.”
“Heightened repression against civil society and the opposition, the exclusion of several political parties, growing restrictions on freedom of expression and the banning of independent media have undermined the Russian people's ability to freely form and express their choice,” the statement said.
A joint statement from the United Kingdom, Canada, Norway, Australia, and New Zealand was also released Monday, calling the vote a “sham”—particularly as it pertained to the four occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Holding Russia’s State Duma elections in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as Russia did in Crimea and Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk and Zaporizhzhia, is a gross violation of Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence, and the UN Charter,” the statement said. “We call on the international community to reject Russia’s attempts to normalise its occupation, condemn the holding of sham elections on Ukrainian territory.”
Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief and a vice president of the European Commission, called the elections “another major setback for Russian democracy” in a post on X.
“The Kremlin silenced dissent, barred the only registered party that opposed its war in Ukraine, and shut out international election monitors,” she said. “The veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia.”

Not the time to soften stance over Belarus, Lithuania says
UNITED NATIONS, Sept 21 - The European Union has no reason to ease sanctions on Belarus, Lithuania's foreign minister said on Monday, arguing that President Alexander Lukashenko's government continues to repress opponents, violate human rights and back Russia's war in Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said earlier in the day that Washington was working on a deal to purchase potash from Belarus, a key sector sanctioned by the EU.
The comments came a week after his administration negotiated the release of political prisoners in Belarus in return for some sanctions lifting, the latest in a year of talks between the two sides.
The US diplomacy is sensitive because Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Of course we would prefer to coordinate on sanctions policy as it is the most effective way to do this, but EU sanctions policy is a bit different," Kęstutis Budrys told Reuters in an interview at the UN General Assembly. "We do not see any reasons why our position on Belarus should soften as Belarus is not changing its behaviour."
The comments underscore a growing transatlantic divergence in approach toward Belarus.
While Budrys welcomed the release of prisoners, of which he said there remained about 1,000, and Vilnius would continue to provide assistance when they were freed, he said the EU should continue applying pressure on both the Belarusian and Russian governments, arguing that sanctions remained effective.
"We see how Lukashenko tries to find ways to get rid of them, and it means that we have to continue," he said.
"On our side, we have to be very exact and continue what works, and that is the pressure on the regime," he said.
The minister, whose country borders Belarus, said Minsk continued to pose a security challenge to the bloc, accusing it of orchestrating hybrid attacks against EU member states.
He cited what he described as the weaponisation of migration flows, particularly affecting Lithuania, Poland and Latvia, as well as smuggling operations, balloon incursions and other activities aimed at undermining European security.
"They are one of the major sources of hybrid activities against the European Union," he said.
The EU's current sanctions framework on Belarus remains in force until February 2027. REUTERS

UK prosecutors charge first person for Rwanda genocide
Vincent Brown is ‘alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others’.
Prosecutors have brought the first-ever charges in the United Kingdom against a man for his alleged role in the 1994 Rwanda genocide.
After a seven-year investigation, Vincent Brown, a 65-year-old doctor who was formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, was arrested and charged on Monday with one count of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of aiding crimes against humanity in Rwanda, prosecutors and local authorities said.

“The charges relate to allegations that Dr Brown took part in the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda in 1994,” Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service’s counterterror division, said in a statement. “He is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others.”
“This is the first time charges relating to the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda have been brought in the United Kingdom,” the statement added.
Brown was first arrested in 2006. His extradition to Rwanda, along with four other men, was refused by a UK court in 2017. “This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes,” Commander Helen Flanagan, head of counterterror policing, said.

Flights canceled, delayed at US East Coast after technical fault
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:47:00 UTC
04:47:00 KST

Flights at several major airports on the U.S. East Coast have been grounded or delayed on Monday following a technical malfunction, the top aviation body said, with reports of a primary circuit cable being cut as a source of the issue.
The technical problems occurred at a key regional air traffic control center, halting operations at every major airport in the New York City area for several hours on Monday, just as numerous foreign leaders were flying in for the U.N. General Assembly.
However, President Donald Trump's flight from Washington to New York was able to depart as scheduled.
The airports affected included JFK, Newark, LaGuardia and Westchester County in New York; Logan International Airport in Boston; Philadelphia International Airport; and Teterboro Airport in New Jersey.
The technical issues happened at the same Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) facility in Philadelphia – the Terminal Radar Approach Control center – that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty International Airport in the spring of 2025.
The center controls approaches and departures, as well as the spacing between aircraft in the terminal's airspace.
Broadcaster NBC News reported that the travel plans of thousands of passengers have been affected.
The FAA has not yet provided any information on how long the disruption might last.
Monday's airport disruption stemmed from two problems, according to Bryan Bedford, head of the Federal Aviation Administration.
On Monday morning, the primary circuit that carries data into that air traffic control facility failed, affecting flights for Philadelphia, as well as Kennedy, LaGuardia and Newark airports, the Federal Aviation Administration said.
The FAA then discovered that the backup fiber optic line had been cut due to construction. Verizon said contractors had dug up and cut the cable that runs along the Amtrak rail line in New Jersey. The company said in a statement that its technicians were racing to get the cable fixed.
By early afternoon, some flights were starting to resume at LaGuardia and in Philadelphia, but significant delays are expected through the rest of the day. Some airlines were allowing their customers to change flights without charging them fees. The FAA advised travelers to check the status of their flights with their airline before heading to the airport.
Bedford told reporters that the agency is working to restore the key connection as soon as possible by installing a new circuit on the primary line, while also working to repair the backup fiber optic line. He said it's not clear how long that will take.
"That fiber break is probably 13 hours to repair. It's massive," Bedford said, according to a video posted online by a CBS transportation reporter.
The primary circuit that failed is due to be replaced as part of the overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system.
Also Monday, the FAA began testing a new computer system that uses AI to help predict schedule conflicts and weather issues to help air traffic controllers reroute traffic.
But that system is initially being tested only in the Washington, D.C., area, so it does not appear to be linked to the outages.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X that around 7.00 p.m. GMT, flights were resuming at LaGuardia Airport and Philadelphia, while flights into Newark and JFK Airports were paused.
"An Amtrak construction crew accidentally cut into a fiber line in New Jersey, which caused a telecom outage and forced FAA to pause flights in the Northeast," Duffy said.
Around 7.00 p.m. GMT, Newark Airport, a key New York City-area hub, had 168 flights canceled and 97 delayed, while Philadelphia had 63 canceled flights and 189 delays, according to FlightAware.

Nestlé’s assets were transferred under the Kremlin’s control, but the company assures that it will &quot;continue operations&quot; in russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
22:44:28 EEST
04:44:28 KST

Nestlé’s assets were transferred under the Kremlin’s control, but the company assures that it will "continue operations" in russia
Kyiv • UNN
Nestlé Russia stated that it would continue its commercial activities "in full." The Kremlin transferred its assets and those of Auchan under the temporary management of L.E.V. Management.
On Monday, the Swiss food giant said that its Russian subsidiary would continue operating in Russia, despite the Kremlin’s decision to transfer control of the assets to a little-known company, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"The Nestle Group in Russia continues its commercial activities in full and declares its intention to unconditionally fulfill all obligations to customers, partners and employees," Russia’s TASS news agency quoted the company’s Russian press service as saying in an official statement.
According to a decree issued on Friday by Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, Nestle’s Russian assets and those of French retailer Auchan were placed under the temporary management of L.E.V. Management — a little-known company with no public track record of operations.
The Nestle statement, quoted by TASS, said that the transfer did not mean nationalization or a change of ownership. The company expressed confidence that cooperation with the L.E.V. Management team would help it continue developing and improve the efficiency of its operations.
Following the announcement of Putin’s decree last week, Nestle — the producer of Nescafe coffee and KitKat chocolate bars — said it would "take all necessary measures to protect its rights and ensure the continuity of business processes in the interests of all stakeholders, primarily its employees."
The Kremlin said that hostile actions by "unfriendly" countries played a role in the decision to take control of Nestle’s and Auchan’s Russian assets.
In previous cases, the imposition of temporary management was often followed by state expropriation, with the assets subsequently transferred to individuals or companies linked to the Kremlin. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that, for now, this was only temporary management.

No median cuts, surface intersections on future high-speed NH corridors: NHAI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:42:30 UTC
04:42:30 KST

A view of the Barapullah Phase-3 elevated corridor that is scheduled to be inaugurated on September 29, 2026, in New Delhi on Saturday. (ANI Photo)
NEW DELHI: New access-controlled high-speed national highway corridors will have no median (divider) openings and no at-grade (surface level) intersections, a move that aims at eliminating conflict points and reducing crashes.It has also been mandated under new NHAI guidelines issued on Monday that these corridors won’t have raised concrete dividers but flush medians — painted centre lanes with thick wire ropes or crash barriers. These will also have advance exit signage at 5 km, 2 km, 1 km and 500 metres to help motorists prepare for lane changes well in advance.The design provisions are aimed at improving safety on access-controlled corridors where cars are allowed to travel at speeds of up to 100 kmph. Delhi-Dehradun Expressway, Ambala-Kotputli corridor and Trans-Haryana corridor are among such highways.NHAI said the guidelines seek to bring uniformity in the planning and design of access-controlled high-speed corridors and ensure consistency in technical standards across projects.“The guidelines will apply to all upcoming four-lane and six-lane greenfield and brownfield access-controlled high-speed national highways,” an NHAI spokesperson said.
Officials said eliminating median cuts and surface intersections will prevent dangerous cross movements and wrong-side driving, while standardised signage and geometric design will improve traffic flow and reduce the risk of high-speed crashes on the new generation of national highway corridors.
The move is significant as govt has set a target of developing 50,000 km of access-controlled high-speed corridors over the coming years.At present, there are no separate standards governing the planning and design of access-controlled high-speed national highways, except for expressways. The new document fills that gap by laying down dedicated norms for highways that are access-controlled but not classified as expressways.The guidelines also specify lane configuration based on detailed traffic assessment and future traffic projections. Depending on the expected traffic volume and the number of structures such as bridges, flyovers and interchanges, these corridors will have a right of way of 60 metres or 70 metres.

Eli Lilly CEO says 700,000 new seniors have started GLP-1s after Medicare coverage, and 70% are on Lilly drugs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:37:01 UTC
04:37:01 KST

Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks told CNBC on Monday that 700,000 new seniors have started GLP-1 treatments since Medicare coverage of obesity drugs launched in July, and 70% of those patients are on Lilly medicines.
In an exclusive interview with CNBC, Ricks called the rollout of coverage "very encouraging" so far, saying its expansion of the broader GLP-1 market "is what we had hoped." His comments offer the latest metrics on how much the coverage is expanding access to the medicines, and who appears to be gaining more momentum among new patients between Lilly and its chief rival, Novo.
The coverage is through a temporary program called "Bridge," which allows eligible beneficiaries to obtain weight loss drugs for a $50 monthly co-pay. The federal Medicare program is for people age 65 and older or with disabilities and covers about 66 million people.
Lilly's blockbuster obesity injection Zepbound appears to be the biggest winner of Medicare coverage so far. Through the program, seniors can get access to Zepbound along with Lilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, Novo's competing Wegovy pill and blockbuster injection under the same name.
"We're capturing about seven out of 10 of those new patients, and a lot are still on Zepbound," he said. "I think we still see physicians focusing on those with the most body weight and the most complications. That's where Zepbound plays a big role."
Lilly's Foundayo plays a larger role for patients who are looking for a convenient treatment option and "maybe just need to lose 25 to 30 pounds," Ricks added. That pill launched in April a few months behind Novo's, but Ricks told CNBC that one-third of new patients on oral GLP-1s are taking Foundayo.
He said he hasn't heard of many logistical issues with the rollout, saying the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services "did a nice job rolling this out," educating physicians and working with both companies and the insurance system.

Does Australia need another baby bonus as it faces a birth rate struggle?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:32:06 UTC
04:32:06 KST

in brief
- Australia faces a choice between higher immigration or having more babies to fix an ageing workforce and shrinking tax base.
- Experts say migration is the most effective strategy to staff essential sectors like aged care long term.
Australia will need to boost its population to support the elderly and the economy in the long term, experts warn, after the government's latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) found that people are expected to live longer and have fewer children.
The report landed as politicians float the idea of bringing back the Howard-era baby bonus and argue over the need to reduce migration.
Independent MP Bob Katter has recently suggested an up-front cash payment of $75,000 per child would reverse the declining birth rate, which is now expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065.
The argument was dismissed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said on Monday that family support policy should be more than just "here's some cash".
However, Australia does face challenging demographic questions, with experts saying the choice will come down to more migrants or more babies.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"We will have a large pool of elderly people that we have to support," Dr Pelin Akyol, research manager at the economic think tank The e61 Institute, told SBS News.
"If we have a smaller pool of people working, then it will be a big fiscal problem in this country — and in every country."
Global and domestic surveys show that most people want to have more children than they end up having, owing to cultural, social, and economic constraints which are difficult to address.
"With AI and everything else going on right now, it is hard to know what will happen," Akyol said. "But what we know at this point is that it's going to affect the economy in a bad way".
The fertility illusion
While the IGR highlights a collapsing birth rate, demographers caution that official metrics paint a distorted picture of Australian family choices.
Peter McDonald, emeritus professor of demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that the country's reliance on international students and temporary visa holders skewed the headline Total Fertility Rate (TFR).
Temporary migrants are often young adults aged 20 to 35 who are in higher education or the early stages of their career. While they are counted as potential mothers, they "hardly have any births," McDonald said, which drives the TFR down.
"That's one of the central reasons why Australia's fertility rate has been falling because the temporary population's been rising," he said.
The birth rate for women born in Australia is around 1.64, higher than the Australian Bureau of Statistics headline fertility rate of 1.48. While this is still below the replacement rate of 2.1, Akyol said the immigration influence on TFR is different in Australia than in other comparable nations.
"In Germany, migrants have higher fertility rate than natives," she said. "But in Australia, it is the opposite".
McDonald also warns against placing too much faith in the long-term projections of the IGR — which assumes net overseas migration will remain flat at 235,000 annually for the next four decades — and that immigration and total births can't be viewed separately as they are "not independent of each other".
"If you can tell me what the birth rate is going to be in 10 years, you're a better man than me," he said. "But if you can tell me what it is in 40 years, then you're a miracle worker."
Is a baby bonus the answer?
Katter's proposed return to former treasurer Peter Costello's cash payment for each newborn child would cost upwards of an estimated $22.5 billion a year for the present 300,000 babies born each year in Australia.
Akyol's research into the 2004 policy indicates that cash incentives do increase the fertility rate, but the effect is "not huge" and, given how different the world is today, "it is not guaranteed we will see a similar effect".
While a $75,000 payment is "huge" compared to the $3,000 of the original policy and "might have an effect", Akyol doubted this was the best use of money when other factors like support benefits also play a key role in family decisions.
McDonald said Australia's tax system has become too narrowly focused on early childcare, making raising older children harder for working families.
"Today, about 58 per cent of families get no family allowance for their children," he said. "It's not just about very young children... supporting families with children is also about supporting older children, and we've gone a long, long way away from doing that."
A median worker claiming both employer and state parental leave would already receive around $48,700 before tax, something McDonald said disadvantages those without full-time employment. Instead of re-introducing lump-sum payments, he calls for a broader review of child equity.
"I think there's a need for an inquiry into the system of child support payments, to deal with two issues: one is the inequity of the system for very young children, and two, the lack of support for older children," he said.
"Children are a social good.... so I think there is justification for supporting families with children; it's called horizontal equity."
"Horizontal equity used to be quite a big thing back in the 1980s ... I think it needs to be revisited."
A national trade-off
To offset a declining taxpayer base, the IGR highlights increasing older workforce participation and leveraging artificial intelligence to automate labour gaps.
However, McDonald questioned the feasibility of expecting Australians to work deeper into their 60s and 70s.
"A lot of people, particularly those who work in physically demanding jobs, do not want to work beyond pension age. They've had enough," he said.
"AI is going to make a big difference to future labour force needs, but AI is not going to wipe the bottoms of people in aged care."
Akyol said current debates around migration could soon flip as birth rates drop across the globe, including in key migrant origin countries such as China and India. With a shrinking global talent pool, nations could shift from seeking to restrict migration to actively competing for skilled workers.
"In the long run, there might really be a competition for getting the best migrants," Akyol said. "Because in all developed countries, fertility rate has been decreasing... and it seems like there is no hope that it will just turn back and increase again."
"There is no easy solution here. There is a trade-off with every kind of policy."
Relying on immigration is the most direct mechanism to address workforce shortages in sectors like aged care, which are already under strain, McDonald said — something he said the government has failed to communicate in its messaging.
"The IGR shows the advantage of a higher level of migration for the federal government's bottom line," McDonald said. "Migrants make our prospects of dealing with a future aged population much better."
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:30:38 UTC
04:30:38 KST

MOS creates basket-like aluminium pavilion at Art Omi in New York
US studio MOS Architects has used aluminium shingles to cover an egg-shaped pavilion at Art Omi in Upstate New York, creating a place to rest that draws stylistically on pre-modern basketry and mid-century futurism.
An experiment in form and material, A Dome with Four Oculi was installed on the expansive Art Omi campus as a place of shelter and rest.
The structure sits on stilts and consists of a shell that MOS compared to a crinoline dress.
It was then covered by aluminium shingles that overlap and are held in place by stainless steel bolts. Combined, the shell is around a quarter-inch thick. It has two portholes on the side that look out into the landscape and is open at the top.
MOS co-founder Michael Meredith told Dezeen that structurally it is like an "upside-down basket", connecting to both the studio's work in easy-to-assemble prefabricated aluminium structures and a focus on the potential for experimentation at small scales.
"We've been working for years with folded aluminium and basically using it like paper, almost like large-scale models," said Meredith.
It was designed to be put together with standard tools in just a few days.
Conceptually, the structure takes cues both from pre-modern basketry as well as from the Airstream trailer.
"There's something of woven architecture in it, almost pre-modern," said Meredith. "Woven structures have an economic use of material, lighter material in this case. There's something nomadic."
"But there's Airstream trailer quality too," he continued. "You can see a bunch of stuff in it."
Beyond the thematic elements, the structure also provides shelter and a place to sit in the fields of Art Omi, which hold dozens of rotating art and architecture installations.
The oculi on the sides of the structure also provide vistas across the field.
Triangular cutouts on the side provide access and give the structure as in a tent.
Viewed from elsewhere, the pavilion has a face-like quality. It almost looks like the top part of the head of the Iron Giant from the 1999 film.
"It's also, as everybody tells us, a little bit ridiculous," said Meredith, who said it was like a Buckminster Fuller dome reimagined by artist Philip Guston. He added that the woven nature of these structures makes it more practical than typical domes, as the sides could be modified and shaped as in basketry.
MOS is well known for its conceptual work and writings.
A Dome with Four Oculi relates to recent writings by the studio, such as its Smaller Architecture book, which calls for smaller architecture studios to experiment.
It was developed partly in response to what Meredith calls a "weird moment" for architecture. The prevalence and desire for bigness have left out an important space that architecture holds for expression.
"Architecture is in a weird moment in general. It used to be a more active part of cultural production," he said.
"At some point, though, it sort of shifted and just feels commercial. Everything just feels like a commodity," he continued.
"So that's what's nice about Art Omi. It's sort of outside the system, and it gives you a chance to reflect and think about something else."
The pavilion was part of Art Omi's fall architecture programming, which included TAELON7's Limbo Engawa pavilion.
Art Omi has been doubling down on its commitment to architecture and, in 2024, announced a series of 18 pavilions designed by established architecture studios such as SO-IL.
In London, Studio Saar created a shield-topped pavilion for London Design Festival, examining Britain's colonial history in India.
The photography is by Michael Vahrenwald.

Parliament ready to convene extraordinary session to pass bills needed for financial support, Speaker says
Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Ruslan Stefanchuk said this at a briefing following a presentation of work on Ukraine’s new Civil Code in Kharkiv, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We are ready [the lawmakers are ready to vote on bills related to Ukraine’s commitments to its partners and the provision of financial support – ed.] when these laws are clear, when they have been discussed with the committees, and when they are submitted to the chamber in a prepared form,” he said.
The Speaker of the Ukrainian Parliament noted that the Verkhovna Rada does not yet have some of these bills.
“There are 45 bills, 18 of which, unfortunately, have not yet been submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine by the government. We are waiting for them to be submitted,” Stefanchuk said.
The Speaker recalled that certain deadlines apply from the moment a bill is submitted or passes its first reading.
“There are 14 days from submission to the first reading and 14 days from the first reading to the second reading – that is the minimum,” he said. At the same time, the timeline for consideration will depend on the number of amendments, he added.
“Unfortunately, lawmakers who call on their colleagues to work more are abusing their right to submit amendments, filing more than a thousand amendments to each bill, which significantly slows down the work of the Verkhovna Rada,” the Stefanchuk added.
Taking the opportunity, Stefanchuk appealed to his colleagues not to abuse the procedure or delay parliamentary proceedings “so that Parliament can work quickly and effectively.”
“As soon as the documents are ready, we are immediately prepared to convene an extraordinary session to vote on all the necessary bills,” Stefanchuk assured.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada had previously rejected three laws that could have unlocked more than $4 billion in international financing for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy Responds to Trump: Ukraine Ready for Energy Truce if Russia Halts Strikes

Zelenskyy Responds to Trump: Ukraine Ready for Energy Truce if Russia Halts Strikes
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly responded on September 21 to US President Donald Trump’s social media statement, agreeing that Russia’s war against Ukraine “must be ended” and confirming that Kyiv is actively discussing diplomatic de-escalation frameworks with Washington.
Following his phone conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” citing the destruction and temporary shutdown of a large number of Russian refineries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Trump called for an immediate end to the “ridiculous and never ending War,” arguing that “the whole World suffers” from the war and pointing to an estimated 25,000 monthly casualties as a primary reason to halt the fighting.
In a statement posted on X, Zelenskyy affirmed that Ukraine has sought peace since the onset of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and highlighted ongoing dialogues with the Trump administration aimed at formulating concrete steps to bring the war to a close.
He explicitly outlined Kyiv’s conditions for a partial energy and infrastructure truce, noting that matching Ukrainian de-escalation measures would depend on a complete halt to Russian attacks against Ukrainian civilian supply systems.
“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” Zelenskyy stated, adding that “solutions are possible” and will be further detailed during bilateral discussions with US partners on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
While expressing willingness to advance reciprocal security guarantees, Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine’s long-range drone technology has permanently altered the dynamics of the war by ensuring that the aggressor state experiences direct consequences.
“It will no longer be the case that only the country under attack suffers,” Zelenskyy stated. “The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will suffer as well. Technology makes this possible”.
The Ukrainian leader’s remarks follow days of intense diplomatic exchanges over rising global energy prices, with Kyiv emphasizing that any halt to its deep strikes on Russian oil facilities remains contingent on reciprocal protection for Ukraine’s own energy grid and critical infrastructure.
Zelenskyy recently proposed a conditional energy de-escalation framework to Western partners, indicating that Kyiv is prepared to halt strikes on Russian refineries if international partners can secure and guarantee a complete end to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy, port, and logistics infrastructure.
In a statement, he emphasized that any mutual halt must be reliable, long-term, and enforceable rather than a brief operational pause. Expressing skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to abide by an agreement, Zelenskyy warned that Russia might seek temporary relief for its domestic fuel markets ahead of elections before resuming strikes.

Trump and Zelenskyy to discuss possibility of granting Ukraine licences to produce Patriot missiles

Call it a win: boredom but no temper tantrums in Burnham’s first face-to-face with America’s King Baby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:18:40 UTC
04:18:40 KST

How do you deal with a problem like The Donald? The simple answer is that you don’t. You can’t. The normal rules of political engagement don’t apply. The US president is like a five-year-old child with the world as his set of toys: a King Baby.
Nothing is ever constant or predictable. What’s agreed one day can be forgotten the next. Any deal can be interrupted with a temper tantrum at any time. Trying to second-guess Donald Trump is a fool’s errand.
So the primary aim of Andy Burnham’s first face-to-face meeting with Trump was to get out alive with his – and the UK’s – self-respect intact. To take no incoming damage. And whatever he did, not to offer the president a third state visit. Keir Starmer never really lived that one down. Putting out on the first date only encourages the other person to think you’re a pushover.
The hoped-for result was a pleasant and almost forgettable bilateral meeting at the United Nations general assembly in New York. It was only scheduled to last 30 minutes, so more like speed dating – one step up from two world leaders shooting the breeze while getting to know each other. Where differences could be acknowledged without causing a major diplomatic incident.
All of which falls pretty comfortably within Burnham’s skill set. Andy’s stock in trade is an easy-going self-confidence. He’s comfortable in his skin in a way that Keir never was. Or maybe the artifice is just better concealed. He understands that trash-talking is all in a day’s work for most politicians. In the past, he may have called Trump all sorts of things. Poisoned politics. Someone who would be unwelcome in Manchester. Well, that was then, this is now. Things change. Just like Trump. Now he would be welcoming the US president to the G20 in Manchester next year. Who would have guessed?
And it all looked to have gone pretty much to plan. Maybe Trump also wanted this meeting to go well. His poll ratings in the US are dire, the midterm elections look like trouble and The Donald needs all the friends he can get – even if he had just tried to lose a few more of them in his speech to the UN earlier. A speech that had been even wilder and madder than many of his previous ones. Still, at least he hadn’t threatened to invade a Nato country this time. And it’s always good to learn of countries you never knew existed. Anyone for “Kazakhistan”?
Taking questions with Trump afterwards, Andy didn’t look quite as self-assured as usual – he seemed very much on edge – but who could blame him for that? This was his first time as prime minister at the UN and The Donald always has it in him to blow any meeting out of the water.
It was Andy who went first, trying to remember what they had just talked about. It had all been a bit of a blur. That was it – they had talked about Iran. In his earlier speech, The Donald had suggested it was a toss-up whether he came to a deal with Iran or whether he annihilated it. On the whole, Andy was in favour of a deal. Quickly if possible. The war was causing a massive hit to the cost of living. He chose not to highlight the irony of Trump calling on Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop bombing Russian refineries as it was playing havoc with the cost of oil. Pots and kettles and all that.
Burnham then bigged up the deal with Saudi Arabia. The one where we send one plane to refuel Saudi fighters that don’t need refuelling because their targets are only a few hundred miles away. Finally, he mentioned the Falklands. By now The Donald was looking a wee bit bored. Unsure where the Falklands are or why they had been talking about them. Perhaps he was wondering why he was looking even more orange than usual.
Then came the actual questions. Was Andy a man with whom Trump could do business? Sure he was, said The Donald. Andy was a “great businessperson”. Really? And by the way he was a lot nicer and a lot more talented than his predecessor. Poor Keir. Not only is he no longer prime minister, but he’s still getting rubbished at meetings he would have been attending. He really can’t buy a break. But that’s Trump for you. Andy shouldn’t relax too much. That will be him getting trashed one day.
On we went. Immigration. Burnham deftly trying to give credit to the immigrants working in the NHS while going on to condemn illegal immigration. Trump was just dreaming of walls and border guards. What about patriotism? Which did the prime minister prefer: Manchester or Manhattan? By now Andy was feeling a bit more self-assured that the whole thing wasn’t about to go tits up, so he joked about the president calling Manchester “some town”. Trump just shrugged. It still is just some town to him, but he wasn’t going to labour the point. He was trying to be on his best behaviour. For a five-year-old.
Then a question on the sanctions imposed on illegal settlements in the West Bank. Trump looked bewildered. Had never heard of them. Andy insisted he had personally called the White House to inform the president of the UK’s intentions. It had been done to maintain the possibility of a two-state solution and to restore trust in politics. This was more like the authentic Burnham. Standing up for what he believed. Trump said nothing. Maybe he actually did recognise the prime minister as an equal.
There was just time for a mention of the proposed handover of the Chagos Islands – It’s a terrible idea,” said Trump unhelpfully, to which Andy gulped “We’re looking at it” – before we closed with Trump insisting relations with the UK had never been better and that Britain was a country on the up. Some of us could distinctly remember The Donald saying the UK was on the slide only last week. But who’s counting?
Then a minder called the impromptu presser to a close and kicked everyone out of the room. Trump looked blank. He often does. Burnham looked relieved. He had got out of his first encounter with the president alive. Both he and the UK were still intact. Chalk this one up as a win.

Experts: Affordable Munitions Could Help USAF in Taiwan Conflict, but More Is Needed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:29:22 UTC
04:29:22 KST

A new think tank report calls for a buildup of U.S. drones and munitions needed for a potential fight against the Chinese military over Taiwan, thought other experts argue the report is missing some nuance in the munitions equation.
The Center for a New American Security’s report, “Drones, Missiles, and the U.S. Munitions Shortage: The Role of Affordable Mass in a Taiwan Conflict,” released Sept. 18, makes the case for increased long-range weapons to strike Chinese military targets to thwart a takeover of Taiwan.
The report, authored by Philip Sheers and Stacie Pettyjohn, notes a gap between the number of targets the U.S. would need to strike and its diminishing stockpiles, given the ongoing use of such weapons in the conflict with Iran.
“In a U.S.-China conflict over Taiwan that is likely to become protracted, the inventory depth and disruption that lower-cost systems can provide will be invaluable to reversing U.S. disadvantages and stopping China from achieving its operational objectives,” Sheers and Pettyjohn write.
To close the gap, the report recommends both stockpiling high-end missiles and massing cheap drones and munitions to overwhelm a Chinese attack. Other recommendations include:
- Multiyear funding and contracts so manufacturers can expand weapons production capacity and the Pentagon can rebuild long-range missile stores
- Funding for cheap, long-range anti-ship and land-attack weapons to quickly fill inventory gaps.
- Standardized shared components across airframes to lower costs and scale production.
- Pairing inexpensive drones with advanced missiles to drain enemy air defenses.
- Prioritizing easily built designs rather than over-engineering
- Routing updates and briefings to Congress on these issues
The White House and Pentagon have taken steps to boost munitions production this year, especially low-cost weapons.
In July, the Pentagon announced multiyear framework agreements with Anduril, CoAspire, and Zone 5 Technologies to mass-produce missiles for the Air Force, followed by a Sept. 17 announcement that Lockheed Martin would expand production of the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The former announcement is part of USAF’s Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, unveiled in the fiscal 2026 budget with plans to ramp up such production to hit 5,300 missiles a year by 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2031.
The current projected five-year budget for FAMM is more than $12 billion for nearly 27,000 missiles.
Retired Air Force Col. Mark Gunzinger, now with AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the CNAS report’s call for more munitions is necessary. But he cautioned that the report’s focus on making weapons affordable needs to be tweaked.
“It should not be about buying cheaper weapons; it should be about how to optimize cost per effect in the battlespace,” Gunzinger said.
The Air Force must fight asymmetrically and maximize the effect of each strike, regardless of munition or platform, and there’s a middle ground for weapons and platform development and procurement, Gunzinger argued.
Precision-guided, specialized weapons such as the Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile and the platforms that deliver them are pricey, and lower-end, short-range munitions for stationary targets have their place, but Gunzinger said defense planners can often make too much of a tradeoff if they focus too much on price to the detriment of capability.
“Now you’ve got something that, ‘OK, you hit a price point, but is it going to survive long enough to do its mission?’” Gunzinger said. “Is it going to be able to shoot its weapon before it dies?”
A Numbers Game
The CNAS report’s operational and tactical focus is countering a People’s Liberation Army attack on Taiwan with strikes against PLA ships—destroyers and amphibious assault ships—and hitting airfields on the periphery of the country, close to the Taiwan Strait.
But it does not include a plan to hit the Chinese mainland interior.
“The paper focuses on denying a PLA joint island landing campaign without considering strategic attacks to deny sanctuaries to the PLA and collapse China’s ability to maintain the offensive,” Gunzinger said. “This risks reducing a conflict with the PLA over Taiwan to a force-on-force math problem, like how many weapons and aircraft are needed to attack PLA forces located in the Taiwan Strait and coastal China. It risks becoming a numbers game.”
Because striking mainland China in a Taiwan invasion scenario might be required, Gunzinger said the current 500-nautical-mile limit of most affordable strike options undermines the CNAS report’s conclusion that more mass will equate to victory.
“China has the capability to project outer and inner rings of airborne and sea-based air defense sensors and shooters to defend its cross-Strait forces and operations,” Gunzinger said.
And using nonstealthy drones to approach the Chinese coastline to then launch affordable missiles doesn’t work either, he said. “This would likely result in losses of the aircraft and their weapons.”
“We win part of the battle,” Gunzinger said. “They win the war.”
Breaking a Stalemate
The numbers-on-numbers approach is what has led to a stalemate in the Russia-Ukraine War, said retired Navy Cmdr. J. Michael Dahm, now a senior fellow for aerospace and China studies at Mitchell.
“Just because you can generate mass doesn’t mean that you’re going to achieve your effects,” Dahm told Air & Space Forces Magazine. “You may be able to keep your adversary off balance, but if you’re not going to then judo throw him into what you want him to do, you’re just engaging in this kind of protracted, endless warfare.”
Throughout the history of the modern Chinese military, it has mostly been defense-oriented, Dahm said. The PLA has airfields dotting its landscape and hardened sites to pull and rotate forces from, as well as a layered air defense network.
What could overwhelm the Chinese defenses, however, is what the U.S. has seen poke through its defenses recently in the Middle East, Dahm said. Iranian air attacks have used a combination of low-end munitions and cheap drones with more expensive and capable missiles fired from various angles, locations, and at varying rates of speed to confuse and defeat air defenses.
This aligns with one of the report’s recommendations—for the Pentagon to develop new operational concepts that pair cheap and high-end weapons for mixed attacks.
“Using low-cost drones in the opening wave to identify air defenses, consume interceptors, and relay targeting data to follow-on missiles offers a promising and sustainable way to create repeated air base disruption,” according to the report. “High-end weapons should be preserved for more challenging targets, while affordable mass should be integrated into strike plans to service soft targets and to saturate air defenses.”
“The Iranians have figured out how to be effective: … send a whole bunch of slow-moving drones with a couple of cruise missiles and a couple of ballistic missiles,” Dahm said.
That’s because modern air defenders must set their systems to track certain ranges, altitudes, and speeds of whatever is in the airspace. And they can’t track everything effectively all at once.
“I don’t want a flock of birds showing up on my radar, so I set the speed gate for higher speed, but how high do I set it for? 100 knots or do I set it for Mach 3? What am I looking for? Range. How far am I looking? Altitude. Am I looking high? Am I looking low?” Dahm said.
Those factors mean an air defense system can’t stop everything.
“The way you overwhelm even the most sophisticated air defense system is you send some slow stuff, you send some medium stuff, and then you send these ballistic missiles that are screaming in from the upper atmosphere at Mach 3-4-5,” Dahm said. “It is hard for any modern air defense system to deal with all those inputs.”
While Iran is using that method against the U.S., Dahm advocates the U.S. use the same strategy in a Taiwan scenario against the PLA.
“That is absolutely what we should be doing,” Dahm said.
For example, to strike a Chinese military ship, such as a cruiser, Dahm said U.S. or coalition countries wouldn’t only send the same type of missile from one direction. They would simultaneously target the ship from air, land, sea, and subsurface platforms with a variety of projectiles at varying speeds and ranges, though the centerpiece of the assault might be an LRASM.
“You might send two LRASMs, but you need to accompany that with some of these more cost-effective missiles,” he said. “It is the reason we need the cost-effectiveness and the affordability, because we shouldn’t have an expectation that all of those weapons are going to work.”
